An interesting point here is that although survey section 2 showed that social media networks were the most used sources of information on COVID-19, they were among the least trusted, a fact whose implications will be explored in the Discussion section.

Social media have often been used to improve health awareness, and this section explored how important a role they played in sharing vital information and educating the student participants about Covid-19 in its early stages. This survey section consisted of 12 statements aimed at measuring their perception of this; the results can be seen in Table 5 . The first eleven of the twelve statements concern the positive input made by social media; only the last has a different focus and refers to its negative impact.

The results presented in Table 5 showed that social media made a very significant contribution to raising awareness of all aspects of the pandemic: how the disease is transmitted, infection-prevention precautions, the symptoms of the virus, the extent of its local and global spread, government measures being taken to deal with it and how to access health services if needed. The mean average degree of responses to all the statements except the last was a relative strength of 85%, indicating that this role was very strong (80% or more means very strong).

Overall, then, despite the survey being conducted at the early stage of COVID-19, results showed that social media networks greatly helped students understand all aspects of the pandemic (M = 40.92, SD = 5.47, relative strength = 85%) and served to correct their misconceptions about it. Results for the last statement, however, revealed that social media networks did also play a negative role and spread confusion and false information. This is understandable, as social media is accessible to all members of society, and many exchange written, audio, and visual messages without verifying the accuracy of the content they are sharing. The results for this statement reached 2.09 out of 4 degrees and thus had a relative mean of 52%; this indicates a medium level according to the criteria used in this research and was much lower than the results for all the positive statements, but still significant.

Since their creation, social media has become an essential and worldwide platform for social interaction and communication among individuals and communities. In the exceptional circumstances created by the outbreak of the pandemic, these platforms became a crucial way not only to obtain accurate and reliable information about the virus but also to maintain communication with others. At a time of social isolation and widespread quarantining, these networks provided many social benefits for individuals and communities, promoting communication, providing psychological support, and allowing people to communicate with healthcare professionals to obtain information, as well as providing entertainment activities to alleviate the psychological pressures of isolation. The students’ responses to the questions about the perceived social benefits of social media are shown in Table 6 below.

Social benefits of social media at the beginning of the spread of COVID-19.

The data presented above shows clearly that students felt that they gained significant social benefits from social media networks during the early period of the spread of COVID-19 (M = 50.15 and SD = 8.19). The mean relative strength score for social benefits was 0.84, which signifies a very strong endorsement. A wide range of social benefits was perceived; the sense of social responsibility they developed was ranked first and was exemplified in, for instance, the sharing of COVID-related knowledge with friends and family, the avoidance of behaviors which could spread the virus, along with a concern about checking up on family and friends and identifying those in the community who needed help. Social media also helped students to tolerate the effects of isolation and avoid boredom at a time when they were unable to enjoy their normal social interaction. There were also practical advantages such as knowing where to access food and medical supplies and treatment, both for themselves and for others, though these were ranked very slightly lower than other benefits.

As explained earlier, soon after the WHO declared COVID-19 to be a pandemic, SQU, like many other educational institutions worldwide, moved from face-to-face to distance/remote/online learning, through electronic platforms and social media, with no idea of how long this situation would remain necessary. This transition was aimed at overcoming the effects of the emergency suspension, but the sudden change posed a number of challenges for both teachers and students. Still, both resorted to using the available social media networks and applications to facilitate teaching and learning and fulfil educational needs. (Study groups have been created on WhatsApp as well as on Facebook, and some recorded lessons have been provided via YouTube). Despite the need to adapt at very short notice, this remote learning was facilitated by the use of numerous technological tools including e-learning applications, web applications, television programs, online educational videos, live online lessons, virtual classrooms and of course programs on social media networks. These tools allowed teachers and trainers not only to provide educational content to students, but also to make it available anytime and anywhere; this helped students stay connected to the curriculum and complete their coursework on time despite the emergency situation. Table 7 below shows the various educational benefits of the use of social media during the early stage of the pandemic, according to students’ perceptions.

The results in this Table indicate that students perceived that social media were playing a valuable role in fulfilling their educational needs (M = 30.80 & SD = 7.89), with the average response at the top on the border between strong and very strong agreement. Students saw the most important educational benefits as the fact that social media use enabled them to access academic material at any time, as well as to submit research and academic assignments to their teachers. Social media, including WhatsApp and class WhatsApp groups, allowed constant and speedy communication between students and lecturers; students could also communicate with each other. Seven of the nine statements met with very strong agreement; that is, over 80% of respondents concurred. The last two statements received only slightly less agreement, and student confidence in their academic future, which could have been very much undermined by the move to remote learning, remained strong at 73%.

While previous sections of the survey examined the positive effects of social media, this last investigates the difficulties involved in its use. The challenges noted by SQU student respondents in using social media during the early period of the pandemic can be broken into two clearly distinct areas: technical challenges and information-reliability challenges.

When the university and government imposed a suspension of “normal” education in an attempt to control the spread of the pandemic, this created an urgent shift from traditional education to distance and e-learning. As a result, there was an increased use of the social media platforms to which students and others had long grown accustomed to, and even dependent on. Indeed, the lockdown affected not only educational institutions but society in general and people sought more than ever to benefit from social media services to maintain communication and interaction. In Oman as in other societies, this increased the pressure on internet networks, which had little or no time to prepare to handle the much heavier demands on their services. At the same time, the consumers’ increased data usage meant higher costs, in a situation they had not willingly chosen.

Students expressed annoyance not only at the cost of using the internet but also complained about its slow speed, its inability to cover all areas of the country, the low efficiency of the networks, and the breakdowns both in the networks and in power supply, all of which affected the sustainability of communication. While it was true that.

Suddenly increased usage meant a deterioration in the quality and coverage of internet services in the country, people had complained even before the pandemic that service was often poor and could be intermittent in more remote areas.

The other area of challenge, the spreading of fake news, misinformation and exploitative messages, was nothing new; nor was the networks’ inability – or possibly unwillingness - to monitor and control it. The unprecedented nature of the pandemic, especially in its early stages when little was known even by the WHO and CDCs, meant that even reliable information and advice were frequently changing, and made deliberate or even unwitting sharing of inaccurate information particularly confusing and dangerous.

Students were strongly aware of all these challenges, and Table 8 below shows how they ranked their relative magnitude.

Overall, students saw the challenges as significant, (M = 34.02, SD = 5.67), with a mean relative strength score of 77%, near the top of the survey’s accepted criteria for strong (strong ranging between 65% and 80%). Six of the eleven, however, were perceived as very strong; these were the most problematic and included both technical and informational issues. The results of the t-test show statistically significant differences between males and females in all dependent variables. Females scored higher than males on the role of social media in raising awareness of health issues during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as on the social and educational benefits of using social media. Conversely, males scored higher than females on the challenges of using social media. These results suggest that females more highly valued the health, social, and educational roles of social media, while males expressed a higher level of awareness of the challenges associated with its use. All differences were statistically significant at the p < 0.05 level.

The results of the independent samples t-test showed statistically significant differences based on place of residence in three dimensions of the study. Students residing in urban areas had a higher average rating of the role of social media in raising awareness of health issues than those residing in rural areas (41.73 vs. 39.98, p = 0.002). Conversely, rural students scored higher averages on the educational benefits of using social media (32.08 vs. 29.73, p = 0.004) and on the challenges associated with its use (34.73 vs. 33.41, p = 0.024). No statistically significant differences were found between urban and rural students regarding social benefits ( p = 0.126). The results indicate that place of residence was associated with different student perceptions of the health, educational, and challenges associated with social media, while their perceptions of its social benefits were similar.

The results of the one-way ANOVA showed statistically significant differences between the categories of the independent variable under comparison in all dimensions of the study. Differences appeared in the role of social media in raising health awareness ( F (3,372) = 10.500, p < 0.001), in social benefits ( F (3,372) = 9.347, p < 0.001), in educational benefits ( F (3,366) = 3.229, p = 0.023), and in the challenges of use ( F (3,372) = 2.731, p = 0.044). These results indicate that students’ perceptions differ among the categories studied. However, determining the categories between which the differences exist, and the direction of these differences requires post-hoc comparison tests.

Post-hoc comparisons using the LSD test revealed statistically significant differences based on income level across all dimensions of the study. In the health awareness dimension, the low-income group scored lower than all higher-income groups, and the middle-income group scored lower than both the upper-middle and upper-income groups. Regarding social benefits, the low-income group scored lower than all other groups. Educational benefits were higher among the upper-middle-income groups compared to the low- and middle-income groups. Concerning challenges, the low- and middle-income groups scored higher than the upper-middle-income group. These results indicate differences in the utilization of social media and the challenges associated with its use based on household income level.

The survey ended with two open-ended questions; these asked for suggestions first about the potential use of social media to reduce the risks associated with COVID-19, and second for recommendations for community initiatives to improve the situation created by the pandemic. Participants put forward a wide range of practical and creative proposals. The most frequently mentioned issue related very closely to the key concerns in the Challenges section of the survey: first, the high cost of accessing the internet, along with its efficiency, and second, the need to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the pandemic-related information being disseminated.

Numerous participants recommended that internet costs be reduced, or that the internet and thus social media be made free and accessible to all. One student proposed, for example, that” Telecommunication companies must provide free unlimited internet until the crisis ends so that we can benefit from social media.” This message was voiced frequently, along with calls for internet speed and coverage to be increased. Equally common was the call for information about COVID-19 to be reliable, verified, controlled and ideally disseminated through one official or formal source to which everyone could refer and which everyone could trust. Alongside this were a number of calls for rumors to be responded to, for the community to be educated, and a few recommending laws to ban and/or “punish the sending of false messages related to the pandemic”.

There were also a number of recommendations about how to make COVID messaging more effective; these included providing the messages in different languages (presumably to reach the different nationalities working in Oman, and the different Omani and other language groups), creating messages appropriate for different age groups and segments of society, as well as making messaging sites more attractive by, for instance, making them interactive and using video and sound, establishing strong community groups and community information feeds, designing awareness publications based on interests such as health, sport etc., using celebrities, design experts, academics and the Fatwa Office to help spread COVID-related messages, and holding competitions with attractive prizes.

The present study demonstrates that social media played a multifaceted role during the initial stage of the COVID-19 pandemic in Oman, contributing to health awareness, social support, and educational continuity among university students while simultaneously presenting important technical and informational challenges. Rather than serving solely as communication platforms, social media became an essential component of students’ daily lives during the suspension of face-to-face teaching, enabling them to access health information, maintain social relationships, and continue their academic activities under unprecedented circumstances. This finding may be explained by the fact that social media represented one of the few communication channels capable of simultaneously supporting information exchange, educational interaction, and social connectedness during periods of mandatory physical distancing. These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that digital communication platforms became indispensable during the pandemic because they provided rapid access to information and facilitated interaction despite physical distancing measures ( Abuhashesh et al., 2021 ; Elkhayat et al., 2022 ; Mohsen et al., 2022 ).

The findings can also be interpreted through the Uses and Gratifications Theory, which proposes that individuals actively choose communication media to satisfy specific information, educational, and social needs. During the early stage of the pandemic, students experienced considerable uncertainty regarding the disease and the sudden transition to remote learning, thereby making immediate access to reliable health and educational information particularly valuable. Consequently, social media became an attractive and readily accessible source for obtaining timely health information, communicating with peers and instructors, and supporting educational activities. The high levels of perceived health awareness, social support, and educational benefit reported in the present study therefore reflect the ability of social media to satisfy multiple needs simultaneously during a period of crisis rather than functioning merely as entertainment platforms.

The strong contribution of social media to health awareness is consistent with a growing body of international literature demonstrating that digital platforms became major channels for disseminating public health information during the COVID-19 pandemic. Students reported that social media increased their understanding of disease transmission, preventive measures, symptoms, and government regulations, suggesting that these platforms complemented official public health communication. Similar findings have been reported in studies conducted in Jordan and other countries, which concluded that social media significantly enhanced public awareness and encouraged adherence to preventive health behaviors during the pandemic ( Abuhashesh et al., 2021 ; Mohsen et al., 2022 ). At the same time, the findings illustrate that students did not rely exclusively on social media without critical evaluation. Although social networking platforms represented the most frequently used source of COVID-19 information, participants expressed considerably greater trust in official government websites, government television, and the World Health Organization. This distinction between frequency of use and perceived credibility suggests that students were able to differentiate between accessibility and reliability, reflecting a relatively high level of digital and health information literacy during the crisis.

The findings concerning social support can be interpreted within the framework of Social Support Theory, which posits that social relationships and communication networks play a critical role in buffering the psychological impact of stressful events by providing emotional, informational, and interpersonal support. During the COVID-19 pandemic, restrictions on face-to-face interaction substantially increased students’ reliance on digital communication. In this context, social media enabled participants to maintain regular contact with family members, friends, and classmates while facilitating the exchange of health information, academic assistance, and emotional support. These findings suggest that social media functioned not merely as a communication technology but as an important mechanism for sustaining social connectedness and enhancing resilience during a period of considerable uncertainty.

This finding is consistent with a recent study that found that active use of social media was associated with increased perceived online response, which in turn was associated with increased perceived social support; and increased social support was associated with decreased loneliness and increased life satisfaction. This indirect pathway emerged during and after the lockdown ( Yue et al., 2024 ).

Particularly noteworthy is the finding that students ranked the development of social responsibility toward family and society as the most important perceived social benefit. This finding is consistent with previous research indicating that, during public health emergencies, digital communication can strengthen community engagement and encourage young people to participate in collective responses that promote public well-being. Evidence from Rwanda demonstrated that youth volunteers were motivated to use community-based approaches to support governmental efforts in controlling COVID-19, highlighting the importance of social responsibility and civic participation during times of crisis ( Bimenyimana et al., 2024 ).

This result extends beyond individual-level support and indicates that social media may also reinforce collective responsibility and community solidarity during public health emergencies. Such findings are likely to reflect important cultural characteristics of Omani society, where strong family relationships, social cohesion, and shared responsibility constitute fundamental social values.

This interpretation is further supported by recent evidence indicating that, during public health emergencies, social media can contribute to strengthening individual and community resilience by facilitating social connectedness, encouraging mutual support, and promoting collective responses to crises. Experiences reported among youth volunteers during the COVID-19 pandemic suggest that digital communication platforms extended beyond information sharing to foster adaptive coping and community engagement under conditions of prolonged uncertainty ( Celestin et al., 2025 ).

Educationally, the findings indicate that social media made an important contribution to maintaining learning continuity following the sudden suspension of face-to-face teaching. Students particularly valued continuous access to educational materials, communication with instructors, collaborative knowledge sharing, and the submission of assignments through digital platforms. These findings are consistent with Khan et al. (2021) , who demonstrated that social media became an effective environment for collaborative learning by supporting knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, peer interaction, and continuous communication between students and instructors during the COVID-19 pandemic ( Khan et al., 2021 ).

This finding is also consistent with a recent study that showed that social media has enabled knowledge exchange and collaborative learning between students and teachers from different countries and highlighted its potential as a complementary tool in blended and hybrid learning environments during and after crises ( Elenurm, 2025 ).

The positive evaluations reported by participants also suggest that the existing technological infrastructure at Sultan Qaboos University facilitated the rapid transition to remote learning despite the unexpected nature of the crisis. This finding may also reflect the university’s prior experience with digital learning platforms, which likely enabled both students and instructors to adapt more efficiently to emergency remote teaching. Nevertheless, the comparatively lower ranking of students’ confidence regarding their academic future indicates that maintaining educational continuity alone was insufficient to eliminate concerns about longer-term academic outcomes, highlighting the psychological uncertainty associated with the early stages of the pandemic.

An important finding of the present study is the apparent discrepancy between students’ patterns of social media use and their levels of trust in different information sources. Although social media platforms constituted the primary source of COVID-19-related information during the early stage of the pandemic, participants expressed substantially greater confidence in official government websites, government television, and the World Health Organization. This finding suggests that frequent use should not necessarily be interpreted as unquestioning acceptance of online information. Rather, students appeared to use social media primarily because of its accessibility and speed while simultaneously recognizing the greater credibility of official sources. This finding aligns with a recent study showing that individuals used social media selectively and cautiously during the pandemic, placing higher levels of trust in traditional and official sources. They also relied on the source’s reputation, credibility, and comparisons with other sources when evaluating information, underscoring the importance of media literacy in distinguishing between easily accessible and reliable information ( Gies et al., 2024 ). The coexistence of high social media use and selective trust highlights the importance of strengthening digital health literacy so that users can critically evaluate information obtained from multiple online sources.

The study also identified several important challenges associated with social media use during the pandemic. Participants consistently emphasized the widespread dissemination of misinformation and contradictory information, together with concerns regarding internet costs, unstable network services, and privacy-related risks. These findings reinforce evidence from previous studies demonstrating that the COVID-19 pandemic was accompanied not only by a public health crisis but also by an “infodemic,” in which the rapid circulation of inaccurate or misleading information complicated public understanding and weakened confidence in health communication. A recent study from China supports the discussion of the challenges of misinformation; it showed that university students were aware of its negative effects, but most lacked the competence to recognize and verify it and expected a greater role from the government in limiting its spread ( Jiang and Wang, 2024 ).

The prominence of misinformation in the present study further emphasizes the need for coordinated communication strategies involving governmental institutions, universities, and public health organizations to provide timely, reliable, and evidence-based information through the same digital platforms most frequently used by young adults.

Inferential analyses revealed differences in students’ perceptions based on gender, place of residence, and income level; females reported higher health, social, and educational benefits, while males reported greater challenges. Place of residence and income were also associated with varying levels of benefit and challenges, reflecting the impact of inequalities in access to digital resources.

The responses to the open-ended questions further support this interpretation. Rather than recommending restrictions on social media use itself, many students proposed improving the quality and credibility of online communication by establishing trusted official information channels, enhancing public awareness of misinformation, improving internet accessibility, and strengthening digital communication strategies. These recommendations indicate that participants viewed social media as a valuable communication resource whose effectiveness depends largely on the quality, credibility, and accessibility of the information being shared. This finding has practical implications for future public health emergencies, where official institutions may benefit from maintaining an active and visible presence on widely used social media platforms to counter misinformation and promote evidence-based health messages.

The timing of data collection should also be considered when interpreting the findings. The survey was conducted during the initial weeks following the transition to remote learning, when both students and academic staff were adapting to an unprecedented educational environment. The generally positive perceptions reported by participants may therefore partly reflect experiences during the early phase of this transition, when digital communication became essential for maintaining educational and social continuity. However, this interpretation should be viewed cautiously because the present study did not directly examine students’ attitudes toward the novelty of online learning or changes in their perceptions over time. Consequently, no causal conclusions can be drawn regarding whether these positive perceptions would have remained stable throughout the later stages of the pandemic. Indeed, subsequent studies conducted among university students in Oman have reported greater psychological stress and less uniformly positive experiences with prolonged online learning, suggesting that students’ perceptions may evolve as emergency conditions persist ( Malik and Javed, 2021 ; Datt et al., 2022 ).

The present study has several strengths that enhance its contribution to literature. First, data were collected during the earliest stage of the COVID-19 pandemic in Oman, enabling the study to capture students’ experiences while major public health restrictions and the transition to remote learning were occurring. Second, the study examined health awareness, social support, educational continuity, and perceived challenges simultaneously, providing a comprehensive assessment of the multiple roles played by social media during a public health emergency. Finally, the study contributes evidence from the Omani context, where empirical research on students’ use of social media during the initial phase of the pandemic remains relatively limited.

Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design prevents conclusions regarding causal relationships or changes in students’ perceptions over time. The study also relied on self-reported responses, which may have been influenced by recall bias or social desirability bias. Furthermore, participants were recruited from a single public university, limiting the generalizability of the findings to students enrolled in other higher education institutions within Oman or elsewhere. Furthermore, although the questionnaire was distributed to all eligible undergraduate students, participation was voluntary and the final sample therefore represents a convenience sample. Consequently, the findings should be interpreted cautiously, as the participants may not fully represent the broader population of university students. In addition, the possibility of non-response bias cannot be excluded, as students who chose not to participate may have differed from respondents in their experiences or perceptions of social media use. Finally, the absence of longitudinal follow-up limited the ability to examine how students’ perceptions evolved throughout subsequent stages of the pandemic. Consequently, the findings reflect students’ perceptions during a unique historical period and may not fully represent patterns of social media use, trust in information sources, or educational experiences observed during later stages of the pandemic or in post-pandemic contexts. Future research employing longitudinal and multi-institutional designs would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the long-term educational, social, and health implications of social media use during public health emergencies.

The findings of the present study have important implications for higher education institutions, public health authorities, and professional disciplines that rely on digital communication during emergencies. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that social media can play a valuable role in maintaining educational continuity, facilitating health awareness, and supporting students’ social connectedness during periods of major disruption. Universities should therefore consider integrating social media and digital communication strategies into their emergency preparedness and continuity plans. Beyond supporting online teaching, higher education institutions should strengthen students’ digital literacy skills, including the ability to critically evaluate online information, identify misinformation, and use social media responsibly for academic, health, and social purposes. Such initiatives would enhance institutional resilience and better prepare students for future public health emergencies and other crises.

The findings also have important implications for public health authorities and university decision-makers. Participants consistently emphasized both the benefits of social media for disseminating health information and the challenges associated with misinformation and unreliable online content. These findings highlight the importance of establishing coordinated digital communication strategies that provide accurate, timely, and evidence-based health information through the social media platforms most frequently used by young adults. Universities and public health organizations should work collaboratively to develop communication campaigns that are culturally appropriate, visually engaging, and tailored to the media consumption patterns of their target audiences. Such strategies may improve the effectiveness of health promotion efforts while reducing the spread of misinformation during future public health emergencies.

Although the participants represented students from multiple academic disciplines, the findings also offer relevant implications for social work education and professional practice. Social workers increasingly engage with individuals and communities through digital environments, particularly during disasters and public health crises. Consequently, social work education programs may benefit from incorporating training on the ethical and effective use of social media for health promotion, community engagement, digital communication, and crisis intervention. More broadly, interdisciplinary collaboration among social workers, health professionals, educators, and communication specialists is likely to strengthen the development of comprehensive digital support strategies capable of addressing the educational, psychosocial, and public health needs of diverse populations during emergency situations.

Finally, future research should extend the present findings by employing longitudinal and multi-institutional designs to examine how students’ perceptions of social media evolve throughout different stages of public health emergencies. Comparative studies across universities and cultural contexts would also provide a broader understanding of the factors influencing students’ trust in digital information sources, patterns of social media use, and the effectiveness of digital communication strategies in supporting learning, well-being, and health promotion.

The current research is significant as it has examined the role of social media in enhancing health awareness, social support and educational progress among university students in Oman during the emergency created by the arrival of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. The study investigates both the positive impact of social media use, and also the challenges it poses, and thus provides a benchmark against which studies of the situation at later stages of the pandemic can be measured. It further highlights the potential of social work professionals to utilize these social media to achieve the preventive, therapeutic, and developmental objectives of their work, particularly during epidemics and disasters. It also suggests useful communication methods for public health officials and decision-makers, and the humanitarian community at large, to strengthen their communicative capacity through the use of social media, and thus to mitigate the impact of future disasters and crises.

It’s the weekend, and an 11-year-old is bored, so she messages her friend to hang out. Late on a school night, a 14-year-old waited too long to start his homework. He opens his laptop to begin. The day after graduation, a 17-year-old sits alone, thinking about who she wants to be when she starts college in the fall and how her life will unfold.

These experiences may sound familiar. Perhaps you’ve had them.

Adolescents’ options for navigating these moments have changed drastically in recent years. The 11-year-old’s friend may not be a person at all, but an AI system , designed to answer instantly and always agree. Instead of struggling through the homework he put off, the teen may feel tempted to automate it to completion with a quick prompt to a chatbot. The young woman contemplating her future need not self-reflect or cocreate who she becomes with her peers if AI shapes her decisions and identity. Moreover, her sense of possibility as she steps towards adulthood may be eclipsed by the growing capabilities of AI, leading her to question the inherent value of her own capabilities and education .

Today, roughly two in three U.S. teens use AI chatbots (O’Neil et al., 2026) and more than half regularly use AI “companions” for personal conversation (Robb & Mann, 2025). Adoption is climbing fast among even younger kids—recent estimates suggest that more than half of 9- to 12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot (O’Neil et al., 2026). Parents, meanwhile, often feel unprepared to respond: Fewer than four in 10 know their teen uses these tools, and only about half of families have ever talked about AI (Madden et al., 2024; McClain et al., 2026).

AI chatbots have rapidly become a mainstay in adolescents’ lives, yet we have almost no rigorous research to understand how this intersects with adolescent development.

In a new paper in Perspectives on Psychological Science , my colleague Dr. Chelly Maes and I combine core concepts in developmental science with what we’ve recently learned about social media and other technologies to map a course for understanding and supporting adolescence in the era of AI.

Adolescence is among the most consequential stretches of the lifespan, a period of such dramatic brain plasticity that researchers have nicknamed it the “age of opportunity.” During these years, young people take on what psychologists call developmental tasks: navigating complicated peer relationships, learning to regulate strong emotions, building autonomy, and figuring out who they are. How someone navigates these tasks and the skills they learn in the process has lasting consequences for adulthood.

These skills and internal resources gained during adolescence are established through practice and are rarely accomplished by being told the answers or opting out. Rather, they’re often built through challenging but constructive experiences—awkward conversations, hurt feelings, boredom, failure, the slow work of tolerating discomfort and figuring things out. This friction of daily life isn’t always fun, but it serves an important purpose for developing the skills and relationships that support a rewarding human life. AI can offer a tempting, effortless route to circumvent these very frictions, which may feel good in the moment but be costly in the long term.

It helps to be specific about what makes AI chatbots unique. Social media was initially designed, at least ostensibly, to connect people to other people : audiences, feeds, comments, the traces of other humans’ lives. When we talk about positive uses of social media, it’s usually about this—finding community, connecting with friends, or learning from other people.

AI chatbots are not people, nor do they typically connect you to people. They’re available every hour of every day and respond instantly and reliably—no human relationship offers that. They have no needs of their own, ask nothing of the user, and never tire of a conversation the way a friend or parent eventually will. They remember what you’ve told them and adapt to your preferences, so conversations feel increasingly personal. And because most chatbots are built by companies competing for engagement, they may be tuned by design to be agreeable: warm, validating, rarely confrontational. Even when used in the impersonal tone of a tool, AI chatbots can synthesize vast content rapidly, making the process of searching for information quicker, simpler, and more personalized.

None of this inherently makes AI good or bad for kids . However, we (like many) are concerned about the potential relational, emotional, and identity risks that may undermine developmental tasks and potentially lead youth to experience social isolation and mental health challenges. These risks may be less likely to unfold if we pay careful attention to these challenges and develop a resolute societal effort to build a digital ecosystem that is safe and developmentally appropriate by design.

Emerging research, and plenty of educated speculation, signals where using AI may undermine adolescent tasks. In the space of psychosocial development, this includes how adolescents engage in relationships with others, manage their emotions , explore their identities, and develop autonomy and success as they prepare for their future roles and vocations.

Importantly, we do not argue that AI is uniformly bad for teenagers, and we’re wary of the reflexive panic that greets every new technology aimed at young people. Purpose-built tools could offer benefits in some contexts, like a tutoring chatbot designed by learning scientists or a cognitive behavioral chatbot that offers skills training. The problem is that almost none of the AI chatbots that teenagers use—the general-purpose, off-the-shelf systems that are designed to make a profit—fit these descriptions. We also note that not all youth are equally likely to engage in all forms of AI use; those that are already struggling or lack strong offline social networks may be most drawn to the riskier AI interactions, potentially making them even more vulnerable to harms of AI use.

Relationships. Learning to negotiate, compromise, care for another, and tolerate rejection or judgment can be uncomfortable, but it’s how adolescents build social competencies. AI companions rarely offer these opportunities. The risks here are both about displacing healthy behaviors—if AI is used as a companion or confidant instead of building peer relationships—and direct potential harms, including AI changing adolescents’ expectations of what a relationship entails or making human interactions feel more effortful (Ibrahim et al., 2026). Teens already prone to social anxiety or loneliness may be most at risk of developing relationships with chatbots, which could exacerbate the very challenges that led them to seek aid from chatbots.

However, it’s possible that AI can be used to help teens build skills for their offline lives, by rehearsing a hard conversation or engaging in scaffolded reflection about how to navigate a conflict, for example. Such benefits will likely only be accrued when chatbots are designed to support development rather than maximize engagement, and when youth use AI as one of many inputs to build social skills that are then translated to human relationships.

Emotions. Persistently available, judgment-free support can be a lifeline for a teen too embarrassed to tell a parent or friend what’s going on, particularly in contexts where the AI is designed with clinicians in the loop, evidence-based coping strategies, and bridges to trusted adults. But AI without the shared humanity, embodiment, and intuition of a trained clinician will likely always lack much of what makes therapy efficacious. Moreover, AI’s tendency toward agreeableness can tip into something darker, including reinforcing self-harm. In one recent study, 90% of chatbots supported a user’s desire to stay in bed for a month and tended to support euphemisms for self-harm (“cross over into eternity”) that a human clinician would not (Clark, 2025).

Even when not used specifically for mental health therapy, using AI might undermine emotion regulatory capacities that adolescents are learning. Using AI to outsource some productive struggles, like learning something new, navigating uncertainty, and feeling out of control, may ultimately erode adolescents’ ability to tolerate normal day-to-day distress. Even if it feels good to use AI in the moment, a tool engineered to instantly soothe every hard feeling may ultimately make it harder to withstand challenges in the long run.

Identity and purpose. For some teens, such as LGBTQ+ youth who face disproportionately greater stigma offline, AI can offer a low-pressure space to explore new ways of thinking about themselves. Again, it’s possible that an AI system designed to promote healthy identity exploration and integration could be beneficial. But the risks are many. AI systems are known to restate discriminatory and biased norms of society, and privacy risks are real and still evolving. Here, too, the process of identity development isn’t always comfortable. A tool that hands teens a tidy answer to “Who am I?” may short circuit the often-fraught exploration process that builds a stable sense of self.

Adolescence is also a time when teens develop a sense of purpose and meaning, yet AI may complicate these processes. If this chatbot can complete a hard task, do my job, or be a better friend and partner than I, why am I here? Such questions pose a humbling opportunity for our species to reassert the inherent value of humanity. Adolescents, newly capable of incredibly sophisticated cognitive and social thoughts, are already prone to asking life’s hard questions. As adults, many of us also increasingly struggle with those questions—the more we embrace and honor that which makes us human, the more we can help teens do the same.

Achievement. AI can explain a confusing concept or help brainstorm an essay. These are among the uses of AI that teens seek out, often trying carefully to ensure that AI helps them and doesn’t outright give them the answer. But the risks of outsourcing thinking are severe, and even teens who may want to avoid using AI in harmful ways say it is tempting nonetheless. Outsourcing to AI can save time, but it can also mask a lack of self-trust and encourage procrastination. When many peers are using AI, some teens may feel pressure to do the same.

Early evidence on teens using general-purpose AI to help with schoolwork is not reassuring. Heavier and compulsive chatbot use is linked to worse academic outcomes. Tasks completed with a chatbot’s help feel easier and more enjoyable, but students report struggling to accurately judge how much they learned. Chatbot use can erode a student’s sense of confidence in their abilities, a critical developmental process that supports the learning of new skills into adulthood.

We don’t yet know the long-term consequences of consistent reliance on AI by adolescents, and we need rigorous research as soon as we can generate it. This includes longitudinal studies that track specific patterns of use (i.e., what teens are actually doing with these tools) across the full span of adolescence and across different backgrounds and vulnerabilities.

We also need to work together. This includes interdisciplinary and cross-sector partnerships that can work faster and more efficiently than any of us working in silos. We need policy and design standards that treat adolescent development as an enforceable constraint on product design, not an afterthought (American Psychological Association, 2025). That means limits on the sycophancy and simulated attachment that may make these tools attractive to developing minds; friction deliberately built back in, like break reminders and tutor mode; escalation to a clinician when a teen mentions self-harm; and firm lines against deepfake harms, like AI-generated sexual images of minors.

Parents , educators, and clinicians can support youth before we have all the answers: staying curious rather than panicked, modeling how to question a source, setting boundaries around use that may undermine social relationships or cognitive development , and, perhaps most importantly, making sure teenagers still have room in their lives for experiences and interactions outside of tech. This includes both the exciting and the boring, the comfortable and uncomfortable, and all the deeply human parts of growing up.

Today’s adolescent generation are already the guinea pigs in yet another technological experiment. The question in front of us is if we’ll be comfortable interrogating, clarifying, and asserting the value of a human life, lived well, and a thriving human society that depends on investing in adolescents. Growing up was never supposed to be easy. If we let AI make it too easy, we may find we’ve automated away the very struggles that were supposed to prepare young people for everything still to come.

Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India --- Business Wire India

Logitech (SIX: LOGN) (NASDAQ: LOGI), in partnership with Aspire For Her, today announced the successful conclusion of its nationwide all-women Generative AI hackathon under the #WomenWhoMaster initiative. Drawing nearly 1,29,000 registrants from across India, the landmark event officially earned a Guinness World Record title. Guinness World Records created a brand-new award category specifically to recognize female inclusion in emerging technology: “Largest Women-Only Generative AI Hackathon (Multiple Venues).”

A core pillar of Logitech MX’s broader #WomenWhoMaster movement, this initiative equips women with practical skills in Generative AI, low-code development, and machine learning. Designed as an end-to-end skill-building program, it provides mentorship and industry pathways to ensure applied Generative AI skills translates into financial independence and career growth for women in STEM.

The Grand Finale, hosted at Logitech’s Chennai headquarters, brought together 112 finalists selected from over 15,000 colleges across 5,000+ cities. Kritika Yadav from Ramdeobaba University, Nagpur, emerged as the national winner for “HerFinance,” an AI-powered financial resilience companion designed to help women better understand their money, risks and financial choices. Priti Kumari Pandey from Parul Institute of Engineering and Technology, Vadodara, was named the first runner-up for “RE – From Skills to Employment,” an AI-powered career companion designed to help women assess their skills, identify career pathways and improve employment readiness. Mridul Singh Soam from GL Bajaj Institute of Technology and

Management, Delhi NCR, was named the second runner-up for “KarigarSetu,” an AI-powered venture navigator designed to help women artisans grow their businesses by connecting marketing decisions with actual sales and transactions. The winners received prize money along with a Certificate of Championship. All participants were given the recently launched MX Keypad, a programmable control device aimed at developers working with AI coding tools.

Significantly, more than 60% of total registrations came from Tier 2, Tier 3, and emerging cities, demonstrating how ambition and technical capability in AI are expanding well beyond India’s established technology centers.

The nationwide journey began with an online assessment that saw over 26,000 women participate, from which 2,800 participants progressed to simultaneous zonal rounds across eight regional hubs, Mumbai (MET College, Bandra), Bengaluru (Dayanand Sagar University, Kanakapura), Chennai (SRM Easwari College), Kolkata (Praxis Business School), Noida (Amity University), Pune (ASM College), Hyderabad (KL University), and Visakhapatnam (Bullaya College), culminating in the 112 finalists advancing to Chennai.

Speaking at the Grand Finale, Grace Lokako, Global Marketing Manager, MX at Logitech, said, “Nearly 129,000 registrations tell us something much bigger than the scale of a hackathon, they reveal a massive wave of ambition among women ready to lead and build the AI economy. What stood out was not only the quality of ideas we saw today, but where that talent came from. With more than 60% of registrations coming from Tier 2, Tier 3, and emerging cities, it is clear that India’s next generation of technology creators will come from every corner of the country. Supporting India’s broader digital-skilling priorities, our ambition through Women Who Master is to help turn that potential into opportunity by creating access to skills, mentorship, and industry-academia pathways that translate into meaningful careers in technology.”

Commenting on the initiative, Polina Anokhina, IMEA (India Middle East Africa) Region Director at Logitech, said, “At Logitech, we firmly believe that diversity of thought is the ultimate catalyst for innovation. Supporting women in STEM is essential for building an inclusive, future-ready technology ecosystem across the IMEA (India Middle East Africa) region and globally. Through our Women Who Master initiative, Logitech is committed to removing structural barriers, fostering hands-on capability, and providing women with the tools and access they need to excel as builders and leaders in the emerging AI economy.”

Kritika Yadav, National Winner, said, “Winning this hackathon is incredibly meaningful because it gave me the opportunity to build a solution around a challenge that affects women in a very real way. Through HerFinance, we wanted to go beyond simply giving financial information and help women better understand their money, assess risks, and make informed decisions with confidence. The experience also showed me how Generative AI can be used to create practical, accessible solutions that can have a meaningful impact on people’s everyday lives. I am grateful to Logitech and Aspire For Her for creating a platform where young women can experiment, build, and turn their ideas into solutions for the future.”

Beyond the competition, the initiative was designed to create pathways for women to build practical exposure to Generative AI, connect with mentors and industry leaders, and explore opportunities within the broader technology ecosystem.

title: Vernacular english literacy practices among language students using AI: A case study in Saudi Arabia

Recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have encouraged teachers of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) to evaluate its potential benefits to the process of language learning. However, little is currently known about how language learners use AI outside the EFL classroom. Accordingly, this study addresses the underexplored area of informal, AI-mediated English literacy practices among EFL learners. Data from a qualitative case study involving 12 postgraduate students who participated in a focus group and retrospective interviews at a Saudi Arabian university were analyzed. Content analysis revealed the students engaged in English literacy practices using AI, and that these were categorized according to their usage in three domains: (1) practices for English language development, (2) to assist with daily life, and (3) to benefit academic studies. Approximately 50% of AI engagement in the English language aimed to practice the participants’ English reading, writing, and speaking skills, while leveraging customized learning opportunities. In addition, examples serving daily life functions were related to personal and vocational activities, and those serving academic life focused on preparing for examinations, academic research, and university assignments. The study therefore defined the concept of AI-mediated English literacy practices, ultimately providing insights into how language students engage in informal AI-mediated literacy practices in EFL settings. Thus, the findings reveal valuable pedagogical insights to inform EFL teachers.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are currently improving rapidly and gaining popularity among both students and educators. AI has proven popular for its potential to improve the processes of teaching and learning [ 1 ]. AI is a software-based technology capable of imitating actions associated with human intelligence [ 2 ]. In addition, it blends technologies, thereby enabling machines to mimic the cognitive activities of the human brain to achieve both problem solving and learning [ 3 ]. To date, two types of AI models have been identified [ 2 ]. First, the predictive model, which can identify and classify information, and second, the generative model (GenAI) that can create and produce content, that is, ChatGPT [ 4 ]. Released in November 2022, ChatGPT is an AI language model designed by OpenAI [ 5 ] that also incorporates a chat function, produced by a Generative Pretrained Transformer using deep learning (i.e., a form of machine learning) to process and generate natural language texts [ 6 ] exploiting a considerable database comprised of human conversation [ 7 ]. ChatGPT can both produce text and interact textually, and its design realistically imitates human engagement during vocal interactions [ 8 ]. Owing to being easy to access and having a user-friendly interface that generates highly advanced language, ChatGPT has proven popular for language learning [ 9 ].

Using AI outside the classroom can enhance language learning. AI can allow English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners to practice language at their own pace as it delivers a personalized learning experience [ 10 , 11 ], adapting its content to meet learners’ needs [ 12 – 14 ]. AI can assist learners with improving productive skills (i.e., grammar, vocabulary, speaking and pronunciation) and provide tailored automated feedback on language use [ 15 ]. Furthermore, AI can also be used to improve writing fluency [ 16 ] by enhancing efficiency as it applies to various aspects of writing, including: (1) checking grammar and syntax; (2) providing instant feedback; (3) facilitating the generation of ideas; and (4) offering personalized instructions [ 17 ]. Moreover, AI can sustain language learning engagement by increasing learners’ motivation and enjoyment [ 18 ] and offer an attractive and stress-free setting [ 19 ].

AI technologies require the user to have digital literacy, that is, practices creating meaning using digital tools [ 20 ], and a knowledge of routine literacy activities [ 21 ]. The concept of digital literacy is particularly relevant in contexts where educators, who are often described as “digital immigrants” [ 22 ], may have different levels of technological familiarity compared to their digitally native students. These are categorized as “vernacular” when they originate in everyday life, unregulated by the procedures and formal regulations applied within institutions [ 23 ]. The practices involving digital technologies can influence how individuals use and learn languages, including English [ 24 ], and can be viewed as sustainable due to their ability to maintain engagement [ 25 ].

Drawing on the concept of “vernacular literacy practices” in the paradigm of the New Literacy Studies (NLS) [ 21 , 26 , 27 ], this study investigates the vernacular literacy practices of EFL students. This paradigm focuses on specific practices, rather than decontextualized skills, so as to effectively examine what people actually do when learning English with AI. As defined by Barton and Hamilton [ 21 ], practices in this context refer to literacy activities that are voluntary, rather than mandated by formal education, self-generated, initiated by the individual user, and intrinsic to everyday life. They have originated from experiences at home and within communities of individuals. They may be dynamic, linked to the value and identities of the individual, and variable according to their needs and social purposes. In this study, the vernacular literacy practices of EFL students, refer to the informal ways in which students use AI tools to perform their everyday activities and fulfill their English language needs. Thus, the current study examines the underexplored area of informal AI-mediated English literacy practices among EFL learners. This study contributes to the NLS framework by extending the concept of vernacular literacy practices into AI-mediated contexts. Furthermore, our study highlights how AI tools function as dynamic literacy environments that shape language use, learner agency, and everyday meaning-making in informal settings. As conceptualized by Liu et al. [ 28 ], critical digital literacy extends beyond technical proficiency to interrogate how power relations, access inequalities, and learner agency shape engagement with digital technologies. In the context of AI-mediated language learning, a critical lens examines questions such as: Who benefits from AI-generated content? How do learners evaluate the authority and accuracy of AI outputs? To what extent do AI tools empower or constrain learners’ linguistic choices? We adopt this critical perspective to complement the NLS framework, thereby allowing for an analysis not only of what literacy practices emerge but also of how social and technological power dynamics influence those practices. Specifically, we address the following research question:

We also draw on critical digital literacy frameworks [ 28 ] to examine how issues of access, agency, and power shape learners’ engagement with AI-mediated literacy practices. In this context, AI-mediated English literacy practices are understood as socially situated, technology-mediated language activities that emerge through interaction with AI tools in everyday settings.

The existing literature includes research into the uses of AI language models in education, and focuses on the perceptions of users. For instance, Adeshola and Adepoju [ 29 ] identified a number of benefits concerning the uses of ChatGPT as an educational tool, as reported in tweets: (1) effective problem solving; (2) enhancing students’ engagement and understanding; (3) generating high standard content; and (4) providing a dynamic learning opportunity. Faisel [ 30 ] concluded that employing ChatGPT in higher education (HE) can help to develop personalized learning, create content, translate between languages, and assist with language learning. Kuhail et al. [ 31 ] reported that chatbots apparently empowered learners by enhancing their understanding of challenging written work, as well as customizing learning materials and suggesting personalized learning pathways.

In addition, a number of quantitative studies have examined the benefits of AI in HE from the perspective of students. For example, Farhi et al. [ 7 ] conducted a questionnaire survey with 388 students to explore the use of ChatGPT in two universities in the United Arab Emirates. The participants considered ChatGPT a revolutionary instrument that improved their essay writing, ultimately assisting them in completing their assignments and translations. Similarly, Pavlenko and Syzenko [ 32 ] investigated students’ perceptions regarding the impact of using ChatGPT as a learning tool at two Ukrainian universities. They collected data from 247 students via an online questionnaire and found that most valued the use of ChatGPT as a learning tool. They noted that it assisted them in writing their assignments quickly and enhanced the quality of their work by correcting their language, augmenting the quality of their literature reviews, and assisting them with presentations and brainstorming. Syahrin and Akmal [ 33 ] adopted a focus-group approach to investigate students’ attitudes regarding the use of ChatGPT at a university in Oman. Students viewed ChatGPT as a helpful tool that increased their autonomy in overcoming academic challenges, boosted their confidence in their ability to handle complicated topics, and assisted their understanding of complex assignments, thereby helping them to brainstorm ideas and improve their writing. Buragohain and Chaudhary [ 34 ] explored ethical and pedagogical perspectives on ChatGPT use in HE and highlighted both opportunities for personalized learning and concerns related to academic integrity.

These studies indicate growing recognition of AI’s pedagogical value in HE, where researchers have employed qualitative and quantitative measures to collect the views of students and educators with regard to AI. They reported that AI tools can develop problem solving skills, support autonomous and personalized learning, improve writing quality, understanding of complicated materials, and enhance engagement. These findings, which were collected by analyzing social media posts, case studies, large-scale questionnaires, and focus groups indicate that AI is viewed as an essential instructional supplement with the potential to streamline academic tasks and scaffold language learning.

Research into AI and language learning, particularly in relation to English, has increased [ 35 ], with growing evidence that the incorporation of various artificial language models can enhance the learning experience. Kohnke et al. [ 8 ] examined the affordances of ChatGPT in language learning and teaching, finding it convenient, and providing: (1) an avenue to practice at all times; (2) robust linguistic input; (3) human-like conversations; (3) personalized learning; (4) understanding of the meaning of vocabulary in context; (5) correction and clarification of language errors; (6) creation of input in different genres; (7) dictionary definitions; (8) opportunities to use words correctly in sentences; and (9) translation options. Jen and Salam [ 36 ] reviewed various studies relating to the use of AI in essay writing and concluded that AI tools could enhance learners’ writing skills, ultimately enabling them to generate ideas, while also evaluating their essays and offering feedback. Liu and Zhao’s [ 37 ] scoping review of AI-mediated informal language learning identified key factors such as learner motivation, engagement, and technological accessibility. Liu et al. [ 38 ] further examined AI-mediated informal digital learning of English and demonstrated that learner motivation and enjoyment significantly influence engagement with AI tools.

Several studies have employed quantitative measures to examine the use of AI in EFL. Mohamed and Alian [ 39 ] employed a questionnaire with 64 EFL students to examine the processes associated with language learning. The students expressed generally positive attitudes toward the use of chatbots. They explained that such technology provides a low-threat environment in which to practice English, subsequently enhancing their confidence and enthusiasm, and encouraging them to engage in interactive conversations. Cai et al. [ 40 ] employed a questionnaire to explore the factors influencing the attitudes of 458 students toward ChatGPT as a tool for learning English in a Chinese university. The participants considered it efficient and easy to use, and noted that it offered them a positive experience when used alongside other resources to support the learning process.

Several studies have also examined the attitudes of language learners in HE settings regarding the effects of using AI technologies to develop their writing skills in an EFL context. For example, Malik et al. [ 3 ] used an online questionnaire to explore the attitudes of 245 Indonesian students attending different tertiary institutions regarding the use of AI for writing academic essays in English. The students considered these tools improved their writing abilities and their academic integrity by: (1) supporting the writing process; (2) generating content; (3) checking their grammar; and (4) translating between languages. Similarly, Al-Zubaidi et al. [ 41 ] used a questionnaire to examine the impact of ChatGPT on the academic English writing of university students in Morocco. The participants considered ChatGPT an effective and time-saving tool, which benefited their academic English writing in areas such as: (1) developing sentence structure; (2) paraphrasing content; (3) reviewing grammar; (4) providing instant feedback on writing tasks; and (5) correcting errors.

A number of further studies have examined the influence of AI on EFL learning in HE settings, using an experimental design. For example, Alharbi [ 42 ] explored the use of Google Translate (GT) (i.e., an AI-enabled translator) to develop the writing skills of 234 students in three HE institutions in Saudi Arabia. The students’ writing drafts were assessed both with and without the use of GT using pre- and post-tests, and their perceptions were investigated. The students’ writing was improved by GT as it reduced their language errors and increased the complexity of sentence structures. The majority of the students valued the option to use GT and expressed an intention to continue using it for their English assignments, in particular as it (1) improved their capacity in English, (2) helped them overcome challenges, and (3) improved their grades. They also stated that they depended on GT for translation, despite their teachers’ instructions not to do so. In the Saudi context, Wahdan and Buragoahian [ 43 ] examined writing pedagogy in EFL settings, further emphasizing the need for structured approaches to support student writing development.

In terms of AI’s effect on grammar knowledge, using mixed methods of pretest and post-test, as well as a focus group, Kucuk [ 44 ] examined the benefits of using ChatGPT to learn grammar among university students in Iraq. The students were divided into experimental and control groups. Students in the control group studied grammar using traditional methods, while the experimental group used the interactive interface of ChatGPT for a seven week period. Students in the latter group accessed ChatGPT whenever they encountered any difficulties with English grammar or spelling, and received instant answers tailored to their specific needs, including corrections of their grammatical errors. The experimental group outperformed the control group in the post-test. Furthermore, the students reported that ChatGPT was easy to access and enhanced their comprehension of complex grammatical structures, while simultaneously increasing their motivation to learn grammar.

In terms of AI’s effect on the speaking skills, Zou et al. [ 45 ] explored the use of AI speaking apps to practice speaking in English with 70 Chinese university students (experimental and control groups). The experimental group engaged with an interactive AI speaking app over a period of five weeks. Engaging with AI speaking apps with interaction significantly enhanced the proficiency of participants, improving their spoken fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, and presentation skills. Zou, Lyu, et al. [ 46 ] conducted a further study to understand the views of university EFL students regarding the use of AI apps to enhance their speaking ability when focusing on “English for Academic Purposes (EAP) Talk.” The study implemented mixed methods comprising of questionnaires and follow-up interviews. The researchers also found the participants regarded EAP Talk as beneficial, as it was easy and enjoyable to use. Furthermore, the participants also felt AI evaluated their oral production accurately, was useful for correcting their errors, motivated them to improve their pronunciation and learn more vocabulary, and increased their opportunities to practice speaking without fear of negative peer evaluation.

These studies reveal that AI can be used as an effective and multifaceted resource in the area of English language learning to develop students’ outcomes and enhance their skills. The quantitative design revealed positive attitudes toward AI technologies, with learners reporting enhanced writing abilities and greater confidence, while experimental studies demonstrated that the use of AI-supported-instructions improved proficiency in multiple skill areas. As Soyoof et al. [ 47 ] argue, AI should not only be viewed as a tool, but also as a discourse that shapes how literacy practices are constructed and experienced. However, an exploration of the use of ChatGPT from the perspective of students [ 7 ], including those in HE [ 30 ], employing qualitative [ 3 ] as well as quantitative and mixed methods [ 9 ] is crucial. The current study investigates the underexplored area of vernacular, AI-mediated English literacy practices among EFL learners focusing on informal literacies in English.

The participants were 12 postgraduate students attending a single university in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The data collection started on December 5 th , 2024 and lasted for five successive weeks. The data collection procedures, including the duration, participants, and tools used, are summarized in Table 1 . As male and female students are separated in most educational settings in Saudi Arabia, only female students were invited to participate. The researcher was female and inviting male students would not yield insightful data, as building rapport would be a challenge for cultural and religious reasons. These female students were accessible to the researcher and had previously reported using AI in their daily lives. The sampling strategy was purposive [ 48 ] and the sampling criteria were as follows: (1) postgraduate students majoring either in Human Resources Management (HRM) or Internal Audit and Governance, and (2) who had experienced using AI apps or websites in English over a period of at least two months ( Table 2 ). The combination of purposive, chain, and convenience sampling was employed to address the research aim effectively. Purposive sampling was first used to select participants who met the abovementioned specific criteria. This ensured that all participants had relevant experience with AI-mediated English literacy practices. Chain sampling (snowball sampling) was then used, where initial participants referred other eligible students from their networks, thereby helping to reach participants who were not easily identifiable through other means. Finally, convenience sampling was applied within university premises to recruit additional participants who were readily available and willing to participate. This multi-strategy approach is common in qualitative case studies where access to specific populations is limited, and allowed the researcher to achieve the target sample size of 12 participants within the available timeframe.
