title: AI becomes the first stop for financial questions people are too embarrassed to ask
content: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how people seek information, whether for health, education, travel or work. Increasingly, it is also changing how people approach personal finance. New res… [+6454 chars]
author: Dr. Tim Sandle
clean_content:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how people seek information, whether for health, education, travel or work. Increasingly, it is also changing how people approach personal finance. New research from Use.AI indicates that many individuals are now turning to AI before seeking help from financial professionals, friends or family members, particularly when dealing with questions they find uncomfortable or difficult to ask in person.

The findings point to an emerging role for AI: not as a replacement for financial advisers, but as an initial, private space where people can explore financial uncertainty without fear of judgement. According to research conducted by Use.AI involving 13,482 adults across six international markets, 57 percent of regular AI users would consider asking an AI system for guidance before speaking to another person about an important financial decision. Nearly half (49 percent) said it is easier to ask AI questions about money that they would feel embarrassed raising with someone else. The results suggest that AI is becoming an early-stage decision support tool rather than simply an information source.

Money remains one of the most sensitive topics in modern society. Many people feel reluctant to admit they do not understand investment products, mortgages, pensions, taxes or debt management. Others may worry about appearing financially uninformed in front of professionals, colleagues or family members.

The survey found that 44 percent of respondents were more comfortable admitting to AI that they did not understand a financial concept than making the same admission to another person. This reflects one of AI’s unique characteristics. Unlike human conversations, interactions with AI are private, non-judgemental and available at any time . Users can ask the same question repeatedly, request simpler explanations or explore hypothetical situations without feeling embarrassed.

In many cases, people are not looking for advice in the regulatory sense. Instead, they are trying to understand basic concepts before deciding whether professional assistance is necessary.

Financial literacy remains a significant challenge globally. According to the OECD , many adults struggle with basic financial concepts such as interest rates, inflation and risk diversification. Understanding these issues has become even more important as consumers face increasingly complex financial products and growing economic uncertainty.

AI appears well suited to addressing some of these knowledge gaps. Modern generative AI systems can explain concepts in plain language, provide examples and tailor explanations to different levels of understanding. The Use.AI research suggests that this capability is already influencing behaviour. More than one-third of respondents reported preferring an initial explanation from AI before speaking with a financial professional. Meanwhile, 38 percent had already used AI to compare financial options or understand financial products. Rather than replacing human expertise, AI may be acting as an educational bridge.

Ihor Herasymov, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Use.AI, describes AI’s role as helping create the “first draft” of a financial decision. This is the stage where a person recognises a problem but has not yet fully defined it. Questions may be incomplete, poorly formulated or mixed with uncertainty. AI provides an environment where these questions can be explored without pressure. For example, a user might begin with a simple question about mortgage affordability, pension contributions or credit card debt. Through a series of interactions, they can refine their understanding and identify the specific issues they need to discuss with a qualified adviser. This process may ultimately improve the quality of human financial consultations because people arrive better informed and with more focused questions.

The growing use of AI in personal finance presents both opportunities and challenges. On one hand, AI has the potential to democratise financial information, making guidance more accessible to people who might otherwise avoid seeking help. This could improve financial literacy, reduce uncertainty and encourage better-informed decisions. On the other hand, AI-generated information is not always accurate. Large language models can occasionally produce misleading or incorrect responses, particularly when dealing with highly specialised, rapidly changing or jurisdiction-specific financial topics.

AI can be effective at explaining concepts and helping users understand options. However, regulated financial advice requires professional expertise, legal responsibility and consideration of an individual’s specific circumstances. Some bodies continue to emphasise the importance of suitable advice and consumer protection when significant financial decisions are involved. Financial regulators worldwide continue to stress the importance of human oversight when decisions involve investments, retirement planning, insurance or other major financial commitments.

The findings also highlight a broader cultural shift. Younger generations have grown up using search engines, social media platforms and digital assistants as primary sources of information. For many consumers, asking an AI chatbot may feel no different from consulting a search engine.

As these technologies become increasingly sophisticated, the first point of contact for financial questions may continue to move away from traditional channels. This does not necessarily mean that people trust AI more than financial professionals. Instead, it suggests that they prefer using AI to prepare for conversations with professionals. This distinction could prove important for banks, insurers and financial advisers seeking to understand changing customer behaviours.

Traditionally, financial advice begins when a customer contacts a bank, adviser or financial institution. AI may be altering that sequence. By the time consumers engage with financial professionals, they may already have conducted extensive AI-assisted research. Their questions, concerns and expectations may have been shaped by conversations with AI systems long before any human interaction occurs.

This creates both opportunities and responsibilities for organisations operating in the financial sector. Companies will need to recognise that customers increasingly arrive with AI-generated information and may expect deeper, more specialised guidance than in the past. At the same time, there is a growing need to ensure that AI systems complement rather than undermine professional financial services.

title: Teaching students to think in the age of AI: Is this the lesson Canada’s schools cannot ignore?
content: Artificial intelligence has become a familiar presence in classrooms. Students now encounter AI-powered tools through search engines, learning platforms, homework assistants and social media. The res… [+5983 chars]

clean_content:
Artificial intelligence has become a familiar presence in classrooms. Students now encounter AI-powered tools through search engines, learning platforms, homework assistants and social media. The resulting debate has often centred on one question: how can schools stop students from using AI to cheat?

According to education experts from Virginia Tech , this may be the wrong question. Instead of focusing primarily on detection, schools should concentrate on helping students develop critical thinking, information literacy and ethical decision-making skills that allow them to use AI responsibly. This perspective has important implications for Canada, where schools, teachers and policymakers are grappling with the rapid expansion of generative AI technologies. Based on reporting from Virginia Tech’s education specialists, the discussion is increasingly moving from prohibition towards responsible integration.

One of the challenges facing schools is that AI is already embedded within the digital ecosystem that students use every day. Attempting to eliminate AI entirely from education may be both impractical and counterproductive. Amy Allen, an associate professor in education at Virginia Tech, argues for what she calls “technocuriosity”, encouraging teachers, parents and students to explore AI with a balanced and informed mindset rather than fear or blind acceptance. According to Allen, this means understanding both what AI can do and the limitations, biases and inaccuracies it may contain.

This perspective aligns with broader discussions taking place in Canada. The Government of Canada has already recognised the importance of digital and AI literacy through initiatives supporting responsible AI development and public awareness. The federal government’s approach to artificial intelligence emphasises transparency, accountability and informed use rather than rejection of the technology.  The challenge for schools is therefore not merely to identify AI-generated work but to ensure that students understand when the technology supports learning and when it undermines genuine understanding.

The emergence of AI has exposed weaknesses in some traditional assessment methods. Assignments that ask students to produce generic summaries, simple descriptions or routine essays can often be completed using AI tools with minimal effort. This has prompted educators to rethink how learning is assessed. Allen suggests that assignments should place greater emphasis on reasoning, evidence evaluation and explaining thought processes. Instead of simply asking students to provide an answer, teachers can ask them to explain how they arrived at that answer and evaluate alternative interpretations.

Such approaches encourage students to engage actively with information rather than simply accepting AI-generated outputs as fact. This issue has particular relevance in Canada, where provinces have increasingly focused on developing competencies such as critical thinking, communication and problem-solving. For example, British Columbia’s curriculum framework places considerable emphasis on “core competencies” designed to prepare students for a rapidly changing world. AI may reinforce the need for these skills rather than diminish them.

In practice, students who can evaluate sources, identify inaccuracies and recognise bias may ultimately benefit more from AI than those who rely upon it uncritically.

The rise of generative AI may create an opportunity to improve educational practice. According to Pamela Gilchrist, Director of K-12 Initiatives at Virginia Tech, teachers can redesign assignments in ways that make student learning more visible. Examples include requiring multiple drafts, asking students to discuss their thinking process, or completing portions of assignments under supervised classroom conditions.

The objective is not simply to identify academic dishonesty. Rather, it is to reinforce concepts such as ownership, honesty and intellectual development. Many Canadian educators are already exploring similar approaches. Several school boards and universities have issued guidance encouraging transparency around AI use while maintaining expectations for original student work. Instead of policing the technology, institutions increasingly seek to establish clear boundaries regarding acceptable use. The result may be a shift away from assessment models that reward memorisation and towards those that evaluate judgement, creativity and understanding.

An important aspect of the Virginia Tech perspective is that AI should not automatically be viewed as a threat. Allen suggests that educators think of AI as a “conversation partner” rather than an “answer machine”. Used appropriately, AI can help students organise ideas, explore unfamiliar topics and receive feedback on their work. Gilchrist recommends a simple framework: “Ask. Check. Create. Explain.”

This framework addresses one of the most significant educational risks associated with AI: the temptation to replace thinking with automation. When students critically evaluate AI-generated content rather than passively accepting it, the technology becomes a tool for learning rather than a substitute for learning.

Canada is particularly well positioned to shape this discussion. The country has established itself as a global centre for artificial intelligence research, with internationally recognised AI institutes including the Vector Institute , Mila . At the same time, Canadian policymakers continue to debate how AI should be governed in contexts ranging from business and healthcare to education.

Schools represent one of the most important arenas for this discussion because today’s students will enter workplaces where AI is likely to play a routine role. Employers increasingly value skills that AI cannot easily replicate, including critical reasoning, ethical judgement, communication and creativity. Educational systems that focus exclusively on preventing AI use may fail to prepare students for that reality. Instead, students must learn how to collaborate effectively with intelligent systems while preserving independent thought and intellectual integrity.

clean_content:
Educators were quick to adopt tech-backed coding curricula, but AI appears to face more scrutiny.

Educators were quick to adopt tech-backed coding curricula, but AI appears to face more scrutiny.

It’s the hot new thing in tech, and it’s where all the jobs are. Students who don’t learn to use it fall behind. And to help them catch up in time, its creators are graciously providing the resources and curriculum for learning it, often pro bono.

That’s the narrative AI companies are pitching schools on right now, but according to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, it’s also how the tech industry has built its influence in classrooms for the past 15 years.

In a new book, Coding Kids , Singer details how tech companies took a central role in promoting computers and coding skills in education, promising computer science skills were the ticket to high-paying jobs. But by the time many of those students entered the workforce, new technologies had thrown that promise into question. Meanwhile, the companies got schools to help them create a new class of would-be workers, and trained students on using their products and software, making them likely future customers.

Now, the AI industry is pitching itself to schools with similar force. “I worry we have collective amnesia,” Singer told me on a recent episode of The Vergecast. “Have we learned any lessons from these past tech cycles in schools that are going to inform the rollout of AI, make sure that it benefits education, and put in the safeguards now — not a decade from now?” Fortunately, in some ways, she believes the answer is yes.

Singer’s book recounts how more than a decade ago, the country’s largest tech companies embedded themselves directly into school curricula through courses for Advanced Placement Computer Science Principles classes. Apple and Microsoft each created their own curricula, featuring their own tools like Apple’s Swift or Microsoft’s Minecraft. “What’s striking about this is you can imagine that parents would not want, say, Pfizer AP Biology, or Northrop Grumman AP Physics, or ExxonMobil Environmental Science AP,” Singer says. She found that those in the medical field would likely understand why — medical students who are trained by a company on how to implant their proprietary device, one expert told her as an example, rarely choose to try another.

Google has also made itself a dominant force in education through its distribution of low-cost laptops called Chromebooks. Singer tracked their ubiquitous adoption across schools through the 2010s, which she says was accelerated even further during the school shutdowns of the covid-19 pandemic. Google also introduced its Classroom app to help teachers communicate things like assignments and grades. By the time generative AI took off, Singer writes, Google was already a key platform provider for many schools, and well-positioned to promote it.

Even when companies weren’t directly involved in education, they backed nonprofit groups like Code.org. Code.org kicked off its viral education campaign with a splashy celebrity-laden video that included tech moguls like Microsoft founder Bill Gates and then-Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, urging kids to learn to code. Code.org founder Hadi Partovi took a startup-style approach to promoting computer science education, and had little planned for how to capitalize on the attention of the video once it took off, Singer writes. He ultimately funneled that attention into a similarly splashy “Hour of Code” campaign across the country, urging schools to engage in entertaining hour-long courses introducing kids to coding building blocks.

At the time, there wasn’t much pushback, Singer found — though there were some attempts at alternatives. One group of academics engaged in a more traditional, methodological approach to testing and rolling out their own computer science curriculum. It had the express goal of diversifying the kinds of students enrolled in such courses, and taught students to think about big questions around the internet and technology, and scrutinize builders’ motivations.

Eventually, backlash arrived. Some recent graduates say they feel let down that they were told to code their whole lives, just to find such entry-level jobs to be diminishing, Singer told me. Some schools are getting rid of ubiquitous Google Chromebooks , and research around the world is finding that adding technology to the classroom often doesn’t have a significant impact on actual learning.

“Most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech”

“I’m not arguing against tech education or tech in schools,” Singer says. “But what I am saying is most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech. They want kids to learn how to be informed citizens in a democracy, and they want kids to figure out what their passions are and who they are and what their beliefs are… And so if we let the tech industry dictate or even heavily influence what happens in schools, then the question we’re asking is, how can we get AI into schools faster? Which is a product question, and not, ‘What are the most important things we want kids to learn?’”

While the AI industry of the 2020s may be pulling from the 2010s playbook, there already appears to be one distinct difference: Parents and school districts are pushing back. Just last week, the nation’s largest school system, New York City, banned elementary and middle schools from letting students use AI in the classroom for the coming school year. A day later, Los Angeles announced an even broader restriction that included high schoolers. And unlike the few-and-far-between critiques Singer documented in the early days of tech’s coding push, there appears to be a vibrant grassroots movement fighting the screen- and AI-ification of the classroom among parents and teachers alike.

“I think schools are beginning to figure it out,” says Singer, who’s “optimistic” that teachers and students are looking for a broader kind of tech education. That curriculum could teach kids “to ask deep questions about how companies are steering us with their technology, how software and AI are designed to affect our choices, and what role students have to use the tools productively. But also to push back if they like, and to not feel like they’re in a world where AI is driving them.”

title: Deep-fake abuse in NZ schools surges as technology races ahead of law
content: The police have seen a rise in AI-generated and deep-fake images in recent years and say one of the biggest challenges is that its becoming increasingly difficult to tell the difference between an AI… [+4035 chars]
author: Jaime Cunningham
clean_content:
There are fresh concerns artificial intelligence deep fakes are evolving faster than New Zealand can keep up – with school students increasingly being targeted.

Netsafe has recorded more than 30 school-related deep-fake reports in the first half of this year – already surpassing the nine in 2024 and 14 last year combined.

Its generative AI (generative artificial intelligence) report said synthetic sexual imagery is one of the two largest AI-related harm types – with rising instances involving students using “nudify” tools on photos of their peers or teachers.

The report said one school-based deep-fake video reached more than 150,000 views.

But the true scale of the problem is unclear, with the Ministry of Education saying it doesn’t collect data on deep-fake incidents involving students.

The police have seen a rise in AI-generated and deep-fake images in recent years – and say one of the biggest challenges is that it’s becoming “increasingly difficult to tell the difference between an AI-generated image and a genuine photograph”.

But Netsafe said many young people didn’t report online harm when they experienced it – meaning there could be incidents that never reach support services.

The threat is prompting some schools to change how they talk about online safety – and what they share online.

Christchurch Girls’ High School has been giving students and families advice about deep fakes, including warning about the risks of publicly sharing photos that can be manipulated using AI.

And Palmerston North’s Takaro School has gone a step further, telling parents it will stop posting photos of students on Facebook from next term. Photos from school events will instead be shared through its private school platforms.

Act MP Laura McClure has been pushing a member’s bill to criminalise the creation and distribution of non-consensual intimate deep fakes for the last 18 months.

It passed its first reading in Parliament earlier this year.

McClure said her bill built on existing laws around revenge porn, which make it illegal to share intimate images of someone without their consent.

She said an amendment to extend those protections to deep-fake and synthetic images was proposed by the Greens in 2022 – but it was not supported by Labour at the time.

“Look at where we are now. Our law isn’t up to date and we’re trying to play rapid catch-up – and the technology moves super fast.”

McClure said trying to regulate or ban the technology itself would be like playing “whack-a-mole”.

Instead, she said making the creation and distribution of non-consensual intimate deep fakes explicitly illegal would send a clear message to young people that there could be consequences.

She said existing revenge-porn laws had helped reduce harm among young people by making it clear the behaviour was illegal.

McClure said students are increasingly becoming aware of deep fakes and what AI can create.

“They know that it’s not technically illegal to do this right now. So there’s no real consequence necessarily for the actions.”

She said she had heard of increasingly disturbing cases, including a girls’ sports team whose team photograph was taken from a school newsletter and manipulated into a pornographic scene.

“I think it’s really horrible and really disgusting and really damaging.”

Netsafe chief online safety officer Sean Lyons said keeping pace with rapidly improving AI tools is becoming increasingly difficult.

“It can feel to many people like a bit of a game of whack-a-mole – we get one step ahead and then the bad guys get one step ahead.”

He said as the tools became better and easier to use, people would find new ways to misuse them.

Lyons said some young people also don’t report deep-fake incidents because of embarrassment and shame.

“Something that might be done as a ‘joke’, or part of banter, can also cause harm simultaneously, even if the intent was humour,” he said.

McClure said the consequences for victims could be severe – including being excluded from education, being unable to return to school or work or withdrawing from social and online spaces.

She said schools also didn’t get the same wraparound victim support they would if another crime happened on school grounds.

The ministry said it worked with Netsafe to support schools and young people dealing with online safety incidents , while providing guidance on generative AI and responsible digital technology use.

But McClure said deep fakes were adding another layer to the country’s existing bullying problem.

“We’ve got a huge problem in New Zealand with bullying in our schools ... but there’s no oversight of how widespread the issue is.”

She said better data would help the education system target programmes – but for now, there is no clear picture of how this abuse is affecting our young people.

McClure said the issue was urgent, as the technology gets better.

Jaime Cunningham is a Christchurch-based reporter with a focus on education and general news. She joined Newstalk ZB in 2023 after working as a sports reporter at the Christchurch Star .

title: Wealthy parents are buying their kids $75,000 AI schooling with guardrails as schools grapple with a literacy crisis
content: Rich families have tried to personalize their childrens education since the days of ancient Greece, when Alexander the Greats father hired Aristotle as a tutor for his son. The AI age is ushering in … [+4920 chars]
author: Mia Osmonbekov
clean_content:
Rich families have tried to personalize their children’s education since the days of ancient Greece, when Alexander the Great’s father hired Aristotle as a tutor for his son.

The AI age is ushering in a new iteration of this behavior as anxiety looms about how the technology will reshape work opportunities for young people and how best to prepare them for an economy that could see less entry-level hiring and more requirements for AI literacy .

Some families are shelling out up to $75,000 per year to send their kids to the AI-powered Alpha School : A spokesperson told Fortune it has more than 1,200 students as it plans to expand to 50 campuses this year . There, students spend two hours per day on core subjects with an AI tutor before devoting their afternoons to workshops designed to hone skills like public speaking and relationship building. Human teachers called “Guides” are still there to get to know and motivate the students, but they don’t plan lessons or grade homework.

“I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends the Alpha School in New York, told Fortune.

Affluent families like Cone’s can curate schooling that integrates AI use with human instruction through places like Alpha as schools nationwide figure out how to teach or restrict the technology, with New York City recently announcing a one-year ban on student-facing generative AI for kids in 2-K through eighth grade. Researchers have warned indiscriminate AI use can erode the cognitive effort needed for learning, but suggested intentionally designed AI tools, like chatbots acting as math tutors instead of giving away answers to problems, can improve learning.

But Huriya Jabbar , a professor of education policy at the University of Southern California, explained that public schools with fewer resources often can’t implement that kind of AI curriculum due high teacher turnover. The thought is someone could be trained in how to engage students with it, but then leave in a year. She also cited other constraints like schools serving low-income students facing more pressure to boost test scores with less bandwidth for innovating new approaches to teaching.

“AI—just like any other tool, technology, curriculum—is going to play out in an already unequal landscape,” Jabbar told Fortune .

Introducing more technology in schools isn’t a new concept, but the rollout of computers to schools since 2014 to help students learn is now being blamed for worsening students’ ability to think.

Neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath testified to Congress screen-based learning was distracting from learning and leading to lower test scores, saying in the hearing “our kids are less cognitively capable than we were at their age.”

“This is not a debate about rejecting technology,” Horvath said separately in his prepared remarks. “It is a question of aligning educational tools with how human learning actually works. Evidence indicates that indiscriminate digital expansion has weakened learning environments rather than strengthened them.”

A similar dynamic is playing out with AI as students use chatbots without the guardrails provided by schools. An estimated 84% of high school students report using AI for homework help, and one in five high schools allow AI use but have no formal policy for it, according to 2025 surveys from College Board, the nonprofit that administers SAT and AP testing. But using AI for homework doesn’t translate to learning for exams. A study looking at AI adoption by 26,811 Chinese students in grades seven through 12 found AI use boosted homework scores by 18%—then tanked exam scores by 20%.

This is happening as foundational literacy skills are eroding. Reading and math performances for 15-year-olds in 38 free-market democracies on the globally watched benchmark Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) reached the lowest average ever recorded , with U.S. students’ average reading scores dropping by 14 points to 490 , the lowest since it began participating in the exam in 2000.

Worsening learning outcomes in grade school follow students to college. Professors previously told Fortune students are arriving to classrooms unable to process long passages and leaning on AI summaries. Gen Z is also reading less than other generations, with Americans between 18 and 25 reporting they read 5.8 books on average in 2025 compared to 12.1 for Americans 65 and older and 8.2 for those between 30 and 44.

But the goal of educators still has to be developing writers and readers even when AI can interpret texts and generate writing, according to Kirsten Peterson, a senior project manager at the nonprofit Education Development Center.

”We want readers who can interpret, question, make connections, recognize perspective, evaluate evidence, sit with ambiguity, and form their own understanding,” Peterson told Fortune . “We have to be really careful not to use AI to remove the very thinking students need to practice in order to become literate.”

A collection of fossils and artefacts recovered from an abandoned quarry in southwestern China has given researchers an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of ancient humans called Denisovans . The items suggest that Denisovans — who lived at the site for at least 30,000 years — crafted bone tools similar to those of the Neanderthals, and were skilled hunters of animals such as deer. “This site’s the full package,” says archaeologist Ben Marwick. “It’s the first site that we have with a long, rich sequence that’s uniquely associated with Denisovans.”

Text messages and weekly 20-minute phone calls from a teacher can improve children’s learning during prolonged school closures . The approach offers a relatively cheap way to support children’s mathematics education when schooling is disrupted by natural disasters, pandemics or other emergencies, say the study authors. In a trial across five countries, kids that received both texts and phone calls improved the most. But text messages alone also improved children's learning compared to a control group.

A prototype tool called ProteinTalks can predict how the cells in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) tumours — which can behave very differently at the molecular level — will respond to various drugs. Researchers trained the computational simulation on millions of protein measurements collected over time from breast cancer cell lines that were treated with dozens of antitumour drugs and drug combinations. The model did a good job of predicting how cells would respond to drugs it hadn’t seen before and real-world clinical outcomes.

The United Nations has voted to phase out use of the Mercator map, a widely used sixteenth-century projection that has been criticized for not representing countries’ sizes accurately. The Mercator map depicts land masses closer to the poles — most of which are in the Northern Hemisphere — as disproportionately large. This can be problematic because people are inclined to conflate size and importance, researchers say. The UN resolution instead endorses use of the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately depicts the relative sizes of land masses. ( Nature | 5 min read )

In 2019, retired topologist Joan Birman received an email from 15-year-old Vasudha Bharathram asking for help in learning geometry. After a few meetings, Birman realized that Bharathram had a knack for the subject, and often solved well-known problems in an unconventional way. Bharathram inspired Birman to revisit a problem that had eluded her for decades : is the Burau representation — the translation of the structure of braids into algebraic objects called matrices — faithful for four-strand braids? This year, a 99-year-old Birman, Bharathram and collaborator Tara Brendle published their answer: yes.

The concerns that researchers might outsource scientific judgement to generative artificial intelligence are valid, but aimed at the wrong object, argues computer scientist Marc Schmitt. The danger is not AI, but people’s assumption that chatbots are producing final answers. Users should treat AI tools as intellectual sparring partners , with which they can develop and hone their thinking. AI developers should encourage this argument-based dialogue with chatbots, and universities should treat a student’s ability to participate in these arguments as a core skill, Schmitt suggests.

To minimize the off-target effects of cancer therapies, researchers need to find ways to deliver drugs to tumours accurately. Some species of bacteria are attracted to the low-oxygen environment in tumours, which makes them ideal candidates to shuttle drugs directly to their target . These bacteria can also be engineered to manufacture the drug inside their cells, and even to sense the conditions of their environment to ensure that they only release their cargo inside a tumour.

Nearly 600,000 New York City public school students will be prohibited from using generative AI during the 2026–27 school year, as the country’s largest school district adopts a dramatically more restrictive approach to the technology.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels have announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI throughout New York City public schools from 2-K through eighth grade. The policy takes effect during the 2026–27 school year and affects nearly 600,000 students.

The restrictions cover generative AI products including chatbots, AI tutors and AI-powered instructional programs. High school students won’t face the same blanket prohibition, but their access will be limited to approved uses as the district introduces AI literacy education intended to prepare older students for workplaces where the technology is increasingly common.

Students in preschool through second grade will generally not use individual learning devices during the school day. Grades 3–5 will be limited to 30 minutes of individual screen time per day, increasing to 45 minutes for middle school students.

Educators can continue using approved tools for tasks such as lesson planning, translating materials and preparing communications. However, the technology cannot be used for several higher-stakes responsibilities, including grading student work, behavioral monitoring, crisis counseling or developing special education plans.

In March, NYC Public Schools released preliminary guidance allowing educators to use the technology for tasks including brainstorming, organizing, scheduling and drafting non-sensitive communications while emphasizing that human judgment could not be replaced. The district subsequently gathered feedback from families, educators and school leaders.

New York introduced a statewide bell-to-bell cellphone restriction during the previous school year, while the city’s latest screen-time rules further reduce how much of the school day younger children spend interacting with personal devices.

New York isn’t claiming AI has no place in education, its approach instead draws a line based largely on age: younger students are being kept away from generative AI while high schoolers will gradually learn how to use it under controlled circumstances.

title: New research shows students experience extreme anxiety when accused of academic misconduct. Unis can do more to help them
content:
Dmitrii Marchenko/Getty Images
Since the launch of generative artificial intelligence (AI), many university students have claimed their teachers have falsely accused them of using AI to cheat. While… [+4716 chars]
author: Guy Curtis, Associate Professor, The University of Western Australia, Amanda White, Associate Professor in Accounting
clean_content:
Since the launch of generative artificial intelligence (AI), many university students have claimed their teachers have falsely accused them of using AI to cheat . While allegations of cheating and plagiarism should be taken seriously, sometimes such accusations have rested on unreliable AI-detection programs.

Unis have always had processes in place to investigate alleged student misconduct. But the impact of these experiences on students’ wellbeing has been mostly anecdotal, and lacking in research .

In a new study , we investigated the emotional impact on students who faced formal academic misconduct investigations.

In 2024, we conducted a large-scale survey , asking uni students about their knowledge of plagiarism. At the end of the survey, we asked 771 of the participants (from two Australian universities) whether they had ever been investigated for academic misconduct. Twenty-two students said they had.

These students were then invited to complete an additional survey about their experiences. This included completing a questionnaire that examined any depression, anxiety and stress they felt during these formal investigations. We also asked these students open-ended questions about their experiences.

We then compared the results of the 22 students with the scores of more than 1,000 students who had not experienced academic misconduct procedures. These scores were collected in a previous study . In addition, we compared results with the psychological norms of more than 2,000 Australian adults .

It’s worth noting that finding students who have been accused of academic misconduct at university is usually tricky for researchers. This is because formal processes are private and confidential to maintain fairness. Because we could not conduct research on students during misconduct processes, we decided to cast a wide net to find students who had faced a misconduct allegation.

We found more than half of the students who had faced misconduct allegations experienced extremely severe anxiety – a score that was in the top 2% of typical scores for anxiety in the general population. We are confident the allegations themselves were the most likely cause of these feelings.

Half of the students also reported severe depression symptoms when facing misconduct allegations. At the same time, only three of the 22 students reported depression, anxiety and stress in the “normal” range.

Although we expected students would report higher-than-normal psychological stress, we were surprised by just how high their scores were. While some students may intentionally plagiarise or cheat, it does not mean they should experience extreme psychological distress as a result of their actions.

We also found a higher percentage of students who faced misconduct allegations did not speak English as their first language. These findings support other research that shows international students are often overrepresented in misconduct allegations.

Some students acknowledged investigation procedures helped them learn more about academic integrity and how to avoid plagiarism in the future, such as by using correct citation methods.

However, when the process was seen by students as punitive, they felt worse. One student said:

I didn’t learn much because my university was not very nice about it.

Our findings also show students experienced increased distress when academic misconduct procedures were drawn out. One student, who reported the process taking about six weeks, noted:

I felt severe anxiety throughout this period […] With the stress of exams and the misconduct, I felt unable to function. I already lived out of home during that period and had to temporarily move back in as I could not function from the anxiety.

Our findings tell us misconduct procedures should not go ahead when based on unreliable evidence.

To avoid incorrect accusations involving AI, unis should reform assessment design so it does not give students the opportunity to cheat using AI. This redesign might involve more supervised exams and in-class demonstrations or presentations.

When investigation procedures are needed, our research suggests unis can make the experience less distressing by providing students with support services, such as access to psychologists and counsellors. Unis should make students more aware of these services, especially international students who are less likely to seek psychological support .

Unis should also use investigations as an opportunity to educate accused students on academic misconduct, and minimise the length of investigation periods to reduce students’ emotional distress.

title: I’ve visited school districts from Tennessee to NYC. American kids are not ready for the AI revolution
content: The first instinct of any school meeting a new technology is often to block it. Calculators, phones, YouTube, and now AI. It isnt necessarily a poor instinct. When youre responsible for other peoples… [+7236 chars]
author: Dora Palfi
clean_content:
The first instinct of any school meeting a new technology is often to block it. Calculators, phones, YouTube, and now AI. It isn’t necessarily a poor instinct. When you’re responsible for other people’s children, and something arrives that nobody yet understands, a block buys time.

I saw this first hand when I visited Hamilton County, Tennessee; a district that takes STEM seriously, and had invited me out to observe its computer science and maker program. I tried to access ChatGPT on the school wifi, but quickly realized it was blocked. The fix was easy: I simply used the mobile data on my phone to access it instead. Every student in that building would have done the same. This is not a district that’s behind or an outlier. It is doing what the majority of over 13,000 school districts in this country have defaulted to.

It reminded me of a story an English teacher told me, about her efforts to stop her class using AI for homework. While marking her students’ assignments, she noticed about a quarter of the essays she was reading looked remarkably similar. She sent an email: ‘If you used AI, please let me know.’ A hundred per cent of the students responded admitting that they had.  Her policy hadn’t succeeded at anything, other than to show her that children aren’t hiding AI from us. Instead, we are hiding from AI, which is costing us the one conversation that would help them.

I’ve been to school districts across the US over the last three years, and I realized I was seeing repeats of this same story: a blanket block failing to stop the use of a technology that has run rampant, and instead only succeeding in moving it out of sight from the adults who should be supervising it. More than a third of entry-level jobs require AI skills, according to Nace’s 2026 Job Outlook Survey . Ultimately, every district that blocks AI is now making a decision about who gets hired in 2030, and simultaneously pretending it isn’t a decision at all.

AI needs to be built with children in mind

The majority of conversations around AI in education usually focus on whether kids might use AI to cheat in an essay. But the stakes are far higher than that: AI is shaping how we all think, and for children in their formative years, it’s shaping how they learn, socialize, and make decisions. The problem is that almost none of the development driving these systems is treating children’s safety as a priority, nor are they building it in a way that allows kids to learn and use it productively. It would seem, therefore, that we’re running a social experiment on millions of kids without knowing the long-term effect.

The people who study young minds are split. In an NBC survey of the American Psychiatric Association and American Counseling Association, 86% of psychiatrists agreed that AI use among teens would inhibit brain development, replacing human interaction with lower-quality synthetic socialisation. However, 64% agreed that children would learn effectively from AI platforms that tailor lessons in a way that those teaching a class of thirty rarely can. Both can be true, but which outcome we get depends on the tools our children can access, and whether anyone is teaching them to use AI productively.

The case for restriction might be strong for social media, but it is weak for AI. Feeds hold a child’s attention, but there is no real reason for a child to be fluent in it. Meanwhile, AI packages its harm and skill in the same product. When we impose blocks that are easily surpassed by VPNs or a Wi-Fi switch, we let AI developers off the hook for children’s safety, and schools to step back from the conversation entirely. Out of sight, out of mind. But this isn’t a sustainable plan.

Today, four out of five students are using AI for schoolwork, according to Stanford’s AI Index. Despite this, only 6% of teachers say their school’s AI policy is clear, and even then, few school districts have worked out a plan for making the transition from a teacher using AI for themselves to using it with thirty or so students.

When you consider the pace of AI’s acceleration, it’s difficult to point fingers. Within two years of ChatGPT’s release, roughly 40% of US adults had tried it; the PC took twelve years. In the years since AI has been developing, global K-12 edtech funding fell by 82% . Schools were asked to absorb the fastest technology shift in modern history with less support than ever. So, school districts are carrying the liability on their own backs: one superintendent I spoke with recently told me his policy is simple – ‘if it didn’t come from us, it’s on you’. A fairly understandable way to manage risk, but ultimately a terrible way to manage a technology moving so fast, as it leaves the teacher the least resourced to act.

Handle it well, and AI could be the greatest equalizer education has ever had. Handle it badly, and we will watch it deepen every single divide we already have. Over 85% of school administrators consider AI education valuable, according to the College Board . Yet, 45% are reporting that access is restricted within their classrooms. The kids who belong to school districts where the only AI policy is no AI will one day be competing for the same entry-level jobs as others who have become literate during their same school years.

During my classroom visits across the country, I see both sides of the coin day-to-day. In some districts, the only AI you see is in an English department’s detection software designed to catch students cheating. In a district right next door, I’ve seen leaders run AI summits for educators, administrators, and AI innovators to learn first-hand how to use and develop frontier technologies so they can best benefit their students. Two districts can be so close in geography and yet headed in completely opposite trajectories. Schools trying to keep AI out of the building think they’re protecting their kids, when in reality, these kids are being left behind.

An example of what can happen when kids are taught to use AI responsibly comes in the form of a 14-year-old boy in Texas. To create greater access to diagnoses in his community, he built an AI app that screens for heart disease in seconds. That’s what’s possible when a child is taught to build with AI instead of just passively consuming it.

Somewhere in a small town in Tennessee, a student is sneaking AI under the desk in a classroom where it’s ‘blocked’. They will use it unsupervised, they’ll try to hide it for fear of getting into trouble, and in the end, all it will have been used for is cutting corners in their assignments.

In my view, we can make a change before students are put at a disadvantage. We need classrooms to be AI-native and provide access to tools that are safe, so students don’t default back to unregulated tools. For this, we need to redesign AI to emphasize education around critical thinking, complex building and ultimately, protecting human agency. The goal has never been for AI to think for a child, but for the child to think better.

Right now, our schools are not ready, and our teachers are not ready, and there is no plan in place to change that. But this generation doesn’t have the time to wait for them.

clean_content:
‘AI won’t destroy humanity - but it could change us forever ,’ says Dr. Uzy Hadad of the Jerusalem College of Technology and urges caution over apocalyptic AI predictions, warning that the greater danger may be humans becoming overly dependent on machines - while powerful economic interests shape the debate over the technology's future.

Artificial intelligence is often portrayed as an existential threat: Machines could escape human control, millions of jobs could disappear, and humanity itself could eventually be placed in danger.

But Dr. Hadad, head of the Artificial Intelligence program at the Jerusalem College of Technology, says the public should approach such predictions with caution - and take a closer look at both the technology itself and the powerful economic interests surrounding it.

"There are a lot of very strange questions here in this whole story," Hadad says in an interview, referring to increasingly dire warnings from researchers and industry figures.

He points in particular to a widely circulated post by a researcher who previously worked at OpenAI and Anthropic and warned of extreme AI-related dangers. While the post attracted enormous attention, Hadad says the intensity of the reaction should itself prompt questions.

He also notes that the technology industry has repeatedly produced dramatic predictions about the imminent disappearance of entire professions - predictions that have not always materialized.

According to Hadad, the debate over AI safety cannot be separated from a major economic struggle over control of a market worth enormous sums.

On one side are the major companies developing proprietary, closed AI models. On the other is the rapidly expanding open-source ecosystem, which allows companies to operate and develop their own models at significantly lower costs.

Dr. Hadad cites the example of a large Israeli company that previously paid enormous sums for access to commercial AI models. After switching to open-source solutions, he says, the company was able to reduce its costs by approximately 90% while also adapting the technology more closely to its needs.

"These big companies are suddenly under pressure," he says.

That dynamic, Hadad argues, should also be considered when examining growing calls for AI regulation.

Regulation may be necessary to protect the public, he says, but it could also have the unintended effect of strengthening the position of existing technology giants and making it harder for smaller companies and open-source competitors to enter the market.

Hadad does not dismiss concerns about artificial intelligence. One of the most immediate issues, he says, is privacy.

Users need to understand what information they provide to AI systems and how that information can be used. At the same time, he notes, the collection of personal information is hardly a phenomenon that began with ChatGPT.

Smartphones, social networks and online services have been collecting vast amounts of personal data for years.

For Hadad, the key to using AI safely is knowing when a human being is still capable of evaluating its output.

"If you ask the AI in a way that treats it as some kind of oracle that will give you the answer, and then you immediately approve it, you can get yourself into trouble," he explains.

When users understand the relevant field and are capable of checking an AI-generated answer and identifying mistakes, however, the technology can become a powerful tool - helping develop ideas, write and edit material, check code and save considerable amounts of time.

Will AI turn against its creators? What about the nightmare scenario in which machines eventually turn against humanity?

Hadad believes much of the public's fear is influenced by popular culture and decades of science-fiction stories.

"Doomsday" scenarios naturally attract attention, he says, making them a powerful tool not only for entertainment but also for generating publicity.

From a technological perspective, he argues, it is important to understand what a language model actually is.

At its core, a language model attempts to predict the next word based on enormous quantities of information on which it was trained. Its increasingly sophisticated capabilities come from systems that connect the model to additional tools and allow it to perform increasingly complex tasks.

The principal danger, therefore, is not necessarily that AI will suddenly become conscious and decide to destroy humanity.

Rather, Hadad says, the greater concern is what humans may choose to do with increasingly powerful technology.

"Like any technology, there is a danger that people will use it maliciously," he says.

Hadad also rejects simplistic predictions of mass unemployment.

AI is already transforming professions, he says, but transformation does not necessarily mean elimination.

In software development, for example, programmers increasingly use AI to generate code. Their role is consequently shifting toward reviewing, correcting and directing the systems.

A similar process could occur in law, accounting and other professions. AI may perform an increasing amount of technical work, while humans remain responsible for professional judgment and accountability.

But this transformation carries its own danger; The danger we should really fear.

Hadad believes society should be much more concerned about what happens when people become dependent on AI for tasks they once performed themselves.

If people become accustomed to allowing machines to read for them, write for them, think for them and solve every problem for them, they could gradually lose the very skills that make them capable professionals and independent thinkers.

He cites computer scientist Cal Newport, who has warned that while social media damaged people's ability to read and concentrate, AI could potentially damage their ability to write.

Hadad says senior software developers have already described this phenomenon to him. Their work has become faster and easier, but sometimes also less intellectually demanding.

Instead of spending hours wrestling with a problem, searching for a solution and thinking deeply about the issue, the machine increasingly performs much of the process.

For Hadad, that is the real warning sign - keeping humans in the loop.

The greatest challenge of the AI era, he says, is therefore not figuring out how to escape the machine, but ensuring that humans remain capable of doing what machines cannot replace: thinking critically, questioning answers, creating and taking responsibility.

The goal is to ensure that behind a product that an AI system can generate is a student who actually understands it.

The safety provisions in the agreement are meaningful, but the standards will only be effective if all AI companies, especially the tech giants, sign on, said Josh Golin, executive director of online safety nonprofit Fairplay. He said the agreement sidesteps the question of whether AI products even belong in classrooms, or at what age they should be introduced.

“I worry that a high-profile framework like this will be misunderstood and schools will think, ‘If they’re doing a good job on data privacy and safety, then that means we should be using the tool,’” Golin said.

The AFT said the agreement, which is legally binding and requires third-party audits for compliance, could set an industry standard. Two other leading AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic , said they also were discussing safety and privacy pacts with the AFT. But Google , the dominant provider of education technology for America's schools, has not said whether it plans to offer similar protections.

As part of the wide-ranging agreement , Microsoft says it will not use student or educator data to train AI systems, apart from a narrow exception for data that could help protect students. It says the data it collects cannot be sold, used for advertising or used for product development.

The agreement prohibits any use of AI companions or features “designed to foster emotional attachment or dependency” and to keep students engaged for longer than a learning task requires. It also includes a range of audit and transparency measures that require the company to disclose to families, in plain language, how its tools work.

“This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” Brad Smith, Microsoft’s vice chair and president, said in a statement. The standards will apply to all schools that Microsoft has contracts with starting Nov. 1, he said.

AFT President Randi Weingarten called the agreement the “first of its kind” and an important step to setting an industry standard in the absence of federal and state legislation on AI in schools.

“We want parents to have control of their kids’ education. We want educators to have control of kids’ education, not ed tech. And that’s what this agreement is,” Weingarten said.

She spoke at a joint news conference with Smith at the headquarters of the United Federation of Teachers, the AFT's New York City affiliate. The headquarters is home to AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction for teachers, which launched a year ago backed by $23 million from Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Along with their yearlong AI moratorium, the school systems for New York City and Los Angeles plan extensive audits of their education technology contracts and AI tools, with a focus on data privacy, transparency and accountability. The ban in New York City applies to all elementary and middle school students, while in Los Angeles it extends through high school.

Weingarten said she contacted Google directly to tell them about the agreement before making it public, in hopes the company would become a signatory.

The company has not responded to a request for comment from The Associated Press on whether it plans to offer similar protections.

“Is Google going to embrace this framework? That is a huge question,” said Golin, the online safety nonprofit chief. He noted schools also use thousands of AI-driven educational technology products produced by smaller companies.

Google found itself at the center of controversy over AI in schools when it announced in August it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. The company says Google Classroom is used by 150 million teachers and students worldwide.

Critics decried Google's move as an escalation of the race between tech giants to make inroads in schools and win over the next generation of AI users. The AI addition to Classroom only affects schools that allow student access to its Gemini app or Gemini Notebook, but it marks a major shift. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

Weingarten said she is also in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic, which both issued public praise for the agreement.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called it an “important milestone for AI safety and privacy in schools.” The company has been working with AFT, it said in a statement, “and we look forward to finalizing our own agreement.”

Anthropic, the maker of Claude, said in a statement, “We applaud all efforts to drive responsible AI use in education.” The company said it was working with AFT to shape “a gold standard for safety and privacy.”

Experts in data privacy say the new standards could help shape the conversation that schools have with AI providers, whether a school is a Microsoft customer or not.

“What I’m hopeful about is that this takes some of the pressure off individual school districts to negotiate with large tech companies,” said Elizabeth Laird, director at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Until now, the negotiating power of schools to secure privacy protections from tech firms often depended on financial clout. “I think this standard makes progress toward not having that type of inequity across school districts.”

Laird commended the agreement for going “above and beyond” what is legally required for vendors working with schools. For instance, Microsoft has committed not to use sensitive data that many companies leverage, such as information about gender, race, age, ZIP code that can be used to identify a person even if their name is removed.

But until others sign on, Laird said, the agreement highlights how difficult it is to set AI standards in the absence of legislation. It also emphasizes that the burden of protecting student privacy should fall on tech companies — not on parents, students or schools.

Microsoft's Smith noted that tech companies have been late to accept that.

“We all know there are important discussions and debates all across the country, about when AI should be used in schools, how it should be used, for what purpose,” Smith said. “It is our role, even our responsibility, to ensure that AI is provided in a form that teachers and kids and parents can trust.”

“We want parents to have control of their kids’ education. We want educators to have control of kids’ education, not ed tech. And that’s what this agreement is,” Weingarten said.

She spoke at a joint news conference with Smith at the headquarters of the United Federation of Teachers, the AFT’s New York City affiliate. The headquarters is home to AFT’s National Academy for AI Instruction for teachers, which launched a year ago backed by $23 million from Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Along with their yearlong AI moratorium, the school systems for New York City and Los Angeles plan extensive audits of their education technology contracts and AI tools, with a focus on data privacy, transparency and accountability. The ban in New York City applies to all elementary and middle school students, while in Los Angeles it extends through high school.

Weingarten said she contacted Google directly to tell them about the agreement before making it public, in hopes the company would become a signatory.

The company has not responded to a request for comment from The Associated Press on whether it plans to offer similar protections.

“Is Google going to embrace this framework? That is a huge question,” said Golin, the online safety nonprofit chief. He noted schools also use thousands of AI-driven educational technology products produced by smaller companies.

Google found itself at the center of controversy over AI in schools when it announced in August it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. The company says Google Classroom is used by 150 million teachers and students worldwide.

Critics decried Google's move as an escalation of the race between tech giants to make inroads in schools and win over the next generation of AI users. The AI addition to Classroom only affects schools that allow student access to its Gemini app or Gemini Notebook, but it marks a major shift. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

Weingarten said she is also in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic, which both issued public praise for the agreement.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called it an “important milestone for AI safety and privacy in schools.” The company has been working with AFT, it said in a statement, “and we look forward to finalizing our own agreement.”

Anthropic, the maker of Claude, said in a statement, “We applaud all efforts to drive responsible AI use in education.” The company said it was working with AFT to shape “a gold standard for safety and privacy.”

Experts in data privacy say the new standards could help shape the conversation that schools have with AI providers, whether a school is a Microsoft customer or not.

“What I’m hopeful about is that this takes some of the pressure off individual school districts to negotiate with large tech companies,” said Elizabeth Laird, director at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Until now, the negotiating power of schools to secure privacy protections from tech firms often depended on financial clout. “I think this standard makes progress toward not having that type of inequity across school districts.”

Laird commended the agreement for going “above and beyond” what is legally required for vendors working with schools. For instance, Microsoft has committed not to use sensitive data that many companies leverage, such as information about gender, race, age, ZIP code that can be used to identify a person even if their name is removed.

But until others sign on, Laird said, the agreement highlights how difficult it is to set AI standards in the absence of legislation. It also emphasizes that the burden of protecting student privacy should fall on tech companies — not on parents, students or schools.

Microsoft's Smith noted that tech companies have been late to accept that.

“We all know there are important discussions and debates all across the country, about when AI should be used in schools, how it should be used, for what purpose,” Smith said. “It is our role, even our responsibility, to ensure that AI is provided in a form that teachers and kids and parents can trust.”

The Vice-Chancellor, University of Lagos, Prof Folasade Ogunsola, has warned that the growing use of artificial intelligence by students could allow them to bypass the learning process and undermine the development of critical thinking. Ogunsola said while AI had enormous potential to transform education, its unregulated use could result in students completing academic tasks without acquiring the knowledge and intellectual skills those tasks were designed to develop. The UNILAG VC spoke during the 8th Lagos State University Research and Innovation Fair, with the theme, “Accelerating National Development through Artificial Intelligence-Driven Research and Innovation,” held at LASU, Ojo, Lagos. Ogunsola stressed that the core responsibility of universities was to develop students’ ability to think clearly, logically and critically, noting that the struggle involved in solving problems was essential to developing the human mind. She said, “Our job is to teach minds to think, and a mind that is not challenged cannot think, because the struggle of working things out is what makes a mind think that builds critical analysis, not giving it out to AI. “We’re beginning to recognise that it might bypass learning, that the students may come into school and leave at the end having not learnt. “ChatGPT, Gemini and others may be leading to erosion of critical thinking and learning skills. Overdependence on AI is not good for brain development, so there have to be guardrails with AI use.” According to her, the challenge facing educators was no longer whether to allow AI in education, but how to ensure that students used the technology as a learning aid rather than a substitute for thinking. She said, “There is nothing wrong with using AI for schoolwork if it is assisting. But if it has taken over, then there are challenges. “Students should not seed their brain to AI but use it as an assistant. Using AI does not make you more skilful.” Ogunsola noted that AI could access knowledge, recall facts and execute processes faster than humans, making it difficult for institutions to police its use, particularly because students could access the technology through their mobile phones. She, however, said banning AI was not a sustainable solution, urging universities to develop teaching and assessment methods capable of determining what students had actually learnt. “Right now, what I see in many places is: so what can we do? How do we do it? Because the students are far ahead of the faculty; they have engaged more. Ninety-four per cent of AI-generated research may go undetected,” she noted. Consequently, Ogunsola said universities would have to redefine the skills they expected students to develop, as AI was increasingly capable of performing tasks traditionally regarded as demonstrations of intelligence. She said, “If we’re going to really start to ensure that the next generation is thinking, we cannot ban AI, but we must find ways to ensure that they use AI to learn, and we have methods to know what they have learned and to force them to think.” Ogunsola cited examples to demonstrate that AI could improve learning when appropriately integrated into education, but warned that institutions must guard against its misuse. King Charles warns tech bosses of ‘existential dangers’ of AI Group trains youths to spot, counter misinformation JAMB explains ‘not admitted’, ‘admission in progress’ statuses She identified other risks associated with AI in education as “academic integrity violations, inaccurate information or hallucinations, data privacy concerns, intellectual property issues, digital inequality and possible job losses.” She said Nigeria could not afford to reject AI because the technology was already widely used by students and could help the country address challenges including shortages of teachers and other skilled professionals. Ogunsola therefore called for clear guidelines and innovative assessment methods that would ensure students continued to develop independent thinking while using AI as a tool for learning. Another plenary speaker and ex-Vice-Chancellor of Covenant University, Prof Adebayo Abiodun, stressed that institutions must develop AI policies to guide its use by students and staff. He noted that AI was beneficial in decision-making, enhancing productivity and gaining data-driven insights, but noted that it would not replace humans. Adebayo called for town-and-gown collaboration, stressing that institutions should integrate AI tools to enhance their operations. Adebayo said, “We need to begin to collaborate with corporate bodies on sensitisation among professionals. The town and gown need to be very strong in collaboration; there should be no disconnect between the university and the professional world. “There should be huge investment by government on AI materials and making AI platforms free and accessible to all users in this regard, and integrating AI tools to assist rather than replace workers.” Outgoing Vice-Chancellor, LASU, Prof Ibiyemi Olatunji-Bello, said the fair afforded an opportunity for innovators to showcase innovations that address the needs of today’s world. She said, “For LASU, this means going beyond adopting AI as a tool. It means asking how our research can use it to solve distinctly Nigerian problems, how our scholars can work across disciplines, how our students can participate meaningfully in an AI-enabled economy, and how partnerships with governments and industry can take research from conception to application.” Chairman of the occasion and Chairman of the LASU Governing Council, Babatunde Ogala (SAN), said the conference was aimed at seeking solutions to accelerate national development. Represented by a member of the council, Taiwo Atolagbe, he highlighted the importance of Nigeria engaging with AI transformation responsibly and purposefully. He also stressed the significance of interdisciplinary collaboration, student participation in an AI-enabled economy, and partnerships with government and industry. The Chairman, Planning Committee for the fair, and Head, Directorate of Research Management and Innovation, Prof Adejuwon Adeneye, explained that the fair aimed at accelerating AI adoption across various sectors. The fair, attended by several scholars, featured presentations of several papers on the efficient use of AI across various fields.

UNSW Sydney says it will introduce new administrative measures to address “academic integrity” as its moves to expand its rollout of OpenAI’s ChatGPT Edu to tens-of-thousands of students.

The AI assistant is being made available to 80,000 students and staff following a limited rollout to 10,000 fixed-term and permanent staff that began late last year.

The deployment, which OpenAI described as a “strategic collaboration”, will also see OpenAI’s technology incorporated into teaching materials, including its AI coding tool, Codex.

A UNSW spokesperson told iTnews that the rollout would be accompanied by a range of academic policy measures, including what it described as an “assessment transformation” that would see it set new “AI modes”.

It will also revise guidance around its expectations “in relation to academic integrity”.

The new AI modes will divide assessments into three categories designed to give students clear directions on when to use the technology: “can”, “can’t” and “must”.

“This will ensure we manage the balance of maintaining trust in our qualifications while supporting the development of AI capability,” the spokesperson said.

At this stage, the university doesn’t view technological tools such as AI watermarking as sufficiently reliable on their own to provide a basis for identifying instances of misconduct or cheating.

“We will continue to monitor the development of technical safeguards noting our position is that any detection tools and watermarking will not be relied upon in insolation for determining misconduct. They represent a tool to support educator judgement,” the university’s spokesperson said.

Sources familiar with OpenAI’s AI development for education settings told iTnews that the company was working on new technological measures to steer students away from cheating behaviours and encourage learning.

For instance, it’s understood that the company is working on measures to detect when students might be trying to take shortcuts in assignments and redirect them back to a safer learning path.

The rollout to students could also bring the university and OpenAI within the reach of the Australian Government's proposed digital duty of care legislation released earlier this week.

The new legislation mainly targets social media platforms and aims force them to give Australian users the ability to opt out of feeds informed by what the government considers to be harmful algorithms.

However, it also captures AI chat bots and assistants, and requires their makers to protect minors from negative content that promotes eating disorders, misogyny or causes serious mental distress.

The university said that ChatGPT Edu would include administrative controls to work alongside OpenAI safety systems designed to “reduce the generation of illegal, dangerous or otherwise harmful content”.

Nevertheless, it said it would keep a close watch on the government’s digital duty of care legislation.

“UNSW is following these developments closely and will keep reviewing and strengthening our systems for identifying, monitoring and responding to issues affecting student and staff wellbeing — including where AI use may be a contributing factor,” UNSW’s spokesperson said.

OpenAI also told iTnews that it was watching the legislation closely and indicated it was willing to work with the government on the bill.

“Providing users, particularly those aged under 18, with a positive AI experience is a priority for OpenAI. We are reviewing the Government’s exposure draft of the digital duty of care bill and look forward to constructive engagement on protecting Australians while enabling them to benefit from AI,” a spokesperson for OpenAI said.

By default, ChatGPT Edu is configured to prevent OpenAI from collecting information into the assistant to train its models and UNSW said that the arrangement would be carried over from the original deployment to staff last year.

UNSW has opted for a revenue model based on tokens for its arrangement with OpenAI rather than licenses.

“UNSW will pay for consumption of tokens, within a fair use limit,” UNSW’s spokesperson said.

OpenAI said that its collaboration UNSW was the first of its kind it had struck within Australia’s academic sector.

The dean of the UNSW Business and AI lead Paul Andon framed the partnership as a national skill-building exercise.

“The collaboration is intended to provide a model for institution-wide, responsible AI capability development – helping more Australian graduates compete globally and ensuring AI-driven innovation flows beyond the campus into businesses, startups, government and critical sectors,” Andon said.
