title: A Kenyan tragically loses his job to AI
content: My wife and I retired from teaching in May of 2020. Our final semester was obliterated by a COVID shutdown. We pretended to teach from a distance, and our students pretended to learn. It was a dishon… [+4958 chars]
clean_content:
Doing jobs Americans won't do might not matter anymore.

My wife and I retired from teaching in May of 2020. Our final semester was obliterated by a COVID shutdown. We pretended to teach from a distance, and our students pretended to learn. It was a dishonorable end to an honorable career, but beyond our control.

During that mostly happy career, I struggled with student plagiarism. All English teachers did in those days of yesteryear. One of my favorites was a young man who stole a friend’s research paper word for word. That would have been obvious enough, but it contained an anecdote about the original author’s mother. The plagiarist didn’t bother to change her full name. Double oops.

I’ve no doubt I bailed out of education just in time for a variety of reasons as I watched education devolve over my career, but at least I didn’t have to deal with AI, used not as an aid to research and writing, but as a means for kids to avoid learning and doing any real, personal work. Sadly, detecting that kind of sloth isn’t always this easy:

An underground industry of ghostwritten research papers has long existed. Ghostwriters have catalogs of papers listing the grades they’ve received. Fork over the cash, and the ghost and the student, for very little effort, are both happy. It hasn’t always worked out so well for students, because teachers have Internet tools for detecting plagiarism, not to mention the ability of competent English teachers to immediately detect when a student’s voice suddenly, miraculously, changes.

Interestingly enough, lazy English teachers and lazy students were sometimes compatible. Rather than go to all the trouble of confrontation and demanding a rewrite, some teachers just assigned a minimal, passing grade, which most cheating kids were happy to accept. Sure, those kids learned nothing, except perhaps about supply and demand.

But with the advent of AI, there’s a new problem: ghostwriters are losing their jobs, as John Hinderaker at Powerline reports:

In this case, by making cheating cheaper and more efficient. The New York Times headlines: “Kenyans Did College Students’ Homework for Years. Then A.I. Arrived.”

Hailing from a farming village in Kenya, Mr. Bundi moved to the capital, Nairobi, in 2011 to be the first in his family to attend university. There, a friend suggested he try a new online job : writing essays for cheating overseas college students.

*** Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day. He balanced completing his public health degree with helping faraway students studying engineering, medicine and computer science to finish theirs. Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments.

One might allow a bit of grudging respect for Bundi’s writing abilities and industriousness. After all, he was a Kenyan doing a job Americans legitimately wouldn’t do, and he didn’t break immigration laws to do it. But alas, all good—bad?—things come to an end:

In 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. At colleges worldwide, students made a simple calculation that has become more pronounced today: Why pay a freelancer in Kenya when ChatGPT could do the job?

Essay work began to thin. Rates fell, and assignments dwindled. Before long, the industry shrank to almost nothing. “I never would have expected A.I. could do this,” Mr. Bundi said.

Not quite a Shakespearean-level tragedy, is it? Consider the tragedy of Brown University economics Professor Robert Serrano. After a December 2025 mass shooting on campus, he advertised take-home exams for an upcoming class that normally attracted 30 students.  Eighty-six enrolled.

The midterm average was 96% in a class that normally averaged 65-80%. The influence of AI was even more obvious because Serrano made the exam more difficult than usual, as students had much more time to complete it.

But by the end of the semester, Serrano regretted the decision. Dozens of students in the class likely used artificial intelligence to cheat and earn perfect or near-perfect scores on their midterm, he said. Serrano in turn made the final exam in-person, which led more than a dozen students to drop the course and even more to fail it. Administrators’ response to the widespread cheating event has been “meek,” he said, and the incident has raised questions about how universities can—and should—respond to AI-enabled cheating at scale.

As in warfare, every new weapon births an effective counter-weapon, and so it is with AI academic counter-weapons. The real issue is whether administrators and politicians will allow teachers to use the nuclear equivalent of failing grades, or even classes, for AI plagiarism.

title: Private schools should not be able to expel children because their parents ask questions
content:
My family recently won an important ruling from the North Carolina Supreme Court allowing our lawsuit against Charlotte Latin School and certain school officials and board members to proceed.
The ru… [+4503 chars]
clean_content:
Private education should not mean that parents surrender every right at the schoolhouse door.

My family recently won an important ruling from the North Carolina Supreme Court allowing our lawsuit against Charlotte Latin School and certain school officials and board members to proceed.

The ruling was not a final decision on the merits. But it gives us the opportunity to pursue our claims arising from what happened to our family in 2021, at the height of the country’s battles over cancel culture, “anti-racism” programs, and political ideology in schools.

At its core, our case raises a question that should concern every parent with a child in a private school: Can a school expel your children simply because you respectfully ask questions about what they are being taught or how they are being treated?

Charlotte Latin and its allies have argued for extraordinarily broad discretion by private schools. Taken to its logical conclusion, that position could leave parents facing an impossible choice: remain silent about something they believe is inappropriate, unsafe, or harmful—or risk having their children removed from school.

That is dangerous. Parents should not have to wonder whether reporting mistreatment, questioning classroom material, or raising a health or safety concern could result in retaliation against their children.

Our lawsuit is not about telling private schools what curriculum they must teach. Private schools have considerable freedom to establish their own educational missions. This case is about accountability.

In 2021, a group of Charlotte Latin parents organized under the name Refocus Latin, and began raising questions about changes we believed were occurring at the school. Among the materials parents brought to the school board’s attention were disturbing images and content , including depictions of Jesus with his throat cut alongside the words “God is Dead,” burning Bibles, pigs portrayed as police officers with their throats slashed, and a gay sex manual in the library.

We presented our concerns to the board. The board chair thanked us for the presentation, assured us there would be no retaliation, and instructed us to continue bringing concerns to school administrators.

Then things changed. Approximately one week later, Head of School Chuck Baldecchi criticized our group during a video conference.

Soon afterward, our then-11-year-old son came to us with concerns about what was happening in his classroom. He told us he had been denied permission to use the bathroom and get water. He also described political discussions that, in his view, portrayed Republicans as white supremacists and made him feel that something was wrong with him because he was white.

Like parents are supposed to do, we asked questions. We requested a conversation with the head of the middle school. Instead, we were asked to attend a meeting with school leadership and were given an explicit written assurance of “no blowback.”

Our children were expelled at that meeting.

The broader issue goes far beyond one family or one school. What happens when a parent discovers something truly dangerous? What happens when a child says he or she is being mistreated? What happens when a parent questions a teacher, administrator, coach, or school policy?

If parents believe that speaking up could cost their children their education and separate them from their friends overnight, many will simply stay silent. That is precisely why basic protections matter.

Following what happened to our family, we founded the nonprofit Coalition For Liberty to push back against the scourge of cancel culture. Our personal lawsuit against Charlotte Latin is our own case; the larger principle, however, affects families across North Carolina and beyond.

Private education should not mean that parents surrender every right at the schoolhouse door. North Carolina lawmakers should examine whether additional protections are needed to ensure that children cannot be arbitrarily punished because their parents raise legitimate concerns, particularly when schools have promised families that concerns may be raised without retaliation.

Schools should welcome responsible parental involvement, not fear it. Parents should be able to ask questions. Children should not become leverage in disagreements between adults. No mother or father should have to choose between remaining silent and protecting a child.

That principle transcends politics. It is simply a matter of parental rights, fairness, and accountability.

The full story, supporting materials, and video are available at HonorAboveAll.org .

Doug Turpin is CEO of Coalition For Liberty, a nonprofit that advocates for free speech, parental involvement, and educational accountability.

title: Many Students Are Sick Of AI
content: The number of targeted AI ads I get as a student is really insane, Eden Daniel told me over coffee. Every time she opened YouTube, she was hit with a barrage of offers to take shortcuts on her school… [+14358 chars]

clean_content:
“T he number of targeted AI ads I get as a student is really insane,” Eden Daniel told me over coffee. Every time she opened YouTube, she was hit with a barrage of offers to take shortcuts on her schoolwork, especially during midterms.

Daniel has a visceral aversion to the technology, framing it as a plague on society that enriches tech billionaires and destroys the environment. Enrolled in the English honours program at McGill University, she saw her position as fairly typical, at least in her department. “We all understand the threat of AI to our jobs and what we’re doing, so it feels almost like a professional betrayal of our own futures.” If her peers were using online tools for proofreading, they had the good sense to hide it, lest they be socially shamed.

Daniel is a perfect example of what The Chronicle of Higher Education labels “the student AI resistors”—young people who refuse to be spoon-fed and want a rigorous education. In fact, when the news broke about graduates in the United States booing commencement speakers who praised artificial intelligence, Daniel texted me to make sure I saw the story. Last December, I wrote about the split among professors surrounding AI. As a college literature teacher, I try to keep these tools out of the classroom, while some of my colleagues focus on modelling proper use. But I’ve since realized that my own understanding was incomplete. I had been looking at AI largely through the eyes of a teacher whose profession was being upended. For my students, the disruption runs deeper: the technology has wrenched their entire educational trajectory off course. In these new waters, I couldn’t tell whether we were allies or enemies. This past semester, I taught a creative writing course where the majority claimed to hate AI. Reading their reflections on breakups and dying grandparents felt like a privilege. Then I dragged myself to a second class where I caught teenagers uploading ten-page short stories to ChatGPT to avoid reading them. Had education really become this much of a charade? There have always been keeners and cheaters, and creative writing classes are easy sells. But the more I talked to people from Daniel’s generation, the more I realized that her peers are in an unnerving position. The old academic norms have crumbled around them, and the new ones have not yet arrived. Torn between their values and their pragmatism, the desire to improve themselves and the fear of being left behind, they’re arguing with each other about AI even more than the faculty are. And, in the end, their debate is what might ultimately shape what education becomes. O f the dozen students I interviewed in the Montreal area, a full half were anti-AI. Eighteen-year-old Chloé Thibault framed her stance as part of her commitment to counterculture: she dyes her hair bright colours, goes to alternative rock shows, and sees the act of creation as “very human, very raw, almost messy.” A strong student who is eyeing a career in politics or law, Thibault was the most vocal proponent of the joys of being challenged. “Obviously, failing and struggling is not fun, but the sense of pride and succeeding afterwards is very, very motivating for me. And I don’t think you’d get that same kick or that same hit from getting a ninety from ChatGPT versus getting a ninety over an essay where you spent six hours in a basement with your cup of coffee and your eyes went criss-cross at the end of it.” Daniel and Thibault are both in humanities programs, but I heard overlapping arguments from those in more technical fields. Arielle Wong, a double major in computational arts and computer science at Concordia University, explained that, for her, it’s a question of ego: “My whole disdain for AI is because I feel like it’s better than me, and it gives me this feeling that I’m worse than a robot or machine.” In her program, she’s encouraged to take a balanced approach, exploring the potential of new tools but not over-relying on them. Though she’s had to unlearn some of the guilt she associates with the technology, she still avoids it as much as possible—“unless I’m really desperate,” she confessed. Wong hopes to find a job in a field like video games where she believes a human touch and sense of artistry still matter. She’s also concerned her commitment to developing her own skills might make her look less employable. “When I look at job offerings, a lot of them will say, like, AI content creator, AI marketing, and stuff like that. So there’s a frustration there.” For fellow Concordia student Wendy (not her real name), doubling down on what she called a “manual” skill set is a luxury for the talented few. As a design major, Wendy accepts that she might end up being an AI prompter, and she’s recently completed a course in “AI and Creativity” to prepare for this new reality. She already uses Claude for scheduling and brainstorming, and she’ll ask ChatGPT to verify whether her idea for an assignment meets a professor’s criteria. The key, for her, is to treat whatever it says as suggestions rather than the truth: “You can’t let the tool be the one who’s controlling you.” The challenge, of course, is determining where that line might be. A survey conducted by the accounting firm KPMG last year found that 73 percent of Canadian students use AI for their coursework, and most agree it has improved their grades. At the same time, 48 percent thought their critical thinking had deteriorated as a result. And that is the paradox in a nutshell: the technology may be helping students succeed at school while making them worse at the skills schools are supposed to teach. What qualifies as critical thinking is also up for debate. Mario Poveda, a science student, argued that he should be allowed to use AI to polish his English essays. “I don’t really use it in the creating part,” he insisted, writing the first drafts himself. Rather, as a native Spanish speaker who attended high school in French, he likes to double-check his grammar and spelling to avoid being penalized for small errors. My French is far from flawless, so I’m sympathetic to his situation. I also think someone’s grade in a college English class should correlate to their capacity to use the language. But when the whole concept of what constitutes “original student work” has frayed, it’s hard to blame him for rolling with the times. Not everyone wants to be a martyr to the cause of human imperfection. S ince the machines are already everywhere, students are making their own decisions about what learning means now—and, predictably, they are reaching different conclusions. James Victor Alvarez, a computer science undergraduate, was the most enthusiastic about the new technology among my interviewees. “I do use AI as I am a very busy person and I can’t really handle everything.” He’ll upload course materials to the application Gemini Notebook in order to produce a midterm study guide and an assignment schedule, which helps him stay organized throughout the semester. He’s aware that the same tool can go much further—turning a whole course into a podcast, for instance, or providing summaries of texts so someone doesn’t need to do the reading. Alvarez is the perfect example of a digital native who keeps up with new models as they’re released. He also likes to reference research to back up his points. For instance, he paraphrased a 2023 Stanford study that found AI detectors are biased against non-native English speakers, in one case flagging over 60 percent of their work as AI generated. He warned that improving these detectors is a lost cause, because “there’s also business on the other side in making AI seem human.” Some applications will insert minor errors into AI-generated text to make the prose look more authentic. Other tools let you upload samples of your writing so they can imitate your style. In short, Alvarez informed me that AI is becoming better and better at plagiarism. And because students have different ethical codes surrounding its use, they are fighting about it. Group projects, always a challenge, are now minefields. Thibault and Wong both mentioned the frustrations of working with people who used AI to complete their sections of group work. Thibault worried about the effect on her marks and reputation. Wong thought it was rarely worth confronting her peers and sometimes just redid their parts. In my problem class last semester, one young woman ranted to me for close to twenty minutes about her teammates’ use of AI for a presentation. I assured her I had noticed and would not be giving everyone the same grade, but I didn’t cut her off. Watching her mirror my own exasperation was too cathartic. For Barbara Roy, seeing her classmates cheat was a particular source of rage. Roy recently graduated from a competitive college program that attracts students who want to go to law school. She claims that one set of friends cheated openly, following a kind of bandwagon mentality: “They were hyping themselves up, basically,” comparing strategies for how to get away with doing less. “It was just laziness,” she insisted, as many of those involved were “super smart.” She argued with them but wasn’t about to snitch on her peers, many of whom were her friends. The problem is that Quebec college students are ranked against each other through a formula known as the R-score. During the semester when she was applying for university, she realized she was being outperformed by classmates who were, for example, shamelessly smuggling phones into in-class essays. “That’s when I realized that my hard work was, in a way, not for nothing but was worth less than I thought because people were cheating.” The experience shook her faith in education. “The system is made so that all that matters is your grades, not what you love to learn, not what you work hard for.” ChatGPT Isn’t Just Changing How We Work. It’s Harming How We Think I Thought My Colleague Was a Traitor for Teaching Students to Use AI. Then We Talked In the Age of AI, Are Universities Doomed? I ’m happy to report that things worked out for Roy: she’s heading to law school at the Université de Sherbrooke next year and very much plans to keep doing her own work. But cases like hers raise the question of who suffers when we aren’t able to enforce basic academic integrity, especially if grades are curved. Will her classmates be held accountable down the line? “I hope they hit a wall, but I don’t know.” At the same time, she finds the idea of her peers being failed or expelled heartbreaking. The students I catch the most easily aren’t in cohorts like Roy’s. Instead, I end up punishing weak students who are patching obvious skill gaps. I’ll see dramatic variations in writing quality between or even within assignments, or they’ll make rookie mistakes like including hallucinated quotations, which makes a plagiarism charge clear-cut. Otherwise, the risk of false positives can be high: Thibault recalled her indignation when a teacher said one of her essays sounded like ChatGPT, and the truth was she’d just sunk a lot of time into it. My interlocutors are probably right, however, when they tell me the vast majority of AI use goes undetected. There are plenty of times I’ve had doubts but no proof. Often, I suspect I’ve just been fooled. One man in his early twenties walked me through how he decides whether to cheat on coursework. He calculates how easily he can get away with it: plagiarism detectors like Turnitin may be flawed, but they’re still a deterrent. He also considers his workload. If he’s at risk of missing a deadline, he might have AI complete his math homework and redo the problems later to learn the material. He also mentioned how, during the COVID-19 pandemic, he felt like 90 percent of students were cheating—and since he wasn’t, his grades suffered by comparison. Above all, though, he uses AI when “the assignment doesn’t really make me a better person and doesn’t really increase anything in my life.” In short, it’s a question of whether or not he cares. From the squeaky-clean side of the aisle, Daniel brought up a similar point. We shouldn’t underestimate student agency; often, they choose to cheat when a required class appears as a roadblock toward what they want to pursue. “Honestly, you could see it as a rebellion against the educational institution as a whole.” M y interviewees had varied advice for teachers who want to limit the impact of AI. For all his interest in new technology, Alvarez highlighted classroom-based activities like debates as an effective counter to its overuse. Wong warned teachers against having AI generate feedback for assignments: students can tell, and it’s demotivating. She also praised one professor who let everyone revise and resubmit their work multiple times for an improved grade. That way, the pressure was off for everything to be perfect from the start, although she conceded this format works best in small classes. The need to strictly invigilate exams became depressingly obvious. Poveda was blunt about some of his classmates’ behaviour: “When the teacher is not looking, they take out their phones, they take a picture, and they just rewrite what’s on ChatGPT.” As much as I appreciated these insights, my favourite moments in these conversations were when they veered off topic. I ended up interviewing Thibault as part of a spontaneous panel with two of her classmates, Raj Matin (anti-AI, because it’s trained on stolen art) and Phillippe Villiard (generally pro). At one point, Villiard started arguing that we should automate all cars for the sake of safety, because “what’s the advantage of, oh, I’m being creative. I’m going to switch into this lane and kill someone.” Thibault shot back, “The part of me that’s a Formula One fan thinks that’s very sad.” Matin complained about people scrolling through social media in class: “To be fair, the teacher was boring, but at least try to pay attention.” And Villiard insisted that one of the most AI-proof jobs out there is hockey referee, because “you want someone to yell at. You want to say, this is a person I hate because he made a wrong call. It’s part of the game.” I suppose I could have begun working on this piece by asking Claude or some equivalent what today’s students think about artificial intelligence. It would have scraped the internet and spit back a series of smooth bullet points—possibly distorting my angle and definitely breaking the terms of my contract but maybe speeding up my research. Yet as I listened to these young people riff off each other, their idiosyncrasies coming into sharp relief, I was reminded of why it’s worth fighting to maintain authentic human dialogue, even if it’s inefficient. I want the mess of dealing with real people. I could have listened to them banter all day. Amanda Perry Amanda Perry teaches literature at Champlain College Saint-Lambert and Concordia University. Though she’s had to unlearn some of the guilt she associates with the technology, she still avoids it as much as possible—“unless I’m really desperate,” she confessed.

Wong hopes to find a job in a field like video games where she believes a human touch and sense of artistry still matter. She’s also concerned her commitment to developing her own skills might make her look less employable. “When I look at job offerings, a lot of them will say, like, AI content creator, AI marketing, and stuff like that. So there’s a frustration there.”

For fellow Concordia student Wendy (not her real name), doubling down on what she called a “manual” skill set is a luxury for the talented few. As a design major, Wendy accepts that she might end up being an AI prompter, and she’s recently completed a course in “AI and Creativity” to prepare for this new reality. She already uses Claude for scheduling and brainstorming, and she’ll ask ChatGPT to verify whether her idea for an assignment meets a professor’s criteria. The key, for her, is to treat whatever it says as suggestions rather than the truth: “You can’t let the tool be the one who’s controlling you.”

The challenge, of course, is determining where that line might be. A survey conducted by the accounting firm KPMG last year found that 73 percent of Canadian students use AI for their coursework, and most agree it has improved their grades. At the same time, 48 percent thought their critical thinking had deteriorated as a result. And that is the paradox in a nutshell: the technology may be helping students succeed at school while making them worse at the skills schools are supposed to teach.

What qualifies as critical thinking is also up for debate. Mario Poveda, a science student, argued that he should be allowed to use AI to polish his English essays. “I don’t really use it in the creating part,” he insisted, writing the first drafts himself. Rather, as a native Spanish speaker who attended high school in French, he likes to double-check his grammar and spelling to avoid being penalized for small errors.

My French is far from flawless, so I’m sympathetic to his situation. I also think someone’s grade in a college English class should correlate to their capacity to use the language. But when the whole concept of what constitutes “original student work” has frayed, it’s hard to blame him for rolling with the times. Not everyone wants to be a martyr to the cause of human imperfection.

S ince the machines are already everywhere, students are making their own decisions about what learning means now—and, predictably, they are reaching different conclusions. James Victor Alvarez, a computer science undergraduate, was the most enthusiastic about the new technology among my interviewees.

“I do use AI as I am a very busy person and I can’t really handle everything.” He’ll upload course materials to the application Gemini Notebook in order to produce a midterm study guide and an assignment schedule, which helps him stay organized throughout the semester. He’s aware that the same tool can go much further—turning a whole course into a podcast, for instance, or providing summaries of texts so someone doesn’t need to do the reading.

Alvarez is the perfect example of a digital native who keeps up with new models as they’re released. He also likes to reference research to back up his points. For instance, he paraphrased a 2023 Stanford study that found AI detectors are biased against non-native English speakers, in one case flagging over 60 percent of their work as AI generated. He warned that improving these detectors is a lost cause, because “there’s also business on the other side in making AI seem human.” Some applications will insert minor errors into AI-generated text to make the prose look more authentic. Other tools let you upload samples of your writing so they can imitate your style.

In short, Alvarez informed me that AI is becoming better and better at plagiarism. And because students have different ethical codes surrounding its use, they are fighting about it. Group projects, always a challenge, are now minefields. Thibault and Wong both mentioned the frustrations of working with people who used AI to complete their sections of group work. Thibault worried about the effect on her marks and reputation. Wong thought it was rarely worth confronting her peers and sometimes just redid their parts. In my problem class last semester, one young woman ranted to me for close to twenty minutes about her teammates’ use of AI for a presentation. I assured her I had noticed and would not be giving everyone the same grade, but I didn’t cut her off. Watching her mirror my own exasperation was too cathartic.

For Barbara Roy, seeing her classmates cheat was a particular source of rage. Roy recently graduated from a competitive college program that attracts students who want to go to law school. She claims that one set of friends cheated openly, following a kind of bandwagon mentality: “They were hyping themselves up, basically,” comparing strategies for how to get away with doing less. “It was just laziness,” she insisted, as many of those involved were “super smart.”

She argued with them but wasn’t about to snitch on her peers, many of whom were her friends. The problem is that Quebec college students are ranked against each other through a formula known as the R-score. During the semester when she was applying for university, she realized she was being outperformed by classmates who were, for example, shamelessly smuggling phones into in-class essays. “That’s when I realized that my hard work was, in a way, not for nothing but was worth less than I thought because people were cheating.”

The experience shook her faith in education. “The system is made so that all that matters is your grades, not what you love to learn, not what you work hard for.”

I ’m happy to report that things worked out for Roy: she’s heading to law school at the Université de Sherbrooke next year and very much plans to keep doing her own work. But cases like hers raise the question of who suffers when we aren’t able to enforce basic academic integrity, especially if grades are curved. Will her classmates be held accountable down the line? “I hope they hit a wall, but I don’t know.” At the same time, she finds the idea of her peers being failed or expelled heartbreaking.

The students I catch the most easily aren’t in cohorts like Roy’s. Instead, I end up punishing weak students who are patching obvious skill gaps. I’ll see dramatic variations in writing quality between or even within assignments, or they’ll make rookie mistakes like including hallucinated quotations, which makes a plagiarism charge clear-cut. Otherwise, the risk of false positives can be high: Thibault recalled her indignation when a teacher said one of her essays sounded like ChatGPT, and the truth was she’d just sunk a lot of time into it. My interlocutors are probably right, however, when they tell me the vast majority of AI use goes undetected. There are plenty of times I’ve had doubts but no proof. Often, I suspect I’ve just been fooled.

One man in his early twenties walked me through how he decides whether to cheat on coursework. He calculates how easily he can get away with it: plagiarism detectors like Turnitin may be flawed, but they’re still a deterrent. He also considers his workload. If he’s at risk of missing a deadline, he might have AI complete his math homework and redo the problems later to learn the material. He also mentioned how, during the COVID-19 pandemic, he felt like 90 percent of students were cheating—and since he wasn’t, his grades suffered by comparison.

Above all, though, he uses AI when “the assignment doesn’t really make me a better person and doesn’t really increase anything in my life.” In short, it’s a question of whether or not he cares. From the squeaky-clean side of the aisle, Daniel brought up a similar point. We shouldn’t underestimate student agency; often, they choose to cheat when a required class appears as a roadblock toward what they want to pursue. “Honestly, you could see it as a rebellion against the educational institution as a whole.”

M y interviewees had varied advice for teachers who want to limit the impact of AI. For all his interest in new technology, Alvarez highlighted classroom-based activities like debates as an effective counter to its overuse. Wong warned teachers against having AI generate feedback for assignments: students can tell, and it’s demotivating.

She also praised one professor who let everyone revise and resubmit their work multiple times for an improved grade. That way, the pressure was off for everything to be perfect from the start, although she conceded this format works best in small classes. The need to strictly invigilate exams became depressingly obvious. Poveda was blunt about some of his classmates’ behaviour: “When the teacher is not looking, they take out their phones, they take a picture, and they just rewrite what’s on ChatGPT.”

As much as I appreciated these insights, my favourite moments in these conversations were when they veered off topic. I ended up interviewing Thibault as part of a spontaneous panel with two of her classmates, Raj Matin (anti-AI, because it’s trained on stolen art) and Phillippe Villiard (generally pro).

At one point, Villiard started arguing that we should automate all cars for the sake of safety, because “what’s the advantage of, oh, I’m being creative. I’m going to switch into this lane and kill someone.” Thibault shot back, “The part of me that’s a Formula One fan thinks that’s very sad.” Matin complained about people scrolling through social media in class: “To be fair, the teacher was boring, but at least try to pay attention.” And Villiard insisted that one of the most AI-proof jobs out there is hockey referee, because “you want someone to yell at. You want to say, this is a person I hate because he made a wrong call. It’s part of the game.”

I suppose I could have begun working on this piece by asking Claude or some equivalent what today’s students think about artificial intelligence. It would have scraped the internet and spit back a series of smooth bullet points—possibly distorting my angle and definitely breaking the terms of my contract but maybe speeding up my research.

Yet as I listened to these young people riff off each other, their idiosyncrasies coming into sharp relief, I was reminded of why it’s worth fighting to maintain authentic human dialogue, even if it’s inefficient. I want the mess of dealing with real people. I could have listened to them banter all day.

An interview from the New York Times revealed that even before AI, college students found other creative ways to cheat the system.

A man from Kenya told The New York Times that he built a lucrative business writing thousands of essays for American college students — until AI ruined everything. Now, students admittedly use AI instead. The academic ghostwriter, Teresios Bundi, told the outlet about the first assignment he ever took, which paid $7 and felt like a “lifeline” for the struggling father, according to the Times interview . “I needed the money,” the now 34-year-old Bundi told the Times in the interview. “I could not sleep that night. I was ready to burn the midnight oil.” But with AI, students seem to see it as a much cheaper way to cut corners with regard to completing coursework.

For years, Bundi’s business plan worked well for him and for others in India, the Philippines, and elsewhere. (RELATED: College Costs Surge 10% Higher Than Last Year, New Report Shows)

Pour one out for the Kenyans who have been helping American students cheat. “Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day … Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments.” pic.twitter.com/3C5uqlojkL

Kenyans were cashing in on the boom of academic ghostwriting. Estimates suggest that some 40,000 people in the capital city of Nairobi were making money doing homework for others, according to the Times.

“Essay writers drove new Subarus, carried the latest smartphones, and booked exclusive tables at clubs,” the outlet reported. (RELATED: Kai Trump Says She’s Been Sobbing, Hasn’t Eaten For Days During College Transition)

“Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day … Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments,” the report continues.

"AI has destroyed Kenyan jobs because American college students no longer hire them to write fake college essays" is not a framing I expected even the NYT to have pic.twitter.com/7DlifkjLE2

Now, thanks to the AI revolution in higher education , Bundi has shuttered his business and has struggled to find work ever since, according to the Times.

“At colleges worldwide, students made a simple calculation that has become more pronounced today: Why pay a freelancer in Kenya when ChatGPT could do the job?” the outlet reported.

Nowadays, millions of college students continue to use AI to help with their studies.

So much so that higher education officials are sounding the alarm, according to research by The College Board.

Almost three-quarters (74%) of college and university faculty report that students are using AI to write essays or papers, and 67% say students admit to making use of it in order to paraphrase or rewrite content, according to the study.

“Faculty are navigating this critical transition, as AI rapidly expands in higher education,” said Jessica Howell, PhD, vice president of Research at College Board said, according to an official press release .

“This research shows that faculty have serious concerns about AI’s impact on critical thinking, original writing, and academic integrity. Faculty, especially those in writing-intensive courses, are asking important questions about how to preserve core learning goals while preparing students for a world where AI will be part of the workplace.”

Even if students do not have AI write them an entire paper - it has the ability to create an outline - so it varies as to what extent college students rely on it to make the grade.

clean_content:
Tutor Intelligence Inc. , a provider of artificial intelligence-powered warehouse robot workers, has launched its second-generation Cassie and Sonny robots, running on the company’s robot foundation models.

Sonny was initially developed as the company’s dual-armed semi-humanoid robot and introduced alongside Tutor’s Ti0 4.5 billion parameter Vision Language Action model. Since then, it has evolved from a research platform into a fully deployable robot capable of autonomous manipulation and mobility in warehouses.

Cassie, the company’s large-format, single-arm robot, was expanded for mobility in warehouses and factories, adding pallet movement and greater physical intelligence. It looks like a giant arm atop a large box with wheels.

“It’s really important for us not only that we build these general robots, but they’re immediately practically useful,” co-founder and Chief Executive Josh Gruenstein told SiliconANGLE in an interview. “We’re in this unique position of building robots that are both generally capable and immediately useful.”

Tutor looked at an industry where humanoid robots are currently “sexy,” but humans already do that fundamental work just fine. Cassie and Sonny represent two separate answers to the same question: What shape can a general robot take if it’s designed around the work rather than around looking like a person?

Cassie provides muscle for moving heavy material in a broad, big box-laden pallet warehouse setting and Sonny works amid shelves where arms and hands make sense for picking up small objects and moving them between bins.

“Sonny is kind of this co-design with Cassie of what is something that is human-like as a robot, but, you know, not designed just to mimic a human, but to do a class of work that humans do,” Gruenstein said.

Cassie in particular can lift 50 pounds and tug thousands of pounds, which Gruenstein described as something of a “loch ness” of a robot moving between pallets doing work. The first-generation of Cassie worked from a fixed position, but is now mobile and can move across warehouse floors.

Back in December, Tutor raised $34 million in Series A funding; in that time, the company built what is essentially a “classroom” for its AI models to run across its Sonny robots in what it calls Data Factory 1 : a 100 “robot factory” where Sonny robots “learn.”

“In robotics, we don’t have like an internet of training data to get the training data to train AI models,” Gruenstein explained.

Robotics has a mild problem. AI models depend on vast amounts of data for pre-training; in robotics, that data is visual and kinetic telemetry that shows them how to do tasks such as picking up objects, what objects look like, where to place them, how to move and so on. Much of this can be done through training, or, as it’s called, “tutoring,” via experts who show the robots how it is done in real settings.

According to Gruenstein, Cassie doesn’t need to reason about everything a pair of hands might encounter. Its physical vocabulary is comparatively small: Identify an object, grasp it, move it and place it. Sonny’s vocabulary is much larger, so Tutor built Ti0, the company’s powerful AI model, and DF1 to attack the corresponding data problem.

“We have this team of tutors staffed internationally that can kind of remote control a robot and teach it how to do a new task for the first time,” Gruenstein said.

After that, the 100 robots in the classroom go through the motions to fine-tune behaviors, smooth out any kinks and prepare the robotic models for what might happen in the field. This is otherwise known as post-training. If an individual robot does a good job, that student’s actions get reinforced in the AI model with a thumbs up, a positive reward; if it does poorly, those actions get a thumbs down. This helps the model learn how real-world behaviors interact with actual hardware.

“We can get robots that recursively self-improve and are superhuman in their performance relative to people,” Gruenstein explained.

title: What Yellowstone, Rwanda and AI Taught Me About Change
content: Over the past two years, Ive spent countless hours talking with teachers, parents, students and school leaders about artificial intelligence. The questions they have are remarkably consistent: How sh… [+8050 chars]
author: Nathan Kraai
clean_content:
By viewing our classrooms as interconnected ecosystems, we can move beyond the surface-level debate over technology to focus on cultivating judgment, curiosity and empathy.

Over the past two years, I’ve spent countless hours talking with teachers, parents, students and school leaders about artificial intelligence. The questions that arise are remarkably consistent: How should schools respond? When should students use AI? How do we preserve authentic learning in a world where answers have become nearly instantaneous?

They’re important questions, but I’ve noticed something interesting about them. Our conversations rarely stay focused on the technology itself. Before long, they drift somewhere deeper. They become conversations about thinking. About curiosity. About judgment. About what learning is actually for when a machine can generate an essay, solve a problem, or summarize a chapter in seconds.

Oddly enough, the most helpful answers I’ve found didn’t come from AI research. They came from Rwanda and Yellowstone National Park.

For years, those two experiences occupied completely different parts of my life. One was a trip that changed me. The other was an ecological story I couldn’t stop thinking about. It took me much longer to realize they were helping me answer the very questions I was now asking about artificial intelligence in schools.

That realization began on a dusty road, on an otherwise ordinary day in Rwanda.

I went to Rwanda as part of a group helping schools transition from French to English in the classroom. That day, I happened to be carrying a yellow jerrycan of water from the watering hole back to the village alongside people who make that miles-long journey every day. Before long, my hands ached and my shoulders tightened. The hard plastic handle dug into my fingers as I wondered how much further we had to walk. The people beside me never seemed to notice the weight. For me, carrying water was extraordinary. For them, it was simply another walk home.

That contrast stayed with me long after I returned home. The walk answered very little. Instead, it left me with a question that has followed me ever since: How do we help students understand realities they have never lived?

That question would resurface years later in a sixth-grade classroom. Our teaching team designed an interdisciplinary unit around Linda Sue Park's novel “ A Long Walk to Water ,” hoping literature, conversations with a friend of mine from Sudan, and local field experiences would help students move beyond learning about water insecurity and begin to care about the people living it.

By most measures, the lesson was a success. Then we sat down to debrief.

“I don’t think it worked,” one teacher said.

Almost immediately, heads began nodding around the table.

No one defended the lesson. No one blamed the students. Instead, we realized we had been measuring engagement when what we really cared about was understanding.

Looking back, I think that meeting changed our teaching far more than the lesson itself. Years of working together had built enough trust for one honest observation to give everyone else permission to be honest too. We stopped trying to protect the lesson and started asking a different question.

Not, How do we make this activity better? But, How does understanding actually grow?

We’ve been refining that project ever since, and that conversation forced us to confront a much larger question: If meaningful change doesn’t happen because of a single lesson, how does it happen?

To understand how meaningful change happens, consider what happened in Yellowstone National Park.

When scientists reintroduced gray wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, they expected the elk population to change. They didn’t expect rivers to change as well. As elk altered where they grazed, willow and aspen trees recovered. Beavers returned. Wetlands expanded. Vegetation stabilized riverbanks. An entire ecosystem began reorganizing itself in ways few people had anticipated.

The wolves didn’t directly reshape Yellowstone. They changed the relationships within the ecosystem. And everything else followed.

Learning about Yellowstone changed the way I thought about change itself. It made me realize that the most meaningful transformations rarely begin by fixing one thing. They begin by changing the relationships within a system. Once I saw that pattern, I couldn’t stop seeing it in schools.

We often assume meaningful change happens by improving the thing right in front of us. We redesign a lesson. We adopt a new curriculum. We write a new AI policy. We expect better outcomes because we’ve improved one part of the system.

The wolves didn’t change the rivers directly. They changed how elk moved through the landscape. That altered where trees could grow, which brought back beavers, reshaped wetlands, stabilized riverbanks, and eventually changed the rivers themselves. One dramatic intervention didn’t drive the transformation. It emerged because relationships within the ecosystem had changed.

I’m beginning to think schools work the same way.

Looking back, our sixth-grade project didn’t improve because we discovered a better activity. It improved because the relationships around the project changed. Teachers trusted one another enough to challenge assumptions. Students were invited to wrestle with ideas instead of simply completing assignments. Learning became less about delivering an experience and more about cultivating understanding.

Once I began seeing schools that way, I couldn’t think about artificial intelligence in quite the same way anymore.

AI isn’t simply introducing another tool into classrooms. It’s changing relationships: The relationship between students and thinking. Between effort and accomplishment. Between teachers and expertise. Between knowing something and finding it instantly.

Those may prove to be the relationships that shape the future of learning far more than any particular AI model or school policy.

That’s why my conversations about AI are almost never about the technology itself. They’re about what we choose to value.

Parents wonder whether students will gradually stop wrestling with difficult ideas if a chatbot can do the work for them. Teachers ask how to preserve productive struggle when every answer is just a prompt away. School leaders wrestle with an even deeper question: If AI can do more of the thinking, what kinds of thinking should remain unmistakably human?

I don’t think there’s a simple answer. What I do know is that answering those questions has required me to revisit experiences that had nothing to do with artificial intelligence — at least not at first.

I keep finding myself returning to that dusty road in Rwanda.

Carrying a jerrycan didn’t help me understand what it means to live with water insecurity. It wasn’t meant to. What it changed was my relationship to the people carrying it beside me.

Our sixth-grade project taught me something similar. We eventually realized our goal wasn’t to create a memorable activity. It was to create the conditions where students might begin asking deeper questions about lives very different from their own.

Increasingly, I think AI presents schools with that same choice. We can use it to remove every obstacle from learning, making every task faster and easier. Or we can become even more intentional about preserving the kinds of thinking that develop judgment, curiosity, empathy and discernment.

Looking back, I don’t think Rwanda, Yellowstone, and AI were ever separate stories.

Rwanda changed my relationship to people whose lives I couldn’t fully understand. Our faculty meeting changed the relationships among teachers. AI is changing the relationship students have with thinking itself.

Rwanda taught me that understanding begins with humility. Our sixth-grade team taught me that meaningful change begins with the courage to question our own assumptions. And Yellowstone taught me that lasting change happens by changing relationships within a system.

Technology will continue to change. Our responsibility as educators won’t.

We still have to create experiences that ask students to think, question, struggle, and understand in ways no technology can do for them. Those were the questions before AI. I suspect they’ll still be the questions long after today’s technology has been replaced by something none of us can yet imagine.

Melania Trump on Tuesday urged students not to fear artificial intelligence — or else they will be left behind.

She made the pro-AI comments as she unveiled tech investments from mega US chip maker Nvidia .

“We need to lead … AI, as a country, and we could see now what they’re learning, and it’s very important. Of course, they need to be vigilant as well,” the first lady told reporters.

“But this is our future, and we need to guide them and teach them what is available. If not, they will stay behind, and we need to be the first in [the] United States to lead.”

Trump touted the benefits of AI during a visit to Mountain View Elementary in North Carolina, where she announced a partnership with Nvidia to bring more AI into the classroom.

The first lady told the students it was “a special surprise to help jumpstart” their learning as the school year began.

Despite a dire warning from researchers about the dangers of AI taking over humanity, Trump offered an optimistic view of the technology and envisioned students building robots they could show off at the White House.

“Dream big and use these AI tools to build something never created before,” Trump told the students. “Maybe one of you will create the next great robot. And if you do, make sure you bring it to the White House to show me!”

Nvidia will provide StudyFetch four-year subscription licenses for 1,500 students in Ashe County School District; and 100 Jetson Nano Developer Kits to experiment with robotics in partnership with Trump’s Be Best program.

After the announcement, the first lady spent nearly two hours visiting classrooms, meeting with students to hear about their work designing video simulations, using robotic arms to accomplish tasks, and using AI to design their own projects.

The kids were just as enthusiastic to see her. One boy, Ryker Hamm, jumped up to give her a hug, and she spent some time talking to him about his lessons.

She complimented one youngster on his passion for AI when he showed her how he wanted to use the technology to help his community, such as tracking damage after a storm.

“You guys are very smart, so keep studying,” she told them.

Her enthusiasm for technology was visible as she joined the students on their iPads to watch their work, admired their projects printed on a 3-D printer and encouraged them to keep learning.

“You are amazing in what you do,” she told them. “You are very smart and you have a big future guys. … You can do anything. Anything is possible. The sky is the limit. Never give up and study hard.”

Melania Trump has become a champion of AI in her husband’s administration , which wants to keep the United States at the forefront of the global economy.

The first lady already launched a coalition called “Fostering the Future Together” dedicated to “enhancing the well-being of children through the promotion of education, innovation, and technology.” At the launch event, she famously entered alongside a robot, the American-made humanoid named Figure 3.

She has hosted multiple events and meetings on the importance of incorporating technology into education, including a summit in March when she brought together the spouses of 38 world leaders.

And she hosted the Presidential Artificial Intelligence Challenge National Champion Awards Ceremony in June.

She’s used AI technology herself, notably to produce the audio version of her 2024 memoir, Melania.

It was the first lady’s fourth visit to North Carolina, and it comes one day ahead of President Trump’s trip to the state.

Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.

Melania Trump, in January 2025, joined the president in touring the damage from Hurricane Helene. She was last in the state in February when she and the president visited troops before Valentine’s Day in Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

President Trump will be in North Carolina on Wednesday to campaign for Senate candidate Michael Whatley in his hometown of Gastonia.

title: Video: Why are AI-generated lies about Finland flooding social media?
content:
"In Finland, schools are shaped like forests each classroom is inside a dome covered in real moss"
"Finland successfully transmits electric power through the air without using physical wires"
The a… [+1835 chars]
clean_content:
"In Finland, schools are shaped like forests — each classroom is inside a dome covered in real moss."

"Finland successfully transmits electric power through the air without using physical wires."

The above are just two examples of the many strange — and misleading — claims about Finland that have started to pop up on social media timelines in recent years.

But what is behind this wave of disinformation?

The images that accompany the texts are clearly generated by artificial intelligence (AI), but platforms such as Facebook have been slow to add "AI info" labels to such content.

The posts often garner thousands of likes, comments and shares — and the accounts that share them can have up to a million followers.

According to a report (in Finnish) by Yle's investigative journalism unit MOT, the administrators of these pages are motivated by the possibility of making money through Meta's Content Monetization programme.

The tech giant, which owns Facebook and Instagram, paid out some 3 billion dollars to content creators last year alone. The initiative rewards posts that generate high engagement — giving administrators a financial incentive to create viral content, regardless of its accuracy.

MOT's investigation revealed that a significant portion of the pages spreading Finland— related AI images are run from India and Pakistan — and this is likely where their target market lies too.

University of Helsinki senior researcher Niko Pyrhönen told MOT that Finland may seem like an "exotic technology paradise" when viewed from afar, and also make the AI-fuelled claims much harder to verify.

"I believe it's easier to build this kind of story about a distant place, or perhaps specifically about Finland, compared to many other countries," Pyrhönen noted.

MOT reported further that the combined follower count of accounts spreading these false claims runs into the millions, suggesting misinformation about Finland is reaching a substantial global audience.

title: California high school grads score 4.0 GPAs but can’t do basic math, professors say
content:
California high school students are scoring more straight A’s than ever but its not necessarily because theyre getting smarter, according to data and education experts. 
The number of college applic… [+7049 chars]
author: Titus Wu
clean_content:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

California high school students are scoring more straight A’s than ever – but it’s not necessarily because they’re getting smarter , according to data and education experts.

The number of college applicants reporting flawless GPAs of 4.0 or higher has doubled over the past decade even as state testing shows a post-pandemic plunge in reading and math comprehension — revealing a grade-inflation crisis that’s sending students who can’t even do fractions into top universities.

Over the past decade, the number of students applying to the University of California system with straight A’s skyrocketed from 52,989 in 2015 to 103,138 for the class of 2025, with a notable jump during the COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2022, according to UC data reviewed by The Post.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

It’s part of a dangerous slide in grading standards as teachers are backhandedly encouraged to hand out inflated marks, according to critics like Glenn Sacks, who teaches social studies in the Los Angeles Unified School District.

“When I was hired at one LAUSD school, the administrator showing me my classroom — a man I liked and respected — told me, ‘Don’t fail too many kids–remember, it’s easier to replace one teacher than 35 students,'” Sacks told The Post.

He cited growing pressure on teachers, which started during COVID and continues today, to eliminate D’s and F’s in order to shore up enrollment and attendance . Teachers were told that a significant number of failing grades meant instruction needed to be revised, he added.

Charles Cole , an education advocate who attended California high schools before graduating in 2001, told The Post that grade inflation has been brewing for decades and has grown worse in recent years.

Cole, who attended much of his high school in Oakland, racked up top marks in high school and felt betrayed when he found out he had to take remedial classes at his California State University.

“Those classes were fairly easy for me. It didn’t take a lot,” Cole said of his high school A’s. “I’m happy and grateful for the grades because it helped me get into college. But the level of preparation was a huge letdown.”

Cole, whose organization The Agentic Institute, formerly Energy Convertors , helps underrepresented students succeed in school, now works with kids in California and across the nation. He said high grades can do students a disservice.

“A large swath of these students are functionally — they’re not on grade level,” he said. “They’re multiple grade levels behind, but they have the confidence of, ‘Hey man, I just graduated with a 3.0. I’m about to go to college.'”

California’s state-mandated test results back up Cole’s observations, painting a grimmer picture on reading and math performance than the high GPAs would indicate. Scores on the Smarter Balanced Summative Assessments, which measures student proficiency in math and English, were an abysmal 57% in English and just 30.5% in math for California 11th graders in the 2024-2025 school year.

They have improved since hitting lows of 54.8% and 27% in 2021-2022, but are generally lower than pre-pandemic times, according to data from the state Department of Education.

While the University of California GPA data includes out-of-state applicants, the vast majority of applicants since 1994 are California residents.

“A 4.0 simply doesn’t distinguish a student in the way it once did,” said Marc Zawel, who co-founded admissions consulting group AcceptU. “In our work with students, we have absolutely seen grades become more compressed at the top.”

While grade inflation may not be the only explanation, the rising numbers of high GPAs make it hard for colleges to figure out who’s actually qualified, Zawel added. It’s why more than 1,200 UC professors claimed in an open letter this year they’ve been forced to teach “middle school” math in calculus and other courses, demanding that the University of California reinstate SAT testing as an admissions requirement.

The UCs removed testing requirements in 2020 to appease lefty activists who claimed the exams were unfair on non-white students, but professors now say it’s fueled rampant grade inflation that’s flooding colleges with unqualified students.

“The current admissions metrics, based primarily on GPA and essays, can no longer reliably distinguish readiness for university-level STEM majors in an era of severe grade inflation and AI-assisted application essays,” the professors wrote in their open letter.

Experts told The Post that new habits formed by the pandemic, when classes moved online, likely accelerated grade inflation. Simon Nicholas, who heads a test-prep tutoring company that’s worked with numerous California students, said COVID led to the rise of ”asynchronous classes” — which students can attend whenever they choose — and a ”downshift in rigor.”

Students can miss a call or not pay attention when they attend, knowing everything will be posted online, Nicholas said.

“The idea that we can do these things online, well maybe we can. But is it as effective as doing things in person? Probably not,” he said, adding that the rise in artificial intelligence is only exacerbating the problem.

Others have blamed education leaders for the grade inflation, saying that there’s an incentive to get every student to pass.

“Some districts are handing out high marks to students who haven’t mastered basic reading, writing, and math, then passing the buck to colleges that are left dealing with underprepared kids,” Sonja Shaw, candidate for state superintendent of education, told The Post.

“That’s not helping anyone. It’s a disservice that Sacramento has ignored for far too long,” she added.

The professors asked the Board of Regents to reinstate standardized testing requirements for admission, and officials say they’re considering that request to take up next year.

“University of California has accelerated its timeline to review and provide recommendations on standardized testing,” the UC system said in a statement.

Nicholas agreed on the need to reinstate testing requirements, saying it could go a long way in fixing grade inflation at high schools.

“It would strongly disincentivize” grade inflation, he said, “because it’s embarrassing to say that, you know, we have 48% of our students or whatever with an A, and they can’t crack a 20 on the ACT.”

“It behooves the school then to be more honest, or to be more scrupulous, or more rigorous about its scoring,” he added.

title: We organized the National Civics Bee — it’s where to start if you want better workers
content: Students are heading back to school in the 250th year since our nations founding. Unfortunately, many of them may not be aware of what the nations founding entailed, as only 22% of eighth-graders in … [+6048 chars]
author: Hilary Crow, Ashley Berner
clean_content:
Students are heading back to school in the 250th year since our nation’s founding. Unfortunately, many of them may not be aware of what the nation’s founding entailed, as only 22% of eighth-graders in this country are proficient in civics according to the most recent National Assessment of Educational Progress .

These students are aware, however, that the world around them is changing, and that AI will have a profound impact on what they need to know to succeed when they leave the classroom. Asked this month which skills will matter most as artificial intelligence reshapes work, teenagers surveyed by Common Sense Media pointed to working well with others, fact-checking and critical thinking, and making sense of complicated information. Employers have been saying much the same thing for years, with only 18% of business leaders believing entry-level hires are ready for today’s workplace.

We tend to treat these as separate worries, one about the health of our democracy and the other about the strength of our workforce. But they actually have more in common than one might think, and there’s a strong case to be made that improving civics knowledge would go a long way toward building the skills students and employers are seeking.

As our nation invests heavily in career pathways, credentials, artificial intelligence, and technical training, we must also invest in one of our country’s most overlooked drivers of workforce readiness: high-quality civic learning.

As the organizers and researchers of the National Civics Bee—a nationwide, nonpartisan civics competition for middle school students—we’ve witnessed firsthand how civic learning can also help students develop the skills employers and students want. This year, more than 20,000 students are participating through over 240 local chambers of commerce and community partners across all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and American Samoa. Students gain civic knowledge and put it to use by identifying issues they see in their communities, researching those concerns from multiple perspectives, developing potential solutions, and discussing their ideas before judges.

In post-competition surveys, 98% of participants identified at least one meaningful benefit from the experience. Nearly three-quarters improved their writing. Many reported greater confidence discussing public issues, a stronger understanding of local government, and more frequent conversations about civic issues at home. Three-quarters said they felt prepared to defend a position on a controversial issue respectfully and thoughtfully.

Consider Emily Brubaker. Born with a rare medical condition that created significant challenges for her family, she entered the National Civics Bee determined to explore a public policy issue that had personally affected her. She researched the topic, built support for her ideas, and traveled to Washington, D.C. to meet with lawmakers to discuss potential solutions. In the process, she practiced many of the same skills employers value in the workplace: research, communication, collaboration, persistence, and the ability to turn challenges into solutions.

Not every middle school student will lobby Congress, but civic learning gives young people opportunities to tackle authentic challenges before anyone is paying them to do so. Experiences like the Bee help students develop the very qualities employers consistently say they need most.

Unfortunately, few young people are given meaningful opportunities to engage with real issues in school, where they can practice and hone skills before entering the real world.

Our nation’s founders saw a citizenry educated in its liberties as a precondition for the republic—a sentiment echoed by Horace Mann half a century later when, as the first Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education, he identified civic education—what he called political education—as a core pillar of a public education system. That sentiment persisted into the 1960s, with high schools commonly requiring three courses in civics and government.

Over time, however, civics has been crowded out by competing academic priorities. Today, most states require just one civics course—and often only a semester—and opportunities to put civic skills into practice are limited: just one-third of high schools offer debate teams, one-quarter offer mock trials, and a mere 20% offer mock elections. Civics instruction is equally lacking in younger grades. A 2022 report from the RAND Corp. on K-5 social studies called out a “ missing infrastructure ,” referring to the gaps in policies, resources, and required testing that encourage classroom instruction on civics.

These gaps are not accidental. They reflect where we put our money. Federal investment in STEM education runs roughly $50 per student each year, while civic education receives less than fifty cents per student. That is troubling for democracy, but it should also worry employers. If students are not learning how institutions work, how decisions get made, how to evaluate competing claims, or how to participate constructively in public discourse, we should not be surprised when they struggle to navigate increasingly complex workplaces.

Technical expertise has never been enough, which is why businesses already invest billions of dollars each year in onboarding, leadership development, and professional training. What if future employees arrived on their first day having already practiced these capabilities for years in classrooms, communities, and civic life?

The National Civics Bee is just one example of what becomes possible when civic learning is treated as an investment rather than an afterthought. As America begins its next 250 years, employers should not wait for the talent pipeline to fix itself. If we want a workforce capable of adapting to change, navigating complexity, and strengthening our communities, those capacities must be cultivated early.

The next generation of leaders, workers, and citizens is sitting in a middle school classroom right now. It’s time to invest accordingly.

title: Teachers are worried AI is taking over the classroom faster than they can stop it
content:
• Epson survey finds 76% of students expect to be able to use AI in their learning
  • Meanwhile, 81% of teachers believe students think AI can do spelling and maths for them
  • Follow… [+3131 chars]
author: Christian Cawley
clean_content:
Are students over-relying on artificial intelligence chatbots? That seems to be the opinion of teachers across Europe, where 80% of educators have expressed concern about the pace of AI entry into the classroom.

A survey of 3,360 people by Epson discovered over two-thirds (68%) of teachers feel that AI use in homework has a negative effect on learning. Conversely, over three quarters of students expect to be able to use AI, with almost 90% already using it once a week for school work.

This research is released as the EU’s AI Act commences enforcement, forcing schools in the European Union to ensure adequate training is provided for any AI tools in use.

Epson Europe’s Educate to Empower 2026 Research surveyed 3,360 people across the EU, specifically France, Italy, Germany, Spain and Poland, as well as the UK. (There is no equivalent to the EU’s AI Act in the UK, although businesses providing services to companies within the EU must adhere to its regulations.)

“AI is developing at speed, and students expect to be able to use it. That means it needs to be managed effectively, with the right governance, guidelines and training in place," said Dr Sarah Henkelmann-Hillebrand, lead for education at Epson Europe.

With 76% of students expecting to be able to use AI and 87% already employing it in some way, the horse has bolted on blocking its use. Instead, the survey finds, the focus should be on teaching skills that cannot be short-circuited by AI.

Henkelmann-Hillebrand notes that “It’s also important to look at how AI can enhance the learning experience. By supporting students and teachers to co-create in immersive learning spaces, using technologies such as projection alongside AI, we can make learning more engaging and collaborative while helping students develop the skills they’ll need for a future dominated by AI.”

While student use of AI is cause for concern where it impacts their ability to learn and demonstrate comprehension, teachers have an additional challenge.

The survey’s findings also revealed that 82% of teachers want more training to oversee the use of AI by students. Additionally – and perhaps more significantly – 78% want training and guidance on how they can use the technology in their own work.

Could it make more sense for teachers to use AI to reduce their admin, than to permit AI use by students? If AI is taking over the classroom, it seems sensible to ensure teachers are fully equipped to encourage skills that AI cannot give students, such as analytical thinking, creativity, leadership, problem-solving, and other uniquely human traits.

content:

Greg LaRose / Louisiana Illuminator
Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and… [+4997 chars]
author: Piper Hutchinson
clean_content:
A survey of higher education faculty in the South found professors are concerned about the political environment around higher education, with some fearing for their physical safety.

The annual survey from the American Association of University Professors included an open-ended question that allowed faculty to detail the problems they’re facing. Compared with previous years, there was a significant spike in faculty scared not only for their careers but also for their physical safety.

“I teach a subject that is now considered ‘controversial,’” a professor in North Carolina wrote. “As a result, I have had a non-student with a gun enter my classroom to intimidate me. I have received an email death threat from a student.”

The AAUP survey polls faculty at schools in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia. The association received about 2,700 responses, with 41 coming from Louisiana universities.

Across the nation, state leaders have put higher education under a microscope. The scrutiny has been particularly acute in conservative Southern states, where changes to education laws have been extensive.

In Alabama, lawmakers eliminated faculty governance at its public institutions, where professors and instructors previously had a say in campus policy decisions.

In North Carolina, faculty are now required to post their course outlines publicly, which survey respondents said has led to them receiving threats.

In multiple states, legislators have passed laws banning the teaching of divisive topics and prohibiting diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

Dozens of faculty members said they had to fight back against angry alumni, political officials and student activists who attempted to get them fired or doxxed them. Doxxing is the act of publishing someone’s private information without their consent in an attempt to bring harm to them.

“I was targeted for harassment and experienced death threats,” a full professor in Virginia wrote. ”I feel less safe doing my job than in the past. I have to think through the consequences of words I write in manuscripts.”

Numerous faculty said they either self-censored or were told not to use certain “off-limits” words such as gender, racism and even transportation because it includes the word “trans.” Some faculty said administrators used AI-screening tools to review their syllabi for certain words.

Some survey respondents reported that the anti-faculty fervor has also spilled off-campus.

“I had to leave my church because the youth pastor expressed from the pulpit that academics were enemies of the faith. This impacts my work as a faculty member as an important aspect of my personal life has become inaccessible,” an assistant professor in Florida wrote.

Faculty also described fears that their students might record them and use their lectures or course materials out of context. The responses mention several incidents in which students publicized faculty comments, assignments or curricula to highlight areas of conflict with their personal beliefs.

At LSU, law professor Ken Levy was suspended in early 2025 after mentioning Gov. Jeff Landry and President Donald Trump in profane comments to his class. Levy fought that suspension in court and lost. His comments came to light when someone shared a video of his lecture with Landry, who posted it online.

The survey also found that 29% of faculty have applied to jobs in other states since 2024 and the same share are considering applying.

The top reason faculty gave for wanting to leave the South was its political climate. Other leading answers included diminished academic freedom, changes to diversity, equity and inclusion policy, low pay, limited LGBTQ+ rights and limits to reproductive healthcare.

Additional findings included 14% of faculty saying they view artificial intelligence as a threat to their academic discipline, and 13% reporting they have lost federal grants since Trump returned to office.

The Trump administration has revamped the government’s approach to academic research funding, which has included cancelling millions in grants and slashing resources for administrative costs related to research.
