The yearly moot court competition is organised by the NDDC for students in law faculties and departments across universities in the Niger Delta states.

Akpata, who commended NDDC for the initiative, said the competition shows the value the commission places on the profession for the transformation of the region.

Akpata said those who are successful in law are those who have the skill to construct good arguments to persuade the listners, noting that advancements in innovation cannot stand to argue in court rooms.

He charged law faculties in universities to invest in the establishment of Moot courts, adding that the process helps the law students build confidence in the profession.

Akpata said: “We are living through a period of extraordinary advancement in technology and innovation like the Artificial Intelligence, AI.

“Most arguments can now be done by machine. But the ability to stand in court and argue what you did not anticipate is what the machine cannot do for you.

High-school students across Asia are pulling ahead of their Western peers, an annual global assessment indicates, as artificial intelligence spurs a worldwide race for talent and reshapes how young people learn .

In a troubling trend, reading, science and math performance among 15-year-olds has continued a decline globally across the board, according to the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment released this week by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

But among last year’s top performers were students in the Chinese cities of Beijing and Shanghai, Chinese provinces Jiangsu and Zhejiang, and the city-state of Singapore. Japan and South Korea were also in the Asia-dominated top 10 across all three subjects, along with the semi-autonomous Chinese city of Macao, and the self-governing democracy of Taiwan.

Meanwhile, secondary students in the US saw their reading scores fall close to 25-year lows, lagging more starkly behind their counterparts in China, which have long held a lead in the exams known for short as PISA – at least in the four major Chinese jurisdictions that submitted test scores.

The exam results come amid an intensifying rivalry between the US and China to outpace the other in technological advancement and direct more funding toward innovation. China has surpassed the US in published scientific reports as well as research spending, on which both nations exceeded $1 trillion in 2024.

However, the growing adoption of AI could significantly impact secondary education, the PISA report warned.

“Most troubling is the decline in the very skills that matter most in the AI age: evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what we read,” Andreas Schleicher, OECD director for education and skills, wrote in the report. “In a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise.”

China’s data for the PISA tests is not without critics - in part because the test only includes students from the provinces of Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, some of the country’s wealthiest eastern coastal areas. Nonetheless, the testing has shown continued drop in US scores over the last decade, that have alarmed many educationalists.

As technology has progressed, student performance has become less linked with national or family wealth, the latest report said. While it’s difficult to determine the exact correlation between the rise of digital tools and test performance, the study identified one challenge as higher digital distraction in the classroom.

Among students from China, Japan and South Korea, fewer than 10% reported that their peers were distracted by digital devices during science lessons, compared with the global average of 28%. As one example of how educators might balance digital tools, the report said Singapore used technology in its classrooms but also emphasized reading comprehension early on.

The proportion of “hasty readers,” or students who rushed through their texts and gave incorrect answers, nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025, the report said. As the average performance among OECD countries in science, reading and math has reached record lows, that could have broader economic implications among the world’s biggest nations.

The 2025 report cited a Stanford University study that performance meeting a basic level aptitude in PISA among all 15-year-old Americans could add over $40 trillion to the US economy over their working lives. However, the percentage of OECD students below that baseline performance increased last year to 20% from 16% in 2022.

Artificial intelligence can summarize an entire semester of coursework in seconds, grade assignments, pass the bar exam and write a legal brief. Meanwhile, the decision to pursue higher education has never faced more scrutiny. Politicians brand universities as ideological factories, parents balk at the soaring price tag, new federal policy caps graduate student borrowing, research funding is under political siege, and enrollment is nearing a demographic cliff.

In short, AI can now perform many of the tasks that once defined the purpose of higher education, even as a degree grows more expensive and harder to obtain. As the first generation raised entirely on smartphones comes of age, the question once whispered is now asked aloud: Why bother?

I’ve been thinking about that question a great deal because my father—my first teacher—died a few weeks ago.

He was 84, and had spent nearly six decades as a pediatrician. Doctors don’t choose pediatrics for the money. What it offered instead was moments like this: My father kept a sewing kit in his office, so he could repair the stuffed animals his young patients brought in for “checkups”—transforming frightened toddlers into trusting ones.

When his medical group considered dropping Medicaid patients, he fought it until the policy died, on the conviction that a child’s care shouldn’t depend on circumstance. Even after retiring, he continued reading medical journals, long after anyone expected him to. He never stopped asking what more there was to learn or how he could better serve his patients.

I took a different path and became a law professor, but I inherited his love for learning and teaching. That inheritance shows up each year, when I take 15 law students to Parma, Italy, where they study alongside students from the University of Parma. We focus on international and comparative law through the lens of climate change and food systems.

Parma is not an arbitrary choice: It sits at the heart of the Po Valley, one of Europe’s most productive agricultural regions and, increasingly, one of its most climate-stressed. The city that gave the world Parmigiano-Reggiano and prosciutto di Parma is also grappling with drought, flooding and the slow transformation of its landscape. For law students studying the intersection of climate and food, there is no better classroom.

Before my father died, I spent weeks designing an architectural walking tour for my students. It looked like a tour about art, history and culture, but that was never really the point. The goal was to teach them how to ask questions.

Why did the Romans establish Parma where they did? Why is an ancient bridge now far from the river it once crossed? And why is it 30 feet under ground? Why does a medieval cathedral feel solid and permanent, rather than light and soaring? Why do cities preserve some historical scars while erasing others?

I finished preparing the tour as my father’s health declined. By the time the students arrived in Italy, it was clear I would not be there to walk those streets with them. Handing them that tour became the last lesson I could give: the instinct to look at something and ask why, curiosity disciplined into a method.

Law is not something confined to heavy casebooks. It is something you learn to see everywhere.

Parma exists because of centuries of decisions about property, water, transportation, taxation, religion and political power. The Romans chose its location because of trade routes, river access and geography. Its bridges, churches, parks and public squares all reflect legal and political settlements reached long before today’s students were born. The challenge is to learn to see those choices, rather than merely admire the surface. A building is never just a building. A patient is never just a patient. A law is never just a law.

Universities, at their best, cultivate exactly that habit of mind. They take the instinct to ask questions and test it against history, evidence and experiences different from our own. Students encounter historians who complicate their assumptions, scientists who demand evidence, lawyers who expose weaknesses in their reasoning, and classmates whose perspectives challenge what they thought they knew. Curiosity may begin alone. Education is what happens when curiosity is refined, corrected and sometimes proven wrong.

That education extends well beyond the classroom. College coincides with one of life’s defining transitions, when young adults begin testing inherited beliefs against lived experience. They learn not only what to think but how to evaluate sources, navigate uncertainty, recover from mistakes and accept that freedom and responsibility cannot be separated. Those lessons are not incidental to higher education. They are among its greatest gifts.

None of this dismisses the legitimate criticisms of modern universities. College has become too expensive for many families. Access remains unequal. Public confidence has declined sharply. Those concerns deserve serious attention.

But they also risk obscuring what higher education is actually for.

If education was simply about acquiring information, AI would already have won. It retrieves facts faster than any professor, summarizes books in seconds, and answers doctrinal questions with astonishing speed. Used well, it can make students more efficient and professionals more productive.

What it cannot do is decide which assumptions deserve to be questioned, which problems are worth solving, or why one answer matters more than another. It cannot teach judgment, empathy, intellectual humility or moral responsibility. Those qualities emerge through sustained engagement with teachers, classmates, difficult ideas and experiences that resist easy answers. It is the difference between diagnosing a child with the flu and sewing their teddy bear along the way.

My father understood that instinctively. He never believed expertise was something you earned once and possessed forever. Education was not preparation for life; it was a way of moving through the world. He remained and taught me to be curious because curiosity made him a better physician—and more importantly, a better human being.

The tour was supposed to end in Piazza Garibaldi, where students could stand in one place and see centuries layered upon one another—Roman foundations beneath Renaissance ambition beneath modern civic life. It was the perfect place to end because, by then, the lesson was no longer really about Parma. It was about learning to see that nothing worth understanding simply is. Cities. Laws. Institutions. Patients. They are all the product of choices, assumptions, compromises and people who believed in curiosity.

AI will almost certainly write better legal briefs than many of my students someday. It may summarize every case they read and answer every doctrinal question they ask. Those developments should change how universities teach.

They should not change why universities exist.

The purpose of higher education has never been simply to fill minds with information. It is to cultivate people who can think critically, question confidently, empathize with the world around them, revise their beliefs when the evidence demands it, and approach the world with both curiosity and humility. My father taught me to remain curious. My education taught me how to sharpen that curiosity. AI can help us find answers. It cannot tell us which questions are worth asking—or what kind of people we should become while asking them. That remains the work of education.

Jonathan Rosenbloom is an associate dean and a distinguished law professor at the Albany Law School in Albany, New York. A co-founder of the Sustainable Development Code, the host of the podcast Insincerely Yours, Earth, and the author of numerous legal texts and treatises, Rosenbloom bridges architecture and law to equip communities with actionable climate solutions.

To mark the start of the school year, Planet Classroom today announced its September Back-to-School Collectio n —six new premieres and four Spotlight selections curated to inspire classroom discussion, critical thinking, creativity, and global citizenship.

Produced by CMRubinWorld , Planet Classroom has grown into one of the world's leading free educational streaming platforms, connecting learners with filmmakers, educators, scientists, entrepreneurs, healthcare innovators, climate experts, artists, and youth leaders through original films and conversations that make today's biggest global challenges accessible to audiences everywhere.

"What Harry and I hoped to create was never simply a place to watch films," said C. M. (Cathy) Rubin , Founder and CEO of the Planet Classroom Network. "We wanted Planet Classroom to become a place where curiosity leads learning, where young people meet extraordinary thinkers and creators, and where every story opens the door to a larger conversation about the future we are building together."

Launched during the COVID-19 pandemic, Planet Classroom has evolved into a global learning community featuring more than 1,000 films created by over 400 filmmakers and curators from across six continents. Today, its growing collection explores the defining issues shaping the twenty-first century—from artificial intelligence and climate change to healthcare, education, sustainability, culture, creativity, and social innovation.

Planet Classroom believes that some of the world's most meaningful learning happens through storytelling.

Its original series—including AI for a Better World, Net Zero Speaks, Problem Solvers, Earth's Champions —and collaborations with organizations including Protect Our Planet (POP), KIDS FIRST! Film Festival , and Actuality Abroad , bring together students with internationally recognized scientists, entrepreneurs, artists, educators, physicians, engineers, environmental leaders, and filmmakers.

Every film is designed to encourage inquiry, discussion, and action while supporting educators seeking engaging, real-world learning experiences for their classrooms.

This month's collection explores some of the most important questions facing today's students.

Artificial Intelligence & The Future of Humanity

M. (Cathy) Rubin . Together they explore creativity, identity, human augmentation, and why our uniquely human imagination may become our greatest strength in the age of intelligent machines.

Students can also explore AI through two new Problem Solvers films: Could AI Replace Colonoscopies For Cancer? , examining how artificial intelligence may improve early colorectal cancer detection, and David at Davos , an original fictional animated short imagining how a young climate entrepreneur works alongside Gemini AI to transform complex climate research into a compelling presentation for world leaders.

In Net Zero Speaks with David W. DuBois , host I van Ransom speaks with New Mexico State Climatologist David W. DuBois about how extreme heat, prolonged drought, water scarcity, dust storms, declining snowpack, and air quality are reshaping everyday life across the American Southwest—and why trusted local climate information is becoming essential for building resilient communities.

Award-winning director Jaime Torres brings audiences to Hoi An, Vietnam, in Hearing & Beyond , the inspiring story of a young deaf woman whose life is transformed through education, friendship, and community.

Meanwhile, creator Cameran Sma ll explores one of popular culture's most beloved franchises in Do Fans Like Disney-Era Muppets? , examining how audience engagement, nostalgia, and storytelling continue to shape entertainment.

September Spotlight: Timeless Stories Worth Discovering

Planet Classroom's September Spotlight also celebrates four remarkable films from its growing archive.

Viewers can experience AIKĀNE , a visually breathtaking animated short inspired by Hawaiian history, mythology, and Indigenous storytelling, directed by Academy Award® nominee Daniel Sousa with Dean Hamer and Joe Wilson; Eternal Illusion, Daniel Gomez Sancho's visually stunning animated art film that transforms personal grief into a moving meditation on healing through sculpture, 3D printing, animation, and movement; Lori Belilove's The Revolutionary at NYFW , an unforgettable New York Fashion Week performance honoring the enduring legacy of dance pioneer Isadora Duncan ; and Jesus Thief , Kyle Wyborski's heartfelt coming-of-age comedy about friendship, faith, forgiveness, and finding the courage to do the right thing.

Together, these ten films reflect Planet Classroom's belief that education extends far beyond textbooks—that stories have the power to spark curiosity, build empathy, encourage critical thinking, and prepare young people to navigate an increasingly interconnected world.

Every Planet Classroom film is available free through the Planet Classroom Network and is designed to support educators, schools, universities, libraries, museums, and youth organizations seeking engaging resources that encourage inquiry, creativity, collaboration, global awareness, and meaningful classroom discussion.

As classrooms reopen around the world this September, Planet Classroom invites educators everywhere to discover new voices, new perspectives, and new conversations that inspire lifelong learning.

Julian Posada and Yair Guijosa-Torres ‘27

When AI became a recurring theme in Professor Julian Posada’s Information, Ethics, and Society class, he was intrigued. Realizing that few courses examine the ethics behind the technology, he determined change was needed. Supported by an AI Course Revision grant from Yale’s Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning, Posada joined forces with undergraduate Yair Guijosa-Torres ’27 through the Center’s Pedagogical Partners program to design a new course focused on AI and its societal implications.

“Instead of focusing on how AI tools can enhance the classroom experience,” Posada explains , “I wanted to create a class that was less focused on information science and more specific to AI ethics and societal issues.”

The Pedagogical Partners program brings instructors and undergraduate students together to collaborate on course design and teaching. The program focuses on creating a reflective space where students and instructors collaboratively think through the classroom experiences they hope to create. Malia Piper and Amanda Valdespino are members of the Poorvu Center’s Teaching Development and Initiatives team and supported Posada and Guijosa-Torres throughout the project. “Julian and Yair both brought incredible care and intention to their partnership,” they explained. “ Faculty often tell us that they appreciate their partners’ insight into the student experience. Student partners are often excited to be making a positive impact on Yale College, while learning more about the teaching process.”

Guijosa-Torres first participated in the program in 2025 as a student partner, an experience that inspired him to learn more about course design. When the opportunity to partner with Posada emerged, he immediately applied.

Most pedagogical partnerships focus solely on making an existing course more engaging and effective for students over a single semester. Posada and Guijosa-Torres’ partnership, however, was a year-long collaboration that included both the design of AI, Ethics, and Society and its classroom instruction.

Before designing the new class, the team first set out to understand how AI was being taught at Yale and beyond. They researched existing syllabi and attended discussions to identify the topics most often covered, as well as those examined less frequently or not at all.

“Many AI courses focus solely on the technology,” Posada said , “without considering how it’s made or the societal impacts on, for example, electricity and water usage or disposal of devices in data centers. We felt strongly that these topics should be included in this course.”

Creating a welcoming environment for multidisciplinary perspectives was a key focus for the team. They invited guest speakers who offered real-world perspectives and created space for students to engage on a range of topics, from AI’s impact on privacy, the environment, and labor to data ethics and responsible innovation. Posada selected the course’s required readings, while Guijosa-Torres applied his perspective as a student to develop activities best illustrating each topic.

Particularly important for Guijosa-Torres was centering the course’s framework around students’ agency in their learning. He suggested offering students three potential options for their final projects: a report detailing an existing problem and potential solution; a community-oriented initiative; or an AI coding project.

“My experience gained through this program,” said Guijosa-Torres, “taught me that if students have agency over their own learning, and the ability to follow their curiosities about subjects that interest them, they are more compelled to complete a project and will learn beyond what is taught in the classroom.”

AI, Ethics, and Society debuted in the spring of 2026 to strong student interest. Admission was highly competitive, with over 100 students from multidisciplinary backgrounds applying for 15 seats. This broad appeal confirmed Posada’s instincts that students across disciplines were eager to explore the topic.

“It’s important to have this class at Yale,” he said. “Courses in computer and data science are often highly technical, while social science courses don’t always engage with how technology intersects with the humanities and society. This course created a bridge allowing STEM students to examine AI’s broader social and ethical implications, while inviting students from the humanities and social sciences to analyze the technology through their own unique perspectives.”

Drawing on his prior experience as a Pedagogical Partner, Guijosa-Torres also proposed a mid-semester survey to assess students’ experience. Posada, Guijosa-Torres, and Teaching Fellow Sophia Cutler used the feedback to develop scaffolded assignments designed to build students’ skills over time. By semester’s end, students presented their final projects at Bulldog Days and Yale’s AI Symposium.

“For me, what stood out in the classroom was Julian’s care in his interactions with students,” reflected Guijosa-Torres. “The students felt appreciated, seen, and also challenged. To me, that is the beauty of a communal relationship that meets the needs of student learning.”

In reflecting on the program, Posada and Guijosa-Torres agreed that the Pedagogical Partners program impacted their careers, as both an instructor and a student. For Posada, this experience allowed him to further his training as a teacher.

“As a researcher, you don’t always take classes in pedagogy,” Posada reflected. “We learn as we teach. Working with Yair was a great experience because he brought a very fresh mind to this class. Collaborating with him on discussions around assignments and exercises was a good learning experience for me, and I look forward to learning more from students in the future.”

For Guijosa-Torres, the program strengthened his desire to become an educator. This summer, he completed a Teaching Fellowship at Breakthrough New York. He will rejoin the Pedagogical Partners program next year as a Lead Mentor and ultimately plans to pursue a PhD to examine critical pedagogies in secondary education.

“It was impactful for me to see that our work shaping the classroom setting had a very powerful effect on the students and their learning,” said Guijosa-Torres. “My experiences have transformed my worldview and really made me value education so much.”

With opportunities available each semester, the Pedagogical Partners program will begin accepting student applications for Spring 2027 in October. Faculty interested in participating in the Spring 2027 or beyond should email askpoorvucenter@yale.edu .

title: Ai is changing the high school classroom, teachers says
content:

But over the past decade, sh… [+8411 chars]
clean_content:
Bodil-Marie Gade has been a high school teacher for 20 years. At the high school of Horsens Gymnasium & HF, she loves teaching students Danish, French, and rhetoric.

But over the past decade, she has seen a shift that worries her.

More and more, she notices a lack of deep focus and concentration among students.

»It’s become harder for students to do an assignment for any length of time«, she says.

»They get distracted by screens incredibly quickly«.

»It worries me a lot, because I think it’s healthy for our brains to be able to immerse ourselves in something for a long time«, she says.

Over the past three years, another threat has appeared in the classroom: the use of artificial intelligence.

Bodil-Marie Gade has just examined the first students from the ’Generation ChatGPT’ – the generation that, for the first time, has had access to artificial intelligence throughout all three years of high school.

»At the beginning of 10th grade, I mostly got astonished looks when we talked about ai. It barely registered at all«, she says.

But then artificial intelligence came roaring in. Slowly, Bodil-Marie Gade began receiving Danish essays that made her suspicious about the use of ai.

Her suspicion arises when she reads essays with an unusually high level of abstraction, where the connection to anything concrete is missing.

»It can also be passages where the language differs so much from the student’s usual way of expressing themselves that it looks like the student wasn’t really involved at all«, she says.

If Bodil-Marie Gade suspects that an assignment was written by ai, she tells the student that she wonders.

»I can’t know with 100 percent certainty whether they used ai«

Aren’t you afraid of accusing someone who actually just used their own brainpower?

»Yes, but we have to have a dialogue about this dilemma. I talk openly with students about the grey areas, so they don’t feel like I’m accusing them«.

This summer, Bodil-Marie Gade graded about 209 essays as an external examiner. During exams, students are monitored, which makes it harder for them to use ai.

She found that students have simply gotten worse at writing. We’re not talking about the occasional misplaced comma or a forgotten present-tense ending, but rather entire sentences that are a mess, where the syntax collapses, she says.

»I sensed a lack of linguistic and cognitive training. It was few and far between. It was very striking«, she says.

Politiken has previously described a random sampling conducted by Danish Upper Secondary Schools that may help show that students used artificial intelligence to such an extent that they were not properly prepared for the written exam.

Over the past decade, students nationwide have received an average between 6.5 and 6.8 on the written Danish exam. But at the 11 schools selected for the random sampling, the students’ average this year was 6.1.

Seventeen-year-old Pippi Lester Hyllested is in 11th grade at Nørre Gymnasium in Brønshøj. She misses a nuanced debate about the use of ai, because she is tired of being a target.

»I think it’s unfair that we high school students are the ones in the spotlight. We are often being shamed for using ai«, she says.

The Danish Evaluation Institute has previously mapped students’ use of ai in high school. The study found that nine out of ten high school students use artificial intelligence in connection with school.

Two out of three students say in the study that at least once they have used artificial intelligence in a way they consider cheating when turning in assignments. Nine out of ten say they have cheated in connection with group work in class.

In early August, Education Minister Magnus Heunicke (The Social Democratic Party) presented an »emergency package« of initiatives aimed at curbing ai cheating at high schools. Among other things, it means students will have to do more written assignments at school while under supervision.

Pippi Lester Hyllested believes that the vast majority of students use ai as a tool. She herself uses ai when there are concepts she doesn’t understand.

»Basically, most of us students actually like learning«, she says.

She also believes the criticism should be aimed just as much at teachers, who themselves use artificial intelligence in instruction. She can see it in the formatting, the language, and open ChatGPT tabs. Sometimes it’s so bad that she feels like she’s being taught by a robot.

»I think it’s hypocritical that students are called cheaters while teachers can do whatever they want«, she says.

Pippi Lester Hyllested describes an »uneasy atmosphere« at the school, because many fear how the exams will unfold. She worries that we will end up celebrating those who drink Red Bull and can perform at their absolute peak under intense pressure for a few isolated tests, she says.

»We risk having some people fall through the cracks of the entire education system«.

Pippi Lester Hyllested feels that trust in young people is disappearing.

»If we get good grades, no one really believes it was because of us. The trust in us has completely collapsed«, she says.

Bodil-Marie Gade is certain that many students use ai. in a sensible way. But many also do not, she says.

»We’re not talking about just a few students in each class using it inappropriately. Unfortunately not«.

»But I do think it’s true that only a few have a real intention to cheat«, she says.

She herself uses artificial intelligence as a tool in daily life, and she has no problem having ChatGPT open in a tab so students can see it.

»But students are at a completely different stage of learning than we teachers are. We have a whole different body of knowledge in the back of our minds that we draw on. They still have to learn that, and it’s a problem if they don’t«, she says.

Bodil-Marie Gade gives grades less often for the work students do at home. Instead, they receive grades for assignments done at school, where she is present.

If it is clear that a student turns in something they did not produce themselves – with or without the use of ai – the school’s rules are that the student receives a warning. A third warning is grounds for expulsion.

Technological development has made her worried. She loves her job as a high school teacher, but she can recognize the feeling of »learning grief«.

»It’s sad when your subject, which you care so deeply about, changes dramatically because of outside circumstances«.

»The entire way I’ve loved teaching for 20 years. Now the rug is being pulled out from under us. We’re on shaky ground«, she says.

Pippi Lester Hyllested would like to see technological literacy as a subject in high school, where students can learn how ai can, in a sensible way, make people smarter.

Bodil-Marie Gade does not rule out that there may be a need for a new subject focused on technological literacy – or at least some dedicated modules. She has also long been calling for more continuing education in artificial intelligence for teachers.

»There’s clearly a lack of instruction in this for all of us«, she says.

Because Bodil-Marie Gade is tired of having to act as an enforcer toward students.

Law schools in the United States have begun banning artificial intelligence in the classroom, according to a Financial Times column Monday (Sept. 7) by Patti Waldmeir.

The University of Chicago Law School is among the institutions imposing these restrictions. For the new academic year, phones, tablets and laptops will be forbidden in core first-year classrooms, the column said.

“The whole point is to do things the hard way—because that’s how you learn,” said William Hubbard , chair of the law school’s AI committee, per the column.

“The hard way” has historically meant using the Socratic method to debate cases and legal principles in front of professors and classmates, the column said. That’s tougher to do with AI.

“The power of AI tools and the legal profession’s eagerness to adopt [them] are at an inflection point, so we really felt a sense of urgency to act,” Hubbard said, per the column, although the school isn’t going as far as imposing a blanket AI ban.

Experience AI equips young people with a meaningful understanding of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning by giving educators the knowledge and confidence to teach these topics in ways that suit their classrooms.

Whether you’re introducing AI to learners for the first time, helping them deepen their understanding, exploring generative AI with them, or integrating AI literacy across the curriculum, Experience AI offers you all the resources you need for free.

Since we started publishing Experience AI resources in 2023, they have been downloaded over a million times in 195 countries, and we have worked with partner organisations in more than 40 countries to train educators to teach AI literacy . Thanks to partners, we have learned a lot about how teachers around the world use the resources in their classrooms, and this has given us direction for what new resources to develop.

Many teachers looking for AI literacy resources are not computing specialists and have very busy timetables. Under pressure to deliver more content without more instructional time, what educators need are resources they can integrate into what they already teach. To support them, we’re now offering an updated suite of Experience AI resources that make AI literacy more accessible, flexible, and relevant.

The resources include those co-developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation and Google DeepMind, alongside those developed independently by the Raspberry Pi Foundation.

The new Discovering AI resources, aimed at learners aged 8–12 and learners aged 13–16, are single lessons for introducing the fundamental ideas behind AI. They support educators with learners who have little or no prior knowledge of AI, and include engaging, age-appropriate activities.

From there, our updated Foundations of AI units let teachers support their learners to develop a deeper understanding of how AI systems work, how they’re trained, and how they can be applied to real-world problems.

And a new and growing collection of thematic resources supports teachers and learners to explore AI through cross-subject topics such as creativity, the environment, and critical thinking.

Experience AI now fully reflects our belief that AI literacy needs to be cross-curricular. Application of AI technologies isn’t limited to neat domains or subjects, so learners’ opportunities to understand them shouldn’t be either.

Education systems vary significantly between countries, and in most national curricula, AI literacy is not yet clearly defined. Nevertheless, teachers are both under pressure to deliver this new topic area in their limited classroom time, and eager to rise to the challenge to support their learners.

So we asked ourselves: how can we help educators to teach AI literacy in any subject without additional lesson time, when we cannot create specific resources for every subject in every education system?

Our answer came from educators themselves. Through our network of global partners , we learned that teachers were not waiting for us to tell them in what subjects the Experience AI resources belonged. They were already adapting them to teach AI literacy in all sorts of contexts. For example, we saw that some educators adapted the resource on AI and ecosystems, which we had developed for Biology classrooms, for their Geography classrooms, where it supported similar learning goals.

This insight into teachers’ classroom practice prompted us to change our approach.

Now, rather than designing resources for a single subject, we design and organise them in themes that fit across subjects, such as environment, creativity, ethics, and critical thinking. So a resource for exploring the environmental impact of AI data centres could be used in Geography, Physics, Citizenship, or Business Studies classrooms. An activity about AI-generated media could prompt discussions in Digital Literacy, Art, or Computing lessons. The same material supports different curricular goals, depending on how teachers choose to use it.

title: America's Two Largest School Districts Impose AI Moratoriums
content:
New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Zohran Mamdani hold a press conference at the Brooklyn STEAM Center on September 2, 2026 in New York. Photo by: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx

author: Chris Mills Rodrigo
clean_content:
New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Zohran Mamdani hold a press conference at the Brooklyn STEAM Center on September 2, 2026 in New York. Photo by: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx

When ChatGPT was released in the fall of 2022, the scale of the impact it could have on K-12 schools appeared obvious. Not only could the chatbot fulfill many class and homework assignments in response to simple prompts, but children and teens had the digital fluency to adopt the technology much faster than their teachers.

The New York City Department of Education was one of the first educational bodies in the United States to act on what many perceived as the threat OpenAI’s new product posed to schooling: in January 2023, it blocked access to ChatGPT on district devices and networks. The nation’s largest school district made the decision shortly after the second largest, Los Angeles Unified School District, banned the chatbot in December 2022.

Other districts across the country soon followed suit, including Seattle , Baltimore , and Oakland , California.

The bans didn’t last though — by May of 2023, then NYC Public Schools Chancellor David Banks was ready to “ embrace ” the potential of ChatGPT, and in August of that year LAUSD Superintendent Alberto Carvalho said his system was looking into a more permissive use policy.

Yet this week, ahead of the start of the 2026-27 school year, these two districts are once again charting out a more restrictive approach to artificial intelligence than the majority of their peers.

On Wednesday, NYC banned student-facing AI in all K-8th grade classes, while allowing a limited set of approved tools to be used for high schoolers, for the upcoming school year.

This new policy is significantly tighter than the guidelines the district had proposed in March, which instituted a stoplight system for judging AI risk that put almost all student use into the “yellow light” category, kicking use decisions to individual teachers. After intense backlash , the district pushed pause on that policy with Chancellor Kamar Samuels admitting the draft “missed the mark.” The district also paused software purchases over the summer.

Later that same day, LAUSD officials announced the district was placing a one-year moratorium on generative AI use on its devices for all of its estimated 378,000 students in a move that caught even school district officials by surprise.

The district had passed restrictions on screen time for students earlier in the summer, but did not previously issue specific rules on AI.

The growing coalitions of parents, teachers, and students who have been pushing for more restrictive AI policies in schools in both cities celebrated this week’s announcements.

At the Los Angeles AI committee meeting where the ban was announced, parents with the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens had to edit their prepared speeches in real time.

You have successfully joined our subscriber list.

“ We are asking our local institut — no, we're thanking our local institution,” said Sandra Martinez Roe, according to LAist. "Thank you, LAUSD for setting an example and knowing that your obligation is to do so.”

The AI Moratorium (AIM) Coalition in NYC called the partial pause a “step in the right direction.” The coalition of organizations featuring teachers, students, and parents launched last fall has been pushing for a complete moratorium on classroom AI for two years.

“We have been overall very pleased with the steps that the mayor and the chancellor have taken around AI in schools with this new policy,” Kyle DeAngelis, a 3rd grade NYC public school teacher in Harlem and member of the AIM Coalition through a rank-and-file caucus of the United Federation of Teachers, told Tech Policy Press.

The coalition still has concerns with the policy they’d like to see addressed — including the creation of AI pilots in some schools, limited restrictions on staff use of AI, and a lack of metrics for evaluating tools — and hopes that a longer term policy is adopted through a democratic process that engages parents, teachers, and students alike.

That new policy should include more restrictions for high schoolers, says Martina Meijer, a fourth grade teacher and member of the same UFT caucus as DeAngelis.

“What we know about AI chatbots, what we know about teen mental health crises, what we know about the tendency of even adults to lean on these chatbots as a form of free therapy makes it really dangerous to ignore the needs of teenagers at this time,” she told Tech Policy Press. “I would just underscore that it's really important that this policy also include high school students because they are extremely vulnerable.”

The nation’s two largest public school districts issuing such restrictions — albeit temporary and, in the case of New York, partial — on AI in classrooms is especially notable given that most school districts have previously shied away from forbidding use.

The news is also indicative of bubbling grassroots opposition to AI, which has manifested itself in widespread data center backlash but is also coming up in, for example, surveys of office workers.

Both districts now have a year to develop longer-term policies on AI in education. Rolling back restrictions like they did with the short-lived ChatGPT bans will almost certainly be met with organized opposition.

“Over the last year, one of the things that has honestly really surprised me is just how quickly this particular movement has taken off,” DeAngelis said. “It’s reflective of what parents and teachers are seeing in their schools.”

AI has its strengths and weaknesses. It’s useful to obtain information, like where is a TV program streaming or who won the Presidency in 1920. But its interpretations are sometimes wrong, as is some of its information. It can write essays, after getting prompts. But when teachers assign essays, they expect students to write them, not AI.

I have corrected AI on several occasions, and the bot quickly apologized. On one occasion, I asked for NAEP scores in a particular state. The AI responded with a slant implying that NAEP “proficiency” was grade level, and those who did not reach it were below grade level. Of course, I pointed out that NAEP itself warns that “proficiency” is higher than grade level and represents “solid achievement, what most of us would call an A or B+. NAEP is not “grade level,” although many reporters think it is. The bot quickly admitted its error.

On another occasion, I asked for the bio of a friend, and AI had confused her with someone else. Again, it made a correction.

AI makes many errors. My college-age grandson told me he never uses it because it’s unreliable.

Worse, it is a shortcut to learning, like copying an answer from an encyclopedia. But it’s more dangerous because encyclopedias are usually subject to rigorous fact-checking. Students who turn in AI essays are not learning. They are cheating.

Dana Goldstein wrote in the New York Times:

The Los Angeles public school system will vastly restrict the use of artificial intelligence at all grade levels, district officials said on Wednesday at a board of education meeting.

The move came shortly after the nation’s largest school system, in New York City, announced it would ban most A.I. through 8th grade . Both developments seem to respond to an extraordinary movement, driven by parents , to push back against the incursion of technology and screens into childhood.

The board of education in the Los Angeles Unified School District previously barred cellphone use during the school day and strictly limited the hours per day students could spend on laptops.

The new A.I. restrictions, reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times, will apply for the current school year, as a board committee considers how to potentially incorporate the technology in the future, according to a district spokeswoman.

Students may still see A.I. summaries on top of Google searches, but will not be able to engage with Google’s Gemini chatbot within those searches, according to the district.

And they will not be able to use chatbot helpers that Google offers inside its Classroom software , including Google Docs, Google Sheets and Google Slides. Google Classroom is near-universally used in American schools.

Nicholas Melvoin, a school board member who sits on the committee studying A.I., said the board had been surprised by district officials’ decision to fully pause the technology for students.

While Mr. Melvoin has led the push to restrict student screen time, he raised questions about the wisdom of a complete A.I. ban for older teenagers, arguing they would need to understand the technology to prepare for college and the workplace.

“High school is where I would have more teacher discretion, with guardrails,” he said — similar to the path New York City officials outlined on Wednesday.

He said his committee would also consider the many big questions about how educators are using the technology, for lesson planning, grading, student feedback and communication with parents.

Los Angeles teachers continue to have access to A.I.

A.I. chatbots can help students learn, acting as a research tool or tutor breaking down complex concepts.

But chatbots can present misinformation. They have also led to an epidemic of cheating , as students prompt A.I. tools to write essays for them or complete problem sets. Even A.I. apps marketed specifically to schools have few blocks to prevent plagiarism or other forms of academic misconduct.

A growing body of research shows individuals who use chatbots can experience reduced critical thinking.

Common Sense Media, an advocacy group, has broadly tested A.I. chatbots and recommended their use be limited for people under 18, in part because they allow students to avoid the productive struggle of learning .

The group has also raised questions about A.I. search summaries, which may prevent students from seeking out multiple sources of information on contested subjects.

Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense, praised the Los Angeles decision, saying it made sense to take a pause on a rapidly evolving technology. While Common Sense believes students of all ages should be given lessons in A.I. literacy to better understand how the technology works, she said that did not generally require classroom access to A.I. tools.

“At this moment, there is oftentimes more danger than opportunity,” Ms. Renteria said. She noted that students would still use A.I. outside of school on their personal devices, and argued that it remains crucial that educators talk to young people about the risks and potential rewards of A.I. use.

New York City banned AI in elementary and middle schools too. I am impressed and very happy that this is happening. So far though, Chicago has, sadly, not taken that step. We may not be the Second City anymore, but I’m hoping we’re the third.

Big Tech is pushing AI into schools as hard as it can because it knows that if they get youth dependent on AI for answers then they will be able to dominate what we think. Google has already shaped our knowledge base by its search algorithms and commercialization. We know what we know because Google tells us what what it wants us to know and ignores anything contrary to its bias.

What’s commonly called “AI” today would be more accurately called simulated intelligence, because only the results resemble what humans consider intelligence. The process used to produce those results isn’t remotely similar to anything we humans would recognize as intelligence, or even thought. The reason it looks intelligent to us is because until now, whenever we’ve seen statements that look like that, they have been produced through reasoning, but that’s no longer the case.

There’s no understanding of concepts, comprehension, or compounding of ideas. It’s a very, very sophisticated version of the feature in text applications that offers suggestions for the next word based on previous words & the first couple of letters a user enters. It’s not a thinking machine; but literally a text processor. It’s in the name: Large Language Model. Responses are generated from statistical algorithms that calculate word sequences using a vast data set (the entire internet) of possible word sequences. No human brain produces a statement this way.

As you pointed out, Diane, AI is most useful when you already know something about the topic being explored. If you don’t recognize & correct mistakes, following responses are based on those mistakes, compounding error by orders of magnitude.

I just used AI to help me devise a plan to move a piano across a carpeted room with only one person lifting. The final result is highly practical & will work with my available resources. However, I had to call out several factual & reasoning errors along the way, based on my rudimentary knowledge of physics & language (e.g., remind it that “zig-zag” means alternating directions). It complimented me profusely each time.

It took me 10 minutes to break ChatGPT with a series of literary analysis questions. Before AI existed, how would you have graded a paper with the answers it produced, & would you have serious concerns about the student’s cognitive skills?

Students who turn in AI essays are not learning. They are cheating.

It’s worse than that. The supposed purpose of cheating is to provide unfailingly correct answers. With AI’s sketchy record, it’s not cheating; it’s cheating badly — like copying answers from a C- (D+?) student!

Also, it’s actually conceivable that a student using tried-&-true🥹 cheating methods might accidentally learn something by copying down correct answers from a reliable source. Even that remote possibility is diminished with AI answers that might or might not be accurate.

Educators, please make sure your students understand the difference between actual intelligence & fancy text processing.

AI is here. It’s not going away. People are going to use it. We can’t change that, but we can change how they understand & view its capabilities & limitations. Educators can have a major influence there. If you believe my perspective above may be useful, please share it wherever you feel it can help.

Really interesting. Does any of this puncture the idea that we ourselves are above that type of thinking? Have I ever had an original thought? I know I have taught students who were nothing more than amalgamation thinkers.

We absolutely do not do that kind of thinking, & couldn’t even if we wanted to. It’s not a “kind of thinking”; it’s not thinking at all. This is not a philosophical issue. Please understand, what current AI’s do to generate answers has absolutely no similarity to anything we’d recognize as thinking. There’s no understanding of concepts, comprehension, synthesis of ideas. It imitates strings of words that have been measured statistically to be likely to occur in particular orders. No human produces a statement that way. The reason it sounds “intelligent” to us is because until now, whenever we’ve heard a statement constructed that way, it was produced by reason & intent, but that’s no longer the case.

When we want to say something — anything: “Good morning,” “How ya doin’,” “I liked that movie because…” — even the most cliche, automatic conditioned statements, we have a purpose in mind, an intention to communicate something. AI’s don’t have purpose; they’re software that assembles sequences of words. Even a student who’s repeating unoriginal derivatives of concepts they’ve heard has understanding & intent. However hackneyed the statement may be, it wasn’t assembled by a mathematical process of stringing words together; there’s still a meaning behind it.

I hope this clarifies the essential distinction: AI does not “think” as we humans understand the process.

The Hollywood Melvoins are wealthy and connected corporate education “reformers” who support school privatization and high stakes testing, so whenever my local school board member, Nick Melvoin supports something that sounds good, as he has a number of times recently, one must be critical. I know from direct experience working in Melvoin’s district that top down mandates requiring the use of specific learning platforms and programs is and has long been the way, the only way. Think Open Court, Read 180, iReady, and so on and so on.

Parents have been complaining to Melvoin about forcing their children to have screen time in school and at home. He made rules that specifically did NOT free teachers from his tech mandates, but instead called for limiting their use — to the same amount of class time my school was already being pressured by Melvoin to use. And the AI restrictions they’re putting in place serve to, if you think about it, force students to stay within the confines of the top down mandated platforms the district is already forcing them to use. Since when does the LAUSD board want teachers or students thinking or writing creatively? They want test prep. They want test practice. They want interim assessments every other week. They want test scores. They don’t want essays.

AI guardrails feel to me like tech greenwashing, like they’re saying, “You must have screen time, but abracadabra, it’s like totally safe now!” They’re selling the tech. A better idea would be to put away the screens. Brains work better with pens. I know it. Parents know it.

With artificial intelligence becoming all-pervasive, the International Institute of Information Technology (IIIT Hyderabad) is setting up a new research centre, the Centre for Educational Technology and Learning Sciences (CETLS), to explore how people, including students and older people, learn in the age of AI, and how to help them improve their cognitive skills.

CETLS will focus on students up to Class 12, higher education, executive training, and learning for the third age. Instead of arguing for a blanket ban on AI in the classroom, the centre plans to focus on helping children improve their cognitive skills. The centre will work with schools to gain insights into the actual learning process, which it can then use to refine and improve educational methods.

Globally known AI thought leader and IIIT-Hyderabad founder Raj Reddy will address the inaugural event on September 5 at the institute’s Gachibowli campus.

By bringing together experts in psychology, learning sciences, cognitive science, and technology, the interdisciplinary centre aims to create compassionate tools and intuitive methods that empower individuals to learn more naturally and effectively alongside AI, an IIIT-H spokesperson said.

Vasudeva Varma, who heads CETLS, said that there was a difference between being a digital native and an AI native. Referring to those born in the 1960s and 1970s, he said they were digital immigrants who grew up in an analogue world.

By contrast, the generation coming of age today interacts with information differently – asking AI for direct answers rather than searching through document collections.

He wondered if human cognitive abilities were at risk of declining or stagnating as machine intelligence rose rapidly. He said that while human intelligence had historically led to better machine intelligence, it is now time for machine intelligence to reciprocate and help human intelligence grow.

Sandeep Shukla, Director of IIIT-H, said they were concerned about whether the knowledge being taught to students remained relevant when generative AI made that information immediately accessible.

He added that they also worried about how to assess students’ knowledge and understanding through homework assignments when generative AI could produce those answers perfectly well.

title: NYC Schools Block Student AI Use Through Middle School
content: New York City will prohibit students from using artificial intelligence in public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14, according to city education officials. The ban is scheduled to … [+5806 chars]
author: Chase Codewell
clean_content:
In a related policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10, according to the announcement. The city's public school technology policies are closely watched by other districts across the country, according to reports. Overview of Ban The prohibition on student AI use extends through middle school, with use permitted only in high school, which begins in ninth grade, according to the education department. Even at the high school level, AI use will be limited to specific purposes, such as learning about the technology itself, according to the policy. Officials said the policy is part of a sweeping overhaul of technology use across the nation's largest school district. In 2023, the school system had previously banned students' use of ChatGPT, though that ban was reversed less than a year later, according to reports. Rationale and Concerns Teachers and parents have warned against AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children's mental health and cognitive development, according to the city's education department. A particular concern cited by officials is an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed "cognitive surrender," along with environmental damage from AI systems. The concerns come amid broader debates about the effects of technology on learning. Education researcher David A. Sousa has noted that gaming and technology have shifted how students learn, replacing periods of concentration with emotional engagement, which changes the nature of the learning process [3]. Schools have struggled to determine how much of an assignment is being completed by a bot while students engage in other activities, according to trends analysis [5]. Policy Details and Exceptions The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments, according to the policy. AI-powered "companion chatbots" offering psychological support will be banned, according to officials. The education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers, sixth through eighth grade, and 30 minutes for elementary school students, according to the announcement. The question remains of how to monitor AI use, since such use often takes place outside the school environment, the department said. The restrictions on AI use differ from the earlier vision of personalized learning systems that some advocates had promoted for students with diverse learning needs [6]. Context and Previous Framework The new rules follow an initial framework published in March that used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for, according to reports. That 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration, and creative projects, drew criticism from many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient, according to reports. In response, the city's schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had "missed the mark" in their communications, adding that his office would carefully review parents' feedback for incorporation into future rules, according to the education department. The city had planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive "guidebook" to take feedback into account, the education department has said. New York State has previously pushed an instructional-assessment technology ideology centered on personalized learning, as described by authors Joseph Farrell and Gary Lawrence [2]. Implementation and Monitoring The education department will establish a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts, and union representatives, according to officials. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York's AI-in-schools policy, according to the announcement. Monitoring of AI use presents a challenge, as much activity occurs outside the school environment, the department acknowledged. The broader question of how AI tools can be integrated effectively while addressing the risks of automation remains an open issue, with some research examining whether AI deployment is cost-effective in various settings [1]. The emergence of large-scale AI systems highlights that such technologies represent broad enabling tools whose full social and economic consequences are still being understood, as noted in analyses of transformative technology development [4]. Conclusion The new policy represents a shift toward restricting rather than expanding AI use in the earliest years of public education, according to the education department. School officials will continue to review how AI might be incorporated at higher grade levels while responding to concerns from parents and teachers, according to reports. The effectiveness of the ban will depend on classroom enforcement and parent cooperation outside school hours, the department said. The taskforce report due in April is expected to provide guidelines for how the district will approach AI use in the coming years, according to officials. References Trends-Journal-2024-01-05. title: NYC: Keeping AI Out of Schools Doesn't Prepare Kids for It
content: On Sept. 2, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for every child from 2-K through eighth grade. That… [+7556 chars]
author: Diana E. Graber M.A.
clean_content:
Posted September 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

On Sept. 2, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for every child from 2-K through eighth grade. That’s nearly 600,000 students, roughly two-thirds of the district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, including high school. The city is also placing new limits on screen time , with recommended caps of 30 minutes per day for students in grades 3-5 and 45 minutes for students in grades 6-8.

Developmentally, this makes sense. Children need foundational skills before they can use a powerful tool like AI safely and wisely. They need opportunities to wrestle with a question, sit with not knowing, make mistakes, work through frustration, and build an argument before a machine builds it for them.

Those capacities are developed through effort and struggle. When a tool consistently removes that while these skills are still forming, it's a hindrance.

But the announcement leaves two big questions unanswered:

According to Common Sense Media’s 2026 census of 1,204 American children ages 9 to 17, 86% already use or interact with AI, and 24% do so every day. Among 9- to 12-year-olds—the very students New York’s moratorium is designed to protect—81% use AI, and 17% use it daily.

Most are not encountering AI at school, either. More than three-quarters use AI on their own phone, computer, or tablet. Only 44% report using it on a school device.

Even if schools decide that students are not ready to use generative AI, that does not mean they are too young to learn about it. It simply means we recognize that AI is an inevitable and ubiquitous part of the world kids live in.

Parents can’t be expected to fill this gap. According to the Common Sense survey, 44% of children say a parent or guardian has never talked with them about how to use AI safely. Even among daily AI users, more than a third have never had that conversation.

So a student can leave an AI-free classroom and walk into a world full of AI—with no teacher nearby and, in many cases, no parent who has ever talked about it. And generative AI is only part of the picture. Artificial intelligence is already embedded in many of the technologies children use every day: YouTube and streaming recommendations, autocorrect and predictive text, navigation apps, search engines, filters, and learning platforms.

Long before children open a chatbot, algorithms are already deciding what they see, what gets recommended to them, and what information rises to the top. We cannot ignore this reality.

For high school students—the students not covered by the moratorium—New York plans to provide two 45-minute AI literacy modules each year. Two. It actually pains me to type this.

The city says those 90 minutes will address what AI is and is not, bias , risks, ethical considerations, and the impact of AI on careers and future skills. These are all important topics, but each requires more than a single lesson. All require foundational knowledge built over time in order for the lesson to stick.

Consider what the city's short list leaves out:

And this is only a partial list; 90 minutes a year cannot do this work.

New York’s moratorium gives educators an opportunity to protect childhood , preserve human-centered learning, and resist the rush to put powerful technology into students’ hands simply because it exists. But keeping AI out of elementary and middle school classrooms cannot mean keeping AI education out too. In fact, this may be exactly the moment to teach it.

Students can learn how algorithms work without using a chatbot. They can investigate misinformation without generating it. They can practice protecting personal information without entering it into an AI tool. They can discuss bias, privacy, intellectual property, healthy relationships, environmental impact, and digital ethics without spending a minute looking at a screen. The strongest preparation may be decidedly low-tech: conversation, discussion, role-play, critical thinking, collaboration , media analysis, and opportunities to work through difficult questions with other human beings.

New York’s 600,000 children will spend this school year living in a world shaped by AI. Many will use it on their own devices, in their own bedrooms, without a teacher nearby and, for nearly half of them, without a parent who has ever talked with them about how to use it safely.

The question is not simply whether children should use AI in school. It is whether we are preparing them with the knowledge, judgment, and human skills they will need to live with it everywhere else.

title: NYC’s AI ban through grade 8 sets stage for rest of US, experts say
content: New York Citys ban on use of artificial intelligence in the classroom for elementary and middle school students in the citys public school system the largest in the country could set the stage for ho… [+5993 chars]
author: Andy Hirschfeld
clean_content:
New York City’s ban on use of artificial intelligence in the classroom for elementary and middle school students in the city’s public school system – the largest in the country – could set the stage for how other school systems in the United States tailor their approach to the use of AI, experts say.

The moratorium, which was announced on Wednesday, will last for one year and will end the use of 40 different educational tools impacting 600,000 students. The ban will not bar teachers from using the technology to create lesson plans.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a news conference on Wednesday.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way.”

Mamdani added that the city will spend the next year studying how the policy will impact students. The city’s public school system will also launch a pilot programme in high schools for a limited number of students.

Among the tools being tested will be the maths AI platform Edia, which will provide “step-by-step coaching” and prompting students to explain their reasoning. Its use will be limited to 20 minutes each week. Another tool, Quill, will be used in English language arts courses and will be limited to 15 minutes each week.

“The mayor is giving schools, parents, scholars the runway to study what the impact on our education system these tools will actually have,” Adin Lenchner, founder of the New York-based political consultancy Carroll Street Campaigns, told Al Jazeera.

“This feels like the kind of leadership that people were actually hungry for — standing up to corporate interests and looking out for students.”

The policy also implements staggered screen-time restrictions, with use limited to less than 45 minutes each day through eighth grade.

The policy also bans “companion chatbots” through high school. City Hall did not elaborate on Al Jazeera’s request for clarification on what that covers.

The moratorium comes at a consequential time for New York City’s public schools. Reading proficiency scores tumbled by 6 percent in 2025 among students in grades 3 through 8.

Experts say that New York City may set the stage for how other school districts approach AI.

“NYC public schools banning AI in elementary and middle schools sends an important message because it is the largest school district in the US. However, it is hard to know the effectiveness of the ban because they haven’t shared the enforcement mechanism,” Margeret Murray associate professor of communication at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, told Al Jazeera.

The mayor’s decision comes alongside a growing number of reports showing that AI use in children’s education can have a negative impact on cognitive development.

A comprehensive review of 400 studies, along with interviews with teachers, parents and other educators conducted by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education, concluded that the negatives of generative AI in the classroom outweigh the positives. However, the report stressed that careful and limited implementation in specific use cases can help enrich learning outcomes.

“It’s in line with the science,” Shaleen Title, an attorney at Rudick Law Group and adjunct professor at Roger Williams University School of Law focusing on emerging sectors like AI, said of the mayor’s move.

“The most important thing about it is that it changes the approach. Before, the approach was to let students use technology without really vetting the risks, whereas now, the default is that the products have to be proven safe before they can be used by students, which I think is the right approach. I think it was a smart reversal on their part.”

One recurring theme outlined in the Brooking Institution’s was what researchers described as a “digitally induced ‘amnesia”, in which students were unable to recall basic factual information about topics they had studied or submitted work on.

That theme continues into adolescence and young adulthood. A January 2025 report in the peer-reviewed sociology journal Societies found that people aged 17 to 25 who relied more heavily on AI had lower levels of critical-thinking ability.

For those bound for university, professors are starting to notice the effects. A College Board report found that 84 percent of faculty believe AI erodes students’ critical-thinking skills.

In a piece published in the Chronicle of Higher Education, a trade publication, an adjunct professor at several universities said his students appear increasingly unable to keep up with reading and writing tasks that students were able to handle a decade ago.

While the city can push back on AI use in the classroom, regulating its use at home will be harder.

“This is something we’ve actually been obviously dealing with for quite a few years. The idea around this policy is to make sure that we get to limitations. I think we ought not to forget that last year there was AI usage in our school,” New York City Public Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said in a news conference when asked about AI use for homework.

“This policy seeks to limit that and seeks to expand our teachers and our understanding of how to combat the external use of AI when it’s used at home.”

The ban does have some exceptions, including for students with disabilities and “multilingual learners”, as well as in environments where students are taking part in “career readiness programs, like computer science”.

“They’re probably going to want to use generative AI in their coding classes, for example. They were also very clear in their announcement that sometimes generative AI will be needed for disabilities and accommodations. So certainly, there’s an exception and a place for it in schools,” Title added.

The announcement also said students will be given access to two yearly AI literacy courses, which are designed to help understand the technology as well as bias and ethical issues that stem from AI use.

AMD and the University of Delhi have partnered to train around 10,000 students in AI and semiconductor technologies over the next year through hands-on learning and industry-relevant resources.

Chip giant AMD and the University of Delhi on Thursday announced a partnership to train around 10,000 students in artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor technologies over the next year.

Under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the two entities, AMD will introduce its ‘AI Engage Developer Program’ to the university. The initiative is designed to equip the next generation of talent with industry-relevant skills, according to a company statement.

“India has the talent and the ambition to lead the next wave of AI innovation. The opportunity now is to give students early access to the platforms and tools that power real-world AI development,” said Jaya Jagadish, Country Head & SVP Engineering, AMD India.

She added that the collaboration aims to help students transition from theoretical concepts to building practical AI solutions.

The programme will provide students and faculty with hands-on access to AMD’s open-source ROCm AI software platform, learning resources and developer GPU cloud credits.

This will enable participants to build, test and deploy AI applications using industry-grade tools.

Students and faculty will gain access to AMD’s AI learning curriculum, technical workshops, open software ecosystems and cloud-based GPU resources for hands-on experimentation.

“This collaboration reflects a growing industry focus on preparing graduates with practical AI skills that extend beyond classroom learning. By combining academic learning with access to modern AI computing platforms, AMD and Delhi University will help create a stronger pipeline of AI developers and researchers to support India’s expanding digital economy,” Prof Yogesh Singh, Vice-Chancellor, Delhi University, said.
