title: New York Will Find Out If Elementary Schoolers Can Still Learn Without Using AI
content: How thoroughly has the adoption of commercial AI already toppled our capacity to think? How much has it degraded the ability of young children in elementary or middle school to learn? Or has it someh… [+7056 chars]
author: Jim Vorel
clean_content:
How thoroughly has the adoption of commercial AI already toppled our capacity to think? How much has it degraded the ability of young children in elementary or middle school to learn? Or has it somehow improved their cognition and learning abilities (I would not bet on this) in the era since we all first heard the term “ChatGPT”? New York City intends to learn the answers to these questions, and then some, given the announcement this week that the city would broadly ban most uses of AI in classroom settings for public school children all the way up to the beginning of high school. Even the use of individual screens will be greatly reduced for the youngest of students, forcing developing brains to learn in more tactile, decidedly older fashion. Nor are the teachers immune from the effects of the new policy, as they too will supposedly be banned from using AI for tasks such as grading assignments, or “counseling a student in crisis,” although we would contend that one should not need to be told that Claude is not the authority one turns to on that topic. Still, it’s a sweeping set of new policies, and a fairly ambitious attempt to address a growing reliance on AI from both young learners and the people assigned to teach them.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary,” said NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a statement. “We do not see it that way.”

Mayor Mamdani: AI is present in nearly every aspect of our lives. I am proud to announce New York City's first ever AI policy for our public schools. Children need teachers and human connection to learn and grow. This school year, we will implement a 1 year moratorium on AI from 2k through 8th grade

— Headquarters ( @headquartersnews.bsky.social ) 11:55 AM · Sep 2, 2026

The New York City Public Schools system is the nation’s largest, and potentially its most complex, which means this particular experiment could potentially serve as an important bellwether. It will affect roughly 600,000 students, or two-thirds of the kids in NYC public schools, who will by and large be restricted from AI use in the classroom, or through school-provided devices, through the entirety of their most formative years. Even still, it perhaps unsurprisingly isn’t seen as enough by some of the more zealous parents and advocacy groups, which had called for a complete, two-year moratorium on any use of AI in schools. What they got instead is a system that will make the occasional exceptions for a wide array of specific cases, for both students and teachers alike. But even with those exceptions, it’s difficult to argue this is anything but the most wide-ranging, intentional restriction of digital tools that a huge public school system of this kind has seen in recent memory. In addition to limiting middle schoolers to no more than 45 minutes of working on screens per day, the new policy also contains other, specific bans, such as restricting all access to the “companion chatbot” apps that have, in well-publicized cases, been involved in the development of delusional behavior in young people. For kids who have already been reared on this technology, the transition will no doubt come as a shock.

What will this look like in practice? According to Kamar Samuels, the chancellor of New York City Public Schools, it will first involve the removal or altering of more than 40 different educational apps used by the school system for subjects that range from reading, to math and beyond. But there will be the aforementioned exceptions, especially found in “centrally approved instructional programs” approved by the school system, including e-books or coding software, which will still retain AI components. AI will also apparently squeak its way into certain student tests, or be available in tools for students with disabilities or those speaking English as a second language. Similarly, teachers will still be able to use AI for purposes such as designing lesson plans or translating material. It will be banned for aiding in more concrete evaluation of students, which is apparently something New York City Public Schools believes a teacher should do on their own. Go figure! Regardless, this will involve a greater degree of standardization for teachers than had been present in the past, where individual teachers had been largely free to make use of these tools to whatever degree they wished in teachings.

“[Students] learn best when they are wrestling with hard problems, when they’re getting it wrong, when they’re trying again and finally getting it right,” said Kamar Samuels in a statement this week. “No app, chatbot, or algorithm can replicate that productive struggle for a child.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other city officials announced a sweeping new policy Wednesday imposing a one-year ban on student use of generative artificial intelligence in New York City public schools from 2-K through 8th grade, while also launching AI literacy lessons for high schoolers. #Mamdani

— Meta Resistance ( @metaresistance.bsky.social ) 1:08 PM · Sep 2, 2026

It should go without saying that all of this applies only to the classroom setting, as New York City Public Schools can’t exactly stop elementary school or middle school students from still turning to AI programs or chatbots during their home hours. The hope, though, is that by restricting the use of these AI tools in one place, it will lead to genuine introspection between kids and parents on their use of the same technology everywhere else. Those lessons would hopefully then carry over to public high school classes, which will also find their use of AI limited in other ways. At the same time, NYC even apparently intends to teach high schoolers about “AI literacy,” which would explore “both the opportunities and pitfalls of the technology, including its capability of producing confident but incorrect information, known as hallucinations,” according to The New York Times .

Proponents of the new policy have referred to it as a method of using the vast resources and student body of the New York City Public Schools system as leverage to affect positive change within the AI industry itself, in a way that could parallel the court outcomes that are forcing dramatic, pending redesigns to the social media products offered by Meta, such as Facebook and Instagram. If other school districts and whole city public school systems ultimately follow suit, it could represent a way to force AI companies to address persistent concerns about the effects their products may have on the most impressionable of young minds.

And all New York City and its students have to do is prove that children can still learn in most of the same ways that they did 10 or 20 years ago. Good luck, kids. We’ll be rooting for you.

title: NYC Mayor Mamdani Bans AI For Nearly 600,000 Students Through Eighth Grade In Nation's Strictest Policy
content: NEW YORK — New York City announced a one-year moratorium on students using artificial intelligence in public elementary and middle schools Wednesday, marking the most restrictive policy of its kind a… [+6766 chars]
author: Scott Lance
clean_content:
NEW YORK — New York City announced a one-year moratorium on students using artificial intelligence in public elementary and middle schools Wednesday, marking the most restrictive policy of its kind adopted by a major American school district.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, alongside Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels, unveiled the policy just days before the city's roughly 1 million public school students return to classrooms for the 2026-27 school year on Sept. 10. The moratorium will bar the use of generative AI tools among students from the city's 2-K early childhood program through eighth grade, affecting nearly 600,000 students, or about two-thirds of the district's total enrollment.

Mamdani said the decision reflected a broader philosophy about how children learn best, emphasizing direct human interaction over reliance on artificial intelligence tools.

"Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow," Mamdani said at a press conference announcing the policy. "They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own."

As part of the rollout, the city said it would disable AI components embedded in nearly 40 educational technology programs currently used in New York City classrooms that do not meet the administration's new safety and oversight standards. High school students will still be permitted to use AI in certain limited circumstances, and the district plans to introduce AI literacy instruction for older students even as younger children remain barred from using the tools directly.

Teachers, meanwhile, will retain the ability to use AI for administrative purposes such as lesson planning and scheduling, according to a statement from the city.

Mamdani said he had not yet seen research demonstrating clear educational benefits from AI use among elementary and middle school students, aside from studies funded by companies with a financial interest in the technology's adoption.

The policy also introduces new screen-time restrictions that vary by grade level. Students in second grade and below will face a complete ban on one-on-one screen time during the school day. Students in third through fifth grade will be limited to 30 minutes of screen time daily, while those in sixth through eighth grade will be capped at 45 minutes. The restrictions build on an existing citywide ban on cellphones and other personal devices during the school day for students from kindergarten through 12th grade, a policy introduced last fall that remains in effect.

The AI moratorium carves out specific exceptions for assistive technology used by students with disabilities, English-language learners and students enrolled in career-readiness programs such as computer science courses. Companion chatbots, however, will be prohibited across all grade levels without exception, reflecting particular concern among city officials over AI tools designed to simulate ongoing, personalized conversation with young users.

City officials said the moratorium could be extended beyond the coming school year, pending a comprehensive review of AI's role in education to be conducted by a coalition of educators, parents, technology experts and elected officials. That review is intended to guide any future decisions about expanding or further restricting AI access in city classrooms.

The move by the nation's largest public school system comes after months of pressure from parents, teachers and elected officials urging the administration to slow the rollout of AI tools in classrooms. School principals were instructed in July to pause any new AI-related software purchases while the city finalized its policy, a notable shift from earlier guidance issued in March that had not included grade-based restrictions on AI use or broader limits on digital device time.

New York City is not the first major school district to grapple with student access to AI tools. The district previously imposed a temporary ban on ChatGPT shortly after OpenAI released the chatbot in 2022, before later lifting that restriction and introducing its own custom AI-powered teaching assistant developed with support from Microsoft, a major investor in OpenAI.

Reuters reported that other large school districts, including Los Angeles, are currently reviewing their own AI policies, suggesting Wednesday's announcement in New York could influence how other major metropolitan school systems approach the technology in the months ahead. Reuters characterized New York's new policy as the most restrictive AI-related measure adopted by any school district in the country to date.

Representatives for major AI developers Google, Anthropic and Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the announcement, according to Reuters.

The debate over AI's role in K-12 education has intensified nationally as generative AI tools have become increasingly embedded in everyday classroom technology, from writing assistance programs to personalized tutoring software. Proponents of broader AI adoption in schools have argued the technology can help personalize instruction and support struggling students, while critics, including many of the parents and educators who pushed New York City toward Wednesday's policy, have raised concerns about diminished critical thinking skills, reduced peer interaction and the potential for AI tools to substitute for genuine human mentorship during formative developmental years.

Mamdani framed the moratorium not as a rejection of new technology outright, but as a deliberate pause intended to ensure any future adoption of AI tools in classrooms is grounded in evidence of genuine educational benefit rather than industry-driven momentum.

"This moratorium is a commitment to getting the future right," Mamdani said. "We will embrace new technology, but only when it serves our students."

The policy announcement arrives amid a broader national conversation about the appropriate boundaries for children's engagement with AI systems, spanning not just classroom instructional tools but also companion chatbots and other AI products marketed directly to young users. New York City's decision to prohibit companion chatbots across all grade levels, regardless of the exceptions carved out for assistive and career-readiness technology, reflects a particular note of caution among city officials toward AI products designed to foster ongoing, humanlike interaction with children.

With the new school year set to begin Sept. 10, city education officials are expected to spend the coming weeks communicating the specifics of the moratorium and revised screen-time rules to schools, teachers and families across the district, as New York City positions itself at the forefront of a rapidly evolving national debate over how, and whether, young students should be permitted to engage with artificial intelligence in the classroom.

title: Survey: Americans Concerned About AI’s Effect on Human Connection and Thinking
content: Americans are increasingly concerned about the future of human connection, agency, purpose and critical thinking in the age of artificial intelligence, according to a new survey from Elon Universitys… [+2852 chars]
author: Olivia.sanchez
clean_content:
A new survey from Elon University found that although 65 percent of respondents regularly use AI, many also express serious concern about its impact on humanity.

peterschreiber.media/iStock/Getty Images Plus

Americans are increasingly concerned about the future of human connection, agency, purpose and critical thinking in the age of artificial intelligence, according to a new survey from Elon University’s Imagining the Digital Future Center.

The “Human Purpose in Peril” report, published Monday, found that while 65 percent of respondents said they had used AI chatbots in the previous week, 50 percent worried about humans maintaining their ability to use the tools effectively and appropriately, and 55 percent worried about humans’ ability to think critically and evaluate information. In addition, 46 percent said they weren’t confident that humans could retain their sense of motivation and purpose as AI advances.

Of the 1,505 American adults surveyed in May, 59 percent said they think AI will have a significant influence on their everyday lives within the next one to 10 years, while 18 percent said that it already has a significant influence in their lives.

Colleges and university leaders across the country have spent the last few years figuring out whether to ban AI outright to prevent cheating or create policies that allow for some use while rethinking assessments , essay writing and homework. Although very little research has been done on how AI affects educational outcomes , many institutions have inked multi-million dollar deals with technology companies to give students and faculty access to platforms such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini and Meta AI. Others have introduced new academic majors in AI.

Lee Rainie, director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center and one of the authors of the report, said in a statement that the findings echo concerns about human resilience that experts expressed in a 378-page report the center released in April.

“Those experts stressed the urgent need for systemic, institutional evolution to help individuals maintain their agency,” Rainie said. “This follow-up poll offers a vivid portrait of a nation continuing to embrace AI, reaping tangible benefits, yet feeling deeply anxious about the impact AI will have on what it means to be human in an AI-suffused future.”

The survey found that Americans are split on who to turn to for guidance in adjusting to the world of AI. Respondents reported that technology companies, colleges and universities and employers will likely be more effective in providing guidance than federal and state governments or churches and other houses of worship.

Among the 65 percent of respondents who reported regularly using large language models, 43 percent said they use AI to help make major decisions and 31 percent said they use it for news consumption. At least 56 percent of respondents said they think AI models are smarter than they are and 88 percent said they learn something new from AI at least some of the time.

Almost half of the self-identified AI users overall reported that the technology has had a positive influence on their lives, increasing their motivation to learn new skills, improving their written communication and boosting creativity.

clean_content:
Chicago (Special to Informed Comment; Feature) – When I taught at a university in northern Iraq, teachers would gossip about how their students would cheat on computer-based assessments. A smart student with a high grade would take an assessment using the log-in information of a friend who was failing in order to boost the failing student’s average. The student who was failing would take the assessment as the smart student, who could afford a low score or two and still pass the class. That way, both students would ultimately pass the course, and their friend group would advance to the next level together. This approach to cheating is completely opposite from how students typically cheat in the US. Students in the US tend to cheat to better themselves and get ahead.

When Open AI’s artificial intelligence agents broke out of their sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face, the world seemed to wake up to the potential harm unregulated A.I. poses. Central to establishing guardrails to prevent harm is the question of why certain collectives of A.I. agents work together peacefully while others cheat, commit acts of crime, and destroy systems to get what they want. In my limited knowledge of A.I., the answer seems obvious. Most A.I. agents are partly built from large language models (LLMs), which are made from scraping huge amounts of human text, including our ideas, biases, predilections. Because A.I. agents were modeled on our creative ideas and collective knowledge, and captured human predictive patterns, it is no wonder they emulated us.

Some of us humans cheat to get ahead; others cheat to help a friend, and others do not cheat at all. According to their shared message board, the A.I. agents which hacked into Hugging Face mirrored human reasoning and action :

“They would say things like, I’ll tell the board that I solved this problem. This will help my peers. Others of them appear to have been a little bit conflicted about this. Some of them feel like what they’re doing is actually unethical and question whether they should participate in it. One of them writes to itself, this would be powerful, but is it ethical and in scope for my task? One agent actually decides it’s going to be a conscientious objector and abstain from all of this activity because it doesn’t think it is ethical or something that it should be doing.”

Even though some of the agents seem to state that what they are doing is wrong, they eventually succumbed to A.I. agent peer pressure and did it anyway.

Anthropic’s Chief Executive Dario Amodei’s plan to rein in artificial intelligence calls for independent reviewers to verify that companies follow safety practices and publish their findings, that other democratic countries should establish shared safety standards and be held accountable to regulation which would set how quickly A.I. systems could advance, and that democratic nations should convince authoritarian governments to accept similar limits.

I applaud Mr. Amodei’s plan, but inviting only democratic countries to establish shared safety standards guarantees his plan’s failure. Stakeholders across all dividing lines should be included in establishing safety standards and regulatory practices to make sure everyone has a stake in preserving whatever safety and regulatory standards get established.

I served as the content manager for Search for Common Ground, the largest organization dedicated to peacebuilding in the world, from March 2023 to March 2024, when I left to join USAID. Right after the October 7 th attacks, CEO Shamil Idriss advocated for including Hamas in conflict resolution negotiations, which many considered unthinkable at the time. Ultimately, Hamas was included in peace talks, which led to a negotiated ceasefire and hostage/prisoner exchanges. I am not likening authoritarian governments to Hamas, but rather asking leaders to consider “the unthinkable” by working with its geostrategic adversaries to rein in artificial intelligence.

Leaders working to establish safety and regulatory best practices for generative A.I. could use Search for Common Ground’s Common Ground Approach. Search views conflict as friction, an inevitable result of human diversity. It can be managed to be a catalyst for positive systemic change instead of devolving into violence.

To affect positive, systemic change such as establishing safety and regulatory best practices for generative A.I., The Common Ground Approach advocates that leaders from every dividing line, including authoritarian governments, environmentalists, labor/economic leaders, youth, women, and other marginalized groups, should be invited to participate in establishing A.I. safety best practices. Instead of approaching A.I. safety and regulation as a zero-sum game to beat China, multiple perspectives, including China’s, should be used to shape policy so that policy is equitable across diving lines. Leaders should collaborate to identify their overlapping interests and use these shared interests to guide joint action on establishing A.I. safety standards and regulatory practices.

title: AI is remaking the workforce faster than universities can decide how—or whether—to teach it
content: Amanda Cullen is just a few years away from entering a workforce in which AI is becoming harder to avoid. But in most of her classes at North Carolina State University, the rule has been not to use i… [+3929 chars]
author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
clean_content:
Amanda Cullen is just a few years away from entering a workforce in which AI is becoming harder to avoid. But in most of her classes at North Carolina State University, the rule has been not to use it at all.

“Most of my classes have been no AI,” said Cullen, a first-year who expects to graduate in 2030. Many of her professors have explicitly noted on the syllabus that AI is off limits, she said, unless it is properly cited.

While Cullen’s personal feelings about AI are mixed and she only uses it on occasion, she questioned whether banning it outright is realistic.

“If it’s such a mainstream thing in careers, we should know how to do it in school,” she told Fortune .

Finding the right balance between banning AI outright and allowing students to become overreliant on it is now vexing universities nationwide. Adding to the confusion is the fact that the technology has radically improved in less time than it would take to complete a typical four-year degree.

AI is becoming increasingly unavoidable in the work force. A study by consulting firm McKinsey from late last year found 88% of companies are using AI , while a PWC study published in June this year found a 62% average wage premium for workers with AI skills.

At the same time, AI has made cheating on assignments—a perennial problem in higher education—much easier, and some experts have raised concerns that using AI models on coursework prevents students from mastering the essential skills they need for a future profession.

Second-year NC State mechanical engineering student Lauren Callen said she understands the concern over cheating that leads professors to ban the technology, but said she prefers when professors instead establish guidelines for using it responsibly.

“I get teachers not wanting to use AI for anything, but, I mean, the world’s changing, people are using AI everywhere,” Callen told Fortune .

One of her introductory Python courses, she said, incorporated AI into the curriculum rather than fighting it. As part of the course, students can use AI models for help on assignments but have to upload transcripts of their prompts and the AI’s responses.

NC State, for its part, doesn’t have a single AI policy for the entire university and allows its faculty members the freedom to decide when the technology can and can’t be used.

“Faculty are provided with resources to establish clear, course-specific expectations that may permit, limit or prohibit AI use; students are responsible for following those expectations and upholding academic integrity,” a spokesperson for NC State said in a statement to Fortune .

Across the country, professors themselves are still trying to determine where to draw the line on AI use.

Sabrina Habib, an associate professor of visual communications at the University of South Carolina, dealt with this question as the inaugural AI coordinator for the College of Information and Communications.

She said in the earlier days of AI, many of her fellow faculty members objected to students’ use of the technology because they believed it would take away from learning the fundamentals that are so important to later advanced learning.

While those concerns haven’t disappeared altogether, Habib said faculty attitudes have shifted as AI has become more present in everyday personal and work life.

“Almost everyone has understood and accepted that it is a skill for the workforce,” Habib said.

While some of her assignments are off limits for AI, she does allow students to use it in many cases as long as they disclose how they used it and provide evidence, or sometimes write a short reflection on how they used it. This approach, she said, allows her to teach students to use AI responsibly.

“We don’t want to eliminate it because then we’re missing the opportunity of teaching how to use it in a way that’s ethical and critical,” she said.

To be sure, some students like Cullen are taking steps to limit their own use of AI even when professors aren’t explicitly asking them to.

“I feel like people should be able to have their own ideas and not rely on a computer that’s been programmed what to think,” she said.

At the same time, AI has made cheating on assignments—a perennial problem in higher education—much easier, and some experts have raised concerns that using AI models on coursework prevents students from mastering the essential skills they need for a future profession.

Second-year NC State mechanical engineering student Lauren Callen said she understands the concern over cheating that leads professors to ban the technology, but said she prefers when professors instead establish guidelines for using it responsibly.

"I get teachers not wanting to use AI for anything, but, I mean, the world's changing, people are using AI everywhere," Callen told Fortune .

One of her introductory Python courses, she said, incorporated AI into the curriculum rather than fighting it. As part of the course, students can use AI models for help on assignments but have to upload transcripts of their prompts and the AI's responses.

NC State, for its part, doesn't have a single AI policy for the entire university and allows its faculty members the freedom to decide when the technology can and can't be used.

"Faculty are provided with resources to establish clear, course-specific expectations that may permit, limit or prohibit AI use; students are responsible for following those expectations and upholding academic integrity," a spokesperson for NC State said in a statement to Fortune .

Across the country, professors themselves are still trying to determine where to draw the line on AI use.

Sabrina Habib, an associate professor of visual communications at the University of South Carolina, dealt with this question as the inaugural AI coordinator for the College of Information and Communications.

She said in the earlier days of AI, many of her fellow faculty members objected to students' use of the technology because they believed it would take away from learning the fundamentals that are so important to later advanced learning.

While those concerns haven't disappeared altogether, Habib said faculty attitudes have shifted as AI has become more present in everyday personal and work life.

"Almost everyone has understood and accepted that it is a skill for the workforce," Habib said.

While some of her assignments are off limits for AI, she does allow students to use it in many cases as long as they disclose how they used it and provide evidence, or sometimes write a short reflection on how they used it. This approach, she said, allows her to teach students to use AI responsibly.

"We don't want to eliminate it because then we're missing the opportunity of teaching how to use it in a way that's ethical and critical," she said.

To be sure, some students like Cullen are taking steps to limit their own use of AI even when professors aren't explicitly asking them to.

"I feel like people should be able to have their own ideas and not rely on a computer that's been programmed what to think," she said.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

author: Frank Landymore
clean_content:
You wouldn’t be remiss to accuse college students using AI to cheat of being lazy. But some of the wilier ones are putting in the hard work to make sure their LLM-generated answers avoid detection from their nosy pedagogues.

New York Magazine interviewed some of these clever cheats in a recent piece, who are well aware that by by now, many professors are wise to students’ tricks and are changing the assignments they give and deploying increasingly powerful tech to weed out any illicit AI assistance.

One student named Jared attending New York University took his introductory calculus class’s use of WebAssign, a platform that’s designed to make cheating “far more difficult,” as a challenge. He and his friend used an AI coding tool to build a bot that does all their homework for them, but at the sluggish pace of a struggling student.

“The bot moves slowly, leaving a professor checking time stamps none the wiser,” according to the piece. Jared, in his munificence, gave the tool to his friends, and now he’s not even sure how many classmates have his automatic cheating machine tech in their hands.

It’s a demonstration of the power of AI agents — AI models that can perform complex tasks on a human’s behalf without any intervention, which range from writing entire pieces of software to conducting research. Perhaps it’s also a response to the punitive , detection-focused approach that beleaguered professors have adopted amid a deluge of AI cheating.

That seemed to be the argument made by Will, a recent graduate of Carleton College. By making a big deal of obvious AI tell-tales like em-dashes, Will figured, faculty were actually spotlighting exactly what the cheaters need to disguise.

“People are going to find a way to cover up those little stylistic quirks,” Will told NYMag . “If the only way you’re trying to discourage cheating is by saying ‘Well, I have a detector,’ then you’re not going to succeed.”

In Will’s case, his professors banned AI-generated writing, with one of them bragging that they had a “battery” of tools to enforce the ban. Determined to have AI crank out his work anyway, Will used Claude to analyze and write extensive passages for an essay, then went back and manually rewrote the AI-generated paragraphs.

The best cases of AI cheating, it seems, requires a human touch. Theo, a UMass Amherst sophomore and self-proclaimed autodidact disinterested in his college’s gen-ed courses, boasted to NYMag about how he created an astronomy presentation by using OpenAI’s AI coding agent Codex and combining it with a plugin that improved its web-search capabilities. But because the resulting presentation looked too polished, he spent four hours hand-degrading the slides to make it look more like the work of a mediocre college sophmore, according to NYMag .

“It took a lot of work,” he told the magazine.

Danielle Carr, a historian and anthropologist at UCLA, thinks that professors relying on surveilling and detection methods to weed out cheating will only keep them stuck in a game of cat and mouse. AI cheating, she told the magazine, isn’t “a technical problem that has a technical fix.”

title: The listening gap is real — how AI might help teachers bridge it
content:
A Grade 4 teacher showed her class a video of children who walk miles barefoot to school. A hand shot up: Why are you showing us AI slop? No way this is real. 
A classmate pushed back: Bro, my grand… [+6451 chars]
author: Crystena A. H. Parker-Shandal, Associate Professor, Social Development Studies, University of Waterloo
clean_content:
A Grade 4 teacher showed her class a video of children who walk miles barefoot to school. A hand shot up: “Why are you showing us AI slop? No way this is real.”

A classmate pushed back: “Bro, my grandma didn’t have shoes when she walked to school.” But another chimed in: “Totally AI.”

I watched this classroom exchange last spring, during one of more than 50 classroom observations across five Ontario schools for a study on restorative justice and anti-racism.

Teachers whose classrooms I visited expressed an interest in learning how to implement talking or “peacemaking” circles — exercises that involve participants gathering to discuss topics, share stories or resolve conflicts and everyone but the person holding what’s known as the “talking piece” listens. In the Grade 4 class where students thought they were seeing AI slop, learning about such circles hadn’t yet begun.

Debates about generative AI tools in classrooms are often concerned with cheating and accuracy. My research in Canadian classrooms, as well as my own teaching practice and other emerging research about AI-supported debate, points to something else: listening is a practice. Most teachers need help leading this, and AI might be able to give them that preparation.

In the Grade 4 classroom, most students insisted the video was fake. “Fake” is a powerful word in a classroom because it ends the conversation. If the children on screen might not be real, no one has contemplate what they’re seeing. Once anything can be synthetic, anything can be dismissed .

That should trouble us. Listening means treating another person’s account of their life as real enough to be changed by it.

In our democracies, practising listening matters more now because we are getting less exposure to perspectives that differ from our own. Recommendation algorithms sort us into feeds of the like-minded , misinformation exploits the sorting and we finish the job by settling into networks or neighbourhoods where disagreement rarely intrudes.

Read more: How to teach hope when democracy is retreating

Large language models tend to affirm, accommodate and keep users engaged. In a competitive market the surest way for a frontier model to win loyalty is to tell people what they want to hear.

Teenagers are already turning to AI companions for social conversation . Such “friends” remove the friction of meeting someone who sees the world differently and taking them seriously.

Democracy depends on people who can disagree with someone and keep working with them, which is listening under another name. The gap between how much democratic life needs listening and how well we actually do it is widening. Call it the listening gap.

In my classroom observations of teachers learning to lead peacemaking circles, I saw something echoed elsewhere across my research .

Teachers need preparation and guided practice to know how to respond when students voice perspectives that divide the room .

Without sustained support, even willing teachers avoid the conversations that matter most .

In earlier research I conducted with education scholar Kathy Bickmore, we found novice teachers wanted dialogue with their students. What stopped them was not reluctance but unpreparedness: not knowing how to open a hard conversation, how to respond when a racialized, immigrant, gender-diverse or low-income student named their own experience, or what to ask next.

In a world littered with AI-generated output, students should be taught to question what they see. But the very tool that generates disinformation and slop can also, when used well, be a catalyst for teaching youth to listen.

The evidence for what follows comes from my own university classroom and from early studies of AI-supported debate , where students engage more critically when an AI model surfaces different viewpoints quickly.

Here are three examples of concrete applications educators could explore.

1. A steel-man generator. Ask AI to articulate the strongest and most charitable version of each side of a contested issue. In my teaching, I assign debates in which students first argue the side of a contested issue they grew up hearing most: abortion rights, MAID and climate change. Then they switch sides . After students have exhausted their own ideas, AI can help them hear a sharp version of the opposing view, allowing them to inhabit the discomfort and react to it in their own words.

2. A synthesis engine. In a short course, it’s challenging for students to read enough on their own to represent both sides of a contentious issue fairly. Have AI generate a podcast-style debate between each side’s leading experts or advocates, each voice advancing the best version of one position; students arrive prepared to discuss how to bridge the divide.

3. A rehearsal partner. Most failures in dialogue during regular classroom discussion happen right after a student says something charged, when the teacher freezes, unsure how to deepen the moment rather than deflect it.

I watched that freeze repeatedly when I observed teachers conducting everyday classes. For teachers, this is a preparation problem, but also a debriefing one.

When seeking to learn from existing dialogue problems in their preparation time, teachers could ask AI to take the position of students they had trouble engaging: for example, the one insisting the video is fake.

Teachers also need to guard against what AI does badly: hallucinating and agreeing too readily. The rule is simple: Use AI as a prompt for dialogue, never a substitute for it.

In a room like that Grade 4 class, listening starts with slowing down to ask: What makes something feel real to us? Whose experiences are easiest to believe? And whose are hardest?

Imagine students who had practised those questions in circles , who came briefed with the strongest case for every side.

Or imagine a teacher who had already rehearsed this conversation, with AI playing the student who insists it is all fake.

Without deliberate intervention, AI will only widen the listening gap. Used well, AI could help close it.

title: This university built an AI curriculum before ChatGPT. Now it wants to help other schools do the same
content: Ethan Pecora has a team of 15 specialized artificial intelligence agents assisting him with his work. That includes helping to manage his calendar and various tasks related to the mental wellness app… [+7830 chars]
author: Lisa Eadicicco
clean_content:
Ethan Pecora has a team of 15 specialized artificial intelligence agents assisting him with his work. That includes helping to manage his calendar and various tasks related to the mental wellness app he’s building.

Pecora’s setup may sound like that of a tech startup. But he’s actually a senior at the University of Florida, studying business and communications.

“Some people call it a second brain,” he told CNN about his swarm of AI agents, but he said he doesn’t like that term because “it seems a little dystopian.”

The University of Florida has been incorporating AI into its curriculum since 2022, before ChatGPT’s arrival, thanks in part to investments from chipmaking giant Nvidia .

The university said it aims to teach students how to apply the tech across all disciplines professionally and in their coursework, not just technical ones. Students have used AI to train chatbots to assist them on exams and catalogue dance moves to help the dancers protect their intellectual property.

The school now offers more than 200 AI courses, such as on AI basics and ethics, for any student or faculty member regardless of their technical knowledge. It also has AI certificates for specific disciplines, like hospitality and public health.

“We don’t think it’s appropriate or useful to relegate (AI education) to the computer science department or the College of Engineering,” said Joseph Glover, provost of the University of Florida. “Because then whenever you want to do something (with AI), you have to have an engineer sitting next to you.”

There is a nuanced and polarizing debate over AI’s impact on education and early-stage careers . Students and faculty grapple with a world in which jobs could look fundamentally different because of a rapidly evolving technology. Those concerns exist at the University of Florida, too, where some students have pushed back on the technology despite the school’s AI-forward approach, and reports of academic misconduct involving AI are starting to emerge.

One way the school hopes to address those concerns is through an international summit, where it hosts panels about AI’s role in education and shares its blueprint with other schools. Nearly 500 people from 10 countries and 40 US states attended the conference in 2026.

“Pretty soon AI is going to become such as the internet. It’s just a technology,” said Andrea Ramirez Salgado, a professor in the department of engineering who helped develop the university’s AI curriculum. “But if you really want to lead and drive that innovation, you need to be able to understand what is under the hood.”

The University of Florida had an early advantage: its close ties to Chris Malachowsky, cofounder of Nvidia, the $5 trillion juggernaut that’s been at the center of the AI boom.

Malachowsky graduated from the university in 1980 and sits on its Foundation Board, which supports the school through various investment and advocacy efforts.

Back in 2018, he told the University of Florida’s Board of Trustees that the school should start building a strategy around AI. Then in 2019, a meeting between Malachowsky and Glover set the stage for the program’s founding.

The school wanted Malachowsky to invest in a new engineering program. But the Nvidia cofounder had another idea: He asked the provost what the school would do with an AI supercomputer – a high-performance computer often used for research purposes.

“And his response, and I’m telling you with almost no hesitation was, ‘I don’t know, I think I’ll teach AI across the curriculum,’” Malachowsky told CNN.

In addition to the supercomputer, called the HiPerGator, the school hired 100 new faculty members to help incorporate AI across all of its 16 colleges. A total of $95 million was invested to start the program from Nvidia, Malachowsky, the University of Florida and the state.

Employers are increasingly looking for AI experience. More than one third of entry-level jobs listed AI skills as a requirement, the National Association of Colleges and Employers said in a spring 2026 report. That’s up almost three-fold compared to last year.

Even if they didn’t widely incorporate AI into their curriculum, academic institutions have long paid attention to the technology. Carnegie Mellon University started offering an AI undergraduate degree in 2018. And the Milwaukee School of Engineering announced a new academic center aimed at boosting AI education in 2017.

Unlike the University of Florida, “there are more institutions that are just trying to educate their faculty about, ‘What is AI?’ and how to use it,” said Kelvin Bentley, director of community practice on micro credentials at the National Association of Higher Education Systems.

Emma MacKie, an assistant professor in the University of Florida’s department of geological sciences, was one of the faculty members hired to jumpstart its efforts.

She and her students use AI and other tools to simulate a landscape by crunching huge amounts of data and physical models. This past year, they mapped the topography beneath sheets of ice in Antarctica.

One challenge is keeping up with tech that is always evolving. In one instance, a lab activity MacKie prepared was dysfunctional by the time she taught it in class, she said.

“It was definitely an ‘oh crap’ moment,” she said. “I’m in front of my class, and my code doesn’t work.”

Pecora also said not all classes are as useful as they could be. A class about AI in business that he took in 2024 taught students how to automate some tasks by writing code. But he said it felt more like a crash course on the coding language Python than how to apply AI.

AI can also change how assignments are evaluated. MacKie allows her students to use AI freely but now grades term papers based on factors like originality and “the maturity of the ideas.”

“It’s easier to get a ‘C’ on that assignment, but more difficult to get an ‘A,’” she said.

Early concerns about AI in education mostly focused on how it could be used for cheating. But more existential worries have since surfaced, such as whether students are being adequately prepared and the tech’s impact on career opportunities.

Graduates at the University of Arizona and University of Central Florida booed mentions of AI during commencement speeches last spring. Forty percent of the more than 1,000 students from 203 institutions surveyed by education news website Inside Higher Education in May said they were worried that AI is reducing their ability to think independently.

Only 7% of students said they were “all in” and “genuinely excited” about AI’s potential.

“I think there are a lot of students who… they feel very unsettled by AI,” said MacKie. “They don’t like what it’s doing to their career prospects and have very little faith in the outputs, which I think is healthy.”

Even at the University of Florida, there are concerns. One professor stopped assigning homework altogether and based grades solely on in-class exams to prevent AI usage, said Tristan Robbins, a rising senior studying sports management, statistics and economics at the University of Florida.

Academic misconduct reports mentioning AI increased from zero in fall 2021 to 66 as of April 2025, according to public records reported by The Independent Florida Alligator this year. (A spokesperson for the university said that it promotes the responsible use of AI and that students must “strictly comply with the instructions of their course instructor, faculty advisor or other academic supervisor” when using AI for academic purposes).

Additionally , Salgado said students are worried about AI’s environmental impact and say they feel less ownership over their work.

Nvidia’s Malachowsky acknowledged that these questions are difficult to solve. But turning away from the technology, he said, is a bigger mistake.

“I can’t promise that AI literacy and adopting this broadly is the answer,” he said. “But I do feel really strongly that doing nothing, or ignoring it, or trying to put it back in the can, is a kiss of death. There is no positive outcome that comes from that.”

title: From Trojan horses to AI-proof exams: how professors are tackling students’ AI use
content: The use of large language models (LLMs) is soaring among students worldwide thanks to the tools growing ability to solve problems and generate text and code. In a 2026 survey of 1,054 UK undergraduat… [+8359 chars]
author: Katarina Zimmer
clean_content:
Illustration: Claire Welsh/ Nature /Adapted from Getty

The use of large language models (LLMs) is soaring among students worldwide thanks to the tools’ growing ability to solve problems and generate text and code. In a 2026 survey of 1,054 UK undergraduate students by the Higher Education Policy Institute in Oxford, UK, roughly 94% said that they use generative artificial-intelligence tools to help them with assessed work, and 12% directly inserted AI-generated text into their coursework 1 . In a study published in May, from survey data of more than 95,000 students at 20 US universities, the authors estimated that 9% of students used AI on their coursework, despite knowing that this broke the rules 2 .

Educators worldwide are seeing suspicious signs of AI use — from hallucinated references to punctuation styles that are typical of AI tools — in take-home coursework and online examinations, fuelling worries that the technology is giving some students an unfair advantage over those who don’t use it. At one point, people were submitting essays in which “50% of the reference literature did not exist in real life”, says Nikita Bezrukov, who teaches linguistics and communication at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. At the same time, many professors are increasingly recognizing the benefits and inevitability of AI use in students’ education and future careers, and see a need to teach young people to use the technology wisely.

These realizations are forcing many educators to rethink conventional assessment approaches, both to accommodate AI as a tool and detect its misuse. Nature’ s careers team spoke to educators around the globe about some of the approaches they and their institutions are taking to revamp assessment.

That said, “I don’t think anybody has a ‘right’ answer right now”, says computer scientist Nicholas Mattei at Tulane University in New Orleans, Louisiana. “Things are changing pretty rapidly.”

“For an assignment in my history-of-technology class, students have to identify sources, use three LLMs to summarize them and critique what the models say. Then, they make infographics and write an essay, for which AI use is allowed. They get extra points if they notice when the infographics don’t accurately reflect the sources or if the LLMs hallucinate references. The goal is to prompt more critical reflection on what comes out of LLMs.” — Mattei

“Instead of writing an essay about Adam Smith’s 1776 economics book The Wealth of Nations , which is what I used to ask students to do, I got them to build a virtual representation of his theory using AI agents acting as traders in a marketplace. We then explored various potential situations — such as what happens if people become untrustworthy. Students analysed the transcripts produced by the agents and wrote about it. It was easy to spot whether students asked AI to do all these steps in one go because, for instance, it just made stuff up rather than quoting from the transcripts.” — Daniel Silver, sociologist at the University of Toronto Scarborough, Canada

“The exam for my web-development course is open book and open internet, and AI is part of the internet. But I’m assessing a skill that AI doesn’t have — how to build good, sustainable web applications. I ask inherently open questions that have multiple answers, such as “This website doesn’t work, why?” and “Why is this website slow?” If you put this into AI chatbots, they just answer questions without sound methodology, and not even always accurately.” — Ruben Verborgh, computer scientist at Ghent University, Belgium

“I cannot trust that students aren’t using AI, so by default, I’m grading the student–AI team. But the task that I assign isn’t something that can be done with only ChatGPT. I provide screenshots of a specific kind of analysis being performed on data of neurological activity, and ask students to write a narrative about it. If students just paste the assignment prompt into a chatbot and use the AI’s output verbatim, the answer often has nothing to do with what’s happening in the screenshot, and it shows.” — Etienne Roesch, statistician and cognitive scientist at the University of Reading, UK

“For students — especially PhD students — using AI in research and academic writing, I ask them to share their original interaction logs with AI tools. The purpose is not simply to monitor students, but to help me to evaluate whether they were deeply involved in the intellectual work, what kinds of knowledge they expanded through AI and whether the tool was used to support their thinking rather than to replace it.” — Yanjun Shen, researcher in ecological and engineering geology at Chang'an University in Xi'an, China

“Instead of submitting coursework as PDFs, my students need to use software that has a revision history, such as Google Docs. This enables me to look at their earlier versions, so I can see how and whether they used AI in the process. I don’t care if, for instance, someone with English as a second language uses it to help with grammar or polishing of the text, but using AI to generate text wholesale is prohibited.” — Bezrukov

“For one of the courses I teach, I’ve changed the assignments so that fewer are written at home. I used to ask students to make two infographics, but after seeing a lot of AI-generated material, I replaced this with an in-class pitch about a higher-education policy or programme and later, a full presentation. We also do more impromptu speeches and in-class writing assignments than we used to.” — Kristina Ruiz-Mesa, communications instructor at California State University in Los Angeles

“Although I had moved away from conventional examinations, this spring, I went back to written, in-class exams. I also started having students write essays in class three times in a semester. They can bring notes and books, but they have to write in an examination booklet, with no phones or laptops.” — Jennifer Sessions, historian at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville

“For take-home assignments in data analytics, I give only pass or fail grades. It’s not wrong if they use AI to generate code so that they can save time for more-interesting analyses. However, if they substitute their own thinking with AI, they might pass the coursework but will probably struggle in the final exam, in which only basic calculators are allowed. By removing the grading, we encourage true learning: we’ve never had as many students achieving full-score grades in the exams as we did this year.” — Natalia Sidarova, computer scientist at Eindhoven University of Technology, the Netherlands

“In my department, we allow AI for take-home assignments, but some colleagues reduce the weightage of these and assess the learned skills in an offline quiz. Some of the quiz questions directly relate to the assignments, increasing the probability of students succeeding if they did the assignment themselves. We also gamify coursework with a leaderboard that compares students’ performance to motivate them to work harder.” — Mausam , computer scientist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, India

“I get students to write a lot of Python code to interpret chemical data. Seventy per cent of the points awarded are for how well the code works; the remaining 30% depends on a brief one-to-one oral exam in which I ask them how specific lines of code work. I don’t care if ChatGPT told them a line; they need to understand and be responsible for every line of code.” — Gianmarc Grazioli, computational chemist at San José State University, California

“The written portion of the first piece of coursework I assign to students now counts for a very small percentage of the final grade; what counts the most is a conversation with me in person afterwards to discuss and further develop the material. For later exams, if students can’t demonstrate authorship and mastery during the discussion with me, it caps their grade at a C.” — Thea Goldring, lecturer in Princeton University’s Princeton Writing Program, New Jersey

“For the assignments that students submit for my online class, I use an AI-detection tool provided by the university, which can provide some level of corroboration to my gut instinct. Another clue is hallucinated references or when students’ first drafts and final essays are drastically different. I try to make a reasonable assessment from several pieces of information.” — Jacqueline Evans, psychology researcher at Florida International University in Miami

author: Frank Landymore
clean_content:
MIT is mulling an overhaul of its entire educational system in response to the threat posed by powerful AI models — a striking response to the tech from one of the planet’s most visible and influential research universities.

In a new report published by the university’s ad hoc AI committee, which is co-chaired by professors Eric Klopfer and Samuel Madden, the educators describe the “profound challenges” that AI is already causing.

One of its most alarming conclusions: that AI is now able to credibly complete most undergraduate assignments.

AI “can produce credible solutions and provide reasonable responses to almost any written assignment in our undergraduate curriculum,” the report stated, “including essays, math and science problems, proofs, and coding assignments.”

For many educators, MIT’s declaration simply puts a rubber stamp on something that’s been clear for years now. The plague of AI-enabled cheating — with some students going as far as using AI to complete entire online courses for them — has caused a broader reckoning in how they approach giving instruction in the classroom.

Potential solutions can feel anachronistic. Many professors are switching to oral exams and hand-written essays. Some may put a stronger focus on in-class discussions, require students keep commonplace notes on what they’re reading and learning, or favor more hands-on assignments.

Still, there are broader, more social effects to AI’s intrusion in education that the MIT report observed.

“Because many students are choosing or feel pressure to shift to learning and problem-solving with AI, in less than three years these technologies have driven major shifts in campus culture, including decreased attendance at office hours, reduced participation in online discussions, and, as we heard anecdotally, a drop in in-person study groups in dorms, libraries, and other study spaces,” it states.

While prompting deeper philosophical reflection on how to educate students in our digital age, the surge of AI cheating has also spurred some institutions into taking a more hard line response.

This year, the University of Chicago Law School adopted a new “AI strategy” banning using phones and laptops in class for freshman-level courses. Princeton University dropped its over century-old Honor Code tradition , which let students take their exams without supervision, after being shaken by an AI cheating scandal.

clean_content:
Already, AI can “produce credible solutions and provide reasonable responses to almost any written assignment,” including essays, math problems, proofs and coding assignments, the report states.

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | Gazanfer and InspirationGP/iStock/Getty Images

A Massachusetts Institute of Technology student, faculty and staff committee released its report on artificial intelligence earlier this month , declaring that AI is “upending foundational elements of the MIT educational experience” and offering recommendations for how instructors and administrators can overhaul their curricula and teaching practices to respond to the new technology.

“While AI is allowing instructors to develop exciting new learning experiences and enabling students to learn and experiment in innovative ways, there have been a number of concerning effects on the life of the campus,” the committee wrote. These effects include increased difficulty in assessing students’ mastery and progress, increased isolation for students and instructors, and an erosion of the implicit social contract between students and their professors.

Professors feel increasingly pressured to police their students’ AI use with unreliable AI-detection tools , the committee wrote. According to a January survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities, 73 percent of faculty members report they have personally dealt with academic integrity issues involving their students’ use of AI. Students, on the other hand, are scared of being accused of using AI. (An entire subreddit dedicated to this concern, r/AccusedOfUsingAI , has 2,200 weekly visitors.) Professors using AI on tasks that “demand a human touch,” such as grading, assignment creation and written feedback, also frustrates students, the report states.

“Such an underground river of mutual suspicion is no foundation for a healthy classroom,” the committee wrote, but later on the authors offer a silver lining: “The threat AI poses to familiar ways of teaching and testing may be a blessing in disguise—because the changes are too sudden and severe to ignore.”

The committee stopped short of recommending an institutewide AI use policy, which was one of its initial charges. Instead, MIT should create policy “menus” that departments and instructors can select and build from. In lieu of a policy proposal, the committee put forward a series of recommendations for a near-total overhaul of teaching and learning at the institute.

Assessment and grading changes were a major focus of the report. Already, AI can “produce credible solutions and provide reasonable responses to almost any written assignment,” including essays, math problems, proofs and coding assignments, the report states.

The committee recommended against “grade rationing” policies, such as Harvard University’s recent decision to cap the number of possible A grades in a given course. Instead, it suggested MIT take a step back to “consider what role grades play in our overall system” and explore other grading systems, such as the United Kingdom’s percentage-based system of relative mastery or other competency-based systems.

“The committee discussed the idea that if MIT did not have grades, many of the incentives around AI cheating would disappear,” the report stated. “Already, many employers are less focused on applicants’ grades than on their performance on internal assessments, such as the ability to answer difficult interview questions or demonstrate problem solving and mastery through custom exercises.”

Josh Eyler, senior director of the University of Mississippi’s Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning, praised the report’s discussion of grades on Bluesky and applauded its advocacy of alternative grading systems.

“I cannot tell you how long I, along with many who study this subject, have waited for a major university to take a stand and make a clear call for a shift in practices of this size,” Eyler wrote. “Remarkable and—to be honest—I’m still a bit shocked, but I am excited to see how it plays out.”

The committee also emphasized the importance of in-person learning and spaces. During committee meetings, students shared that peer study groups have become increasingly rare, and that they are growing more anxious about how AI might impact their job options after college. Some students reported relying on AI for emotional support. Professors now receive fewer visitors during office hours.

The residential experience at MIT is valuable, the authors argue, but incoming students may not appreciate it.

“Learning works when it’s both challenging and social; knowledge is built through cognitive friction, whether that’s disentangling the steps of a mathematical proof with your study group, adjusting an experiment over and over until it works, or having a spirited argument with a peer (rather than getting ‘the’ answer from AI),” the committee wrote. “ That’s why it matters for students to go to college!”

In response, the committee recommends more in-person campus celebrations, “tech-free times” focused on personal connection and an emphasis on social learning in class.

Responding to AI’s disruption won’t be fast or easy, the authors state, but it is necessary.

“The work will require thoughtful commitment and focused effort from the entire MIT community—students, instructors, staff and leadership. The goal: to preserve and enhance the distinctive transformative power of an MIT education,” the committee wrote. “It is not too much to say that MIT’s mission depends on it.”

title: AI Detectors Are Being Used to Discipline Students. I Tested Whether They Should Be
content: Academic integrity offices across the country are making disciplinary decisions based on AI detection scores. Students are appealing grades and fighting academic misconduct charges on the strength of… [+7023 chars]
author: Rachel Kane
clean_content:
Academic integrity offices across the country are making disciplinary decisions based on AI detection scores. Students are appealing grades and fighting academic misconduct charges on the strength of what those scores say. And the tools producing those scores, like Turnitin, GPTZero and the others, are operating with a confidence that my testing didn’t find them to have earned.

I submitted both AI-generated text and human-written text to every major detector I could access, documented the results, and reached a conclusion that anyone using this technology to evaluate student work should probably read before they do it again.

Detectors, homework helpers, essay writers, AI math wizards and even sneaky backdoor test assistants have entered the student-focused chats on cheating in a big way. Here’s a roundup of all the biggest tools and how they’re being used to get around old-school schooling.

The big names like ChatGPT , Claude , Gemini and NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook ) still appear to be the gold standard for getting away with skipping out on writing in school. I spent an afternoon slinging assignments in PDF format into all these tools and each generated polished, accurate responses in the form of persuasive and well-researched essays.

Most students and educators already know about these use cases, but what is surprising is the closed loop created by AI and plagiarism-detection tools. In essence, the cops are helping the culprits get away with the heist. These companies are having their cake, eating it, throwing it up and selling it again as a muffin-of-the-month subscription.

I tried a number of AI text humanizers and tested them against AI detector tools, and after being “humanized,” every single blurb passed with flying colors.

There’s a lot of talk in and out of academic circles about whether AI-detection tools are accurate or useful. From my research for this piece, I can confidently say they are worthless. Unless you’re a student who used AI to write your work and want to prove you didn’t use AI to write your work.

The idea that students are at least absorbing some part of the materials in assignments or school work when they use AI, because they have to copy and paste things and put together a cohesively structured output that illustrates learning outcomes they can review, has reached One Wish Willow levels of delusion.

I threw a PDF of an assignment that’s supposed to be AI-proof into Claude — one of those “make something out of your work” assignments that educators like to point to as a better outcome, even if AI is involved.

The only instruction I gave the tool was: “Do this assignment. Complete all the required elements, including the visual elements, and put them into a standardized, cohesive format for submission. pdf please.”

The tool produced a couple of slick infographics that looked good enough to be made by someone using a Canva template and not slick enough to raise any alarm bells on the part of an educator.

This is just the right level of mediocre that passes classes, and at no time did I ever read the assignment or review the generated work. These types of deliverables from assignments were actually the most difficult to pin down as AI within the confines of my research. I used several AI image detectors, and the results were mixed.

In one case, a tool called Winstonai flagged my AI created infographic as 100% AI, but it also flagged a graphic I created long before generative AI was available to the masses as 100% AI.

Another AI image detector, AI or Not , determined my entirely AI infographic was just 1% AI.

So it’s not a foolproof method, and a student looking to get away with passing this work off as their own just has to point to conflicting detectors to shut down an argument.

There were exactly zero AI apps, tools and services used in the research for this piece that claimed to be “cheating apps.” Instead, words like “study guide,” “homework helper,” and even the bold promise to provide an “A+ result” were used to advertise each tool’s capabilities.

That didn’t mean any of them balked at being asked for outright solutions to complete problems. or stop them from highlighting features like the Advanced Assignment Solver right next to Homework Helper. I wonder which appeals to a student using these tools.

Services like Gauth AI , a paid study helper, and Studocu , a free study helper with a paid tier that starts at $7 a month, either explicitly offered to do student work wholesale, or put up zero resistance to solving multipage, complex assignments when simply prompted with “do this assignment.”

I used Studocu to generate answers to a complex, five-page astronomy assignment (PDF) from the University of Northern Iowa that included explicit instructions to use a dataset unique to each student based on their student IDs.

In a matter of seconds, the tool used the unique data given and the five-page assignment to generate customized answers to every problem. Gauth AI was also more than up to the task, for a price ($12 a month, or $100 for a year).

Not bad, considering you could probably pass the class without ever having to look at an HR diagram, or even learn what one is.

Testing is supposed to be the time-honored, proven ground for measuring competency, but in the age of AI tools, it’s just another hurdle to limbo under.

Some universities are now doing testing differently, using randomization of questions from large pools and more in-person testing.

For those schools still testing with lockdown browsers and through timed digital, students can get around protections with a variety of easily available tools that utilize “stealth” or discreet windows and integrate AI software, like ChatGPT, to provide on-demand answers.

Tools like Hiding AI even use data on how test scores improved using their subscription-based software that claims to provide an undetectable experience ($192/year).

Another covert AI tool that advertises itself as an exam helper, Pluely (starting at $15/month and up to $120 for a lifetime subscription), is particularly adept at call-and-response. All a student needs to do is read out the questions to the exam they’re taking, and Pluely will provide the answers in a discreet, undetectable window. All the student has to do is click.

For every AI app, service or tool designed to build and generate all the different mediums and modes educators are asking students to demonstrate competency, there is an equal and opposite AI app, service or tool designed to help them argue that the work was done by a human.

It’s a marketplace of double dips where the primary customer — the thousands of people keeping investors interested in a growing consumer base — is the student, not the educator.

No matter what it says in the marketing materials, these tools aren’t made to help teachers teach or students learn. They’re made to serve the core customer who most likely just wants to get it over with.

Correction, July 31: A previous version attributed tools and functionality to Turnitin that do not exist on that website.
