title: Schools are starting to teach AI literacy. For many, that means helping kids see chatbots' flaws
content: Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school aud… [+7320 chars]
author: Jocelyn Gecker
clean_content:
Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school auditorium and talked about inviting AI into the classroom.

The teachers and principals watched as an instructor prompted an AI tool to “create a map of the world.”

The result drew gasps of disbelief and laughter. Projected on a large screen was a map riddled with bizarre errors . Mali was spelled “Mail.” Egypt was identified as “Sopth.” In place of Libya was something simply called “Africa.” Dozens of other countries' names were misspelled or written in pure gibberish.

“If you ever want kids not to over trust these tools, try the map demo,” said the instructor, Amanda Bickerstaff, founder and CEO of AI For Education, an organization that helps schools draft AI policies and train teachers and students in what she calls safe, ethical and effective use of the technology.

After initially trying to ban AI use, a growing number of U.S. public schools are trying a new strategy: encouraging classroom experimentation, partly so students can see its shortcomings, including generative AI’s notorious tendency to “hallucinate,” or fabricate information.

AI literacy has become a buzzword of this back-to-school season as educators try to strike a balance between equipping students with the skills they need for an AI-driven future while preventing them from outsourcing their thinking to chatbots.

There is no single definition of what AI literacy means, or how it should be taught. Tech giants like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic offer schools training sessions in how to use their AI tools . But for educators, there is a growing consensus that AI literacy is about more than learning how to use generative AI and write good prompts.

“Good AI literacy,” said Rebecca Winthrop, director of the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution, “includes knowing when not to use it.”

Some districts build their own approaches on AI literacy

Thirty-seven states have now published official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint. South Carolina is not one of them.

So the state’s second-largest school district set out to do it on its own, said Lucas Clamp, deputy superintendent of the 50,000-student Charleston County School District. “It has been a huge endeavor.”

A year ago, the district contacted AI for Education, which helped draft guidance for Chicago Public Schools, Houston and dozens of other districts.

Phase 1 was laying the foundation. The district developed an AI policy, seeking input from teachers, students and parents.

The district organized student focus groups and learned that student AI use was ubiquitous but unguided. Teachers and students said they were navigating the technology on their own and wanted clear rules and instruction.

Studies show a majority of teenagers and teachers nationwide are using AI for schoolwork, but they're teaching themselves how to use it; very few say they have a technical understanding or have received formal training on how it works.

Schools and parents are eager to avoid mistakes made with social media , where kids were left to explore the online world without learning about addictive algorithms, comparison culture and other downsides that have been linked to a youth mental health crisis and dwindling attention spans.

As the school year begins in Charleston, Phase 2 kicks in: training. Teachers and middle and high schoolers will get a mix of online and in-person instruction on how AI tools work and how to use them effectively.

The student course walks through familiar scenarios — like asking a chatbot to help with a research paper — to show that generative AI might deliver wildly inaccurate information, including made-up studies, with unflinching authority. “Always verify any factual information you get from GenAI, especially for your classwork,” the course advises.

A section on data privacy cautions against sharing personal information with AI tools because conversations can be stored, used for data training and potentially leaked.

High school teacher Ray Knauer attended the summer training and left with “teachable moments” for his AP Research class. He plans to show examples of AI bias and hallucinations to fuel student discussions.

“We’re all trying to figure this out right now: What’s the right balance so we don’t scare students away from AI but don’t encourage them to run to it,” Knauer said. “We have to teach students: You can’t just get an answer and move on. You have to use analytical skills and dig deeper.”

Some states offer top-down guidance on AI in classrooms

Utah was an early pioneer in taking a statewide approach to AI in education.

In 2024, the board of education named Matt Winters as its AI education specialist, making Utah the first state to create a full-time position overseeing the technology in schools.

Over the past year, Winters led AI training for over 7,000 teachers, almost a third of Utah’s public school instructors. He is helping districts shape AI policies, which they are required by state law to have in place by July 2027.

“There is a clear method from the top in Utah,” said Chris Agnew, director of the Generative AI for Education Hub at Stanford University. “When you’re tackling big change, it’s easier to have coherence if everyone is singing from the same hymn book.”

A handful of other states have since replicated Winters’ post, including Maine, West Virginia and Georgia.

In other states, a patchwork of AI approaches has emerged, with variance from one school district to another. Extensive AI literacy training requires steep investment, raising concerns that kids in under-resourced districts might not get the same attention.

In Utah, training starts with the basics of how AI works to teach an understanding of AI bias, hallucinations, ethical concerns and data privacy needs, Winters said. Teachers can then pursue additional training on specific tools.

“If I had to give advice: Figure out how to make training accessible to everyone,” said Emma Moss, who oversees AI at the Canyons School District and also led an eight-person team that traveled the state doing over 150 AI literacy trainings. The training was funded by a $500,000 AI literacy grant from a local healthcare provider. “We said, ‘We will come to you.’ Whether you are in a rural area or urban, it didn’t matter.”

The state has also played a key role in procuring AI tools, Winters said. He negotiated data privacy agreements along with discounted prices, which has allowed rural and under-resourced districts to get access.

“Everyone needs to understand what this technology is and how it works,” said Winters, who cautions against blanket bans. “AI literacy is much larger than saying: ‘Don’t use AI.’ It’s about how we can prepare kids for the future.”

Changing adult mindsets is also key, said Kristina Yamada, the state Board of Education's digital technology specialist.

“I think teachers need to change their mentality about students using AI to cheat,” Yamada said. There has always been cheating, she said. It’s up to teachers to speak students’ language and convince them they can’t rely on AI for all the answers.

For younger kids it means starting to talk about AI early, with conversations like, “People can lie. A program can lie. A robot can lie,” Yamada said. “For older students it’s different: ‘Sure, you can use ChatGPT to write computer code . But when the program stops working, you need to be able to fix it.’”

A federal framework… [+10340 chars]
author: Zena Chamas
clean_content:
States have different approaches to AI integration into classrooms. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke )

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) technology could have significant implications for the future of education, according to one of Australia's leading AI education experts.

A federal framework for ethical and responsible AI use was released by the Albanese government in 2023, which focused on protecting students and assisting educators.

While it was intended to set national standards for AI use, since then state education departments have adopted their own approaches in an effort to clamp down on AI-enabled cheating.

Recently, the New South Wales government proposed a major overhaul of the Higher School Certificate (HSC), pushing to ban unsupervised take-home assignments for year 11 and 12 students to combat AI cheating.

It was prompted by more than 1,000 recorded cheating cases in 2025 and rising concerns over AI in writing student essays.

University of Technology Sydney professor in AI and Education, Leslie Loble, said AI in learning spaces could have implications that "go beyond cheating".

"The process of learning relies on converting the working memory of new information into retained memory and knowledge.

She said AI gives "short-term" boosts, keeping the user reliant on it for more answers.

"What we're seeing in the research is that we're increasing dependency, and it becomes a vicious cycle because we're not converting that information into long-term knowledge," she said.

States have different approaches to AI integration. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke )

Professor Loble said the NSW government's proposal was a step in the right direction but "we have to take the threats and risks seriously".

While warning there was a "basket of risks", Professor Loble said there was evidence that students who were falling behind in class could benefit from using AI tools to catch up.

"For students, there is growing evidence that AI tools can be helpful for kids who are falling behind. On the other hand, there's definitely a basket of risks."

The NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) developed a policy on the use of AI in schools in 2024, which states that unapproved use of AI in completing assignments is a breach of academic integrity.

Under that protocol, students must complete a learning unit called All My Own Work (AMOW) before they are eligible to take HSC courses and to be awarded the HSC.

In South Australia, the approach to AI in schools stands out nationally. The SA government has embraced AI in public education rather than banning it.

They partnered with Microsoft to develop a ChatGPT-style AI tool for classrooms, called EdChat.

South Australia has rolled out EdChat, a large language model similar to ChatGPT or Claude, something no other state has done so far.

EdChat was delivered through a partnership with Microsoft and is branded as a custom, secure generative AI tool for public high schools.

After trialling the software, the SA government said a broader rollout would facilitate safe and productive technology use.

It was an example of how AI tools can be used to help students who need it, according to Professor Loble.

"The tool challenges the student through further questioning and providing some information but not the answer, to essentially have a much more robust approach to learning built into the tools.

"These are examples of how you can have design standards that will give us greater confidence of the technology in schools," she said.

A Department of Education spokesperson told the ABC that the state government recently announced a nation-leading royal commission into AI commencing in October this year.

"Our teachers are supported to use a range of assessment types including oral, written, multimodal and performance modes so that evidence of learning is collected in multiple ways.

"It is expected that teachers' professional judgement continues to be applied when assessing a student's work," the statement said.

In Victoria, the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) provides advice on how schools use AI, and sets standards for academic integrity.

Those standards state that students must submit work they have produced on their own, acknowledge the resources they used to complete it and must not plagiarise or otherwise cheat.

Individual schools are left to adjudicate on whether suspected cases of AI use have breached the VCAA standards.

A VCAA spokesperson told the ABC in a statement that the authority required work submitted for assessment to be the student's own, except where assistance was explicitly permitted and acknowledged.

"The vast majority of work students do to complete their VCE certificate is already completed under supervision in class.

"The best integrity control is our teachers — they know their students and monitor their progress as they complete take-home tasks to make sure their work is their own.

"We continue to explore ways to protect academic integrity with respect to AI," the statement said.

Professor Loble says Victoria is leading the way in screen time restrictions for primary schools.

Starting in term 1, 2027, the Victorian government has introduced strict daily screen time caps and device rules for all state primary schools.

The rules state that schools must not invite or allow families to purchase or bring their own student digital device to use at school from Prep to year 6.

It's "worth a conversation" if this should become a national standard, Professor Loble said.

"Screen time caps, age standards, should those be national standards? These are the sorts of things that ministers should be considering," she said.

The Queensland Department of Education and the Queensland Curriculum Assessment Authority (QCAA) work together to protect the integrity of the state's Certificate of Education qualification.

The QCAA provides advice to schools about academic integrity, which includes a course on the subject that all students must complete during their senior years.

They work together to support schools and maintain the Queensland Certificate of Education qualification by supporting a balanced approach to teaching and assessment.

The Department of Education said in a statement that the QCAA provides advice to schools about academic integrity in its policy and procedures handbook and requires students to complete an academic integrity course during senior schooling.

"Digital tools, including emerging technologies such as AI, are used in the classroom where they add value to student learning. Schools continue to maintain an appropriate balance between digital and non-digital learning.

"Decisions about device use and how technology is integrated into learning and assessment are made by principals in consultation with their school communities," the statement added.

Western Australia has adopted the federal government's Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools.

That was a "good place to start", but Professor Loble said there were gaps that needed to be filled to minimise risks.

In a statement sent to the ABC, the WA Department of Education said they were monitoring developments in generative AI.

"Developing an understanding of the ethical use of AI is an important part of the Western Australian Curriculum from pre-primary to year 12.

"Schools with year 11 and 12 students are required to implement a senior secondary assessment policy which provides information to those students, their parents/guardians, and teachers on authentication of student work, including cheating, collusion, plagiarism, appropriation, and unacknowledged use of artificial intelligence applications," the statement said.

In the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), policy on AI cheating and academic integrity is governed by the ACT Board of Senior Secondary Studies (BSSS) alongside the ACT education department.

Each school sector in the ACT has its own policies on the use of AI technology.

An ACT government spokesperson told the ABC in a statement that the number of breaches for cheating across the ACT was extremely small, with about 0.1 per cent of all assessments having recorded academic integrity issues.

"These issues include but are not limited to the use of AI," the statement said.

"Assessment in all schools is externally reviewed twice yearly through system moderation days, with schools provided with targeted written feedback about the assessment in each course, focusing on elements such as validity, academic integrity, and quality," the statement said.

Longitudinal mapping is also undertaken to monitor risk, and support mechanisms have been put in place to assist schools to identify and maintain improvement, the statement added.

Like WA, education departments in Tasmania and the Northern Territory have adopted the federal government's framework.

The NT Council of Government School Organisations tracks AI deployment to balance equitable student access against risks such as bias and diminished human connection and has oversight.

AI use is permitted under the AI framework, but it empowers individual public schools to develop their own localised processes to meet territory expectations, according to the NT Department of Education.

The Tasmanian Department for Education, Children and Young People (DECYP) regulates AI tools via risk assessments, permitting low-risk systems like Microsoft Copilot for staff while restricting unvetted student apps, alongside managing recent safety and deepfake controversies.

A DECYP spokesperson told the ABC in a statement that AI apps and websites have been blocked for all students on DECYP devices and networks.

"The Department has policies, procedures and support resources for principals and teachers related to generative AI in schools, including an academic integrity guide," the statement said.

There are no take-home exams used as part of the end-of-year external assessment program for year 11 and 12 senior secondary courses in Tasmania.

Low-risk approaches can work to the student's benefit, but it's important not to miss out on using AI as an enhanced learning tool, Professor Loble said.

"What we are seeing now is widespread use of AI by teachers and students.

"So it's become so much more integral," she said.

Professor Loble called for consensus among state departments on AI in schools.

I was not surprised by recent news that online classes have become swamped by artificial intelligence cheating , eroding academic integrity. From the second I heard about “asynchronous” studies, I thought of the word’s negative connotations: not happening or existing simultaneously, out of sync, allochronic, unsynchronized.

“You have to sign up for the 20-hour Canvas computer course,” my boss had informed me.

“I tried it. That software is too complicated for me and I don’t need it,” I told her. “Other teachers got permission to skip it, so I requested a waiver.”

As a popular college creative writing professor who’d filled up in-person sections every term for 25 years, I worried I was too much of a Luddite to learn new cyber tricks. Yet I’d actually adapted to and enjoyed easy Zoom live video meetings, which mirrored my regular courses. I assumed I’d just get an exemption to avoid the Canvas Learning Management System requirement.

Instead, when I didn’t complete the tutorial, the algorithm canceled my classes. Checking the university’s website, I saw that my list of 50 current students disappeared overnight. While two younger male colleagues were somehow excused from the cyber course prerequisite, I was dismissed after a quarter of a century of service, and I was distraught.

Reading about the 8.63 million workers who have been laid off this year reminded me of the shock I felt. I couldn’t afford the lost income. My husband needed surgery that year and we weren’t sure if he could keep working. Plus I’d loved teaching, and for years my employer had offered me praise, awards and touted the high return-student ratio I’d helped to build. I’d never planned to retire or change my course load.

I’d adapted when the Covid-19 pandemic closed our brick-and-mortar building and gave middle managers and commercial consultants more authority. Admittedly technophobic, I had students help me recreate my in-person classes with Zoom, the platform used by 90% of U.S. colleges. For two semesters, I dressed up to teach from my living room laptop, receiving excellent evaluations. Why switch to complex, problematic software? “If it ain’t broke don’t fix it,” I told my boss.

Researching the asynchronicity the institution was promoting, I saw it involved pre-recorded lectures, no live meetings and homework submitted by email 24/7 — no personal interactions. Although the software has taken over 41% of the U.S. education market , it isn’t user-friendly. Every user I knew complained it was inconsistent, illogical, cluttered, had clunky navigation and ignored accessibility standards.

Indeed, the Canvas learning management system, chosen by non-teachers and non-writers, had nothing to do with educating, reading or writing. It was financed by venture capital firms and hedge funds, and aimed to increase profits from overseas clients.

“Why is IT and the administration controlling how I teach successful writing instruction?” I asked my boss, rallying against the corporatization of academia. Indeed, the Canvas learning management system, chosen by non-teachers and non-writers, had nothing to do with educating, reading or writing. It was financed by venture capital firms and hedge funds , and aimed to increase profits from overseas clients. Like the billionaire geniuses who created social media that wound up depressing, dumbing down and dehumanizing civilization, the motives of these companies were purely financial.

They were pushing the antithesis of the intimate learning style my literary program had once promoted. A simple Google search of this management software continues to show on-going issues due to outages, ransomware breaches , cyberattacks and tech glitches that caused global classes and exams to need rescheduling.

“You can use Zoom on Canvas,” I was told.

But why would I? Changing my live, synchronous video classes could ruin the miraculous process, where students read their personal essays aloud, critique each other, bring in revisions, meet with newspaper and magazine editors for question-and-answer sessions, then publish their work. Hands-on instruction offers guidance, monitoring and inspiration. The human interaction, back-and-forth questions and follow-ups are essential to keep their stories authentic and anti-AI — a system that is proving to be detrimental to teaching writing skills .

Telling a colleague that the software was too anonymous and complex for me, he suggested that I “pay an IT guy to do it.” Since my tech guy made house calls for $100 an hour, it would cost me $2000 to have him run the 20-hour course so I could keep a low-paying gig using a process that could wind up hurting my instruction.

Still, I actually considered this — until I read a quote by author Erica Williams Simon: “Don’t ever attach yourself to a person, a place, a company, an organization, or a project. Attach yourself to a mission, a calling, or a purpose only. That’s how you keep your power and your peace.” Reading those words, I realized I had to be more loyal to myself than to the bureaucratic institution whose judgement I no longer trusted.

A freelancer by day, I’d appreciated teaching’s miraculous equation: I did my job, they paid me the first of every month. But after years of fighting for my own bylines, my ambition now was to help my students thrive, make a living and not repeat my mistakes. The steady checks from the university took the pressure off my pages as they championed my books with launch events in their auditoriums, sharing good reviews on their vast website. I debated if I was wrong to care more about pleasing my students — who were there only temporarily to finish two or four-year degrees — than my higher ups in permanent positions with power over me.

After 23 years of struggle and 60 rejections, I’d sold a hardcover memoir to Random House that led to a series of books. Education, my second love, was worth rethinking too.

The day my classes were deleted in 2021, I did an emergency phone shrink session where my therapist reminded me that with stints as a poet, novelist and journalist, I was well-versed at reinvention. After 23 years of struggle and 60 rejections, I’d sold a hardcover memoir to Random House that led to a series of books. Education, my second love, was worth rethinking too.

Since my teaching method focused on getting published, I’d already offered thousands of former students continued support in a Facebook group. After I lost my longtime gig, I decided to launch my own private computer course, based on strategies I’d perfected for decades. If only a few students enrolled, I’d still teach at a loss until I gained momentum. Posting social media fliers for free, I was taken aback when 80 people of all levels and backgrounds signed up for my first session, from ages 14 to 90. It was exhilarating as strangers and former pupils popped in, from India to Brazil to Ukraine to a block away from where I lived. For some it was before sunrise; others stayed up well past midnight in their time zone. For those who’d insisted that only self-paced classes would attract the market share of international business, the people taking my classes ironically spanned 50 countries.

I revised the syllabus to accommodate the expanding model. When there was an issue, I scheduled seminars, makeup sessions and phone office hours at different times to supplement the meetings and assignments. Because of the popularity of the virtual course, I was able to give scholarships to those who’d studied with me in the past but couldn’t afford the sequel, as a way to help see their projects through.

The results were stunning. A California high schooler who broke into top newspapers was offered a full scholarship to Stanford. An undergrad became a magazine staff writer and received a free ride to Columbia’s MFA program. A Michigan teacher’s first essay led to three bestselling novels from Farrar, Straus and Giroux. A single mother from Trinidad landed a six-figure deal for a Random House memoir. I laughed when a protégé called me a digital nomad in the gig economy, like him. A few thanked me with national clips lauding my virtual teaching venture.

I was surprised when, post-Covid, my old university offered me my in-person teaching job back. By then I was making six times my old salary. Additionally, hearing of the institution’s employee strikes, dismissals and downsizing due to lower enrollments, I respectfully declined. I was more secure in my own domain. After all, I’d never lay myself off, push any convoluted apps down my own throat, replace me with AI or let students use chatbots to supplant themselves.

Now I teach one in-person course a term at a different college. Other nights I’m still Zooming, setting the rules and opening the gates, grateful to my former employer for helping me develop a personal method of teaching that still has legs 30 years later.

Turns out I hadn’t flunked technology after all. In my fifth decade, I’d found a web-learning technique that was workable and empowering. All that’s needed is a laptop, students, and a teacher who shows up at the same time.

title: The Results of Middle and High School Students Using AI Are Extremely Ominous
content:

author: Frank Landymore
clean_content:
New research gives us a grim portrait of how rampant AI usage is affecting young students’ academic performance and learning.

In a study that tracked nearly 27,000 students in China between the ages of 12 and 18 (grades 7-12), around 80 percent reported using AI models like DeepSeek and ByteDance’s Doubao. The remaining 20 percent, who abstained from using AI, formed the control group.

What the researchers from Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong found, as reported by The Economist , point to an alarming trend. After six months, the homework scores of students who used AI rose by 18 percent across all subjects, while the time it took them to complete each assignment fell from 64 minutes to 45 minutes on average — a 30 percent reduction.

But were they really learning, or were they using AI as a crutch to breeze through the assignments? This is where the findings get ominous: the AI-using students earned scores on monthly exams that were 20 percent lower than their classmates who didn’t use the tech.

This upends decades of conventional wisdom. It used to be the case that students who got good homework grades tended to do well on their exams, too. Now it’s the opposite: it’s these supposed best performers who end up doing the worst when it’s time to bust out the blue books.

To those on the ground, this likely doesn’t come as a surprise. A Brown University professor, for example, noticed this academic year that his students did suspiciously well on a take-home midterm , with the average score in the high 90s, and half of the students getting perfect grades.

Suspecting that AI had a hand in the phenomenon, he confronted his class about their suspected cheating and changed it so the final exam would be taken in-person. His hunch turned out to almost certainly be correct. The average score on the final collapsed to just 48 percent, when previously the average had never dipped below 65 percent. Dozens of students didn’t even bother to take the final — the majority of them being those who had gotten perfect scores on the midterm.

Other research has explored AI’s cognitive effects on learning. An MIT study published earlier this year found that students who used AI to help write an essay showed lower brain activity compared to the students who didn’t. Alarmingly, the AI group struggled to quote their own essays, and when they were later asked to write a paper without AI help, their brain activity stayed at a reduced level. Mirroring those findings, other studies have showed that AI impairs critical thinking and have associated it with memory loss .

This latest study illustrates academic trends rather than cognitive ones, but it dovetails with what those studies are showing. In addition to the plunging exam scores, it also found that the worst learning losses came in social science subjects, followed by STEM and language courses. Intriguingly, the AI users who took around the same amount of time to complete their homework as non AI users had smaller learning losses, though the losses were still present.

The study also adds to the concerns around AI’s role in grade inflation , which has skyrocketed in recent years. Recent research found that that the percentage of A grades in college courses that were considered vulnerable to AI cheating — which were typically in the humanities and engineering — have surged by 30 percent since the release of ChatGPT.

title: The trick to getting kids to stop trusting AI: Ask it to draw a map of the world
content: Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school aud… [+7502 chars]
author: Jocelyn Gecker, Russ Bynum, The Associated Press
clean_content:
Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school auditorium and talked about inviting AI into the classroom.

The teachers and principals watched as an instructor prompted an AI tool to “create a map of the world.”

The result drew gasps of disbelief and laughter. Projected on a large screen was a map riddled with bizarre errors . Mali was spelled “Mail.” Egypt was identified as “Sopth.” In place of Libya was something simply called “Africa.” Dozens of other countries’ names were misspelled or written in pure gibberish.

“If you ever want kids not to over trust these tools, try the map demo,” said the instructor, Amanda Bickerstaff, founder and CEO of AI For Education, an organization that helps schools draft AI policies and train teachers and students in what she calls safe, ethical and effective use of the technology.

After initially trying to ban AI use, a growing number of U.S. public schools are trying a new strategy: encouraging classroom experimentation, partly so students can see its shortcomings, including generative AI’s notorious tendency to “hallucinate,” or fabricate information.

AI literacy has become a buzzword of this back-to-school season as educators try to strike a balance between equipping students with the skills they need for an AI-driven future while preventing them from outsourcing their thinking to chatbots.

There is no single definition of what AI literacy means, or how it should be taught. Tech giants like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic offer schools training sessions in how to use their AI tools . But for educators, there is a growing consensus that AI literacy is about more than learning how to use generative AI and write good prompts.

“Good AI literacy,” said Rebecca Winthrop, director of the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution, “includes knowing when not to use it.”

Thirty-seven states have now published official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint. South Carolina is not one of them.

So the state’s second-largest school district set out to do it on its own, said Lucas Clamp, deputy superintendent of the 50,000-student Charleston County School District. “It has been a huge endeavor.”

A year ago, the district contacted AI for Education, which helped draft guidance for Chicago Public Schools, Houston and dozens of other districts.

Phase 1 was laying the foundation. The district developed an AI policy, seeking input from teachers, students and parents.

The district organized student focus groups and learned that student AI use was ubiquitous but unguided. Teachers and students said they were navigating the technology on their own and wanted clear rules and instruction.

Studies show a majority of teenagers and teachers nationwide are using AI for schoolwork, but they’re teaching themselves how to use it; very few say they have a technical understanding or have received formal training on how it works.

Schools and parents are eager to avoid mistakes made with social media , where kids were left to explore the online world without learning about addictive algorithms, comparison culture and other downsides that have been linked to a youth mental health crisis and dwindling attention spans.

As the school year begins in Charleston, Phase 2 kicks in: training. Teachers and middle and high schoolers will get a mix of online and in-person instruction on how AI tools work and how to use them effectively.

The student course walks through familiar scenarios — like asking a chatbot to help with a research paper — to show that generative AI might deliver wildly inaccurate information, including made-up studies, with unflinching authority. “Always verify any factual information you get from GenAI, especially for your classwork,” the course advises.

A section on data privacy cautions against sharing personal information with AI tools because conversations can be stored, used for data training and potentially leaked.

High school teacher Ray Knauer attended the summer training and left with “teachable moments” for his AP Research class. He plans to show examples of AI bias and hallucinations to fuel student discussions.

“We’re all trying to figure this out right now: What’s the right balance so we don’t scare students away from AI but don’t encourage them to run to it,” Knauer said. “We have to teach students: You can’t just get an answer and move on. You have to use analytical skills and dig deeper.”

Utah was an early pioneer in taking a statewide approach to AI in education.

In 2024, the board of education named Matt Winters as its AI education specialist, making Utah the first state to create a full-time position overseeing the technology in schools.

Over the past year, Winters led AI training for over 7,000 teachers, almost a third of Utah’s public school instructors. He is helping districts shape AI policies, which they are required by state law to have in place by July 2027.

“There is a clear method from the top in Utah,” said Chris Agnew, director of the Generative AI for Education Hub at Stanford University. “When you’re tackling big change, it’s easier to have coherence if everyone is singing from the same hymn book.”

A handful of other states have since replicated Winters’ post, including Maine, West Virginia and Georgia.

In other states, a patchwork of AI approaches has emerged, with variance from one school district to another. Extensive AI literacy training requires steep investment, raising concerns that kids in under-resourced districts might not get the same attention.

In Utah, training starts with the basics of how AI works to teach an understanding of AI bias, hallucinations, ethical concerns and data privacy needs, Winters said. Teachers can then pursue additional training on specific tools.

“If I had to give advice: Figure out how to make training accessible to everyone,” said Emma Moss, who oversees AI at the Canyons School District and also led an eight-person team that traveled the state doing over 150 AI literacy trainings. The training was funded by a $500,000 AI literacy grant from a local healthcare provider. “We said, ‘We will come to you.’ Whether you are in a rural area or urban, it didn’t matter.”

The state has also played a key role in procuring AI tools, Winters said. He negotiated data privacy agreements along with discounted prices, which has allowed rural and under-resourced districts to get access.

“Everyone needs to understand what this technology is and how it works,” said Winters, who cautions against blanket bans. “AI literacy is much larger than saying: ‘Don’t use AI.’ It’s about how we can prepare kids for the future.”

Changing adult mindsets is also key, said Kristina Yamada, the state Board of Education’s digital technology specialist.

“I think teachers need to change their mentality about students using AI to cheat,” Yamada said. There has always been cheating, she said. It’s up to teachers to speak students’ language and convince them they can’t rely on AI for all the answers.

For younger kids it means starting to talk about AI early, with conversations like, “People can lie. A program can lie. A robot can lie,” Yamada said. “For older students it’s different: ‘Sure, you can use ChatGPT to write computer code . But when the program stops working, you need to be able to fix it.’”

content: It’s back-to-school season, and Google is getting in on the academic action. The company announced on Wednesday that a dedicated student hub, featuring a suite of AI study tools, will now be availabl… [+3500 chars]

clean_content:
It’s back-to-school season , and Google is getting in on the academic action. The company announced on Wednesday that a dedicated student hub, featuring a suite of AI study tools , will now be available on its Gemini AI assistant and through Google Search.

The dedicated study hub can be found within Gemini and contains a suite of tools, including a study notebook , customized flash cards and practice quizzes to help with research and assignments.

According to Google, this set of learning tools is meant to act as a virtual study partner.

“By streamlining administrative study tasks or digital clutter, like organizing files and sifting through a screen of open tabs, it means students can spend more time and energy engaging with their class material,” a Google spokesperson told CNET.

Students will be able to ask Gemini to dig into a topic they’re researching and then switch tasks while the tool compiles the information in the background. When the report is finished, Gemini will send a notification and be available to discuss the report’s details and participate in a question-and-answer session to help the student better understand the findings.

Students will also be able to chat conversationally with Google Live regarding multi-step research papers to better understand the topic in question.

Other educational features in Gemini include AI-generated 3D simulations, tables and grids, made after the student enters a specific prompt. A student who’s writing a paper on DNA can enter a prompt like “Show me how DNA works in 3D” and be presented with interactive visuals they can use to explore a DNA model.

Students also can generate simulations using Google Search to better understand complex topics. Science students can search for “pH scale” and see visual results in an interactive AI overview.

Stick with AI Mode in Google Search, and you can ask follow-up questions about the topic in question to dig deeper into a subject.

Customized quizzes can now also be created through Search. Students can enter prompts for subjects ranging from science and math to foreign languages. A student preparing for the SAT could ask, “Create a quiz with the most commonly tested vocabulary words to help me prep for the SATs.” Search will then generate a quiz based on the prompt.

Students can upload files like PDFs, images, docs and more to Search, and the platform can create study documents to keep things organized and easy to follow. You can consolidate scribbled notes, ideas from class or feedback from lectures into one-page reports that outline the bullet points.

Google is offering college students in the US a free year of Google AI Pro, which normally costs $20 per month. The plan includes four times higher usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini Spark, Gemini features in apps such as Google Docs and Gmail, Google Health Premium and 5TB of storage.

Google is also bundling Google AI Pro with YouTube Premium for up to 70% off. For more information on Google’s student deals, head here .

Google’s announcement of its new AI study tools comes one day after OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens , a version focused on younger students’ education. As more AI companies enter the education market, Google’s expansion into AI-powered learning could have a significant impact on the space.

That said, the growing use of AI in education has raised questions about where study help ends and cheating begins.

In July, Princeton University began proctoring exams after concerns about the proliferation of AI-related cheating. Many schools have implemented tools for AI detection and imparted strict rules on AI use, while wrestling with how to draw the line between limited use for minor tasks and major ones, such as essay writing.

Students seem unlikely to give up AI entirely, and AI companies will continue to encourage it, but schools will continue to face its various challenges.

title: Teachers Warn That Students Are Losing the Ability to Think as They Lean on AI for Everything

clean_content:
Students across the country are using AI models to complete assignments and write entire essays. Some of this constitutes cheating, but in many cases schools are allowing students to make some use of AI tools.

This is a slippery slope. As some experts argue, any intrusion of automation into the writing process isn’t just threatening students’ composition skills, but their entire ability to think.

“Writing is a technology for thinking,” cognitive psychologist Ronald T. Kellogg told the New York Times in a new essay mulling the consequences of sidestepping the hard work of writing.

Writing, the piece notes, helps develop all sorts of cognitive faculties, including building our working memory, executive planning skills, and our metacognition, or the ability to be aware of your own thinking.

For all the romanticism around writing, it’s also a form of drudgery. Kellogg says that drafting a basic essay is as mentally taxing as digging a ditch is physically exhausting. You have to really rack your brain to find the right word and organize ideas in a way that makes sense to a broader audience. When they’re manifested in the real world, you revise your ideas by going over them yourself or asking for feedback.

Writing, in other words, is inextricable from the labor that goes into it. And so when you bring in a piece of machinery that offers to do the process for you, it’s no longer writing, and by no extension, no longer exercising the brain.

An MIT study earlier this year found that people who used AI while they wrote an essay showed lower brain activity compared to people who didn’t . Moreover, the people who composed with AI struggled to remember a single line from the essays they just produced, with their brain activity staying at a reduced level even when they were later asked to write again without an AI’s help.

As the NYT piece notes, though, few people would willingly dig a ditch, and the same goes for writing. But there’s no part of the writing process than can be offloaded to an AI without some cost, warned Steve Graham, a writing expert and educational psychologist at Arizona State University.

Building off that warning, the NYT ‘s Dana Goldstein pondered: “If writing is thinking, then any part of the struggle that is outsourced to technology amounts to relinquishing some freedom to perceive. How will students ever know what they really think of anything — whether it’s ‘The Crucible’ or AI itself — if they ask a machine to spit out an answer for them?”

Schools and colleges are grappling with how to rein in students’ use of the tech. Some are returning to using pencil and paper to write essays and oral exams. Others are banning digital devices in freshman courses, and Ivy League schools like Princeton University have dropped Honor Code traditions that let students take tests and exams unsupervised.

If there’s a silver lining, it’s that many students have to come to realize on their own that using AI to write an analysis of, for example, assigned literature, is robbing them of their own education.

“You’re not strengthening that muscle by actually analyzing these really hard texts,” a college junior told the NYT . “They’re meant to be hard.”
