clean_content:
Associate professor David Bourget created a program called MATCHA, designed as a walled garden in which users can access word processors and online research materials but not AI tools, for students in a second-year course. Nicole Osborne/The Globe and Mail

As the fall semester begins at universities across Canada, professors are grappling with a fundamental challenge of the artificial-intelligence era: How do you assess students when cheating has never been simpler?

Research essays and other take-home written assignments can be conjured from thin air with a prompt to Claude or ChatGPT.

And ferreting out such subterfuge is hard because many Canadian universities forbid or discourage professors from using AI-detection software, said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

“We ban the use of AI detectors as unethical because they’re not 100 per cent accurate,” Prof. Daley explained, referring to Western’s policy.

Opinion: Universities should stop treating AI as a cheating problem

When cheating is easy and cheaters can’t easily be caught, instructors must get creative. Here is how four professors in different fields at one university are remaking their assignments for the new AI reality.

For the past few years, Western University philosophy professor David Bourget tried to assign essays that were AI-resistant. He asked narrow questions and picked obscure readings that, as far as he knows, stumped early versions of ChatGPT.

But as large language models (LLMs) improved, “all of these techniques stopped working,” Prof. Bourget said. “Then I had to turn around and, like everybody else, rethink how I do things.”

This year, he is running a pilot project where about 130 students enrolled in Introduction to the Philosophy of Mind, a second-year course, will research and write essays in an on-campus computer lab under the watchful eye of a teaching assistant.

Students will bring their own laptops. The supervisors, using QR codes on their phones, will sign the students in to external servers for MATCHA , a software program that Prof. Bourget designed as a walled garden in which users can access word processors and online research materials but not AI tools.

The program, which stands for Modern Authoring Tool for Certified Human Authorship, has other features that record the work that goes into producing an essay, including research notes, early drafts and edits. Prof. Bourget co-founded a company to license the program.

The supervised nature of the lab keeps students from using AI on a secondary device, such as a phone, and typing the results into MATCHA.

As a bonus, the lab will bring students and their teaching assistants together for what would otherwise be a virtual course. Prof. Bourget will be delivering his lectures online.

“My goal,” he said, “is to make cheating hard again.”

Selma Purac, the undergraduate program chair at Western’s Faculty of Information and Media Studies, realized the traditional essay was in peril in the fall of 2023, less than a year after the launch of ChatGPT.

She was marking a batch of 40 papers for a mass communication class she had taught for years. Thirty of the essays were remarkably similar. They read nothing like the student writing she was used to grading. Twenty-eight employed a word that Prof. Purac had never seen in a student essay, one she now recognizes as a favourite of ChatGPT’s. (She declined to reveal the word, saying she’d rather not give away the AI tell.)

Prof. Purac didn’t want to abandon essays. Writing them taught her students to read critically, develop strong arguments and find their voices. “But those skills were being degraded by the way in which my students were using LLMs,” she said.

Instead, Prof. Purac decided to reimagine the essay. Two years ago, she started breaking down her assignments into worksheets. She gave her students time outside of class to conduct research and outline their arguments, including pulling direct quotes from source material. Then, she had them write their essays in class with pen, paper, their worksheets and supervision.

For example, in her third-year course, Children, Advertising and Consumer Culture, she had for years assigned a close reading of an advertisement.

Opinion: The cheating generation is asking us to help them stop

Before LLMs, students selected ads and composed their assignments at home. Now, Prof. Purac distributes a three-and-a-half page worksheet, which must be completed in point form, at least three weeks in advance of a two-hour, in-class writing period.

“I really like the way it demystifies the traditional essay,” she said.

Students studying at Western’s Ivey School of Business know they’ll be expected to use AI in the workplace. So Guneet Kaur Nagpal, who teaches marketing management and digital marketing analytics to undergraduates, had to find a way to teach students to master AI without losing the ability to think critically.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal developed a marketing strategy simulation tool called plAIbook that allowed her students to use generative AI as an assistant in solving business case studies. The program caps the number of prompts students can give AI and sets strict time limits.

The tool garnered positive feedback from faculty and students after it was piloted in 10 sections of a marketing class last spring. Prof. Kaur Nagpal built it as one of Western’s Generative AI teaching fellows. She and two other professors have been seconded to the university’s Centre for Teaching and Learning for two years to develop and assess new ways of teaching with AI.

On top of developing plAIbook, Prof. Kaur Nagpal and her colleagues overhauled some classic assignments. In the pre-ChatGPT era, she gave groups of students 48 hours to compare two legacy brands and develop a marketing plan for the weaker of the two. Now she asks groups to develop marketing plans in 24 hours, using AI, for newly minted brands from sources such as the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter or the start-up incubator Y Combinator.

She also traded a week-long take-home exam for a four-hour, in-class exam with the help of AI. Unfortunately, when she quizzed students orally on the material, she discovered that some who scored well on the written final with AI couldn’t even define simple terms.

“It’s telling and it’s troubling,” she said.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal plans to increase the weight of oral tests this fall.

Western history professor William Turkel was on sabbatical in the 2024-2025 academic year when he realized that generative artificial intelligence was improving at a clip that would force him and his colleagues to teach differently.

He changed the name of his third-year Digital Research Methods class to Digital Research Methods with Artificial Intelligence. He told his students to use AI as much as they liked, including as a virtual teammate for group projects.

But he warned that the standard fare spit out by an LLM would net only an average grade.

If students wanted higher marks, they would have to do something more ambitious. One example: Dispatch an LLM or multiple LLMs to comb through thousands of digitized texts at U.S. presidential libraries, and compare what American leaders said in real time about the Vietnam War to facts that emerged later in the Pentagon papers.

Prof. Turkel is also one of Western’s generative AI teaching fellows. He thinks students are better off embracing the inescapable new technology.

“How many undergrad students become professional historians? One in 100? One in 200?” he said. “The rest of them are going to workplaces where they can’t pretend AI doesn’t exist.”

title: Parents of students with disabilities find private school vouchers come with a catch
content:
CINCINNATI — The meeting with staff members of Cincinnati Christian Schools began with a prayer. Then they told Mike Grimmer and Linda Kelly that their granddaughter could no longer attend the private school. Annabelle Kelly had enrolled there three months earlier, in August 2025, in a program specifically for students who struggle in mainstream classrooms. […]

The post Parents of students with disabilities find private school vouchers come with a catch appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
author: Pepper Stetler
clean_content:
CINCINNATI — The meeting with staff members of Cincinnati Christian Schools began with a prayer. Then they told Mike Grimmer and Linda Kelly that their granddaughter could no longer attend the private school.

Annabelle Kelly had enrolled there three months earlier, in August 2025, in a program specifically for students who struggle in mainstream classrooms. Annabelle, 15, has Rett syndrome, a genetic condition accompanied by significant cognitive and developmental delays. Her grandparents, who took legal custody of Annabelle when she was 5, believed that the small, faith-based setting of CCS would be a better fit than the local public school. She received a voucher from the state through a school choice program specifically for students with disabilities, which authorized paying CCS up to $29,750 for Annabelle to attend tuition-free.

But at the meeting in November, Kelly said, the school’s director of academic support services told her and Grimmer that Annabelle’s physical and educational needs were too extensive for her to continue at CCS. If they wanted her to stay, Annabelle would need an aide to work with her one-on-one, and her grandparents would need to pay the additional cost, roughly $25,000 per year.

Disability advocates warn that as private school voucher programs spread, more parents will find themselves in similar straits. Federal protections for students with disabilities don’t apply to private schools, and neither the schools nor voucher programs like the one Annabelle qualified for are required to inform parents that they waive certain rights when they leave the public school system. When Congress passed legislation last year establishing the nation’s first federal voucher program , it did not include language that disability rights groups had lobbied for that would have required private schools receiving federal funds to follow the law known as the Individuals with Disabilities in Education Act.

“If there are public funds being spent, public protections need to be afforded,” said Chris Roe, director of state policy at the Council of Parent Attorneys and Advocates, a policy advocacy organization that provides training and guidance in special education law. “At the very least, states that provide voucher programs should be required to inform parents of the rights they are giving up.”

Kelly said the decision from CCS came despite the family being transparent about Annabelle’s needs when they applied to the school: They shared medical information, copies of her academic evaluations and her learning plan from the public school she attended. The then-eighth grader attended three trial days at the school before enrolling, and several previous conferences with teachers had gone well, her grandmother said.

“We were blindsided by the school’s decision,” said Kelly.

Raymond Kochis, superintendent of Cincinnati Christian Schools, declined an interview but said in response to written questions that the costs of educating Annabelle exceeded what had been determined initially. “When a student’s needs evolve,” Kochis wrote, “the school works with the family to determine the most appropriate level of support.” (According to Kelly, Annabelle’s needs had not changed, and school officials quickly dismissed any alternative solutions she proposed.)

Related: 10 things to know about Trump’s new school voucher program

Private school voucher programs have proliferated in the United States in the last decade. The number of students with disabilities in these programs has grown too: In the 2025-26 school year, Annabelle was one of more than 200,000 students nationwide either using vouchers meant specifically for students with disabilities or enrolled in the country’s largest voucher programs, compared with more than 180,000 the year prior.

The federal school voucher program goes into effect next year. After failing to persuade Congress to include language stating that voucher programs and participating private schools must comply with IDEA protections, COPAA and other disability rights groups are focused on pressing states that choose to participate in the program to enforce the IDEA even for private schools.

Signed into law in 1975, the IDEA states that everyone ages three to 21 with a disability must be provided a free public education that meets their particular needs. In collaboration with parents, public school districts must develop an individualized education program, or IEP, establishing learning goals and plans appropriate for the student. The law also states that students with disabilities must be taught alongside children without disabilities “to the maximum extent appropriate.” Today, 8 million public school students are served by the IDEA.

While voucher programs like the one Annabelle received, Ohio’s Jon Peterson scholarship, are publicly funded, participating private schools like CCS control their own admissions and enrollment decisions. Students using a private school voucher are considered “ parentally placed ,” and private schools are not required to follow an IEP or uphold any IDEA protections. Families that use these vouchers sacrifice key civil rights afforded by the IDEA, including protection against discrimination and removal from the school based on a disability.

Kelly doesn’t remember, when filling out the scholarship application and enrolling Annabelle at CCS, being told that the rights and protections that apply to students with disabilities in public schools do not extend to private schools. Since students must have an IEP to qualify for the Jon Peterson scholarship, she assumed that the IDEA’s rules and policies would be followed.

In a response to written questions, a spokesperson for Ohio’s Department of Education and Workforce said there are multiple safeguards for students with disabilities who attend private schools. The department’s website never explicitly states that private schools are not required to comply with the IDEA’s mandates and regulations. But it does mention on a page of regulations that if a student is enrolled in a school that is not public, it is “not obligated to provide the child” with a free appropriate public education. Ultimately, the private school is not required to follow the IDEA, and parents have little recourse if the school chooses not to.

However, as states expand their voucher programs, more are aiming to serve students with disabilities. States including Florida, Indiana and Ohio award more voucher money to these students to account for the additional costs of educating them. Texas’ Education Freedom Accounts program gives priority to students with disabilities and their siblings. As of June 2026, more than one in four Texas students awarded a voucher for the coming school year has a documented disability.

Ohio is one of at least nine states that have created voucher programs specifically for students with disabilities. On paper, the policies of Ohio’s Jon Peterson scholarship, established in 2012, seem more rigorous than others. For example, schools receiving scholarship funds are expected to employ staff with special education training and credentials. If a school formally declines to enroll a child, it must provide the scholarship applicant with a reason in writing. Schools receiving scholarship funds are also expected to provide the student’s assigned public school district with records of how the IEP was implemented and how the student is progressing toward its goals. But there are no consequences listed for schools that do not follow these rules.

Data published by the state Department of Education and Workforce suggests that many students only use Jon Peterson scholarships for a short time. In 2025, 8,680 students received a scholarship. Just over half of those students had participated in the program for three years or more. Reasons students might leave the program include transferring to a different voucher program, moving to a different district, graduating, or returning to public school.

Voucher rules for students with disabilities vary dramatically nationwide. For example, Florida’s program for students with disabilities — which has the most participants of any program in the country (140,147 in 2025-26)  — does not require students to have an IEP to access the program: A valid diagnosis from a medical professional is also accepted. Oklahoma’s scholarship for students with disabilities requires participating schools to provide services and accommodations for those students, but it does not require private schools to document IEP implementation or hire appropriately credentialed special education staff.

A January 2026 report by COPAA outlined challenges it said private school choice programs raise for students with disabilities, many due to a lack of regulations and oversight. Most states do not require private schools to keep data on whether they are effectively educating students with disabilities, the report noted, and, according to Roe, states do not have to publish data on voucher programs, which could provide an opportunity for accountability.

Roe, lead author of the report, said these programs might initially appeal to families that  have struggled to get public schools to follow their children’s special education plans. “Parents are enticed by the idea that they don’t have to fight their public school anymore for what they should be getting under the law,” he said. “But then they realize there are few schools that will take a child with nonverbal autism or with Down syndrome.”

Related: Young kids with and without disabilities can learn side by side. One state has instead kept them apart for years

When Kate White, who is now 11, started preschool at her local public school in the suburbs of Cincinnati, her mother, Nicole White, noticed she wasn’t developing many communication skills. Kate has Down syndrome and has had chronic ear and airway complications since birth, which were affecting her ability to learn.

Nicole White worried the local public school couldn’t provide the support Kate needed and began looking around for alternatives. Eventually she found the St. Rita School for the Deaf. When she asked school administrators if they could help a student with Down syndrome who was learning American Sign Language, White recalled, “They said ‘absolutely;’ they didn’t bat an eye.” She enrolled Kate at St. Rita in 2019 with support from the Jon Peterson scholarship. At first, White said, “it was phenomenal.”

But as Kate got older, White wanted a more traditional curriculum for her daughter that emphasized numbers, letters and colors alongside ASL. White was also concerned that the environment at St. Rita did not include students of all learning types and abilities. “I wanted her to be exposed to what the world is like,” she said.

Kate’s IEP called for occupational and physical therapy, but St. Rita eliminated those services before her third year. School administrators told White that school budget cuts were to blame. In 2022, Kate returned to her local public school district, which for her mother seemed like the least bad choice. “I was looking at the students ahead of her at St. Rita’s and there were four students in the graduating class. I didn’t want that for Kate, but I wanted the support that St. Rita’s gave its students. So what do I do? Where do I go?”

In a response to written questions, Angela Frith, president of St. Rita, said that the Jon Peterson scholarship does not cover the full cost of educating a student at the school. Families now have to pay a third-party clinic out of pocket or use private insurance or Medicaid if they want to get occupational and physical therapy on site.

COPAA’s Roe said he worries experiences like White’s will become more common. Private schools meant for students with disabilities can provide valuable support, he said, but students sacrifice an opportunity to learn among nondisabled peers.  “If parents are looking for an inclusive environment, private schools are problematic,” Roe said. “There are a lot of barriers.”

Annabelle did not attend school for several months after CCS did not welcome her back, but eventually Kelly enrolled her in ninth grade at Princeton High School, her local public school. She says Annabelle is happy there. “I made assumptions about Princeton based on what I knew about the school 20 years ago,” Kelly said, “back when special education was completely segregated.”

Her granddaughter is now making progress on her IEP goals, Kelly said. Annabelle reports that her favorite class is gym, which she takes with a diverse group of other high school students. Said Kelly: “Annabelle is now where she needs to be.”

title: OPINION: We’ve been treating college as a career plan, but it’s failing too many students
content:
In one of Denver’s wealthiest suburbs, where median family income tops $150,000 and nearly every kid is expected to go to college, students are now lining up for trade certifications. Their parents aren’t worried; in fact, most of them are championing the move. For decades, Americans have been treating college as a career plan, spurred […]

The post OPINION: We’ve been treating college as a career plan, but it’s failing too many students appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
author: Pat O’Donnell
clean_content:
In one of Denver’s wealthiest suburbs, where median family income tops $150,000 and nearly every kid is expected to go to college, students are now lining up for trade certifications.

Their parents aren’t worried; in fact, most of them are championing the move.

For decades, Americans have been treating college as a career plan, spurred by the “college for all” movement — a decades-long educational and political push that aimed to make a four-year college degree the standard expectation and primary goal for all high school students. The data show that it doesn’t work.

Although 88 percent of college freshmen say getting a good job is “a main reason” they enrolled , more than half of college graduates are underemployed a year out, working jobs that don’t require a degree. A decade later, 45 percent still are.

These aren’t students who dropped out or gave up. They did everything right and still couldn’t find their footing.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter .

The problem isn’t that college doesn’t matter. It’s that college has become an expensive career exploration strategy, with no exit ramp for students who may need one. No wonder confidence in higher education is slipping.

It does not have to be that way. The opportunities for those without a four-year degree are exploding. The U.S. faces an annual shortage of nearly 712,000 workers with certificates and associate degrees in fields where workers without a bachelor’s degree can earn upward of $55,000 a year, Georgetown University’s Center on Education and the Workforce found.

The jobs are there. The pathways to them are not.

One course correction to the “college for all” movement is playing out in Denver’s Cherry Creek neighborhood, where high school students are participating in a program that offers real-world skill building and trade certifications, ranging from computer science to aviation to health science.

Students split their time between the program and their regular classes, with transportation provided to and from their home high school. When I visited the program, I met three students who were all headed down different paths: One intended to pursue a bachelor’s degree for engineering. Another was interested in an associate degree for construction management. The third was excited to earn an industry credential to become a chef.

The common thread they shared was that they were all locked in on their career paths. They had real experience in the field from the Cherry Creek Innovation Campus and clarity that they were moving in the right direction. Most Cherry Creek students still end up enrolling in college, but they do so with direction and purpose.

Georgetown’s ROI data shows that associate degrees and certificates often deliver a higher return on investment than bachelor’s degrees in the first 10 years after completion, although the data also shows that ROI for bachelor’s degrees pulls ahead at 15 years and then widens the gap thereafter.

That nuance matters: For students who need economic traction now, shorter-term credentials can be the smarter first move.

The “college for all” movement, while well-intentioned, has created a false binary between academic preparedness and workforce skills. Programs like Cherry Creek’s not only improve engagement in high school and college-going rates but also offer a more defined pathway into the workforce.

In my former role as CEO of a public charter school foundation, I was fortunate to be able to support the journeys of hundreds of students from college acceptance to college graduation. But it’s the journeys that didn’t work out as planned that have stuck with me the most.

Take, for example, the experience of a student from Oakland who I met through our career coaching program. She grew up wanting to be a nurse and had enrolled in a nursing program for a bachelor of science degree, diligently setting out on her long-awaited career path and becoming the first in her family to go to college.

But she had never been exposed to real-world healthcare or nursing work in high school, and she got two years into her program before realizing nursing wasn’t for her. She transferred to a community college, worked at a fast-food restaurant, and went through what she now calls “a lost phase.”

Two years gone; not because she failed, but because the system never gave her a chance to figure out her path before she enrolled. What’s worse, most students in this situation are left saddled with student loan debt. We can do better.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected

If we want to meet the needs of a rapidly shifting economy — one in which college graduates can’t find good-paying jobs and employers can’t find graduates with the right skill set — we need to stop treating college and career readiness as separate tracks.

It’s time for families to stop picturing shop class when they hear “vocational training.” That’s a stigma born from a past of underfunded, poorly constructed programs that filtered kids out of opportunities rather than into them.

Today those programs look vastly different. Take, for example, nonprofit Ridgeline’s maritime career exploration program for high school students in the San Francisco Bay Area, where rising 11th and 12th graders get hands-on paid career experience in a variety of maritime fields such as ship engineering, ferry and container ship operations and port management. Some maritime jobs require apprenticeships; others require a degree from nearby Cal Poly Maritime Academy. Many pay six figures.

It’s time to set a new standard: Every high school should offer students the opportunity to graduate with a diploma and an industry-recognized credential or documented work experience.

Honor the choice to skip college while giving those who want a degree more purpose. Everyone wins.

Patrick O’Donnell is CEO and co-founder of Ridgeline, a nonprofit that connects Bay Area students from underserved communities to high-wage, high-demand careers.

title: Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students
content:
Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students Olivia.sanchez Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM The enrollment growth has been accompanied by growing pains, leaders say, as they figure out how to house, feed and teach more students. Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

The enrollment growth has been accompanied by growing pains, leaders say, as they figure out how to house, feed and teach more students.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
author: Olivia.sanchez
clean_content:
Morgan State University’s enrollment grew by 42 percent between 2019 and 2024, according to federal data.

Concerns about enrollment plague college leaders across the country, who fear what will happen to their institutions as fewer 18-year-olds graduate from high school and fading faith in higher education deters others. But even as many predominantly white, regional and private colleges struggle to fill seats, some historically Black colleges and universities are seeing heightened—in some cases record—interest, applications and enrollment.

As one expert put it, the increased interest in HBCUs can be explained by a long-standing message on a digital billboard on a Baltimore campus: “Morgan State University, where Black lives have always mattered.”

Across the country, 42 of 101 HBCUs grew their enrollment between 2019 and 2024, according to federal data. Many increased head count significantly in that period: Howard University grew by 50 percent, Morgan State by 42 percent, Virginia State University by 27 percent and Elizabeth City State University by 23 percent. Since then, enrollment has continued to climb, according to several colleges that provided enrollment figures to Inside Higher Ed . (Some predominantly white institutions have also seen unexpected enrollment gains .)

Not all HBCUs have been so lucky. A few have maintained relatively stable enrollment, while others faced major enrollment declines and, in the case of St. Augustine’s University in North Carolina, serious financial trouble and bankruptcy .

But among those seeing an upswing, experts said a combination of factors is driving the interest. For one thing, students are growing more aware of HBCUs—thanks to high-profile HBCU alumni such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and the ever-growing use of social media to document campus life. At the same time, students may be deterred from predominantly white institutions for a number of reasons, including acts of racist violence like the 2020 murder of George Floyd , the Supreme Court’s ban on the consideration of race in admissions and the Trump administration’s campaign against all things diversity, equity and inclusion .

“Seeing this on display really calls us to understand what we call ‘home’ and where we are thriving—in environments that were created for us and that are foundational to our identities,” said Leslie U. Ekpe, a professor of higher education at East Texas A&M University. “We talk about belonging in higher education and how critical it is to one’s well-being and success, and I think HBCUs have paved the way to show that Black students are welcome, they’re celebrated.”

Ekpe, who researches minority-serving institutions, said heightened interest in HBCUs serves as a reminder that “we should have never been looking at HBCUs through a deficit lens.”

Howard University’s student body grew by 50 percent between 2019 and 2024, federal data shows.

Michael A. McCoy for The Washington Post/Getty Images

But more students means more pressure on HBCUs to accommodate them. Jorge Burmicky, a professor of higher education leadership and policy studies at Howard University, said that as enrollment grows, HBCU leaders must consider the demand on faculty and staff to meet students’ needs.

Students need to be connected with advising and tutoring, gain entry to required classes, get help from financial aid officers when necessary, and access mental health services in a timely manner, Burmicky said. As part of a separate research project, Burmicky recently interviewed faculty and staff from six HBCUs, many of whom reported struggling to meet student demand as enrollment at their institutions grew.

“It’s fine for us to celebrate growing enrollment—for a lot of HBCUs that’s been a blessing. But equally as important is making sure that we are investing in the capacity so that we’re not so stretched thin," Burmicky said. “Because the reality is that it doesn’t just hurt faculty and staff, it also hurts the student experience.”

Kara Turner, senior vice president of enrollment management and student success at Morgan State, said the university’s enrollment growth can be attributed not just to the growing interest in HBCUs in general, but also to her institution’s concerted recruiting effort.

During the pandemic, university officials realized they could reach more students using virtual recruitment sessions and campus tours, she said. Eventually they hired a recruiter based in the Midwest to expand the university’s geographical reach.

The effort paid off: Enrollment exploded from 7,151 students in 2019 to 12,477 in 2026. But that rapid growth has created new challenges.

In the last few years, the university has built three new residence halls (two of which are open now) and remodeled several others. To fill the gaps, the university leased units from nearby apartment complexes so that students could still get their housing through Morgan; others are being temporarily housed in hotels until the new residence halls open, Turner said.

“Of course there are growing pains when you grow and you grow fast. But the university has been nimble,” Turner said. “We wanted the students. The students were interested and we wanted them and so we said, ‘All right, we’re going to figure this out.’”

North Carolina A&T University, which grew from 13,300 students in 2021 to 15,713 this fall, also put students up in hotels as a new residence hall was under construction.

Beyond housing, university leaders have had to consider how their swelling student body can get their financial aid and register for classes on time, said Dawn M. Nail, the university’s interim associate vice provost for enrollment management. The university moved the treasurer, registrar and financial aid offices into one building to make the process more efficient.

The pressure on HBCUs has manifested in different ways. Howard University disenrolled 502 students over the summer and then re-enrolled about 200 , after officials said the students hadn’t met their payment deadline. Keyana Scales, Howard University’s senior vice president for enrollment management, told WJLA News 7 that it was a matter of reduced resources. A spokesperson from Howard declined to answer questions about enrollment growth for this article.

At some HBCUs, the enrollment figures do not necessarily reflect the extent of their increased popularity. For example, Spelman College in Atlanta has seen such a rise in applications that the admissions rate went from 51 percent to 19 percent in the last five years, largely because leaders have chosen to keep enrollment relatively stable.

“There’s a real energy to it. A more geographically diverse and competitive applicant pool means more perspectives in the classroom, even as we stay intentional about our size,” Chelsea Holley, Spelman’s director of admissions, said in an email.

Holley said the college is building two residence halls because they want to accommodate all the Spelman undergraduates who choose to live on campus for all four years.

“Our goal isn’t to become huge,” Holley said. “We’re a small liberal arts college, and we want to expand the resources that support students throughout their time here, not the number of seats.”

Byline(s) Emma Whitford Texas Professor Suspended for 16 Months Without Recourse
Emma Whitford Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

Clyde Barrow and his lawyer have repeatedly asked for updates and details on his case and have been met with silence and redirects at all levels.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
author: Emma Whitford
clean_content:
Barrow said he hasn’t heard anything more from UT Rio Grande Valley officials since October.

Inside Higher Ed | Clyde Barrow | Gabriel V. Cardenas/AFP/Getty Images

For the past 16 months, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley political science professor Clyde Barrow has been barred from his classroom, office and campus.

To this day, he has yet to learn why exactly the university placed him on what he considers an “indefinite suspension,” though he believes it has to do with his vocal and frequent criticism of campus leadership, he said. The American Association of University Professors and the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression have also asked the university for answers on Barrow’s case and received little to no response.

Barrow was placed on paid administrative leave May 15, 2025, while the university investigated “allegations of possible [rules] violations” and “inappropriate conduct,” according to the email notice from College of Liberal Arts Dean José Dávila-Montes, which Barrow shared with Inside Higher Ed .

In the email, Dávila-Montes noted the “action is not disciplinary in nature” and didn’t include any details about rules Barrow was accused of having violated or what “inappropriate conduct” might have referred to. When Barrow followed up, Dávila-Montes declined to answer his questions and directed him to human resources, Barrow said.

“They’re calling it a paid investigative leave, but it’s actually an indefinite suspension,” he said. “One of the things I’ve asked many, many times—and my attorney has asked many, many times—is have any complaints been filed against me? And up to this point, there has not been a single complaint filed by a student, a staff member or a faculty member.”

Over the next several months, Barrow participated in a couple of interviews related to the investigation, and in September 2025, he received a report that detailed dozens of email exchanges in which Barrow was critical of department leadership or policy. In emails and during meetings, Barrow spoke openly against a new policy that he said increased faculty workloads and was implemented without adequate faculty input. He also criticized the provost’s “unilateral” installment of new evaluation standards, as well as the appointment of Dongkyu Kim as then-interim director of the School of Political Science, Public Affairs, Legal and Security Studies. Faculty favored an external search, but the provost chose Kim, who was leading what was then the political science department.

Barrow was critical of Kim. For example, in one April 2025 email to Kim and two others, Barrow wrote that he had “heard many faculty complaints about department meetings” from colleagues, including that the meetings had become “unfocused, undisciplined, and disorderly” under Kim’s leadership and that they did not follow Robert’s Rules of Order, as dictated by the department’s bylaws.

“It is also widely recognized that university policies are routinely violated and shared governance is replaced by a dictatorial style, which ignores the sound advice of faculty,” Barrow wrote in the email to Kim. “The complaints about Department meetings are about the poor quality of leadership and meeting management … The complaints, Mr. Kim, are about YOU.”

Kim did not respond to Inside Higher Ed ’s request for comment Wednesday. In a statement, UT Rio Grande Valley spokespeople said the university “is following its established policies and processes regarding this personnel matter. Because the matter remains ongoing, the university will not comment further.”

University officials told Barrow his emails amounted to “inappropriate behavior” and “professional misconduct,” and that by criticizing Kim and the new policies, he had “challenged the dean,” Barrow said. After receiving the report, he asked for a decision on his case.

“I said, ‘OK, the investigation is over. You’ve issued your report. The dean is now obligated to make a decision, and you have three options under your own policies: You reinstate me and find that there’s nothing here, you issue a sanction less than termination or you start termination proceedings,’” Barrow said. “But the response was ‘The investigation is still underway.’”

Barrow is uncertain as to why he was singled out for suspension—his opinions of the new policies and college leadership are shared by colleagues, he said. College of Liberal Arts faculty members—in groups and then as a whole—wrote at least three letters to Dean Dávila-Montes over the past year with their concerns about the workload and evaluation policies, according to emails Barrow shared with Inside Higher Ed . In August, the UT Rio Grande Valley AAUP chapter sent a letter to Interim Provost Can Saygin, stating that “major academic decisions are too often being made without meaningful faculty consultation while simultaneously increasing the administrative and instructional burdens placed upon faculty members.”

“They think I’m a ringleader or something,” Barrow said of administrators. “I think [my suspension] is also to send the message: If we can take him out without any due process and without any legitimate charge against him, we can do this to any of you.”

Barrow said he hasn’t heard anything more from university officials since October. In the meantime, he’s been working with an attorney paid for by FIRE’s Faculty Legal Defense Fund. A couple of weeks ago, his lawyer reached out to the University of Texas system office for an update.

“Once again, crickets. Dead silence. No response at all,” Barrow said. It was the system office’s nonresponse that prompted him to go public with his case.

The Texas American Association of University Professors, as well as the AAUP national office, has been advocating for Barrow since last summer. In July 2025, the AAUP wrote to UT Rio Grande Valley President Guy Bailey to “urge that the administration immediately rescind the suspension imposed upon Professor Barrow” until he is afforded a hearing before faculty, which has not yet happened, Barrow said. That same month, in a letter to Dávila-Montes, then–President of the Texas AAUP Brian Evans wrote to “convey our concern” about the treatment of Barrow and called on the university for more information about the allegations against him.

Barrow assumes university officials are hoping he’ll give up. But he plans to keep fighting, he said.

“I’m not a slacker. I’m not dead wood. I’ve got 13 books published—in fact, I’ve published three books while I’ve been on suspension,” he said. “It’s a policy of intimidation and threats to quiet faculty, because the … issues with evaluation standards, workload, appointments—that’s going on across the whole campus.”

The killing of Charlie Kirk on Sept. 10, 2025, during an event at Utah Valley University was witnessed by thousands of people.

Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images News/Getty Images

Charlie Kirk’s family announced a wrongful death notice Wednesday, paving the way for a potential lawsuit against Utah Valley University officials, who, they allege, did not provide proper security at the outdoor event where Kirk was killed on Sept. 10, 2025, the Associated Press and other news organizations reported .

A rooftop sniper fatally shot Kirk at a university-approved event hosted by his conservative student organization, Turning Point USA. Kirk’s estate and heirs filed the notice against the university, its former president, its police department and the state of Utah, alleging that the shooting “came against a well-known backdrop of risk” and was the result of a “series of stunning failures and reckless decisions.”

“Those decisions ultimately rendered Mr. Kirk helpless to the rooftop shooter in an assassination that could have been avoided had the UVU Parties only taken reasonable steps to plan and oversee a safe event,” the notice reads.

It is dated Sept. 9—a day shy of the one-year anniversary of Kirk’s death, which marks the statute of limitations for signaling a potential lawsuit. Under Utah law , a wrongful death lawsuit must be filed within two years of the death.

The notice states that students had flagged concerns about easy access to surrounding rooftops and that the risk of such a shooting “should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year.”

A review conducted by the Associated Press following the incident showed that UVU did not fly a drone over the event, which drew about 3,000 attendees, nor did it conduct bag checks or use metal detectors—practices that AP noted are standard safeguards at major public events.

A UVU spokesperson told the AP that the university was aware of the notice and would address it in a manner “consistent with our established processes.” The news organization also contacted the Utah Attorney General’s Office, which said it does not comment on potential litigation.

title: When Basic Needs Go on Credit
content:
When Basic Needs Go on Credit Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM New Trellis Strategies research finds students with unpaid credit card balances experience greater financial strain and difficulty concentrating on schoolwork. Byline(s) Joshua Bay When Basic Needs Go on Credit
Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

New Trellis Strategies research finds students with unpaid credit card balances experience greater financial strain and difficulty concentrating on schoolwork.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
author: Joshua.Bay
clean_content:
Nearly nine in 10 student cardholders surveyed by Trellis Strategies reported using credit cards for basic needs.

For some college students, covering basic needs means taking on debt. Some put expenses such as food, housing and transportation on credit cards, and many carry unpaid balances as they manage the costs of college. New research from Trellis Strategies suggests that financial strain can follow students into the classroom, making it more difficult to focus on their studies.

The data comes from the postsecondary research and consulting firm’s 2025 Student Financial Wellness Survey , which drew more than 65,000 responses from undergraduates at 153 institutions in 23 states, including over 32,000 credit card users. It found that 54 percent of respondents reported using a credit card in 2025, up from 43 percent in 2018.

Fewer than half of student cardholders (47 percent) pay their balance in full each month, the survey showed. Among those carrying a balance, 88 percent said they worried about covering basic monthly expenses, compared with 61 percent of those who pay in full. Some 60 percent of students carrying unpaid balances also reported difficulty concentrating on schoolwork due to financial stress , compared with 43 percent of those who pay their balances in full.

Bryan Ashton, managing director at Trellis Strategies and co-author of the report, said the findings highlight the financial pressures students can face as the cost of living rises while their options for borrowing to cover expenses outside of tuition remain limited.

“We have limitations on what we can do with student loans, especially federal student loans, because of caps,” Ashton said. “But when indirect costs go up—cost of living, housing, food, transportation—we don’t really see the ability for students to increase borrowing without going to the private market. So sometimes credit cards become the one way that students can close that indirect-cost gap.”

Basic needs on credit: The report found that 88 percent of student cardholders reported using credit cards for basic needs such as food, housing and transportation.

While 75 percent of student cardholders reported paying their credit card bills on time, 14 percent said they struggled to do so. Among students who do not pay their balances in full each month, that share rises to 31 percent.

Ashton said using a credit card to pay for basic needs is not necessarily a problem. The bigger concern is what happens when students cannot pay off those expenses and begin carrying revolving debt from month to month.

“The bigger challenge is the number that are not then able to pay off that expense,” Ashton said. “As you get into these revolving credit situations, one of the concerns that we have is ‘What is the credit limit attached to these? When will we run out of that opportunity?’ And then, secondarily, the higher [annual percentage rate] that students are paying to finance those expenses during that period of time.”

Alexandra Penrose, research analyst at Trellis Strategies and co-author of the report, said financial pressures do not remain separate from students’ academic lives.

“When we struggle to fully pay off things in life, it then automatically bleeds into our academic work and studies,” Penrose said. “It’s really hard to separate financial pressures from what students are doing in school.”

Among students using credit cards for basic needs, 58 percent expressed concern about their ability to cover monthly expenses, and roughly one-third said their overall debt felt unmanageable.

As interest accumulates on unpaid credit card balances, Ashton said, students can find themselves increasingly struggling to catch up, which can take a mental toll.

“We see that with credit card utilization, too, because that interest compounds so quickly that the inability to catch up can drive some of the anxiety and depression we see in students.”

Addressing financial strain: The report notes that helping students better understand how consumer credit works, including responsible use and repayment expectations, can reduce the risk of debt accumulating to unmanageable levels.

Ashton noted that institutions often allow students to pay tuition with credit cards. While that can be a routine way for some students to finance their education, he said credit card payments can also signal financial strain. Institutions could provide students with information about credit and repayment when they choose to pay tuition by card, he said.

Colleges can also help students reduce their reliance on credit cards for basic needs by connecting them with public benefits that can offset the costs of food, housing and other necessities, he added.

“Continuing to educate on the role of interest and what it means to use credit is important and something that we’ve gotten away from on campuses over the last couple decades,” Ashton said.

Penrose said institutions can offer lower-cost alternatives to credit cards, including payment plans, while also embedding financial education into courses to help students understand how to manage their expenses.

“When students use these high-interest credit card options to pay for their educational expenses, it should be a signal for institutions that there is a need that needs to be addressed for students to successfully go through college,” Penrose said.

title: 2 in 3 Harvard Professors Say AI Has a Negative Impact on Class
content:
2 in 3 Harvard Professors Say AI Has a Negative Impact on Class Emma Whitford Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Emma Whitford 2 in 3 Harvard Professors Say AI Has a Negative Impact on Class
Emma Whitford Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
author: Emma Whitford
clean_content:
Most Harvard professors now have explicit policies about how and when AI can be used in their classrooms; only 3.5 percent said they didn’t have any such policy.

Nearly two-thirds of Harvard University faculty members said artificial intelligence has had a “somewhat negative” or “very negative” effect on their courses, according to a recent survey of more than 460 professors in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences conducted by The Harvard Crimson , Harvard’s student newspaper. Last year, 42 percent of faculty said the same.

Most Harvard professors now have explicit policies about how and when AI can be used in their classrooms—only 3.5 percent said they didn’t have any such policy, down from 10 percent the year prior. At the same time, only 4 percent of professors “entirely permit” AI use in class, down from 8 percent last year, the Crimson reported. About a quarter of professors prohibit all AI use in class, up from 20 percent last year.

Harvard leaders have recently leaned into AI. Earlier this month, Harvard College Dean David Deming suggested that professors accept or encourage AI use in writing and project-heavy courses. President Alan Garber praised AI use for research during an address on the first day of classes.

According to the survey, social science faculty most often allow AI use in class—84 percent said they permit at least some AI in their courses, compared with 79 percent of science and engineering faculty and 63 percent of arts and humanities faculty.

Nearly nine in 10 faculty members reported receiving student work that they knew or believed was produced using AI—though only 64 percent reported feeling “somewhat or very confident” in their ability to distinguish between AI-generated and student-created work, the Crimson reported. Only 12 percent of faculty respondents said they referred cases of unauthorized AI use to the honor council this past year, up slightly from 10 percent the year prior.

title: Parents Are Bringing AI to the IEP Meeting. How Should Teachers Respond?
content: Using AI in IEP meetings can benefit parents and teachers – if done correctly.
author: Adam Stone
clean_content:
Using AI in IEP meetings can benefit parents and teachers – if done correctly.

Credit: Frame Stock Footage / Shutterstock

EDITOR’S NOTE: This article has been updated to clarify language about educator response.

The individualized education program (IEP) process generates a big stack of papers, full of terminology that parents may not understand. In response, some parents have begun using artificial intelligence to better understand IEPs and prepare for teacher meetings. Kimberly Morris, who taught pre-K through the 2025-26 school year, saw this firsthand.

Morris would set school goals in the IEP, “and some parents would then utilize AI as a way to create a home goal,” she says.

Morris, who is now a curriculum and instruction specialist supporting early childhood learning at Unlocking Children’s Potential of Central Florida, didn’t mind that parents were using AI to align home efforts with school goals. But as the conversation around AI use transparency grows in classrooms, some wonder whether parents should disclose if they used AI to prepare for an IEP meeting.

Concerned parents might use AI in several ways during the IEP process, says Elizabeth Laird, director of equity and civic technology at the Center for Democracy and Technology. “A parent might turn to AI to learn more about the process and what their rights are, what their child’s rights are,” she notes.

Laird thinks that’s not necessarily a bad thing. “AI can play a role in democratizing access to information about the process itself, as well as being a starting point for thinking about what types of accommodations parents may want to ask about,” she reasons.

For many parents, “just because you’re a parent of a child with a disability doesn’t mean you automatically understand all of these things related to your child’s IEP,” says Olivia Coleman, an assistant professor in the School of Teacher Education at theUniversity of Central Florida. “They’re using it to translate the jargon, any acronyms. It’s helping them to draft questions.”

Parents are putting their child’s IEP into AI models “and then having it put it into plain language, like, ’What is this thing and what does it mean?’” says Coleman, who is also a co-principal investigator at the Center for Innovation, Design, and Digital Learning.

Morris, the curriculum and instruction specialist, sees an upside to parents using AI in IEP meetings. “They can become more of a team member alongside the teacher, occupational therapist, physical therapist and speech therapist,” she says.

But there are risks. For example, when a parent’s AI-generated contribution to the meeting sprawls to 20 or 30 pages, “it’s going to take a teacher the majority of their day just to read through a request,” says Phyllis Wolfram, executive director of the Council of Administrators of Special Education. “It will slow down the process.”

“AI is not an IEP expert,” Laird adds, noting that the AI’s outputs can be inaccurate. With that in mind, she counsels teachers and parents to reflect together on the AI’s findings. A key aspect of the IEP process, she notes, “is its emphasis on bringing different subject matters together to collaborate, to identify what is the best path forward for an individual child.”

Here’s where federal law enters the picture. The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) provides privacy protections for parents regarding their children’s education while the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) offers additional privacy protections for students receiving special education.

With FERPA and IDEA as the legal backdrop, parents should not put identifiable personal data like medical diagnoses and legal documents into AI. The tool could potentially train on that data, which risks that information becoming publicly visible. The data also may be at risk of being exposed in a security breach, if the AI provider gets hacked.

Some argue that parents need to be candid about their AI use for that collaboration to be effective. Some parents were upfront about AI when meeting with Morris. “When I would report on a goal, they also had input and would say, ‘Hey, I created something at home and I used AI for that.’ I thought that was really cool, that parents stepped out of their own mindset to think about how to incorporate those goals at home,” she says.

Even if parents don’t disclose, teachers and others could spot AI-generated text. “Right now, the information that parents are providing to school districts regarding their IEP meetings is much lengthier, and it carries some legal jargon that doesn’t typically come from parents,” Wolfram says. “Most educators will know when they’ve received something written by AI.”

If teachers do want parents to disclose AI usage, they can make a strong case for that, Laird believes. After all, in schools across the country, “parents are demanding from their school to know whether and how AI is being used,” she says.

The key is to avoid being defensive if AI is being used in the IEP meeting, says Coleman. “We don’t want to pit anyone in the IEP team against each other. We want to work together.” For the IEP process to meet its intent, she adds, participants need to trust each other, and “transparency builds trust.”

Parents might consider using AI for a number of reasons as they prep for an IEP meeting:

To verify their rights against local state guidelines

To translate unfamiliar jargon or bridge a language gap

To generate questions to help guide the process

In all these cases, educators say they’d prefer parents disclose their AI use, so that everyone can align in what is supposed to be a collaborative process. Parents should also double-check with local and state rules to make sure they are allowed to use AI with their IEPs.

Morris counsels teachers to assume that some parents will use AI. “I have created the IEP and I know my role and goals as well as those for the student and parents,” she says. How the family responds is up to them, “and I’ve always kept an open relationship with the parents that I have worked with,” she adds.

In the spirit of collaboration, teachers can model appropriate transparency and disclosure etiquette with parents. “We can’t make disclosure mandatory, but we can practice it and set an example,” Coleman argues. “Teachers can say up front, ‘We’re not against AI use, but we’d really appreciate you also being transparent, and this is why.’ We want to make sure we’re all on the same page,” she says.

With trust in place, Wolfram notes, the teacher can talk openly about the AI outputs a parent brings to a meeting. “The educator can say, ‘Let’s talk about those recommendations. Do you see those as different from what we’re already doing? And if so, let’s talk about why you think that’s needed,’” she says.

The AI discussion requires some finesse, but Morris thinks it’s worth the effort. “I want parents to be advocates, and to understand exactly what is being told to them on their child’s IEP,” she says.

title: College enrollment rate among recent high school graduates ticks up
content: The National Student Clearinghouse Research Center found improvement across both high- and low-poverty high schools.
author: Laura Spitalniak
clean_content:
The National Student Clearinghouse Research Center found improvement across both high- and low-poverty high schools.

Matthew Holsapple, the clearinghouse's senior director of research, called the improvements in persistence modest but an indicator of positive trends.

“What stands out most is that graduates of high-poverty high schools saw the largest gains in both enrollment and persistence," he said in a statement Thursday.

Among 2023 graduates of these schools who enrolled in higher education, 76% returned to college for their second year, compared to 74.3% from the previous cohort.

A significant majority of students who graduated from low-poverty high schools in 2023, 90.6%, persisted to their sophomore year. That's up slightly from 89.4% among the class of 2022.

The immediate college-going rate wasn't the only metric that improved.

Among the high school class of 2023, 58.7% of students from high-poverty schools enrolled in college within two years of graduating, up from 56.6% among the class of 2022. At low-poverty schools, that share rose from 75.9% among 2022 graduates to 77.9% among 2023 graduates.

College enrollment within two years also ticked up among high school graduates regardless of where they attended school. Urban schools saw the biggest increase. Among their 2023 graduates, 67.1% attended college within two years of graduating. That's up from 65.2% among 2022 graduates.

The gains among 2023 graduates from other high schools were smaller. The rate rose 0.4 percentage points year over year to 60.9% at rural high schools and 0.2 percentage points to 70.4% at suburban high schools

title: Kirk family alleges ‘stunning’ security failures at UVU led to the figure’s death
content: Charlie Kirk’s heirs could sue Utah Valley University, arguing that it should have done more to protect the right-wing figure.
author: Ben Unglesbee
clean_content:
Charlie Kirk’s heirs could sue Utah Valley University, arguing that it should have done more to protect the right-wing figure.

The family’s attorneys, with the firm Parkinson Benson Potter, argued that UVU should have beefed up its security measures given Kirk's prominence and in light of U.S. political violence preceding the event, including the attempted assassination of President Donald Trump on the campaign trail.

“Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie,” they wrote. “Those decisions ultimately rendered Mr. Kirk helpless to the rooftop shooter in an assassination that could have been avoided had the UVU Parties only taken reasonable steps to plan and oversee a safe event.”

A UVU spokesperson said in an email Wednesday that the university was aware of the Kirk family’s claims and that it addresses legal matters through its established processes. “Our focus remains on supporting our campus community,” the spokesperson said.

The Kirk family attorneys alleged several security failures, including:

The letter’s allegations came as a notice of claim that could form the basis of a potential lawsuit. The threat of litigation over Kirk’s death highlights the tight spot many colleges face when campus groups invite controversial speakers to campus.

Disallowing such figures from speaking raises concerns about free speech, while allowing them can incur heavy operating costs for those events.

Shortly after Kirk’s death last year, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression argued that colleges had “a moral and legal obligation to redouble their efforts to protect free speech as well as their campus community.”

Yet FIRE warned that “administrators must not pass those security costs along to speakers or use security concerns as pretext to cancel a speaker’s appearance.” The organization pointed to a 1992 U.S. Supreme Court case limiting the use of security fees by public campuses for events based on administrators’ judgments about the potential hostility toward speakers and their messages.

But eschewing security fees can lead institutions to absorb high security costs in an age of tight budgets.

One famous example is the University of Florida spending $500,000 on security when the white supremacist Richard Spencer came to speak on campus in 2017 .

The University of California, Berkeley likewise spent $4 million the same year to protect a handful of speakers over the course of one month. The university later settled a free speech lawsuit over security fees and moving speaking locations away from the campus center for controversial right-wing speakers. UC Berkeley paid $70,000 and agreed not to charge fees tied to concerns speakers’ ideas will “provoke disturbances.”

Not long after those speaking events, Columbia law professor Suzanne Goldberg described a situation “where a commitment to free expression has enabled provocateurs not only to spew hostile messages into our communities but also to divert extraordinary levels of resources to protect their messaging.”

title: West Point civilian speech policies ruled unconstitutional
content: The military academy blocked faculty from discussing personal opinions while teaching and speaking at certain events without preapproval.
author: Laura Spitalniak
clean_content:
The military academy blocked faculty from discussing personal opinions while teaching and speaking at certain events without preapproval.

During the first month of his second term, President Donald Trump ordered military colleges to ban “promoting, advancing, or otherwise inculcating” certain views his administration deemed “un-American, divisive, discriminatory, radical, extremist, and irrational.”

Soon thereafter, West Point leadership issued an institutional memo requiring faculty to obtain departmental approval for any outside engagements at which they would identify as West Point professors and talk about their “disciplinary areas of expertise."

West Point professor Tim Bakken, a civilian who has taught law at the military academy since 2000, sued over the policy last September . In his complaint, he alleged it was part of an institutional effort to “control, chill and suppress faculty speech.”

Bakken also said that S hane Reeves, then the dean of West Point’s academic board, told faculty it was wrong to share personal opinions or “advocate for a particular position or ideology” when teaching students — an allegation that West Point did not refute in court filings.

Reeves, who has since become the president of the University of Wyoming , is also facing a lawsuit over allegations he stifled instruction about climate change while at West Point via faculty retaliation.

Both the formal policy and Reeves' directive violated the First Amendment rights of civilian faculty , Seibel wrote in her Sept. 8 ruling .

This month's legal victory is not the first Bakken has won against West Point. A federal judge in 2012 ruled that the military academy had retaliated against Bakken for reporting hiring and pay discrepancies between retired military officers and qualified civilian candidates.

title: How La Salle University bounced back from enrollment losses
content: Daniel Allen, the Catholic institution’s president, spoke with Higher Ed Dive about regrowing by refocusing on recruiting and strategic fundamentals.
author: Ben Unglesbee
clean_content:
Daniel Allen, the Catholic institution’s president, spoke with Higher Ed Dive about regrowing by refocusing on recruiting and strategic fundamentals.

Last fall, La Salle University reported its largest incoming class in six years, with roughly 900 new undergraduate students. Its first-year student body ballooned by 40% from the previous year, and the number of transfer students grew by 60%.

That growth was more than welcome for La Salle, a Catholic institution in Philadelphia co-founded by the Brothers of the Christian Schools, a faith organization of nonclergy — it was crucial after years of declines and financial pressures.

Between 2019 and 2024, La Salle’s fall headcount plummeted by just over 36% to 3,153 students, according to federal data. With shrinking enrollment came operating losses — to the tune of $17.9 million in fiscal 2024 and $16.3 million in fiscal 2025 .

Its financial statements from those years had “going concern” warnings, accounting language indicating an entity might not have the financial resources to sustain itself over the next year. During that time, La Salle freed up cash by selling property and refinancing debt.

Even worse: Last summer, the Middle States Commission on Higher Education warned La Salle that its accreditation was at risk over its standards on financial resources — a message no college leader wants to hear. Accreditation loss renders institutions ineligible for federal student aid. But this May, about a year later, MSCHE gave La Salle a clean bill of health, saying it was fully compliant.

President Daniel Allen, who joined La Salle in 2022 , spoke to Higher Ed Dive about the institution’s journey back from its earlier precarious state and how it rebuilt enrollment by refocusing on the basics.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

HIGHER ED DIVE: How did you diagnose your enrollment problem in such a way that you can find a potential treatment?

DANIEL ALLEN: There are schools that are doing well despite the demographic cliff, and it gives you an opportunity to think differently about what you need to do from a strategy perspective. For us, we looked at how we were recruiting prospective students and how we were talking about and positioning the university in the market with those prospective students and their families.

There were a couple things that were super-important that we found out. One, most schools will recruit three classes of students at a time. So they're communicating with and engaged with high school sophomores through the senior year. La Salle was only recruiting one class at a time. Fundamentally, you're behind everybody because they've been talking to students for two years, and you're just getting into the mix.

Also, we're in Northwest Philadelphia. We were recruiting students from parts of the country where we said, “Why would a student from that city, that state, that part of the country be interested in coming to Northwest Philadelphia? That's probably not a good match.” So we fundamentally changed where we were going to recruit students. For example, we think that we have a better alignment with a student from Chicago who's at a Christian Brothers high school than, say, a student who's going to high school in Maine.

On the narrative side of things, what we found was that in our marketing and our communications, we talked a lot about the ascribed characteristics of students. La Salle is a great place for students from Philadelphia who are the first in their families to go to school and who may need a Pell Grant to go to college.

We are really proud of the work that we do with that demographic of students. And yet, that was only like 35% of our students. It's not the entire university. What we were concerned about is the student who's not the first in their family, who doesn't need a Pell Grant, who's not from Philadelphia, saying, "Man, I really like La Salle, but all I hear from them is ‘first generation Philly kids,’ and that's not me.” What we want to do is talk about La Salle in the marketplace in terms of the things that we do really well, and the things that we are doing that are different from, say, a Temple or a Drexel.

What are those things you do differently?

First and foremost, we compete with schools that are bigger than us. What we say to prospective students and their families is: “We really do care about you as an individual student. And from the president of the university on down, folks will know you by name, and you literally have the ability to send the president of the university an email and get a response. If you are interested in an environment where you will be known for who you are, we think we do that exceptionally well.: I've told prospective students and families on visit days, “Look, if you’re interested in going to a school that six weekends a year is going to have 80,000, 90,000 people at a football game, and massive Greek life and that sort of thing, you should leave now. You're just not going to be happy.”

When you came up with this slate of strategies, how did you determine their potential? How did you gauge whether a strategy might be successful before you actually start trying to execute it and devote resources?

Folks try to get too cute with strategy. There's this desire to be innovative, be cutting edge. In the end, it's pretty simple. We knew that you just can't recruit one class at a time. If your competitors have been talking to students for two years, they're ahead of you.

We also know that — for the type of school we are, the values we have and what we think we're really good at — being relational and knowing our students personally in the recruitment process, and not treating them to mass emails and cold informational communications, was something that was going to work for us because it’s part of the branding.

We talk about La Salle being a place that cares about you as a person and that is going to provide a hyper-personalized experience — you have to show them that before they actually start.

We're not trying to chase R1 or R2 status. We're really focused on students, student success, and what happens in the classroom. Revisiting and recommitting why we are in this business to begin with, and why this particular university was founded, has been fundamental to the change.

With the enrollment turnaround you've had, do you feel comfortable that the momentum will carry through into the future?

I do. I feel comfortable with what we are building. We're not making wild projections such as growing 10% every year in our first-time class. We think that the growth that we have had is absolutely sustainable.

We also have to be focused on what the net tuition revenue is and what our discount rate is. I've said [to the board], “Look, I could get you more students than what we have, but we're probably not going to make as much money, because we're going to have to heavily discount to get more students.”

In some respects, one could say we're in the business of postsecondary education. We're not in the business necessarily of making money, but we need to generate revenue in order to strengthen our mission, enhance the quality of the experience for our students, and reinvest in our own faculty and staff and their programs. We have to be focused on generating more revenue year over year. At times, we become too focused on whether we're growing enrollment.

In 2027, we are projecting a net-positive operating margin on a cash basis. When you throw in depreciation and those other things, then we're looking at break-even or running a small deficit.

That was not true for ‘26. It was negative.

And you're anticipating positive margins going forward?

It better be the case going forward. We can't lose money every year. That's just not a sustainable model. We’ve got to get that fixed.

What do you think are still your biggest challenges on the horizon, and your biggest opportunities?

The biggest challenge will continue to be financial — it is running the university in a way generating enough revenue year over year so that we can make investments.

The biggest opportunity that we have is in thinking creatively about how we can generate some of that revenue through philanthropy and fundraising. There is an opportunity to engage with our alumni community, which really does care deeply about this university and has a real commitment to what we're doing.

We talk a lot about not chasing the latest shiny new toy. What's the next big idea? Well, higher education is such that the next big idea fades away in three or four years, and then you're chasing the next big idea. We need to focus on what is it that we do well, what is it that we have been called to do in terms of our mission with the population we serve, and not be distracted by the desire to have some big new bold idea that nobody's ever thought of before.

title: Week in review: DOJ sues remaining states over tuition laws

We’re rounding up last week’s stories, from Florida’s public education shutting out undocumented students to the stalled fight to ban legacy admissions.

The State University System of Florida’s board of governors will ban undocumented students from attending its selective institutions beginning in the 2027-28 academic year. That decision, combined with a similar vote by the Florida State Board of Education in July, means undocumented students will be effectively locked out of the state's public higher education system.
