title: Let’s work to keep our students while we still have them
content: According to research I recently saw , About 16% of young people ages 18 to 24 are not in employment, education, or training. Researchers call them NEETs, or disconnected youth. After 35 years in public education, I read the number a different way.
author: Paul DeAngelis, Concentric Educational Solutions
clean_content:
According to research I recently saw , About 16% of young people ages 18 to 24 are not in employment, education, or training. Researchers call them NEETs, or disconnected youth. After 35 years in public education, I read the number a different way. Almost every one of those young adults sat in somebody’s classroom a few years ago. Somebody had them at 14. Somebody had them at 16, the year they missed 32 days and the system recorded the absences and moved on.

Disconnection at 20 is rarely a surprise. It is the final step in a long slide, and most of the slide happens while a student is still enrolled and still within reach. We are not powerless in that window. Unfortunately, we are simply working in it alone.

A seventh grader starts missing Mondays. The attendance clerk calls. The counselor pulls him in. The principal sends a letter. Everyone in the building follows the script, and none of it touches the actual reason, which turns out to be a mother working a 6 a.m. shift with no one to get three kids out the door. No letter fixes a schedule. No suspension fixes an unmedicated asthma condition or a family two weeks from an eviction.

Schools see the warning signs first, earlier than any other institution in the community. Schools also have the least authority to resolve them. A superintendent and board controls the budget, calendar, and staff. They do not control housing stock, bus routes, clinic hours, or the hiring practices of the largest employer in the county. The barriers keeping a 13-year-old out of class live almost entirely outside the buildings they lead.

The people who do control those things are already in town. The mayor. The community foundation with a board looking for something durable to fund. The workforce board with employers begging for workers and no pipeline. The health system. They are all working on youth outcomes in their own way, in their own rooms, on their own timelines, and most of them have no idea which specific children in their community are sliding right now.

School leaders are the only ones with the standing to pull those rooms together.

I do not say this to flatter my colleagues. It is a plain fact about how communities work. The superintendent sits with the mayor. Districts hold the trust of parents who will not answer a call from a local official but will answer one from a school. No other local institution touches as many households on a Tuesday morning. When a superintendent asks a foundation director and a workforce board chair to sit down, they sit down.

What we have not done, often enough, is spend that standing early, on behalf of students who are still in front of us.

Convening is not another task force. I have sat through enough of those to know the difference. A task force produces a report. A working partnership produces a name, a next step, and someone accountable for taking it.

Start with the students showing the first signs, not the ones already gone. Bring partners a real list of children whose attendance is slipping this month.

Then, get to the why, which means going to the family rather than waiting for the family to come to us. Housing. A car. A child at home. A health problem nobody screened for. We have spent years counting absences and almost no time understanding them, and counting has never moved a single number on its own.

Then, decide who acts on what. The foundation funds the transportation gap. The health system opens an after-hours slot. The workforce board gives a 16-year-old a paid summer placement and a reason to stay enrolled. The district keeps the case open until attendance recovers.

At Concentric Educational Solutions , we work with communities building that kind of shared front, and Concentric360 , the platform we launched this week that gives partners one coordinated way to see who is slipping, understand the barriers behind it, and connect a family to the support needed to reverse course. The tool matters far less than the decision to sit at the same table, and the decision belongs to leaders.

I hear the objections every week – district leaders are stretched thin. The budget is flat. Enrollment is down and the levy failed. But the question is never whether we can afford improvement. The question is whether we can afford to wait. A sixth grader missing 30 days becomes a sophomore with no credits, and a sophomore with no credits becomes a 20-year-old outside every system built to help him. Waiting moves the cost to emergency rooms, courtrooms, and shelters, where the price runs higher and the outcomes run worse.

Boldness here does not require a bond issue. Boldness looks like a superintendent calling her local partners and saying, I have 200 children sliding right now, I know their names, and I am not willing to hand them to you in six years as a workforce problem.

We have these young people today. Keeping them connected, supported, and on a path to graduation is the choice leaders must make now, together, before another student slips away from the classrooms.

Paul DeAngelis, Regional Partnerships Director at Concentric Educational Solutions, spent 35 years in Michigan’s public schools. He is committed to empowering school leaders to break down the barriers keeping students out of class.

title: Quit saying “I’m not a math person”
content: It’s quite rare to hear someone say, “I can’t read” or “I’m illiterate so I don’t read.” On the other hand, lots of people claim that they’re “not a math person.” The phrase isn’t just “I don’t like math.”
author: Dr. T.J. Vari, MaiaLearning & Thomas O’Brien, Winward Academy
clean_content:
It’s quite rare to hear someone say, “I can’t read” or “I’m illiterate so I don’t read.” On the other hand, lots of people claim that they’re “not a math person.” The phrase isn’t just “I don’t like math.” It’s “I’m not a math person,” signifying that they don’t know how to do math, not just that they don’t like it. We believe this single sentiment is significantly impacting students’ perceptions of math in school and their efficacy with it in life. As educators, what we say matters, especially when talking in front of impressionable students.

Our central argument is that no one should be so comfortable with saying the statement: “I’m not a math person,” but we stress this even further for educators, which includes anyone who works in a school, has influence over students, and might say something like this in front of them. We’ve heard it before from teachers, school administrators, support staff, and district leaders. When a school official says this in front of students, the message is clear: Math is optional, even for successful adults. Our guess is that it simply devalues the need to be able to do math because a successful person who even works in academia brushes it off with ease.

The societal consequences might be even more damaging, though. Many high-paying jobs require the ability to do math, including the use of algebraic reasoning, statistical analysis, and advanced computation. These jobs often also require a degree in a STEM or business-related field, and these degree programs, especially for selective colleges and universities, typically screen applicants based on the level of math education that gets reported on their transcript. This is not abstract–in fact, according to the National Science Board , in 2023, full-time STEM workers had median earnings of $76,000 in comparison to $55,000 for non-STEM workers. In other words, a student who doesn’t progress to pre-calculus, for example, might be denied entrance into a university program to study cybersecurity. We don’t think it’s a stretch to go from hearing an adult devalue math skill acquisition to not electing to take upper-level math courses to being unable to study in a certain major to not having access to higher paying jobs.

We also believe that statements like “I’m not a math person” are more detrimental for already-marginalized students in under-resourced schools and communities. When students already have limited exposure to people with high-paying jobs in math-heavy careers, the only people who might have influence over their perception of the importance of math are the educators in their schools. This means that we not only need to quit saying “I’m not a math person,” and instead begin to emphasize the critical need for math skills to be able to reach postsecondary success after K-12. We say that we want every student to reach for their dreams, but what if you’re unintentionally putting up barriers to them?

Our call-to-action is simple: Please stop saying “I’m not a math person.” Don’t say it, don’t think it, and especially not in front of young people. Instead, try saying: “Math has not always come easily to me, but I know it matters, and I’m still learning.” This small shift in language has major implications; instead of treating math as optional, it demonstrates that we are all life-long learners of it, even when it requires persistence. We know that adults, mentors, teachers, and school leaders have a dramatic influence on students, their mindset about school, and their future achievements. What seems like a harmless and innocent thing to say could be creating significant damage over time. We’re asking that you quit saying it and start challenging others when you hear it. We hope that this is just one step in the right direction for the creation of a world where we’re all “math people.”

Dr. T.J. Vari is the Senior Director of Product Strategy at MaiaLearning , with a focus on postsecondary planning for students worldwide. Dr. Vari is a former deputy superintendent, middle school assistant principal and principal, and high school English teacher. He’s the cofounder of TheSchoolHouse302 , a leadership development firm, and the coauthor of seven books on educational leadership, which are the basis for his speaking engagements, coaching, and leadership development institutes. Thomas O’Brien is the Vice President of Success & Engagement at Winward Academy , where he supports hundreds of schools, districts, and after-school programs across the country in achieving their college and career readiness goals. Prior to joining Winward Academy, Mr. O’Brien served as a nationally recognized high school principal and award-winning math teacher, leading innovative efforts to improve student achievement and access. He writes a blog about math instruction, education technology, and school leadership. His forthcoming book will be released this summer.

title: 5 questions to help every district leader make better decisions
content: As budgets remain tight and expectations for measurable student growth increase, every instructional decision carries greater weight. Choosing one initiative often means delaying another, making it even more important to separate promising ideas from approaches supported by stronger evidence.
author: Steven L. Miller, Ph.D., K-12 Research Consultant
clean_content:
Every district leader has experienced it.

A new instructional program promises stronger student achievement. An intervention arrives with compelling testimonials. A technology platform highlights impressive pilot results. The presentations are polished, the early outcomes are encouraging, and the potential seems significant.

The challenge isn’t finding innovative ideas. It’s deciding which investments are most likely to improve learning across an entire district.

As budgets remain tight and expectations for measurable student growth increase, every instructional decision carries greater weight. Choosing one initiative often means delaying another, making it even more important to separate promising ideas from approaches supported by stronger evidence.

A recent meta-analysis examining implementations of Penda Learning synthesized findings from 13 independent studies involving more than 33,000 students. Among them was a large, multisite evaluation conducted across 46 schools and nearly 19,500 students. That study found an average 21% gain in science achievement, with students approximately 20% more likely to reach science proficiency than peers receiving traditional instruction. Although the research focused on science intervention, its leadership lessons extend well beyond a single subject area.

Whether evaluating curriculum, instructional technology, intervention or professional learning, these five questions can help district leaders distinguish promising ideas from evidence-based investments.

1. Are we evaluating evidence—or anecdotes?

Every instructional initiative has a success story. A neighboring district reports impressive gains. Teachers describe positive classroom experiences. Conference presentations showcase encouraging early results. Success stories can spark interest. They should not drive districtwide decisions.

Before making a major investment, leaders should ask whether results have been demonstrated across multiple schools, diverse student populations, and varied implementation settings. The broader the evidence base, the greater confidence leaders can have that the findings are repeatable.

Meta-analyses are particularly valuable because they test whether similar patterns emerge across multiple independent studies rather than relying on one successful implementation. For district leaders, that broader view helps distinguish results that are promising from those that are more likely to be replicated across different schools, student populations, and instructional settings.

Successful implementation depends on more than the resource. High-quality materials, professional learning, instructional leadership, coaching, and time for teachers to refine practice all matter.

When vendors or publishers present positive student outcomes, one of the most valuable follow-up questions is not simply, “What resource did the district use?” It is, “What conditions made implementation successful?”

In the 46-school study, teachers received structured professional learning before implementation, along with ongoing classroom support and professional learning communities throughout the school year. Those supports were part of the intervention—not separate from it.

Before investing, leaders should evaluate not only the quality of the resource but also whether their district has the capacity to implement it successfully.

3. Does the research reflect students like ours?

District leaders serve diverse communities, and research should reflect that reality. A promising result becomes more meaningful when leaders can see that it extends beyond one school, one grade level, or one type of learner.

Across the research, students averaged a 21% gain in science achievement and were approximately 20% more likely to reach proficiency. Positive outcomes were also observed across reported ethnic groups, both male and female students, and among students attending Title I schools, English learners, and students with disabilities.

The practical question is not simply, “Did students improve?” It is, “Did students with different needs and starting points improve?” Evidence of gains across diverse populations gives leaders greater confidence that an investment can support the full range of learners they serve.

Education often measures what is easiest to count: participation, instructional minutes, training hours, or software usage. Those metrics matter, but they do not necessarily reflect learning.

One important finding involved student mastery. Students mastering learning activities with at least 80% accuracy demonstrated greater gains on the nationally normed NWEA MAP Science assessment than students who simply spent more time using the program. The meta-analysis found a clear dose-response relationship, with higher levels of mastery associated with progressively greater achievement gains.

For district leaders, the implication is straightforward: establish meaningful measures of success before implementation begins so initiatives are evaluated by student learning—not participation alone.

5. What will we learn from this investment?

Every significant instructional investment is more than a purchasing decision—it’s an opportunity for organizational learning. The strongest district leaders do not simply ask whether a program worked. They ask why it worked, what implementation conditions contributed to the results, what challenges emerged, and how those lessons should shape future decisions. That mindset helps districts become more disciplined consumers of research and more thoughtful evaluators of innovation.

The meta-analysis reinforces this principle. Rather than relying on one successful implementation, it found consistent results across multiple studies, schools, grade levels, and student populations. That breadth of evidence gives district leaders greater confidence that the findings are likely to translate across different educational settings.

Whether evaluating curriculum, professional learning, instructional technology, or intervention, the broader lesson is the same: Stronger instructional decisions come from asking better questions, learning from implementation, and building on what the research continues to reveal.

Steven L. Miller, Ph.D., is an education researcher who studies the relationship between academic achievement, economic mobility, and workforce development. He has served as a research consultant for multiple K–12 education organizations and regularly writes about the intersection of education policy, learning science, and economic outcomes.

title: Why K-12 cybersecurity education needs practice, not just awareness
content: Students are already making cybersecurity decisions every day. Giving them a list of rules is not the same as teaching them how to recognize a threat.
author: Paul Cuffe, GetIntoCyberJobs.com
clean_content:
Students are already making cybersecurity decisions every day. Giving them a list of rules is not the same as teaching them how to recognize a threat.

K-12 cybersecurity education matters because U.S. schools are more dependent on technology than ever, while the threats facing them continue to evolve. CoSN’s U.S. State of EdTech 2026 report, based on responses from more than 600 education technology leaders across 44 states, found that cybersecurity remains their number one technology priority. At the same time, 65 percent identified insufficient cybersecurity staffing and the lack of a dedicated budget as leading barriers to addressing those challenges.

School districts invest in firewalls, identity protection, filtering, monitoring, multifactor authentication, and endpoint security. All of those controls matter, but they cannot make every decision for the person sitting in front of a screen. Eventually, a student or staff member receives a message, follows a link, shares information, or is asked to log in somewhere and has to decide whether to trust what they are seeing.

That human decision is why cybersecurity education deserves attention alongside technical security.

My own perspective comes partly from years spent supporting and managing IT in British secondary schools. At Ken Stimpson Community School, I worked in an environment serving around 1,200 students. I later managed IT at South Hunsley School, which served roughly 2,300 students. The terminology and education systems are different from those in the United States, but working with technology at that scale taught me something that translates directly to U.S. K-12 environments: technical controls can reduce risk, but they cannot remove the need for people to make good decisions.

Knowing the rule is not the same as recognizing the threat

Most students have heard basic online safety advice. Do not share your password. Do not click suspicious links. Be careful about what you post online.

The challenge begins when the threat does not look suspicious.

A phishing message might use a familiar logo, appear to come from a service the student recognizes, and warn that an account will be disabled unless they act quickly. A link might look genuine at first glance. Generative AI is also making convincing text, images, audio, and other content increasingly easy to produce.

In those situations, cybersecurity becomes less about remembering a rule and more about making a judgment. Who actually sent this? Does the request make sense? Where does the link go? Why am I being asked for this information? Can I verify the request another way?

Students need opportunities to practice answering those questions before the consequences are real.

Give students the opportunity to get it wrong safely

Instead of simply telling students not to click suspicious links, schools can put a realistic but safe message in front of them and ask what they would actually do.

Would they follow the link? Check the sender? Report the message? Ignore it?

A simulated phishing exercise can allow students to make the decision first and then explain what they noticed or missed. Perhaps the sender’s address is slightly different from the genuine organization. The message might create artificial urgency, point to an unexpected domain, or ask for information the legitimate organization would not normally request.

If a student makes the wrong choice during an exercise, no account has been compromised and no data has been lost. Instead, the mistake becomes the lesson.

That is one reason simulations and game-based activities can work particularly well for K-12 cybersecurity education. Students can make a choice, see the consequence, understand why it happened, and try again. The same approach can be applied to password reuse, social engineering, unsafe information sharing, suspicious downloads, and AI-generated or manipulated content.

The individual threat will change. The habit of stopping and asking, “Why should I trust this?” has much more staying power.

Cybersecurity belongs in digital literacy

Practical cybersecurity education should not be limited to students pursuing computer science or technology careers. Most students will never become cybersecurity analysts or network engineers, but almost all will rely on online accounts, email, cloud applications, and connected devices throughout their lives.

That makes basic cybersecurity judgment part of digital literacy.

CISA takes a similarly broad view in its Protecting Our Future report on K-12 cybersecurity. The agency says school leaders need to establish and reinforce a cybersecure culture and makes clear that IT and cybersecurity personnel cannot carry that responsibility alone.

Students should be part of that culture, not simply users being protected by it.

None of this requires U.S. districts to add another semester-long course to an already crowded curriculum. Short exercises can still teach useful habits.

A teacher could spend 10 minutes comparing two emails and asking students which one they trust and why. Students could work through a situation in which someone has already clicked a suspicious link and decide what should happen next. They could examine a message, image, or online claim and identify what they would check before believing or sharing it.

These activities do not require a cybersecurity lab or specialist equipment. What matters is the thinking behind them: stop, examine the information, question what is being requested, make a decision, and explain the reasoning behind it.

U.S. schools cannot prepare students for every phishing email, scam, impersonation attempt, or piece of manipulated content they will encounter. The threats will change too quickly for that.

What K-12 cybersecurity education can do is help students build habits that remain useful as technology changes: pause before acting, question unexpected requests, verify information, recognize when something does not make sense, and know when to ask for help.

The aim is not to turn every student into a cybersecurity professional. It is to let students practice making cybersecurity decisions while getting one wrong is still a learning opportunity rather than a real security incident.

Paul Cuffe is an IT and network professional with more than 20 years of experience across education, enterprise, and public-sector technology. He currently works in government IT network management, holds Cisco CCNP Enterprise certification, and created GamingForLearning.com and GetIntoCyberJobs.com, two free educational projects focused on interactive learning, cybersecurity education, and pathways into technology careers.

title: The compliance trap waiting on the other side of Title II
content: Every few years, something shifts how schools think about accessibility. A law changes, a new technology arrives, or a group of advocates succeeds in bringing attention to the topic. Right now, it's Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
author: Luis Pérez, CAST
clean_content:
Every few years, something shifts how schools think about accessibility. A law changes, a new technology arrives, or a group of advocates succeeds in bringing attention to the topic. Right now, it’s Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The Department of Justice has updated Title II to require compliance with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, Level AA, for all public school digital content: curriculum platforms, grading systems, parent communication tools, online assessments, third-party instructional materials. Larger districts have until April 2027. Smaller ones get until April 2028.

Here’s what worries me about that deadline. I’ve watched districts treat requirements like this one as a finish line before, and I’ve watched a vendor run a scan, a box get marked complete, and the work quietly stop right when it should be starting.

I’ve been at CAST for nearly nine years. Before that, I was a graduate student who almost didn’t finish his degree. I was identified with a visual impairment after starting a program in instructional technology, and I spent a long time trying to figure out how to get through a field that relies so heavily on vision. Eventually I transferred into a special education program, not because I gave up, but because that department was practicing Universal Design for Learning (UDL). My professors offered content in multiple formats. Assessments could be completed in different ways. I could access what I needed to actually learn, not just survive.

That flexibility wasn’t a workaround. It was good teaching, by design and for everyone, and it’s exactly what every district in the country is now legally required to build.

The instinct, understandably, is to hand Title II to one department: Someone audits the website, a vendor runs a scan, and compliance turns into a technical problem with a technical fix.

That instinct will leave districts exposed. Accessibility doesn’t live in one department. It shows up in procurement decisions and in the documents a teacher creates. A district that buys a learning management system for 50,000 students just made an accessibility decision that touches every one of them, whether anyone framed it that way or not. Compliance isn’t something that happens once at the top of an organization. It happens every day, at every level, which means leadership has to set the vision while the work lands in classrooms, procurement offices, and curriculum committees. Everyone needs to actually be talking to each other. I call this leading from the middle, where leadership and the grassroots meet in the same conversation.

This is where districts have real leverage they aren’t using. Accessibility requirements belong in every RFP a district issues. Make them a condition of the contract, not a line item buried in it. Ask vendors for their Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) and ask how recently it was updated. Ask whether the tool was tested with actual disabled users, not just run through an automated checker. And ask what happens when the next version launches, because software updates constantly, and a tool that passed an audit in January can fail one in June. If a vendor can’t answer those questions, that’s information too.

We draw a line between technical accessibility and what we call practical accessibility. A site can meet every criterion in WCAG 2.1 AA and still be genuinely hard to use if the people building it never designed alongside the people who’d rely on it. We don’t design for people with disabilities. We co-design with them, because that’s the only way to catch the assumptions we didn’t know we were making and end up with something people actually want to use, not just something that scores well on a checklist.

What this looks like for students and teachers

Teachers do not need to become accessibility specialists. I hold a professional certification in accessibility, and it took real time and training to earn. That’s not what I’m asking of educators who already have so many demands on their time.

What I am asking is that teachers learn five or six foundational practices : proper heading structure, descriptive link text instead of “click here,” and image descriptions on any visual in a handout or worksheet.

The first few times may feel unfamiliar. By the tenth time, it’s a habit.

For students, the stakes are simpler than any of this. If you can’t perceive the content, you can’t make meaning from it. Accessibility is the floor UDL stands on, not the ceiling. It’s the difference between a student who can access material and one who can actually engage with it and understand and be understood.

But those habits won’t take root if the district isn’t modeling them. A school system asking teachers to build accessible materials while running an inaccessible website is sending a contradictory message. You can’t ask for something you’re not demonstrating yourself.

We built one of the first web accessibility checkers back in the 1990s. We called it Bobby, after the unarmed policemen in the UK whose job is to help people, not catch them. That’s still how we think about this work: support, not a gotcha. Title II has created real momentum. Administrators who never thought seriously about accessibility are in the conversation now, and that’s genuinely good. But accessibility never really finishes. It becomes a set of systems and habits that keep moving as the tools change underneath them.

The deadline is real. What districts build between now and April 2027 will decide whether Title II becomes a turning point or a temporary fix.

Luis Pérez is Senior Director of Disability and Accessibility at CAST , the nonprofit education research organization that originated Universal Design for Learning. He holds certification from the International Association of Accessibility Professionals and has spent nearly nine years working at the intersection of UDL, accessibility, and inclusive technology.

title: AACTE releases national framework on AI in educator preparation
content: A new national framework from AACTE (American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education) aims to help educator preparation programs (EPPs) navigate the rapidly changing role of artificial intelligence in education.
author: ESchool News Staff
clean_content:
A new national framework from AACTE (American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education) aims to help educator preparation programs (EPPs) navigate the rapidly changing role of artificial intelligence in education.

The framework, AI Framework for Educator Preparation , developed through collaboration among members of the AACTE Programmatic Advisory Committee on Innovation and Technology, AACTE leadership, Board of Directors, and external reviewers, reflects a shared commitment to ensuring that AI strengthens educator preparation while keeping human relationships and professional expertise at the center.

“Artificial intelligence presents both tremendous opportunity and significant responsibility for educator preparation,” said Cheryl Holcomb-McCoy, Ph.D., AACTE President and CEO. “AACTE’s Framework reflects our commitment to ensuring that technology serves, not supplants, the expertise, ethics, and professional judgment of educators.”

The widespread adoption of AI is changing what educators need to know and what they need to be able to do. EPPs have a critical role in ensuring that future educators can evaluate AI-generated information, recognize bias and limitations, protect student privacy, promote equitable access, and make sound decisions about how AI fits into teaching and learning.

The framework centers this work on four interconnected areas:

Together, these areas position AI literacy as a matter of professional practice, not simply technology training.

This new framework marks the beginning of AACTE’s continued work on AI and educator preparation as technologies and their applications in education continue to evolve, and is available as a resource for EPPs seeking to prepare future educators for an AI-enabled profession.

title: Career readiness in the AI era needs decision practice, not just tool access
content: Schools are racing to teach students how to use AI. That is necessary, but it is not enough. The workplace advantage will increasingly belong to people who can decide when an AI output is useful, when it is incomplete and when it is wrong.
author: Gleb Tsipursky, PhD, Disaster Avoidance Experts
clean_content:
Schools are racing to teach students how to use AI. That is necessary, but it is not enough. The workplace advantage will increasingly belong to people who can decide when an AI output is useful, when it is incomplete and when it is wrong.

Stanford Digital Economy Lab’s August update shows why this matters. The employment shortfall for U.S. workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations widened from 15 percent in the July 2025 data vintage to 19 percent by June 2026. The easiest early-career tasks are exactly the ones AI can often handle first.

Schools therefore need to treat AI as a practice partner for judgment. A student can use AI to summarize background information, but then should be asked to identify what evidence is missing. AI can propose a solution to a science problem, but the student should test its assumptions. AI can draft an argument, but the student should compare sources, identify tradeoffs and defend a final position.

That progression can start young. Elementary students can compare an AI answer with a trusted text and explain differences. Middle school students can work with conflicting evidence and choose what they trust. High school students can tackle messy career-connected cases in which there is no single correct answer and must document how they reached a decision.

The goal is not to make every student an AI specialist. It is to make students harder to fool and faster to develop. Schools should measure whether learners can verify claims, recognize exceptions, ask for missing information, communicate uncertainty and take responsibility for a conclusion.

Recent news has highlighted career readiness as a systemwide progression and has also stressed that AI should strengthen rather than replace human expertise. Those ideas belong together. If AI handles more routine production, schools should spend more time on the reasoning and responsibility that machines cannot own.

The best preparation for an AI-shaped labor market is not simply more exposure to AI. It is more practice making decisions when AI is in the room.

Gleb Tsipursky, PhD, a behavioral scientist, CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts, and author of The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results (Georgetown University Press, 2026).

title: Building an everyday equitable practice for AI in schools
content: AI technology is advancing rapidly in schools, but research is increasingly showing that Large Language Models (LLMs) lack the common sense, morality, and knowledge of individual classroom dynamics needed to be truly equitable.
author: Chelsie Thielen, Winona State University
clean_content:
AI technology is advancing rapidly in schools, but research is increasingly showing that Large Language Models (LLMs) lack the common sense, morality, and knowledge of individual classroom dynamics needed to be truly equitable.

Many districts handle AI with blanket policy statements inspired by guidance from state departments of education, such as the Minnesota Department of Education’s Guiding Principles for AI in Education . These frameworks and the documents they inspire are a solid starting place, but lack the detail needed to solve the daily equity issues surrounding LLMs in the classroom. Furthermore, in all but a handful of states, they remain non-binding frameworks rather than required policy mandates.

The issues classroom teachers are facing will not be solved from a vague, general statement placed in a district handbook or tacked at the bottom of a syllabus. Ethical AI implementation in schools is an active, ongoing practice that demands technical scrutiny, broad stakeholder input, and accessible, timely professional development for educators and administrators to protect student agency and equity.

AI is far from a neutral tool and can carry considerable systemic and socio-cultural risks into classrooms:

Operationalizing equity: A three-part practice

To prevent AI from reinforcing classroom disparities, administrators and educators must shift from passive compliance to a continuous, three-part cycle of technical scrutiny adapted from researcher M. Lockwood’s Equity Bias Framework :

Transforming ethical guidelines into practice requires concrete strategies that equip educators with tools, training, and institutional support needed to govern AI responsibly:

None of this suggests that districts should simply ban AI; quite the opposite. Blocking these tools out of fear of plagiarism is both short-sighted and counterproductive. Our students will enter a global workforce where AI collaboration is already the baseline standard, and where their peers from around the world have been well-trained in these technologies. To compete, they will need to know AI’s limits, its strengths, and how to use it responsibly. But if we are going to prepare them for that reality, we must first master these tools ourselves, moving beyond superficial bans and passive policies to build an everyday practice grounded in technical scrutiny, human judgment, and uncompromising equity.

Chelsie Thielen has taught middle and high school language arts in Minnesota for 17 years and is a doctoral student at Winona State University.

title: We stopped waiting for the teacher pipeline–we built our own
content: Every hiring season, school districts ask the same question: Where are the teachers? We stopped asking and started building.
author: Bonnie Toffoli & Kimberly Wood, Orange County Public Schools
clean_content:
Every hiring season, school districts ask the same question: Where are the teachers? We stopped asking and started building.

Florida’s Orange County Public Schools (OCPS) is one of the largest districts in the country, and over the last several years, we’ve built what we now think of as a cradle-to-career teacher development ecosystem. This is not a singular program, but rather a set of pathways built on the idea that the people most likely to become great teachers, and stay, are already in our buildings, communities, and high schools. Our job is to find them early and clear the path between where they are and where they want to go.

The traditional teacher pipeline where students enroll in a college of education, graduate, get certified, and apply to a district is producing fewer and fewer candidates every year. We know this. Education school enrollments have been falling nationally for more than a decade, and the graduates who do enter the field often choose districts close to where they trained. For a large urban system like OCPS, that means competing for a smaller hiring pool against every other district. We also know that posting more jobs on more platforms and hiring sites wasn’t going to fix this problem.

If the traditional pipeline was narrowing, we needed to widen the path from a different direction. So, we started looking inward, at the people already in our schools who had the makings of great teachers but no clear way to get there. The added benefit, we’d come to realize, is that the people you grow tend to stay.

Paraprofessionals are the heart of this work. They’re in our schools every day, students know them, families trust them, and they already understand the intricacies and culture of their schools. What many lack is a clear, supported path to the front of the classroom. That’s where the opportunity is to offer support.

We partnered with local higher education institutions to build two distinct pathways, because everyone thrives under different circumstances, especially when you’re returning to school as a working adult. One partner runs a small, personalized cohort with blended evening coursework, and just entered its eighth cohort. An additional partner provides a scholarship-based program that folds candidates into its larger college of education.

When we sit with a candidate, we want to build a relationship with them and get to know them as we’re trying to meet them where they can succeed. We ask: Are you a learner who’ll do well in a big university setting, or have you been out of school for 15 years and need something more guided? Do you have kids at home and no room for in-person evenings? The right program depends on who you are as a learner, as a person, and what you’re juggling while making this commitment.

For candidates who can’t leave their school at all, we built a third pathway option through a national partner: a residency model that turns on-the-job classroom work into micro-credentialed college credit. No travel to a college campus. No outside coursework. Your classroom work counts as coursework.

This summer, our first cohort in the residency model program graduates. Several will graduate and be certified in elementary education, while the majority will graduate and certify in ESE, where vacancies are consistently high. In 2024–25, 100 percent of participants received satisfactory ratings, which tells us the model holds up where it matters most: in front of students.

One of our fastest-moving programs came out of a 2023 state statute most districts were still figuring out. The paid senior intern pathway allows qualified education students to serve as teachers of record in their final semester, full-time, with pay, benefits, and FTE count, just before they graduate college. We launched a pilot in spring 2024 with 11 students, nearly all through our local university and college partners. After the initial year, we brought principals and university faculty together to collaborate; we discussed all of the program benefits and adjusted supports that were necessary. A year later, we had 14 paid senior interns in a single semester. The pathway has continued to flourish since its inception, growing a little more with each school year.

There were some questions along the way. But providing principals with an overview of the selection process and program criteria gave a clearer picture of the caliber of the intern entering the program. Some universities set GPA and testing requirements above the state’s minimums, and every candidate needed a college letter of recommendation. These were students who had already shown they were ready to teach. In several cases, they were the same candidates principals had hoped to hire mid-semester before this intern program existed.

Looking ahead, the newest piece of our teacher ecosystem is a high school academy pathway, piloted at two of our high schools near a major university corridor. Through a dual enrollment partnership with a local college, students can complete the prerequisites for an education bachelor’s degree before they graduate, earning both their high school diploma and an associate’s degree at the same time. They leave the academy ready to enter our OCPS pathways program or any bachelor’s program in the state, with hands-on experience working with pre-K students they got without ever leaving campus.

To ensure we are reaching every student who wants to teach, we are branching out beyond the obvious candidate. We’re working with guidance counselors to find students who haven’t considered teaching yet, but who would thrive in the position. These are the students who are good with younger children, who light up in service roles, and who might not have a clear direction but have every quality you want in a teacher. From here, those students can feed into one of our pathways, and some will come back to us as paraprofessionals while they finish their degrees. Our goal is to grow educators from our own communities, so the teacher at the front of the classroom grew up in the same neighborhood as the students in the desks. We have found that teachers who come from the community they teach in tend to stay, helping retention rates.

None of this works without solving the practical problems that doom programs before they start: funding. When a paraprofessional in a high-needs school reaches the internship phase of their education degree program, they can’t afford to take unpaid leave.

We worked with our staffing partner, Kelly Education , to arrange substitute coverage during those rotations, sending a coordinated list of names, schools, and coverage dates so that every absence was planned and covered in advance. The paraprofessional doesn’t lose a paycheck. The classroom doesn’t lose continuity — this is what ensures the program survives. Any district with a staffing partnership should be asking whether it can be structured to support teacher development, not just daily coverage.

Over time, our substitute teacher pool has become one of our most reliable recruiting grounds. We track the number of substitutes who convert into full instructional hires each year, and the numbers have been consistent: these are people who already have bachelor’s degrees, who already love what they’re doing in our classrooms, and who are ready to make it permanent. Our recruiting team meets with them individually, walks them through certification pathways, and recruits actively at substitute orientation events for our alternative certification program. They aren’t strangers to our schools; they’re already part of them.

Retention starts at the first conversation

Relationships run through everything we’ve built. Every person on our recruiting team is a former teacher. They answer the phones. They follow candidates from a college event through onboarding and into year two. We have new hires walk in and say, “I remember meeting you at a local college two years ago.” As large as OCPS is, every candidate should feel like they’re working with the smallest, most personal district they’ve ever encountered.

Our two-year induction program adds on-campus mentors at every school, weekly support resources, and stipends for mentor teachers. This structure showcases to new teachers that the district takes their success seriously.

If you’re a district just starting this work, start small. You don’t need to create five programs at once. Pick one pathway, build one university relationship, and make it work for the candidates in front of you, in your community. From there, offer more than one modality, because your candidates aren’t one type of learner. And remember: the teacher shortage isn’t only a recruiting problem; there is a retention factor, too. The district that answers the phone, follows up, and makes a candidate feel supported before they’re hired is the district they’ll want to stay in. OCPS has built multiple pathways to meet the evolving needs of future teachers.

Bonnie Toffoli is senior director of talent acquisition and programs at Orange County Public Schools in Orlando, Florida. Kimberly Wood is assistant director of talent acquisition and programs at Orange County Public Schools.

title: A blanket screen-time ban won’t fix what’s broken in edtech
content: Many parents, policymakers, and educators are worried about screens in schools. They’ve observed the positive effects of cell phone bans and are wondering how edtech might contribute to real issues, including declining attention spans and learning loss.
author: Todd Wirt, Discovery Education & Former Public School Superintendent
clean_content:
Many parents, policymakers, and educators are worried about screens in schools. They’ve observed the positive effects of cell phone bans and are wondering how edtech might contribute to real issues, including declining attention spans and learning loss.

In my years as a superintendent, I saw plenty of edtech that should never have been sold to schools. It was bought on a vendor’s promise, with no evidence it worked. But I saw at least as many capable tools fail for a different reason: There wasn’t a plan for implementation, instructional clarity, or educator support when the “boxes” were opened.

I have seen schools hand teachers carts of devices with nothing but login instructions. I have watched principals celebrate 1:1 programs without being able to say what students would do on the devices, or how anyone would know if it was working. I have sat through board meetings where learning plainly had not improved despite the expense, and no one could explain why.

Conversely, I served as a high school principal in a district that was well ahead of the curve on technology implementation. We invested deeply in teacher professional development and changed how we taught to deliver on the outcomes we had promised. We used a defined set of technology solutions to increase engagement, enhance exposure, and differentiate based on need. However, the power was always in the hands of the classroom teacher to decide when technology was most impactful and which tools best met the needs.

I understand the concerns now driving legislatures and school boards across the country. Los Angeles Unified recently voted unanimously to ban district-issued devices in early grades, cap screen time across all grade levels, and audit every educational technology contract in the system. At least 17 states are moving legislation forward, while four states have already signed laws. Parent coalitions are showing up to board meetings with signs that read “Schools Beyond Screens.”

While frustration is warranted, broad restrictions unintentionally eliminate high-impact instructional uses together with the practices policymakers are rightly trying to address. Arbitrary time limits divorced from context don’t create balance. A 20-minute block of passive consumption is not inherently “better” than a 40-minute block of active, meaningful learning.

The question we should be asking is whether students are thinking, creating, discussing, and applying, not simply whether they are looking at a screen. A student passively scrolling through short-form videos for hours is fundamentally different from one using a simulation to explore chemical reactions, engaging in an interactive lesson that adapts to their level, or collaborating with peers on a problem that mirrors real-world challenges. Rules that treat all screens the same do not protect children from bad technology. They wind up making legitimate , effective , teacher-led instruction enabled by technology disappear.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) updated its guidance on digital media in January, and it got this right. Instead of fixed screen-time limits, the AAP calls for quality over quantity. The question isn’t how many minutes a student spends on a screen. It is whether a teacher incorporates it into instruction with a purpose and whether it is developmentally appropriate. In this model, teachers leverage real-time data and flexible content to differentiate instruction. Students actively engage with concepts through simulations, media, and creation tasks that make complex ideas tangible. That’s what active learning looks like, and evaluating whether screen time meets that standard requires informed judgment by educators, supported by the right training and tools.

The focus on quality over quantity allows room for a more nuanced conversation, including recognition of a changing workforce and evolving communities. Today’s students will work alongside tools that did not exist when they were in kindergarten. Preparing students responsibly means building the digital fluency and AI literacy to assess sources, interact with AI agents, and adapt to new jobs. That’s possible through purposeful, constructive technology use, supervised by teachers who model critical thinking and keep the focus on learning.

I work in edtech now, so let me say what the industry should be saying for itself. Too many tools have been sold on novelty, and the experiences they produced are exactly what parents are reacting to. Some vendors have overpromised on “innovation” and underinvested in teacher preparation. Pretending otherwise is how we ended up here.

The questions districts should ask before any technology purchase are simple, even when the answers are not: Is there independent evidence this tool works with students like mine, at this grade level, in this subject? Will teachers receive real pedagogical training, not just a feature tutorial? What are the specific learning outcomes, and how will the teacher know if they are being met? If district leaders cannot answer those questions, the problem isn’t the technology. It is the planning and support that should have surrounded it.

The district leaders I hear from are asking these exact questions. They are not debating whether to use technology but instead are pressing for evidence on which tools work, for which students, in which subjects. And they are worried that across-the-board bans will sweep away the instruction that does work along with the instruction that doesn’t. Lawmakers and parents are right to push for answers. So are the educators trying to get the work right.

But the answer isn’t to wall classrooms off from the technology students will be expected to use as adults. The work is harder than that: careful procurement, deep teacher preparation on the why and the how, and clear measurement of student outcomes. That kind of discipline produces edtech implementations that serve students with greater precision than broad restrictions can.

We have a real choice right now. We can let legitimate frustration push us toward blunt policies that eliminate effective tools alongside ineffective ones, or use this moment to invest in the intentional implementation and educator support that too often have been missing. The first path is easier. The second is the one that serves students and prepares them for success in a technology-rich future. Before we unplug the classroom, let’s fix what’s really broken. We are going to get exactly what we design for, or exactly what we ignore.

Todd Wirt is a former public school superintendent and currently serves in a leadership role at Discovery Education. The views expressed here are his own.

title: Beyond spotting deepfakes: Teaching multilingual learners to interrogate AI
content: Long before computers entered our homes and classrooms, photographs helped shape what people believed. Images carried a particular kind of authority: We did not simply look at them; we often treated them as evidence.
author: Nesreen El-Baz, ESL Educator
clean_content:
Long before computers entered our homes and classrooms, photographs helped shape what people believed. Images carried a particular kind of authority: We did not simply look at them; we often treated them as evidence. They helped audiences understand events they had never witnessed themselves and gave distant stories a sense of immediacy and truth.

Yet images have never been neutral witnesses. They can be selected, cropped, staged, retouched, captioned, or removed from their original context. Photographic manipulation predates the digital age. What artificial intelligence has changed is not the possibility of visual deception, but its speed, accessibility, scale, and increasingly convincing realism.

Today, students can encounter an AI-generated photograph, a cloned voice, or a convincing video of an event that never occurred—all while scrolling through the same feed where they see authentic news and messages from friends.

For multilingual learners, this deserves particular attention. Visuals often bridge linguistic gaps, making concepts accessible before students have the language to fully explain them.

But when images can be generated, manipulated, or taken out of context, visual access must be paired with visual questioning.

This is not because multilingual learners are inherently more susceptible to misinformation.

Rather, if we use visuals as a bridge to understanding, we must also teach students to question their source, context, and credibility.

One response to deepfakes is to teach students how to spot them: Look for distorted hands, unusual shadows, unnatural facial movements, or inconsistencies in the background.

These clues may help, but they have a limitation: AI is improving. The visual flaw that exposes an AI-generated image today may disappear tomorrow.

Students therefore need to move beyond asking:

“Does this look real?” and learn to ask: “What evidence do I have that this is real?”

Research from Stanford’s Civic Online Reasoning initiative found that students often struggled to judge the credibility of online information, challenging the assumption that growing up with technology makes young people skilled evaluators. Professional fact-checkers used a different strategy: lateral reading—leaving a questionable page to investigate its source and seek independent evidence.

Applied to deepfakes, the lesson is simple: Don’t just look more closely at the image.

For multilingual learners, teachers can make both the thinking and language of verification explicit: What do I see? What is the claim? Who created it? Where else can I check? What evidence do I have? Students can discuss their reasoning with a partner or in their strongest language before communicating conclusions in English, supported by frames such as This source claims…, I questioned this because…, and The evidence does/does not support…

Google Arts & Culture’s Odd One Out, which asks students to identify an AI generated image among authentic artworks, offers a low-language-entry way to practise this reasoning.

Teachers can move beyond simply spotting the “fake” by asking students what made them question the image, what evidence supports their judgment, and where else they could check.

Questioning AI-generated content is only part of AI literacy. Students also need opportunities, with appropriate safeguards, to understand how it is constructed. A useful progression is to interpret, generate, and evaluate.

Interpret: Students examine an image or video, considering its source, framing, context, purpose, and audience. For multilingual learners, visuals provide an accessible entry point, while structured discussion develops the language needed to express increasingly complex interpretations.

Generate: Students might create two AI-generated images of the same fictional event, changing the perspective, wording, or framing of the prompt. They then compare what changed, what was emphasised or omitted, and which version appears more convincing.

The goal is not simply to learn prompting, but to experience how choices shape the story an image appears to tell.

Evaluate: Students return to the evidence: Who created this? What supports the claim? What do reliable sources say? What might be missing? What would make me reconsider my conclusion? In doing so, they use academic language to question, corroborate, challenge, justify, and revise.

This progression reflects higher-order processes in Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy: students analyse how visual meaning is constructed, apply their understanding through creation, and evaluate claims using evidence, context, and credibility.

Linguistic scaffolding does not lower expectations; it gives multilingual learners greater access to these sophisticated cognitive processes.

These skills extend beyond AI-generated content. A genuine photograph paired with a false caption can mislead. An authentic video removed from its original context can distort an event. The larger goal is therefore not simply to teach multilingual learners how to detect AI. It is to give them the tools and language to evaluate claims and evidence.

Stanford’s research offers an encouraging message: these skills can be taught. Studies evaluating Civic Online Reasoning instruction have shown that students can improve their ability to judge the credibility of online information.

Importantly, we do not want students to leave our classrooms believing that nothing can be trusted. Skepticism without the skills to investigate can quickly become cynicism.

The goal is not: “Everything could be fake.”

It is: “I don’t know whether I should trust this yet. Let me find out.”

Schools have legitimate reasons to establish boundaries around AI, particularly around privacy, safeguarding, age, and assessment. But boundaries need to be accompanied by education.

This is especially important for multilingual learners. We have long recognised the power of visuals to make learning more accessible. In the age of generative AI, we need to extend that principle: access to visual information must be accompanied by the tools to interrogate it.

Keeping AI outside the classroom will not keep it outside students’ lives.

We do students a disservice if they leave school knowing how to avoid AI but not how to question an AI-generated image, investigate its source, corroborate its claims, or decide whether it should be shared.

Our responsibility is to give every learner—including those still developing the language of instruction—the tools and language to interpret what they see, generate responsibly, investigate what they encounter, and evaluate what deserves their trust.

Because in the age of deepfakes, perhaps the most important question we can teach a student to ask is not: “Is this real?” but: “How do I know?”

Nesreen El-Baz is an ESL educator with over 20 years of experience, and is a certified bilingual teacher with a Master’s in Curriculum and Instruction. El-Baz is currently based in the UK, holds a Masters degree in Curriculum and Instruction from Houston Christian University, and specializes in developing in innovative strategies for English Learners and Bilingual education.

title: Financial education must not sacrifice student privacy
content: Financial education is gaining real momentum across the United States. More states are adopting mandates, more schools are adding graduation requirements, and more policymakers are acknowledging that students need practical preparation for the financial decisions they will face as adults.
author: Vince Shorb, National Financial Educators Council
clean_content:
Financial education is gaining real momentum across the United States. More states are adopting mandates, more schools are adding graduation requirements, and more policymakers are acknowledging that students need practical preparation for the financial decisions they will face as adults.

That progress matters because every student will eventually make consequential choices involving money, including renting a home, paying for higher education, starting a job, using credit, buying insurance, and planning for long-term financial security. Strong financial education can help young people approach those decisions with greater knowledge and confidence.

Recent analysis from the National Financial Educators Council, however, identified a serious gap in how some states are implementing that education. In ten states and Washington, D.C., financial education standards or legislation direct students to complete classroom activities involving documents that can require personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, birthdates, home addresses and other sensitive details.

The documents include W-4s, financial-aid applications, loan forms and banking paperwork. Students should understand how these forms work, but standards that call for their completion without explicitly requiring sample data or protected classroom versions create an unnecessary risk that real personal information could be entered, collected, or stored.

The problem is not the subject matter. It is the absence of safeguards.

Students can learn the purpose, structure, and use of financial documents without entering real personal information. Classroom versions should remove, redact, or block sensitive fields rather than rely solely on instructions telling students to leave them blank or provide fictional information. Directions can be misunderstood or overlooked, while a well-designed form prevents sensitive information from being requested in the first place.

There is no educational justification for exposing a minor’s identity data. A Social Security number combined with a name, birthdate and home address can provide much of what an identity thief needs to damage a child’s credit and financial future. Because minors rarely monitor their credit histories, the harm may stay hidden for years, surfacing only when they apply for financial aid, seek employment, rent an apartment or open their first credit account.

In the states examined, the relevant standards and legislation do not clearly require redacted forms, educator privacy training, secure handling procedures or protocols for storing, transmitting and disposing of sensitive information. That omission creates a preventable student privacy risk and points to a larger problem in how financial education policy is sometimes designed and implemented.

Classroom realities compound the danger. Once personal information is written on a form or entered into a digital document, a series of practical questions follows. Will the assignment be collected, graded, or stored? Could it be uploaded to a learning management system, sent by email, printed, left on a desk, or discarded in an ordinary trash can? Will a third-party platform retain any of the information?

Teachers should not be expected to answer those questions on their own. Most are not trained as privacy officers, compliance specialists, cybersecurity professionals or records-management experts. Asking them to handle sensitive student information without clear guidance creates risks not only for students and families but also for educators, schools and districts.

Poorly designed requirements could also undermine public confidence in financial education itself. Advocates have spent decades working to establish the subject as a serious part of K-12 education. If its expansion produces avoidable privacy failures, the resulting loss of trust could weaken support for programs that students genuinely need.

The deeper issue is policy design. Financial education is too often treated as a simple addition to graduation requirements rather than as an academic subject requiring rigorous standards, qualified educators, strong curricula, meaningful accountability and built-in protections. Legislatures can pass mandates, but the infrastructure needed to carry them out, including time, training, resources, oversight and implementation guidance, does not always follow.

Other areas of education routinely build in safeguards when classroom activities present foreseeable risks. Science laboratories have safety procedures, student health records receive privacy protections, and online learning platforms undergo data-security reviews. Financial education should be held to the same standard.

States can start by requiring protected classroom versions of any financial, employment, tax, student aid, loan, banking, insurance or benefits documents used in instruction. Sensitive fields should be removed, redacted or blocked, and standards should explicitly prohibit students from entering real Social Security numbers, birthdates, home addresses, wage information, account details or other personal data except through a legally authorized and properly secured process.

Teachers should also receive basic privacy and compliance training before leading activities involving financial forms. Schools need clear procedures for collecting, grading, storing, transmitting, retaining and destroying assignments that could contain personal information. Any third-party platform used for financial education should undergo an appropriate privacy and security review before students are asked to use it.

State departments of education should examine their existing standards and issue prompt clarification wherever protections are missing or ambiguous. Policymakers who supported financial literacy legislation should likewise determine whether the language they advanced may have unintentionally created opportunities for student data to be exposed.

None of this is an argument against financial education. It is an argument for delivering it responsibly.

Students should learn about taxes, employment forms, banking, credit, financial aid, loans, insurance and long-term planning. They should understand what financial documents ask, why the information matters and how different choices can affect their lives. Practical instruction, however, does not require real student data. Redacted forms that block students from entering personal information can still provide meaningful experience without compromising anyone’s privacy.

Some may argue that teachers can simply instruct students to use fictitious information. That is not an adequate policy. If a standard directs students to “complete a W-4” or “complete a loan application” without requiring a protected classroom version, safety depends on every educator independently identifying and correcting the problem. Sound policy should build in protection by design rather than leave it to individual judgment in thousands of classrooms.

Others may dismiss the concern because the documents are used only as classroom exercises. An assignment involving minors and sensitive personal information does not become harmless simply because it is educational. Whenever Social Security numbers, birthdates, addresses or family finances could be disclosed, privacy safeguards must be part of the lesson’s design.

The National Financial Educators Council has begun contacting federal agencies, state departments of education, attorneys general, state boards of education, policymakers and other relevant offices to request review and corrective action before the next school year. That timetable matters because every year these gaps remain, another group of students may face an entirely avoidable risk that may not surface until long after the assignment has been forgotten.

Financial education is too important to implement carelessly. If we expect students to become financially capable adults, we need instruction that is practical, rigorous, safe and professionally designed, with privacy protections, educator training and accountability built in from the start.

The principle is straightforward: Teach the concepts, explain the documents, prepare students for real financial decisions and protect the child.

No student should have to risk identity theft to learn financial literacy.

Vince Shorb is the CEO of the National Financial Educators Council .
